If you would like to go deeper into a specific boundary—for example, the indication limits for robotic THA in Crowe IV DDH, or preoperative planning strategies for robotic assistance in scoliosis with Cobb angle > 80°—we can continue there.

Reduced tactile feedback removes an important warning signal: the surgeon may know where the instrument is without fully appreciating how much force it is applying or what tissue resistance has changed. The consequences differ for bone cutting, screw insertion and soft-tissue handling. First, the premise needs qualification. Not all orthopaedic robots lack haptic feedback. Some provide resistance at virtual cutting boundaries, and surgeons using handheld instruments through robotic guides may retain some direct sensation. However, a virtual boundary is not the same as feeling actual bone hardness, cortical breakthrough or soft-tissue tension. stryker.com Surgical task Information lost when tactile feedback is reduced Potential consequence Osteotomy and bone preparation Changes in cutting resistance, transition between cortical and cancellous bone, and the sudden release when the far cortex is breached. Delayed recognition of breakthrough can allow tool overshoot and injury to structures beyond the bone. Inappropriate cutting force or prolonged tool contact may also become harder to recognise. Screw placement Resistance during tract preparation, cortical contact, insertion torque and loss of purchase. The surgeon may recognise skiving—sliding off the intended entry point—or cortical breach less readily. Excessive advancement or tightening may damage bone or compromise fixation. Soft-tissue dissection and retraction Tissue tension, compliance, gripping pressure and the resistance separating tissue planes. Excessive traction or compression can cause tearing, crush injury or injury to nerves and vessels. During suturing, excessive tension can cut through tissue or break the suture; insufficient tension can leave an insecure repair. These are plausible mechanical consequences supported by drilling experiments, clinical descriptions of robotic screw-placement failures and experimental soft-tissue studies. They should not be interpreted as proof that absent haptics independently increases complication rates in every orthopaedic procedure. PMC For osteotomy, geometric accuracy and tissue safety must be assessed separately. A robot may maintain the planned cutting plane accurately, but that alone does not establish safe cutting pressure or temperature. Thermal injury depends on factors such as irrigation, cutting speed and the cutting cycle; experimental robotic osteotomy studies demonstrate this. I would not attribute thermal necrosis directly to absent haptic feedback, because that causal relationship is not established. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov For screw placement, the particular concern is false reassurance from navigation. If the vertebra moves after registration, or the tool deflects or skives, the displayed trajectory may not reliably represent the actual screw path. Reduced tactile information removes one additional opportunity to notice the discrepancy. This makes independent checks of registration, the tract and final implant position important; imaging and, where appropriate, neurophysiological monitoring supplement rather than replace surgical judgement. Clinical series document registration errors, movement, skiving and soft-tissue interference as causes of robotic placement problems. PMC For soft-tissue dissection, visual deformation becomes the main substitute for touch. That requires the surgeon to watch tissue stretch and instrument contact closely, which can increase attention demands. In a preclinical study involving 28 surgeons, instrument force feedback reduced forces during several robotic tasks. However, this evidence is largely from general robotic surgery and experimental models, so its direct applicability to orthopaedic clinical outcomes remains uncertain. Also, in many established joint-replacement and spinal robotic workflows, soft-tissue exposure and dissection are still performed manually. PMC From a practical surgical perspective, the response is controlled instrument advancement, adequate exposure and tissue protection, reliable irrigation, repeated verification of navigation, and readiness to stop or use conventional instruments when the visual, mechanical and navigation findings disagree. Haptic boundaries and force sensors can help, but neither substitutes for these checks.

机械臂的活动范围与角度限制，在临床中是一个真实存在、可以被管理，但无法被完全消除的约束。它并非总以“够不到”这种极端形式出现，而更多表现为对体位摆放的隐性约束、深部操作时稳定性的下降，以及在有限空间内避障能力的不足。对于术者而言，这意味着机器人的“精准”并非无条件，它的前提是手术室空间、患者体位与规划路径三者必须与机械臂的运动学包络（kinematic envelope）达成妥协。 特殊体位：约束是“前置”的，而非术中才显现 机械臂的物理尺寸和底座设计，直接框定了患者体位的可摆放范围。这种约束在术前摆位时就已经生效。 在脊柱俯卧位手术中，一个具体的量化限制是：由于机械臂需要从特定角度接近术区，手术床下缘到患者皮肤的高度被建议小于32 cm，对于肥胖患者尤其需要注意控制身体侧面的厚度，否则机械臂的轨迹空间会被躯干挤压。在骨盆骨折的仰卧位手术中，约束来自底座而非臂展：天玑机器人的机械臂底座较大，需尽可能安置于麻醉机对侧，这直接倒逼患者的体位和术者的站位必须据此调整，若需双侧植钉，则必须提前规划麻醉机与机械臂的位置以预留空间。在关节置换中，Mako系统的机械臂需置于患肢侧，且手术床需尽量靠近麻醉机及健侧边，以“为床尾端的无菌器械和患者侧的机械臂留出较充分的空间”。这些都不是术中才会遭遇的问题，而是在铺巾之前就已经被“写入”了体位摆放的决策之中。护理规范明确要求，调整体位时需同时确认“机械臂的活动范围是否顺畅”，并将此作为体位摆放的验收标准之一。 深部术区：可达性之外，更关键的是“稳定性” 当操作目标位于深部骨科术区时，活动范围的限制以一种更隐蔽的方式产生影响：它未必阻止机械臂“到达”目标，但可能迫使机械臂以接近其运动学极限的姿态进行工作，从而削弱其在负载下的稳定性。 脊柱手术领域的一项对比观察指出了一个关键事实：“机器人工作空间小，小型机器人驱动力小，难以对抗软组织张力，造成机械臂移位”。这意味着，在深部操作中，即使机械臂的末端在几何上到达了规划点，当它需要穿过较厚的软组织或对抗持续的组织张力时，有限的工作空间可能使它无法选择一个力学上更优的支撑姿态，从而在负载下发生位移，影响置钉精度。此外，自由度数量直接决定了在受限空间内的灵活性。仅提供5个自由度（5 DoF）的系统，可能只能在一种或两种特定姿态下实现给定轨迹，这严重限制了其围绕牵开器、椎弓根螺钉塔等术野内障碍物进行避让的能力。当目标位于深部且周围布满器械与组织时，这种“姿态选择的贫乏”会转化为操作上的笨拙与风险的上升。 系统的应对：从“被动避让”到“主动规划” 面对这些限制，当前的临床策略已经从单纯的术中小心，前移到了术前规划与系统算法的主动规避。 路径规划中的软限位与奇异点规避是核心防线。机械臂的“奇异点”（singularity）是一种运动学构型，在该构型附近，机械臂会丧失某些方向的运动能力。规避策略包括：在规划阶段提前预警并尝试规避路径上的奇异点，或设置软限位以避免出现不可达位姿。当系统检测到机械臂接近奇异位形时，可通过算法施加约束力使其避开奇异位形继续运动。对于深部操作中可能发生的体位意外移动（如患者术中咳嗽），系统的应对是实时监测并进行位置补偿，但这本质上是一种补救，其精度上限仍受制于机械臂在补偿姿态下的可达性与稳定性。 辅助工具与替代方案是工程层面的补充。对于刚性机械臂在受限空间中可达性不足的根本性缺陷，研究方向包括将刚性连杆机器人与连续体机械臂（continuum manipulator） 结合，后者能够“增强在手术中常见的难以进入的空间中的可达性”。在临床实践中，导向器与保护套筒的使用虽然“延长了植钉路径上的轴向操作距离”，但也同时意味着需要在体位摆放时局部适当垫高以预先调整角度，以补偿这种延长带来的角度灵活性损失。 临床视角的总结 机械臂的活动范围与角度限制，其临床影响可以归结为一句话：它将手术操作的空间约束，从术者手部的“自由度”转移到了机械系统的“运动学包络”之上。在特殊体位中，这种约束表现为对患者摆放方式的前置性规定；在深部术区，它表现为机械臂在极限姿态附近工作时抵抗软组织负载能力的下降，以及因自由度不足而丧失的避障灵活性。当前的临床实践已经形成了一套“规划先行、布局补偿、算法规避”的管理框架，但这一框架的有效性，高度依赖于术者和团队是否在切开皮肤之前，就已经将机械臂的物理存在作为一个必须被规划进去的“参与者”，而非一个切开后才开始互动的“工具”。承认这一约束的存在，并在术前规划中为其预留空间与姿态的冗余，是让机器人的精准度在深部、在特殊体位下仍然可信的前提。

面对高昂的设备与耗材成本，病例筛选的核心逻辑需要发生一次根本性的转变：从过去基于“疾病诊断”的宽泛准入，转向基于“价值密度”的精细化筛选。成本效益并非机器人技术的固有属性，它高度依赖于病例选择、机构手术量和支付环境。筛选的目标，是让每一例机器人手术所消耗的额外资源，都能对应一个在传统技术下难以实现或风险显著更高的临床获益。 筛选的锚点：识别“价值密度”最高的病例特征 根据现有卫生经济学与临床证据，高“价值密度”的病例通常具备以下一个或多个特征，这些特征使得机器人的精准度或微创优势能够直接转化为可测量的资源节约或结局改善。 第一，解剖复杂、传统技术精度瓶颈显著的病例。 这是机器人价值最确凿的领域。在脊柱外科，机器人辅助腰椎融合术的增量成本效益，被明确指向置钉困难或流程复杂的病例，而非所有腰椎融合的常规应用。具体而言，经皮固定、解剖变异、多节段手术和翻修等场景，传统技术下置钉偏差风险和辐射暴露显著上升，机器人的机械导向价值在此处最为突出。一项针对L4-L5滑脱的微创手术经济学分析为此提供了量化支撑：尽管机器人 upfront 成本更高，但由于其降低了手术 invasiveness 和手术时间，在2年随访期内，机器人辅助组的每QALY成本为11,839美元，而对照组高达76,848美元，后者是前者的约6.5倍。这揭示了一个关键逻辑：在复杂病例中，机器人通过减少术中“隐性消耗”（如出血、手术时间、并发症处理），可能将高额的固定成本分摊后，反而获得更优的长期经济学表现。 第二，机器人精准度已显示出转化为长期结局优势信号的术式。 在关节置换领域，并非所有术式的经济学证据都同样积极。全髋关节置换（THA）的匹配队列研究在高量中心并未观察到机器人辅助带来临床意义的患者报告结局改善，且每例成本高出约1000美元，住院资源利用无差异甚至更高。在这种“精准度未转化为可测量结局差异”的场景中，筛选的优先级应显著降低。相比之下，全膝关节置换（TKA）在15年以上随访中开始显现无菌性生存的潜在优势，这为将资源向预期寿命较长、对远期翻修风险敏感的TKA患者倾斜提供了初步的卫生经济学依据。部分经济模型甚至提示，当假设机器人手术能完全消除翻修时，TKA和部分膝关节置换（UKA）才具备成本效益——这从反面界定了筛选的极端边界：只有当病例的翻修风险足够高、且机器人的精准度有望实质性降低该风险时，高投入才具备经济学上的合理性。 第三，能够被“病例集中”效应放大的场景。 单例手术的成本效益，与机构的年手术量和流程成熟度深度绑定。骨科机器人的投资回报存在一个病例量阈值。有研究估算，年全膝关节置换量超过200例，可能在2年内抵消相关成本。在高量机构中，机器人相关成本可被减少的并发症、缩短的住院时间和改善的出院指标所部分抵消；但这种抵消效应依赖于将合适病例相对集中地安排给固定的、熟练的机器人手术团队，而非分散使用。将机器人手术“打散”到低频率、多术者的模式中，装机调试和流程中断的固定时间成本将被反复支付，单位病例的经济效率会急剧恶化。 机构层面的筛选策略：从“买设备”到“建项目” 病例筛选不是术者个体的孤立决策，它嵌在机构层面的资源配置逻辑中。那些能从机器人投资中获取真实价值的项目，其共性不在于购买了最昂贵的系统，而在于将机器人视为需要精心运营的“基础设施”而非“展示品”，并围绕它构建了可重复的、以合适病例选择为前提的工作流。这意味着筛选策略必须包含负向清单：对于解剖正常的初次THA、传统技术已高度优化且机器人精准度未显示增量结局获益的常规病例，应审慎限制或明确排除在优先使用机器人的范围之外。这与国家医保支付政策“引导优先应用于复杂手术、防范滥用”的导向是一致的。 支付环境：筛选的外部约束与杠杆 病例筛选的经济可行性，最终受制于支付端对机器人附加成本的覆盖方式。当前的政策演进正在改变筛选的算式。国家医保局对手术机器人实行与主手术挂钩的系数化收费，按“导航、参与执行、精准执行”分档定价，参与度更高、功能更复杂的手术可获得更高收费系数。这意味着，在复杂病例中使用机器人的“精准执行”功能，其附加收费的合法性基础更强，而在简单病例中，收费系数可能无法覆盖真实的资源消耗。此外，租赁与服务化模式正在降低医院的固定资产门槛，使得筛选决策可以更多地基于病例组合的临床价值，而非迫于尽快收回设备折旧的压力。对于尚未达到理想病例量的机构，远程手术协作也被探索为一种将技术能力与病例需求进行跨区域匹配的资源配置路径，其单独设立的收费项目为这种模式提供了初步的支付框架。 需要坦诚说明的边界 必须指出，上述筛选逻辑所依赖的卫生经济学证据，其成熟度和可移植性存在显著局限。多数成本效果分析（CEA）基于特定国家的支付体系、价格水平和随访时限，直接移植到我国临床环境中的外部有效性仍需本地真实世界数据验证。脊柱机器人领域的经济学证据变异性很大，且高度依赖机构特异性因素，部分模型甚至在7年设备寿命内未能实现财务盈亏平衡。因此，任何筛选框架都不应被视为一份静态的“准入清单”，而应是一个需要本机构利用自身病例组合、成本结构和支付数据持续校准的动态决策工具。从执业视角看，最审慎的姿态是：承认在常规病例中机器人精准度的边际临床价值尚不足以确证其经济合理性，从而将有限的高成本技术资源，集中投向那些传统技术的精度瓶颈或风险敞口最为确切的复杂病例。这既是临床合理性的要求，也是在当前证据阶段对医疗资源负责任的使用方式。

Robot- or navigation-assisted fixation often reduces the surgeon’s radiation exposure, but it does not consistently reduce the patient’s cumulative dose. The determining factor is the imaging workflow—particularly whether navigation requires additional CT or three-dimensional scans. Imaging approach Patient exposure Surgeon/staff exposure Conventional fluoroscopy Increases with imaging duration, repeated views, patient size, and procedural complexity. Repeated exposure to scatter while working near the patient. Fluoroscopy-based robotic/navigation guidance May decrease when fewer guidewire adjustments and repeat images are needed; savings are not universal. Often lower because staff can step away during acquisition and use stored images during instrumentation. CT/cone-beam CT-based guidance Can exceed conventional fluoroscopy, especially for short procedures or when scans are repeated. Low-dose protocols can substantially change the comparison. Usually markedly lower during scanning if staff leave the room or stand behind appropriate shielding. For example, a randomized thoracolumbar trial measured surgeon exposure of 21.7 versus 70.5 μSv with robotic versus conventional fixation—approximately 69% lower—despite no significant reduction in fluoroscopy time. This illustrates why fluoroscopy time alone is an inadequate measure of dose. Randomized trial Conversely, CT-based navigation studies have reported higher patient exposure. A randomized imaging-protocol study demonstrated a fivefold reduction in patient exposure using low-dose acquisition, emphasizing that the protocol matters as much as the technology. CT-navigation study, low-dose trial Cumulative exposure should include the entire relevant imaging pathway: planning CT, intraoperative scans, fluoroscopy, repeat registration scans, and postoperative imaging. Machine-reported dose indicators and personal dosimeter readings measure different things and should not be added or compared directly without medical-physics interpretation. For high-volume surgeons, practical protection should include: Reduce radiation at source: use suitable low-dose protocols, pulsed fluoroscopy, tight collimation, last-image hold, and avoid unnecessary magnification or repeat scans. Use distance and shielding: step away during exposures; leave or shield during 3D acquisition. Wear an appropriate apron, thyroid collar, and protective glasses, and use movable or mounted barriers where feasible. Keep hands outside the primary beam. During lateral fluoroscopy, stand on the detector side where practicable, because scatter is greater on the tube side. IAEA protection guidance Health surveillance should be driven by measured exposure and local occupational-health requirements. Use correctly positioned personal dosimeters; high-exposure work may warrant under-apron and collar badges, dedicated eye dosimetry, and ring dosimeters. Review results regularly, investigate unexpected increases, and combine exposure records across hospitals. Occupational-health review should address suspected overexposure and arrange eye assessment where indicated; routine blood tests cannot substitute for dosimetry. IAEA worker guidance, multi-site monitoring guidance I would not promise a universal percentage reduction or a “safe” annual case count: exposure varies substantially with procedure mix, equipment, technique, and protection.

**机器人或导航通常能减少术者的职业辐射暴露，但患者总剂量不一定同步下降。**关键取决于影像采集方式、扫描次数及团队流程，而不是是否使用机器人。 1．患者与术者的剂量为何可能出现不同变化？ 技术方式 对患者的影响 对术者的影响 传统二维透视置钉 剂量随定位难度、反复调整和置钉数量增加 术者常需在患者旁操作，持续接受散射线，长期累积值得关注 二维影像导航或机器人导向 减少反复定位、导针调整时，可能降低剂量；仍需计入全部配准及验证影像 通常可减少近距离透视操作，降低职业剂量 术中三维扫描、CT导航及配套机器人 单次扫描增加剂量；能否抵消减少的透视，取决于扫描范围、低剂量协议、固定节段和重复扫描次数 扫描时人员可撤离或进入屏障后，职业剂量往往明显降低 一项脊柱CT导航研究显示了这种差异：患者暴露可能增加，而术者暴露减少。不过其设备和比较条件较早，不能用其中的倍数代表现代所有系统。脊柱CT导航研究 因此，**不能只比较透视秒数，也不能将设备显示的mGy、剂量面积乘积或CT剂量指标直接相加，作为人体有效剂量。**患者应核算术前、术中及必要术后影像的整体负担；术者则应以个人剂量监测为依据。 2．高手术量术者应怎样防护？ 建议把防护嵌入每台手术流程： **减少出束：**采用满足成像需求的低剂量、脉冲透视和限束，利用末帧保持，避免不必要的放大与重复扫描。 **增加距离和屏蔽：**三维扫描时尽可能撤离或站到屏障后；必须在场时使用合适的移动铅屏，并按设备几何布局优化站位。 **保护眼、甲状腺和躯干：**规范使用合适的防护围裙、甲状腺围领及带侧防护的铅眼镜，并定期检查防护用品完整性。 **手离开主射束：**不能依赖铅手套把手放入照射野；自动曝光系统可能因此增加输出，使手部及患者剂量反而上升。OSHA防护说明 高手术量中心还应按术式审查剂量，查找高剂量病例的原因，例如肥胖、复杂解剖、反复配准或扫描，而不是仅统计年手术台数。 3．个人监测与健康随访如何安排？ 以中国大陆职业健康管理为主： **规范佩戴个人剂量计。**穿铅衣工作时采用内、外双剂量计方案；眼和手暴露较高者，由放射防护人员评估增加眼晶状体及指环剂量计。佩戴位置和剂量换算须由监测机构指导。国家核安全局监测说明 **定期复核累积剂量。**我国管理办法规定，外照射监测周期一般为30天，最长不超过90天，个人剂量档案终生保存。异常升高或异常偏低，都应核查佩戴和工作情况，不能等到超限才处理。职业健康管理办法 **接受专门的职业健康检查。**按上岗前、在岗和离岗等要求管理；在岗检查通常为1～2年，必要时增加临时检查。重点结合剂量记录，关注眼晶状体、皮肤及标准规定的其他项目；普通年度体检不能替代职业健康检查。GBZ 98—2020 **没有一个通用的“每年做多少台就不安全”的界线。**高手术量术者最有用的管理依据，是实际个人剂量及其趋势，而非透视时间、手术例数或血常规正常与否。健康随访用于发现问题，不能替代日常降低暴露。

以执业骨科医师的视角来界定机器人的适应症与禁忌症，核心不在于罗列一份静态的疾病清单，而在于建立一个基于分型与解剖复杂度的分层决策框架。机器人的价值并非在所有场景中均等，它最确切的定位是：在传统技术因解剖复杂、视野受限或二维信息不足而面临精准度瓶颈时，提供一种可规划、可验证的解决方案。因此，适应症的界定应从“疾病诊断”深入到“分型特征”，而禁忌症的判断则需区分“绝对的技术禁区”与“需要审慎权衡的相对边界”。 脊柱区域：以“解剖可规划性”与“畸形可代偿性”为分型轴 脊柱机器人应用最成熟的领域是椎弓根螺钉置入，但适应症的宽窄在不同节段和分型中差异显著。 上颈椎（C1-C2） 是机器人优势最无可争议的区域。该区域解剖结构复杂，毗邻椎动脉和脊髓，传统徒手置钉的风险极高。2025年《机器人辅助上颈椎内固定手术指南》的表述相当宽泛：适用于所有需上颈椎内固定的患者，涵盖创伤、畸形、退变、肿瘤、感染等病因。这一推荐背后的逻辑是，上颈椎手术对精准度的基线要求已经超越了“经验校正”所能可靠覆盖的范围，而机器人能够将操作精度稳定在亚毫米级，从而系统性地降低这一特定解剖区域的风险。可以说，在上颈椎，适应症的界定更多取决于患者能否耐受手术和能否获得合格的导航影像，而非具体的疾病分型。 胸腰椎区域的界定则需要更细致的分型考量。2024年《中国机器人辅助胸腰椎手术指南》列出了广泛的适应症：创伤性（爆裂骨折、骨质疏松性压缩骨折）、退变性（滑脱、椎间盘突出、椎管狭窄）、畸形（侧凸、后凸、先天性重度滑脱）、肿瘤及感染。然而，这一宽泛列表的真正临床意义，需要结合2026年RA-TLIF共识来理解。该共识明确指出，机器人相较于传统透视引导的优势在椎弓根纤细、解剖变异和翻修手术中才“巨大”地凸显出来。换言之，在常规的初次单节段腰椎退变手术中，机器人提供的边际精准度增益可能并不足以构成决定性优势；而当分型特征指向解剖标志模糊或丧失（如严重畸形导致的椎弓根形态变异、翻修术后瘢痕化改变）时，适应症的权重才显著上升。共识中提及的“Ⅰ~Ⅱ度腰椎滑脱优先”，也暗示了对于高度滑脱或严重不稳的病例，其适应症地位需要更审慎地评估，因为这类病例的挑战往往在于复位策略与整体力线重建，而不仅仅是单枚螺钉的轨迹。 关节区域：以“力线可量化性”与“骨缺损可代偿性”为分型轴 关节机器人的适应症界定，核心矛盾在于技术精准度提升与患者选择获益之间的不确定性。2026年亚太专家共识（ASIA）在肯定机器人改善截骨精度、假体位置和力线的同时，坦承“最佳力线与平衡目标及其长期临床获益仍不明确”。这意味着，适应症的界定不能简单地以“能否使用机器人”为标准，而应追问“哪一类分型特征的患者，其精准度增益最有可能转化为临床价值”。 在初次全膝关节置换（TKA） 中，机器人对于严重内翻或外翻畸形的病例具有明确的理论吸引力，因为它能够在三维空间中执行个体化的力线调整，并提供截骨前的软组织平衡定量参考。然而，共识同时强调了一个关键的排序原则：当软组织平衡与刚性机械力线目标发生冲突时，应优先保证软组织平衡。这一原则实际上划定了适应症的边界：机器人是执行个体化平衡策略的工具，而非强行追求某一固定力线数值的理由。对于轻度畸形、软组织条件良好的膝关节，传统技术已能取得可预期的结果，机器人适应症的紧迫性相对较低。 在全髋关节置换（THA） 中，适应症更多聚焦于髋臼假体空间位置和肢体长度/偏心距重建。共识指出机器人改善了髋臼杯定位和肢体长度重建，但脱位率或翻修率的降低尚未被证实。因此，对于髋臼发育不良（DDH）继发骨关节炎、髋臼骨缺损等分型，机器人辅助髋臼杯精准安放的适应症逻辑较强；而对于解剖正常的初次THA，其必要性则需结合患者个体因素和术者判断来权衡。 关节翻修是一个需要特别讨论的场景。在骨缺损严重、解剖标志丧失的翻修病例中，机器人基于三维建模的配准能力具有明确价值，能够帮助在 distorted anatomy 中定位旋转中心和骨缺损边界。然而，这也是禁忌症最需要被强调的区域：金属植入物产生的伪影可能严重干扰影像配准，骨缺损的严重程度（如Paprosky III型以上）可能导致机器人规划所依赖的骨性参考系不复存在。因此，翻修适应症的界定高度依赖于术前影像评估能否生成可靠的三维规划，而非翻修这一行为本身。 创伤骨科：以“移位可控性”与“复位可闭合性”为分型轴 在创伤领域，机器人辅助经皮螺钉固定的适应症与禁忌症之间的界限，比脊柱和关节更为锐利，主要取决于骨折移位程度和能否实现闭合复位。 以髋臼骨折为例，适应症被明确限定于无移位或仅有轻微移位的骨折；禁忌症则清晰地指向粉碎性骨折、高度移位骨折、以及股骨头突入盆腔需要切开复位的病例。这一界定反映了机器人技术的本质局限：它精于在已获得满意复位的前提下，精准执行内固定物的置入，而不擅长处理需要复杂开放的复位操作。对于Tile C型骨盆环骨折，机器人联合复位架可实现微创固定的前提是新鲜骨折且螺钉进点区域未粉碎；陈旧性骨折因复位困难而被排除在适应症之外。因此，创伤领域的适应症界定可以提炼为一个简洁的决策节点：骨折分型是否允许以闭合方式获得可接受的对位，并使螺钉进点具备可规划的骨性基础。若答案为否，则应归入禁忌或相对禁忌。 贯穿各领域的通用禁忌症框架 在上述领域特异性分型之外，存在一组跨领域的禁忌症，需要以“绝对”与“相对”的二分法来理解。 绝对禁忌症指向那些使机器人系统赖以工作的基本前提失效的状况：手术部位活动性感染（违反无菌原则且感染性骨破坏使参考系不稳定）、严重凝血功能障碍或无法耐受麻醉（手术本身的风险压倒精准度考量）。此外，无法获得满足手术要求的导航图像（如患者追踪器安放位置不可行、影像质量不足以完成配准）在胸腰椎指南中被列为明确的禁忌条件，因为这是系统运行的技术前提，而非可以权衡的风险。 相对禁忌症则是一组需要在获益与风险之间进行个体化权衡的因素，它们并非“不能做”，而是“需要更审慎地论证”。严重骨质疏松（如T值<-3.5） 会降低螺钉的把持力，使精准置入的螺钉仍可能因骨质量而松动，此时机器人的价值需与骨水泥强化等策略综合考量。严重肥胖（BMI>35） 可能通过增加组织厚度影响追踪器安放和影像配准质量，并增加手术整体风险。既往手术史导致的解剖结构异常或内固定物存留，在脊柱翻修中可能是机器人发挥优势的场景，在关节翻修中却可能因伪影而成为障碍——同一个因素在不同领域中的禁忌权重是反向的，这正是分型化界定的意义所在。儿童骨骺未闭合被列为相对禁忌，因为骨骺这一生长中的骨性参考系可能影响配准的长期稳定性及规划逻辑，但在特定创伤或畸形病例中，其必要性仍需个案评估。 从执业医师的决策视角来看，界定适应症与禁忌症的本质，是完成一次从“疾病标签”到“技术-解剖匹配度”的翻译。机器人不会因为一个诊断名称而自动成为适应症，也不会因为一项相对禁忌的存在而被简单排除。我的判断路径通常是：首先确认导航图像与参考系能否可靠建立（技术前提），其次评估该分型的核心难点是否恰恰落在机器人擅长的“规划-执行”闭环之内（分型匹配），最后在精准度增益与手术时间、成本、以及患者骨质量/软组织条件等风险因素之间进行权衡（个体化决策）。只有在这三层过滤之后仍然指向净获益的病例，才构成一个真正意义上的适应症。

Yes—current navigation and robotic assistance can reduce screw-placement deviation, particularly compared with freehand or conventional fluoroscopy-guided techniques. However, improved placement accuracy does not automatically establish fewer serious complications. This is an evidence-informed orthopedic surgical perspective; I am not a practicing surgeon. Three-dimensional planning helps select the entry point, trajectory, screw diameter, and length. Navigation provides positional feedback, while a robotic guide helps maintain the planned trajectory. A multicenter randomized trial supports improved pedicle-screw placement accuracy with robotic navigation. Randomized clinical trial From a surgical decision-making perspective, several qualifications matter: Accuracy and clinical safety are different outcomes. Fewer cortical breaches are desirable, but nerve injury, vascular injury, and revision surgery are relatively uncommon. Studies may demonstrate better accuracy without being large enough to establish a reduction in these complications. Robotics is not consistently superior to modern navigation. A comparative clinical study found no significant adjusted difference in screw malposition between robotic and navigation-guided placement. The benefit depends on the platform, anatomy, and surgical workflow. Comparative study Assistance introduces its own failure modes. Registration errors, reference-frame movement, tracking interruption, and instrument deflection or slipping can cause the actual trajectory to differ from the displayed plan. A clinical series documented navigation errors despite generally favorable results. Clinical series These functions provide a useful additional safety layer when the surgeon verifies registration, checks anatomical plausibility, and confirms placement when indicated. The strongest evidence concerns spinal pedicle screws; I would be cautious about extending the same conclusion to every orthopedic screw procedure or claiming that assistance prevents intraoperative error generally.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the honest answer is that the maturity of protocols for converting from robotic to manual operation is uneven and procedure-specific. There is no single, universally adopted “orthopedic robot-to-manual conversion protocol” in the way that, for example, laparoscopic conversion-to-open protocols exist. What exists instead is a patchwork of platform-specific manufacturer instructions, specialty society guidance, institutional checklists, and team-based simulation training—some of which are well developed for predictable technical failures, but far less standardized for the specific crisis of an acute vascular or nerve injury during orthopedic use. 🦴 Spine: Guidance Exists, but Conversion Triggers Are Technical, Not Crisis-Specific In spine surgery, the robotic workflow has an inherent structural advantage for emergency conversion: the robot is typically semi-active or supervisory, meaning the surgeon retains the drill or instrument and the robot provides trajectory guidance rather than autonomously executing the critical step. This design means the “conversion” is often less drastic than in teleoperated systems—the surgeon can simply resume freehand technique using the same exposure or percutaneous track. The 2024 Chinese guideline on robot-assisted thoracolumbar surgery includes recommendations on intraoperative decision-making and precautions (recommendations 7–11), and the literature explicitly recognizes that reference frame loosening, registration failure, or discrepancy between the navigation display and actual anatomy should prompt the surgeon to pause and re-verify, with backup plans emphasized. A structured intraoperative emergency checklist for intelligent orthopedic robots has been developed using the SHEL model (Software, Hardware, Environment, Liveware), producing 5 primary, 15 secondary, and 35 tertiary items covering software failures, hardware failures, environmental issues, personnel issues, and interaction failures. This is a meaningful step toward systematization, but it is a generic adverse-event checklist, not a vascular-or-nerve-injury-specific conversion algorithm. The specific clinical decision of when to abandon the robotic trajectory and how to expose and repair a vascular injury remains dependent on the individual surgeon’s open surgical skills and the immediate availability of vascular or neurosurgical support. 🦵 Joint Replacement: The Most Quantified Conversion Data, but Focused on Technical Abortions Arthroplasty provides the most robust numerical data on conversion, but the reasons for conversion are predominantly technical failures of the robotic workflow, not acute neurovascular crises. In a consecutive series of 429 robotic-assisted total hip arthroplasties (RA-THA), intraoperative abortion and conversion to manual THA occurred in 17 cases (3.96%). The leading causes were pelvic array loosening or malposition (1.17%), inaccurate bone mapping or construction (1.40%), and inaccurate initial registration (0.93%). A broader review has cited abortion rates due to robotic, navigation, or process-link problems as high as 22%. The 2026 Asia-Pacific expert consensus on robotic hip and knee arthroplasty explicitly defines “the ability to safely convert to conventional surgery when necessary” as a core component of robotic competency, alongside normal workflow operation, anomaly recognition, and fault management. This is a significant statement of principle: the consensus recognizes that traditional arthroplasty skill constitutes the safety net when the robotic system fails. However, the consensus does not prescribe a step-by-step conversion protocol for an acute vascular injury—it establishes the expectation of convertibility as a training and credentialing requirement. 🚨 The Genuine Gap: Acute Neurovascular Crisis in Orthopedic Robotics The literature on robot-to-open conversion for hemorrhagic crisis is far more developed in general, thoracic, urologic, and gynecologic surgery than in orthopedics. Studies describe high-fidelity simulation programs for emergency robotic undocking in thoracic surgery, with teams successfully converting from robotic to open within 5 minutes of attending arrival at the bedside. These programs use progressive scenarios including pulmonary artery bleeding, open conversion, and hemodynamic instability, and have been shown to reduce critical missed steps through structured checklists and team-based training. The principles are transferable, but the orthopedic application is lagging. An acute vascular injury during robotic spine surgery—for example, a vertebral artery injury during cervical pedicle screw placement or an iliac vessel injury during sacropelvic fixation—demands the same non-technical skills: rapid recognition, clear communication, coordinated undocking, and immediate open exposure. Yet the orthopedic-specific simulation literature for this exact scenario is sparse. The field acknowledges that robotic surgery inherently increases the demand on communication because the surgeon may be away from the bedside or focused on a console, and that non-technical skills—leadership, decision-making, situational awareness, stress management, and teamwork—become instrumental. These are precisely the competencies that simulation training builds, but orthopedic programs have been slower to adopt them than general surgery programs. A specific technical consideration for orthopedic conversion is that many orthopedic robots are mounted or docked to the patient’s anatomy via a reference frame or array. An emergency undocking must account for the physical disconnection of this hardware without causing secondary displacement or injury. Manufacturer user manuals for robotic platforms do include conversion-to-manual procedures and manual instrument movement instructions as part of their alarm-response chapters, but these are platform-specific technical instructions, not clinical crisis-management algorithms. The surgeon must integrate the mechanical steps of releasing the robot with the clinical steps of achieving hemostasis or decompressing a nerve. 💎 The Bottom Line The protocols for converting from robotic to manual operation in orthopedic surgery are partially mature, but not uniformly so. For predictable technical failures—registration error, array loosening, system fault—the maturity is reasonably good: arthroplasty registries quantify the conversion rate, expert consensus defines convertibility as a competency, and structured adverse-event checklists exist for orthopedic robots. For acute vascular or nerve injury, the maturity is substantially lower: the crisis-management simulation and undocking protocols that are well established in thoracic and general robotic surgery have not been systematically translated into orthopedic training, and the published orthopedic guidance tends to address technical workflow failures rather than acute neurovascular catastrophes. As a practicing surgeon, I would state the practical implication plainly: the safety of robotic orthopedic surgery in an emergency depends less on the existence of a written protocol and more on whether the surgical team has rehearsed the conversion under realistic conditions, whether the surgeon retains the open surgical skills to manage the complication independently of the robot, and whether the institutional environment provides immediate access to the necessary specialist support. The direction of travel is toward greater systematization—checklists, simulation, and competency-based credentialing—but the evidence base for orthopedic-specific neurovascular crisis conversion remains thin, and I would not describe it as fully mature.

For an experienced arthroplasty surgeon, initial workflow efficiency often improves after approximately 7–20 robotic TKAs and 12–35 robotic THAs. These are planning ranges—not validated thresholds for independent practice or patient safety. Some surgeons and teams require substantially more cases. The endpoint matters. A prospective TKA study identified a seven-case learning curve for operative workflow, with no detectable learning effect on component-positioning accuracy. Another robotic knee platform reported approximately 20 cases. TKA workflow study, seven-axis platform study For THA, one contemporary study reported 12–17 cases, but a larger single-centre study identified operative-time stabilization after 41 posterolateral and 73 direct-anterior cases. Because different surgeons performed the two approaches, that difference cannot be attributed to approach alone. Contemporary THA study, approach-specific study From a surgical programme perspective, I would structure introduction as follows. These are practical recommendations, rather than a universally validated training protocol. Phase Recommended structure Before the first patient Complete platform-specific training, planning exercises and cadaver-based practice covering exposure, tracker placement, registration, instrument access and conversion to conventional surgery. Rehearse the complete workflow with the theatre team. Cadaveric training preceded clinical adoption in the cited seven-case TKA study. Initial clinical cases Use an experienced arthroplasty surgeon and a consistent team. Arrange on-site supervision by a surgeon experienced with that platform; manufacturer technical support complements clinical supervision. Begin with straightforward primary cases using the surgeon’s familiar approach and implants. Supervised progression Continue supervision until planning, registration verification, safe execution and troubleshooting are demonstrated consistently. Do not end proctoring solely because a predetermined case number has been reached. Scheduling and volume Allow additional operating time and avoid long gaps between early cases. Concentrate initial cases among a small trained group. A three-surgeon THA study associated higher case frequency with faster efficiency gains, but cannot establish a universal minimum annual volume. Volume study Ongoing review Audit consecutive cases for total theatre and operative time, registration failures, conversions, positioning outliers, pin-related injury, infection, readmission and reoperation. Review problems before expanding complexity or throughput. There is no well-established universal number of proctored cases, cadaver procedures or annual robotic arthroplasties that guarantees safety. Local credentialing and platform requirements should be met, with progression based on observed competence and outcomes. Early accuracy can be acceptable while operations remain slower. Conversely, reaching an operative-time plateau does not establish that rare complications have been controlled. The programme should preserve adequate time for verification and maintain immediate access to conventional instruments and surgical expertise.

从执业关节外科医师的视角看，机器人关节置换的学习曲线并非一条单一的曲线，而是“操作效率”与“临床精通”两条相互交织但拐点不同的曲线。新开展中心最常见的失误，是将“手术时间不再明显延长”误判为“已经跨越学习曲线”，从而过早放宽病例选择。效率的拐点来得很快，但安全边界的建立要慢得多。 学习曲线的真实形态：一个“快速入门、缓慢精通”的分层过程 全膝关节置换（TKA） 的效率拐点出现得相当早。基于累积和（CUSUM）分析的研究将机器人TKA的学习过程划分为三个阶段：初期学习期（第1–9例）、能力提升期（第10–52例，进入平台期）、优化表现期（第53–80例）。另一项研究将显著的时间下降定位在第41–50例的区间，此后手术时间稳定在约90分钟的平台。但文献中报告的“学习曲线长度”跨度极大，从6例到43例不等，这种离散性本身就提示：“多少例跨越”的答案高度依赖于所测量的指标（总手术时间、截骨步骤时间、还是工作负荷评分）以及术者既有的计算机辅助手术经验。一项2026年的研究甚至报告，在已有机器人经验的手术团队中，第3例即可将手术时间从65分钟降至55分钟的稳态，这更接近于“平台内转移”而非“从零学习”。 全髋关节置换（THA） 的曲线形态略有不同。CUSUM分析一致地将初期胜任力（competency） 的阈值定在12–17例（不同系统分别为MAKO 13例、七轴系统17例、影像导航系统12–17例），而巩固精通（consolidated proficiency） 则需要38–43例。国产ARTHROBOT系统的学习曲线报告为约20例。一项范围综述汇总了多个平台的数据，手术时间在13–17例的学习阶段后趋于稳定，但注册时间的改善和肢体长度/偏心距测量一致性的提升，则在更晚的阶段才显现。 将两条曲线并置，可以形成一个对临床决策至关重要的区分：“效率拐点”约在10–20例，“精通平台”约在40–50例，而THA的巩固精通可能延伸至40例以上。 新开展中心的起步方案设计，必须以较长的那条曲线为基准来规划病例选择和监督强度，而非以较短的那条来宣告“毕业”。 新开展中心的起步方案：以“结构性约束”替代“个人悟性” 现有证据最一致的建议，是将早期病例集中在一个固定的、经过系统培训的团队手中，并以前置性的结构化监督覆盖风险最高的阶段。 第一，导师带教应覆盖“前10例”这一风险窗口，而非象征性到场。 基于THA学习曲线的推荐明确建议，新中心的结构化实施方案应包括制造商培训加上初始5–10例的 proctoring（现场督导）。导师的角色不应仅限于“在台上看着”，而应覆盖病例选择、术前规划审核、以及注册失败或轨迹异常时的即时决策。一项针对儿科脊柱机器人的 mentorship 模型显示，结构化的导师制可以在维持可接受的安全性和效率的同时，将新技术整合进新术者的实践；但该研究也警示，在初始训练期应格外谨慎，以避免并发症。对于关节置换，导师制的关键价值在于帮助新团队识别那些“看起来能做、但早期阶段不应该做”的病例——例如严重僵硬膝、既往内植物存留、或显著骨缺损——这些恰恰是Q13中讨论的相对困难场景，应推迟到效率平台建立之后再逐步纳入。 第二，尸体/假骨培训应聚焦于“注册与故障排查”，而非重复截骨步骤。 机器人关节置换早期的时间损耗和安全隐患，主要不在截骨本身（截骨在传统手术中已高度熟练），而在于注册的可靠性、追踪器安放、以及光学信号遮挡时的恢复策略。一项尸体研究提示，即使是经验丰富的外科医生，首次在尸体上进行机器人TKA时也可能出现比手工操作更高的叠加误差（stacked errors），这恰恰说明尸体培训的价值不在于“证明机器人更准”，而在于暴露和纠正那些在活体手术中代价过高的流程性错误。培训设计应刻意模拟注册失败、参考架松动、光学阵列被遮挡等场景，让团队在无患者风险的条件下建立故障排查的肌肉记忆。 第三，例数门槛应分层设定，并与病例复杂度准入挂钩。 结合TKA和THA的证据，一个审慎的分层框架是： 0–10例：仅限解剖正常、无既往手术史、BMI适中的初次置换，导师全程在场或即时可及。 11–25例：可逐步纳入中度畸形（如内翻<15°），但仍应排除严重僵硬、严重骨缺损和翻修。 26–40例：若团队效率已进入平台且无注册相关不良事件，可开始审慎评估DDH（Crohn I–II型）或轻中度屈曲挛缩等Q13中获益明确但技术门槛较高的指征。 40例以上：在THA中可考虑进入巩固精通阶段，逐步纳入更复杂的翻修或严重畸形病例；TKA的优化表现期通常从50例后开始。 这一框架的核心理据是：早期病例的“简单化”不是对机器人能力的浪费，而是对学习曲线成本的必要控制。在注册可靠性尚未经过充分验证的阶段引入解剖困难的病例，会将“学习机器人”和“挑战困难解剖”两个风险源叠加，而这两者本可以分开管理。 控制早期手术时长与并发症的结构性策略 手术时长的控制，关键在于将“非手术时间”移出关键路径。 学习曲线早期的时间增量，主要集中于装机、注册和系统调试，而非截骨本身。CUSUM研究识别出注册时间是早期效率的核心瓶颈——计算机注册时间的改善（约21.5%）在达到精通后才显现，而系统bug和患者高BMI在前50例中会显著延长注册时间。因此，早期效率策略应包括：在患者入室前完成系统开机、自检和器械准备；将术前规划审核前置到手术日前；以及为每一例预设“注册失败后的备选方案”（如转为导航或徒手），避免在手术室内进行开放式的问题解决。一项2025年的研究显示，机器人TKA组每30例的平均手术时间递减（97.6→86.6→76.7分钟），且并发症率无差异，提示在结构化推进下，效率的改善可以不伴随安全性的牺牲。 并发症的控制，核心不在机器人本身，而在于“避免在学习期做超出团队当前能力边界的决策”。 综述证据明确指出，机器人TKA在学习期与精通期之间，假体生存率和假体相关并发症率无显著差异，但早期术后阶段可能出现更差的临床结局。这意味着，学习曲线的主要风险不是“机器人做错了什么”，而是术者在流程不熟练时，倾向于用“个人经验干预”去覆盖机器人的规划——例如在注册不理想时强行继续、或在软组织平衡与规划冲突时放弃个体化判断。2026年亚太共识对此的表述是：当软组织平衡与刚性力线目标冲突时，应优先保证软组织平衡。在学习期，这一原则应被进一步收紧：当注册质量或规划可靠性存疑时，应优先转为已验证的替代技术（导航/徒手），而非在机器人平台上“试一试”。将“中转”视为一种成熟的术中决策而非失败，是早期阶段最重要的安全文化。 综合判断：一条以“分层准入”为核心的起步路线 将学习曲线的证据与起步方案的要素整合，一个新开展中心的合理路线可以概括为： 阶段 例数范围 病例准入 监督强度 核心目标 效率建立期 1–10 解剖正常初次置换，排除僵硬/骨缺损/翻修 导师全程在场或即时可及 将注册时间和装机流程标准化 能力提升期 11–25 可纳入中度冠状面畸形，仍排除困难解剖 导师术前审核规划，术中可远程支持 注册稳定性与故障排查的自主性 平台巩固期 26–40 审慎纳入DDH（轻中度）、屈曲挛缩 定期病例复盘 将效率平台转化为可重复的临床路径 精通拓展期 40+（THA）/50+（TKA） 逐步纳入翻修、严重畸形、骨缺损 按常规高难度病例管理 在维持安全边界的前提下扩展适应证 “多少例跨越学习曲线”的临床含义，不应被理解为“到了某一天就突然具备了独立处理一切病例的能力”。它更准确的表述是：约10–20例后，团队具备了安全执行“简单病例”的流程稳定性；约40–50例后，才逐步具备将机器人的几何确定性应用于“复杂解剖”的决策成熟度。 新开展中心最审慎的姿态，是在效率曲线已经平坦之后，仍然刻意延迟困难病例的引入，直到注册可靠性和故障排查能力已经被反复验证。学习曲线的成本，最终不是由手术时间的长短来衡量的，而是由在团队尚未准备好时接诊的那个困难病例来定义的。

Robotic guidance can improve pedicle screw accuracy by several percentage points, but the size of the benefit depends on how accuracy is defined, the robot used, and the comparison technique. A larger benefit in deformity or revision surgery is plausible, but is not conclusively established. From a surgical decision-making perspective, it helps to distinguish Grade A placement, meaning no pedicle breach, from Grades A+B, commonly considered radiographically acceptable placement, allowing a breach of less than approximately 2 mm. Two direct comparisons illustrate the magnitude: Study Accuracy measure Robotic guidance Freehand with fluoroscopy Absolute improvement Randomized thoracolumbar trial: 234 patients, 1,116 screws Grade A 95.3% 86.1% 9.2 percentage points Same trial Grades A+B 98.7% 93.5% 5.2 percentage points Retrospective thoracolumbar comparison Grades A+B 93.4% 88.9% 4.5 percentage points These are individual study results, not a pooled estimate or guaranteed performance. The randomized trial primarily involved degenerative and traumatic conditions. Randomized trial, retrospective comparison In spinal deformity, rotated vertebrae and narrow or distorted pedicles make three-dimensional planning particularly useful. One comparative scoliosis study reported accuracy of 96.7% with robotic navigation versus 80.4% with freehand placement, a 16.3-point difference. However, a large difference in one cohort does not prove that deformity consistently increases the treatment advantage; case selection, surgeon experience, and imaging methods can affect the comparison. Scoliosis study In lumbar revision surgery, robotic planning may help when previous surgery has altered the usual landmarks. An 81-patient retrospective comparison found Grade A placement in 93.6% versus 87.2% of screws, approximately 6.5 percentage points higher with robotics. Grades A+B were 98.5% versus 96.9%, only 1.6 points higher. Thus, revision evidence supports improved accuracy but does not establish a larger advantage than in primary surgery. Revision study Clinically, I would regard robotics as potentially valuable when safe trajectories are difficult to reproduce. I remain uncertain about a precise thoracic-versus-lumbar benefit or a consistently greater benefit in complex cases, because many studies combine levels and lack direct subgroup comparisons. Better CT accuracy also does not necessarily translate into a proven reduction in neurological injury or reoperation.

**截至目前，关节登记数据库与中长期对照研究尚未一致证明：机器人关节置换能降低总体翻修率、延长假体存留，或持续改善患者报告结局。**定位与力线更准确的优势较明确，但“更准确→平衡更好→翻修更少”这条链条，尚未被完整证实。 这里将“注册研究”理解为关节置换登记数据库研究；它与随机试验注册、医疗器械注册研究不同。 1．翻修率与假体存留率：应按术式分别看 术式 代表性结果 临床解读 全膝置换 2026年英国NJR研究中，匹配后5年假体存留率为机器人组 98.6%、传统组 98.5%，翻修风险无显著差异 数值相差0.1个百分点，不能据此宣称机器人减少翻修 全髋置换 同期NJR研究中，匹配后两组5年存留率均为 98.8%，总体翻修风险无显著差异 与假体位置异常相关的一组翻修原因出现降低信号，但未转化为总体翻修减少 单髁置换 部分研究显示再次干预减少；但2026年NJR研究对全膝和单髁的总体结论，均未证实机器人降低早期总体翻修风险 结果尚不一致，不能把单中心优势当作普遍结论 上述NJR研究平均随访约2.5年，最长评估至5年，并非所有患者都完成5年随访。全膝与单髁NJR研究、全髋NJR研究 更长期的全膝证据也未显示明确优势：一项至少随访10年的随机试验报告，15年时以翻修或无菌性松动为终点，两组假体存留率均约 98%。但这是较早期机器人系统的结果，不能直接代表当前所有平台。长期随机试验 2．患者报告结局：部分早期优势，尚未形成稳定的中长期差异 患者报告结局应看疼痛、功能、关节感知及生活质量，而不是仅看X线。 2026年多中心RACER-Knee随机试验中，12个月遗忘关节评分为机器人组 49.2分、传统组 50.2分，调整后差值为−1.5分，未发现有临床意义的优势。它属于短期证据，不能回答远期存留问题；上述长期全膝试验也未发现WOMAC等结局明显改善。RACER-Knee试验、长期全膝试验 全髋方面，前述NJR研究未纳入患者报告结局，不能用其存留率结果推断疼痛、功能是否更好。 3．为什么力线与平衡改善，未必带来翻修减少？ 首先，更准确地执行规划，不等于规划目标对每位患者都最合适。不同力线策略、软组织处理和假体设计，会共同影响结果；术中测得的间隙，也不能完全代表负重活动时的动态稳定性。 其次，翻修还包括感染、假体周围骨折、脱位等原因，许多并非单靠截骨精度就能避免。传统置换的存留率本已较高，要证实额外的小幅改善，需要很大的样本和足够长的随访。 最后，登记研究存在选择偏倚：机器人患者可能更年轻、健康，术者病例量也可能更高。全髋NJR研究中，未匹配时的部分优势在匹配后减弱，说明不能把差异全部归因于机器人。全髋NJR研究分析 **临床上可以说，机器人提高了部分操作的可重复性；目前仍不宜承诺它能让关节“用得更久”。**也不能把“未发现显著差异”解释为已证明完全等效，尤其是现代平台10年以上的比较数据仍需积累。

从骨科创伤的决策角度，**最适合机器人辅助经皮内固定的，是确需手术、已获得并能维持满意复位、存在安全螺钉通道，而且徒手定位较困难的骨折。**机器人主要帮助把螺钉放准，不能弥补复位不良，也不能替代正确的固定方式选择。 1．哪些骨折值得优先考虑？ 骨折或损伤 适合考虑的情况 关键限制 骨盆后环损伤：骶骨骨折、骶髂关节脱位或骨折脱位 需要固定，闭合或有限切开复位满意，CT确认存在安全骶髂或经骶通道；通道狭窄、常规透视定位困难时尤其值得评估 不能仅凭Tile分型决定使用。高度不稳定损伤可能需要联合前环固定或腰盆固定，单纯骶髂螺钉未必足够 髋臼前柱、后柱及部分耻骨上支骨折 需要固定，移位较小或能获得满意复位，骨折形态适合长通道螺钉固定 关节面压陷、明显粉碎、关节内游离骨块或不能满意复位者，通常不能仅靠经皮螺钉解决 股骨颈骨折 已决定采用保头内固定，复位满意，拟使用空心螺钉等平台支持的固定方式 机器人可辅助螺钉布局，但不能保证避免股骨头坏死、不愈合或股骨颈短缩 骨盆与髋臼机器人技术指导，将移位较小，或能够闭合、有限切开复位的损伤列为适合评估的范围，而不是所有骨盆、髋臼骨折。骨盆髋臼机器人技术指导 股骨颈骨折的小型对照研究支持机器人改善定位、减少透视使用，但不足以证明长期保头成功率一定更高。股骨颈骨折对照研究 2．哪些情况下属于低价值或多余使用？ **原本适合非手术治疗的稳定骨折：**不能为了使用机器人增加手术指征。 **定位简单、常规操作可靠的病例：**若预期准确性、安全性或流程没有实质增益，增加装机、配准和耗材可能得不偿失。 **术式选择本身不合适：**例如部分高龄移位股骨颈骨折，经综合评估更适合关节置换，就不应为了使用机器人而选择保头螺钉固定。年轻患者的高剪切、粉碎性股骨颈骨折，也不能因机器人能放置平行螺钉，就忽略更合适的固定构型。 3．哪些情况下不宜实施机器人辅助经皮置钉？ 没有安全骨性通道，或无法避开重要神经血管。 复位不满意、不能维持复位，或螺钉构型无法提供足够稳定性。 影像质量、配准或参考架固定不可靠，机械臂无法安全到达。 需要紧急止血、清创、解除压迫或处理关节内病变，却因等待机器人延误必要治疗。 其中前两项往往意味着“经皮螺钉方案不适合”，不只是机器人不能用；后两项可能需要改用其他辅助方式或手术入路。相关技术指导也明确列出无法安全规划、经皮螺钉不能有效固定及机械臂不可达等限制。技术指导中的适应证与禁忌证 **复杂骨折并不自动意味着机器人更合适。**最重要的顺序是：先选对治疗与固定方案，再完成复位，最后判断机器人能否在具体置钉步骤中增加价值。对具体骨折类型，目前还缺少足够证据给出“哪一种获益最大”的统一排名。

For an experienced arthroplasty surgeon, a reasonable planning estimate is approximately 15–30 cases for initial robotic workflow proficiency, with 30–40 or more sometimes needed to approach conventional operating times. These are estimates—not credentialing thresholds or proof of competence. The distinction between technical accuracy, workflow familiarity, and speed matters: Robotic TKA: One institutional study reported approximately 30–40 cases before operative times became comparable with conventional TKA. Considerable variation existed between surgeons. TKA learning-curve study Robotic THA: A randomized study identified a 13-case learning phase for one platform. Another study found approximately 20 cases for a high-volume surgeon, while lower-volume surgeons did not show the same clear improvement. These findings should not be transferred directly between platforms or surgical approaches. THA randomized study, surgeon-volume study From an arthroplasty programme perspective, I would recommend the following structure. The numbers below are practical planning suggestions, not universally validated requirements. Train the surgeon and a consistent operating-room team before launch. Complete platform-specific instruction, observe an established service, and rehearse setup, registration, tracker placement, and troubleshooting. Cadaver training should cover the complete procedure, safe instrument access, and conversion to conventional surgery. Course attendance alone should not establish competence. Use an experienced, platform-specific proctor for the initial clinical cases. A practical starting arrangement is 5–10 proctored cases, with additional supervision whenever needed. Independent practice should depend on demonstrated competence in registration verification, planning, execution, and recovery from errors—not simply completing the prescribed number. Begin with routine primary cases. Initially avoid severe deformity, ankylosis, major bone loss, and complex retained hardware. Keep the surgical approach and implant familiar while learning the robotic workflow. Concentrate early experience. Launch with a small group of surgeons and a stable team. Where feasible, schedule one or two robotic cases weekly to avoid long gaps. There is no well-established universal annual minimum volume that guarantees safe robotic arthroplasty. Allow additional theatre time and review performance. An initial allowance of approximately 20–30 extra minutes per case is reasonable, adjusted to local experience. Audit operative time, registration failures, conversions, component-position outliers, wound problems, pin complications, fractures, and early reoperations. Review progress after roughly 10, 20, and 30 cases, rather than automatically increasing case complexity. Published series often preserve placement accuracy during early adoption, but complication events are too uncommon to conclude that the learning phase carries no additional risk. Progression should require acceptable accuracy and safety alongside improving efficiency; faster surgery alone is an insufficient endpoint.

From a practicing orthopedic surgeon's perspective, the answer is yes—limitations in reach and angular range do affect surgery in special body positions and deep anatomical sites, but the impact is highly platform-dependent and is increasingly mitigated by design and preoperative planning rather than being a fixed, insurmountable barrier. The constraints are real and clinically documented, but they manifest less as a categorical inability to perform a procedure and more as a set of geometric and kinematic boundary conditions that must be respected through robot base positioning, patient positioning, and trajectory planning. 📐 The Nominal Specifications: Generous but Not Infinite Modern orthopedic robots are not severely limited in raw reach or angular range on paper. A representative technical specification for an orthopedic navigation and positioning system lists a robotic arm reach radius ≥800 mm, joint range of motion ≥360°, and an effective working space of ≥200 mm × 200 mm × 200 mm. The "Tianji" (天玑) platform uses a 6-degree-of-freedom arm that the manufacturer states can cover different body parts and angles across the whole body. Another serial orthopedic arm has a full length of 850 mm, six DOF, with each DOF rotatable to ±360°. These numbers suggest that the arm itself is rarely the limiting factor in isolation. The clinically meaningful constraints arise when these nominal capabilities intersect with patient anatomy, table position, and the presence of other objects in the surgical field. 🛏️ Special Body Positions: The Constraint Is Often the Base and the Bedside, Not the Arm The most practical limitation in special positions is not the arm's reach but the robot's base footprint and its interaction with the operating table and anesthesia equipment. In pelvic fracture surgery using the Tianji robot, the robotic arm base is relatively large and must be positioned on the side of the operating table opposite the anesthesia machine to avoid interfering with the surgeon's standing position. When bilateral screw fixation is required, the positions of both the anesthesia machine and the robotic arm must be planned in advance to reserve sufficient operative space. This is a configuration constraint: the robot may be able to reach the target in theory, but the physical footprint of its base and the need to keep the surgeon's workspace clear can make certain setups impractical without repositioning the patient or the robot. Patient position itself also determines whether the robot can be deployed. One technical specification states the system is compatible with supine, prone, or lateral positions, but compatibility does not mean equivalence. In spine surgery, the robot is often mounted on a side rail of the Jackson table, and the reference fiducials may be attached to the robotic arm rather than directly to the patient's bony anatomy—a configuration in which patient movement (e.g., coughing) can degrade accuracy because the arm-mounted reference does not track the spine independently. This is not a reach limitation per se, but it is a positioning-related limitation of the robotic setup that affects accuracy in ways that vary with body position and patient stability. For sacral instrumentation, a specific collision problem has been described: during S2 alar–iliac screw placement, the robotic arm can collide with the patient's body, preventing completion of the planned screw placement. This is a direct example of an angular and spatial constraint imposed by the patient's own anatomy in a specific position (prone, with the pelvis and sacrum exposed), rather than a deficiency of the arm's nominal range. 🦴 Deep Orthopedic Sites: Where Reach Meets Geometry Deep sites—the acetabulum, the pelvis, the sacrum, and the deep posterior spine—are where the interaction between reach and angular range becomes most consequential. Acetabular and pelvic surgery. The bone-mounted or table-mounted configuration of many orthopedic robots introduces a rigid geometric relationship between the robot base and the target. In acetabular preparation, the system may enforce a conical stereotactic boundary of approximately 10–15° deviation from the acetabular axis to protect against soft-tissue injury and over-penetration. This is a deliberate angular constraint rather than an incapacity, but it illustrates that the effective working angular range at depth is a subset of the arm's full range, defined by safety and anatomy. In confined spaces such as behind an acetabular implant, a dexterous robotic system has been reported to cover 91% of the workspace in cadaveric debridement studies, which is a favorable figure but still leaves a margin of inaccessible volume. Deep spine and sacropelvic fixation. The S2AI screw collision described above is the clearest documented instance of a deep site where the combination of patient anatomy and arm geometry limits the achievable trajectory. In pelvic trauma, the robot's arm must reach through a soft-tissue corridor to a deep bony target, and the system's rigidity means it does not correct its position for external deviating forces—in one reported case, the surrounding soft tissue and erector spinae muscles pushed the arm medially by a few millimeters, causing the navigated drill to skive and necessitating conversion to freehand navigation. This is a compliance limitation that becomes clinically relevant specifically in deep, constrained corridors where soft tissue can exert lateral forces on the arm. ⚙️ The Mitigating Strategies: Planning, Pose Optimization, and Design The clinical response to these limitations is not to accept them passively. The literature describes several systematic mitigations. Preoperative base pose optimization. Because of kinematic limitations, selecting an optimal robot base location and surgical access point is essential to avoid reachability problems. Capability-map methods have been developed to preoperatively determine whether a given robot base pose can reach all planned trajectories for a specific procedure, using pedicle screw placement as a validated use case. In practice, this means the surgeon or team can simulate the arm's motion before the case and adjust the base or patient position if a planned trajectory falls outside the reachable workspace. Patient positioning as a reach-enabling maneuver. In pelvic surgery with the Tianji robot, the patient can be locally elevated during positioning to pre-adjust the screw trajectory angle, specifically to avoid interference from surrounding equipment and to bring the planned path into the arm's favorable working envelope. This is a deliberate use of patient positioning to expand the effective reachable workspace. Collision avoidance and joint-limit management. Modern systems incorporate collision-stop functions (e.g., stopping at a collision force ≤80 N) and real-time position compensation if patient movement is detected. Some control architectures allow the remote center of motion to be repositioned in response to detected collisions, thereby improving arm reach and reducing the likelihood of collision. However, these are safety and recovery mechanisms, not solutions to the fundamental geometric constraint; when a collision prevents completion of a planned screw, the surgeon must decide whether to adjust the plan, reposition, or convert. 💎 The Bottom Line Reach and angular range limitations are clinically relevant in special positions and deep sites, but they are better understood as geometric and logistical constraints than as hard technological failures. The arm's nominal reach (≥800 mm) and joint range (≥360°) are generous, yet the effective workspace at depth is narrowed by safety boundaries (e.g., 10–15° conical limits in acetabular work), patient anatomy (e.g., S2AI screw collision), soft-tissue forces that a rigid arm cannot correct, and the physical footprint of the robot base in relation to the anesthesia machine and surgeon's station. These constraints are managed through preoperative base-pose optimization, deliberate patient positioning to bring the target into the favorable envelope, and collision-detection and compensation features—but they are not eliminated. As a practicing surgeon, I would state clearly that the question of whether a given deep or awkwardly positioned case is feasible is answered not by the robot's specification sheet alone, but by preoperative planning that confirms the planned trajectory lies within the reachable and collision-free workspace for that specific patient setup; when that confirmation cannot be obtained, the robot is not the appropriate tool for that trajectory, and conventional or navigated freehand technique remains the correct fallback.

从卫生经济学的严格视角审视，机器人辅助脊柱手术的成本效果并非一个“是”或“否”的二元结论，而是一个高度条件依赖的区间。椎弓根穿破与翻修成本的降低，在理论模型上具备抵消高额前期投入的潜力，但这种潜力能否在真实世界中兑现，取决于一组极为苛刻的前提条件。关于年手术量的收支平衡阈值，文献给出的答案同样分裂：在理想化的高效运营模型中，约200例/年可能在2–4年内回本；而一旦纳入真实世界的不良事件与效率损耗，多数情景下设备在其7年寿命内根本无法实现收支平衡。 抵消的逻辑：理论上的确成立，但依赖于未被真实世界数据充分检验的假设 支持“翻修减少可以抵消成本”的证据，主要来自基于模型的外推，而非在真实世界中对总成本的直接观测。 一项被广泛引用的模型分析估计，在557例胸腰椎手术中采用机器人辅助，每年可避免9.47例翻修，并通过缩短手术时间、住院时间和减少感染，总计节省约608,546美元。另一项网络荟萃分析进一步给出了每例患者的节省估计：机器人相较于CT导航可节省4,086–4,865美元/例，相较于徒手透视则可节省7,317–9,654美元/例。西班牙的一项10年预算影响分析也报告了每位患者平均1,011欧元的净节省，其构成中再次手术的减少贡献了793欧元，住院时间缩短贡献了1,523欧元。 这些数字勾勒出了一条清晰的传导链：精准度提升→翻修减少→高成本的翻修被低成本的初次手术所替代→节省额累积并覆盖前期投入。翻修手术本身的费用是高昂的，因此“避免一例翻修”在经济账本上的权重，确实足以在模型中抵消相当数量的单例耗材成本。单例耗材费用的报告范围差异很大，从约200美元的无菌铺巾和 fiducials，到800–1,200美元的专用一次性耗材，部分系统甚至可达1,500美元/例。相较于翻修手术的总体费用，这一量级的单例增量是可控的。 然而，这条传导链的每一个环节，在真实世界中都面临摩擦。 真实世界的“隐性成本”如何颠覆模型 2025年发表于《The Spine Journal》的一项研究，为上述乐观模型提供了一个必要的修正。该研究从FDA MAUDE数据库中提取了1,346例机器人脊柱手术不良事件，并据此构建了涵盖不同年手术量、手术室成本和并发症率的189种经济情景。其核心发现是：在所有189种情景中，机器人系统均未能在其7年有效寿命内实现财务收支平衡；即便在最优条件下（最高手术量、最低并发症率），收回初始投资也需要33.8年。 这一颠覆性结论的根源，在于模型纳入了此前被忽视的“流程中断成本”。研究发现，机器人相关不良事件导致的平均手术延迟为58.1分钟，其中因精度问题（占并发症的66.4%）引发的延迟尤为突出，而34.4% 的不良事件最终导致机器人被术中弃用，弃用时的延迟进一步延长至71.4分钟。这些分钟数是直接的手术室成本——在一个年手术量本已很高的中心，每一分钟的非计划延迟都在侵蚀机器人本应带来的效率收益。换言之，机器人精准度在“理想病例”中节省的翻修成本，在“真实故障”面前被流程延迟和弃用造成的沉没成本部分抵消了。 一项Becker's的报道也印证了这一判断，指出机器人脊柱手术“尚未显示出任何投资回报（ROI）”，其高昂成本在“利润微薄”的支付体系中只是增加了管理费用。 年手术量阈值：一个被“效率”和“并发症率”调节的条件性数字 关于“多少例能收支平衡”，现有证据指向的是一个区间，而非一个确定的常数。 在理想化的高效模型中，阈值相对较低。 一项成本效果分析报告，在200例/年的手术量下，净现值在约2.08年后转为正。西班牙的预算影响分析则显示，在一个逐步采用（年手术量从213例增至330例）的情景下，全部资本投资在3.83年内回收。这些模型的一个共同特征是，它们假设了相对稳定的流程效率和较低的并发症/弃用率。 但在纳入真实世界不良事件后，这一阈值变得遥不可及。 前述189种情景的分析，其“最优条件”已经包含了“最高手术量”，却仍然得出33.8年回本的结论。这意味着，当并发症率和由此导致的流程中断达到真实世界观测到的水平时，单纯增加年手术量不足以将项目推过收支平衡点。手术量越高，每一例中因故障导致的58分钟延迟和潜在的机器人弃用所造成的累计损失也越大。一项伞状综述的结论与此一致：成本效果证据“高度依赖于机构因素，如手术量和效率”，大型行政数据库研究甚至报告机器人病例的医院收费更高（单节段腰椎融合的机器人组平均收费为154,673美元，非机器人组为125,467美元）。 因此，对于年手术量阈值的诚实回答是：如果机构能够将机器人相关不良事件的发生率、弃用率和由此导致的流程延迟控制在极低水平，那么约200例/年的手术量可能在数年内实现收支平衡；但如果真实世界的故障模式在经济模型中得不到有效抑制，那么无论年手术量多高，在设备的经济寿命内实现回本的概率都极低。 阈值本身不是决定性的变量，“每一例手术的流程可靠性”才是。 临床视角的审慎结论 将上述证据并置，机器人辅助脊柱手术的成本效果呈现出一个清晰的条件性结构： 椎弓根穿破和翻修成本的降低，在“翻修确实被避免”且“机器人本身不引发新的流程中断”这两个条件同时成立时，具备抵消设备与耗材成本的理论能力。 但真实世界数据表明，后一个条件在当前的系统可靠性水平下并不稳定成立。精度问题恰恰构成了机器人相关并发症的最大来源，而由此引发的术中延迟和弃用，直接侵蚀了精准度本应带来的经济收益。 对于考虑开展此项目的机构而言，比追问“多少例能回本”更具操作性的前置决策是：本中心的流程成熟度、团队经验和系统维护水平，是否足以将不良事件率和弃用率压制到使经济模型中的“节省”通道得以开启的程度？ 如果答案是否定的，那么高手术量本身并不能解决经济性问题，它只会以更快的速度累积每一例中未被消除的效率损耗。在当前的证据阶段，将机器人定位为在特定复杂病例中换取确定性、而非在全院层面实现投资回报的工具，或许是更符合真实世界数据的选择。

The best candidates are fractures for which percutaneous screw fixation is already appropriate, reduction can be achieved and maintained, and accurate targeting through a narrow bony corridor is difficult. Most fracture-navigation robots guide screw placement; they do not themselves reduce the fracture. From an orthopedic trauma decision-making perspective: Fracture pattern Suitability for robotic assistance Sacroiliac disruptions and selected sacral/posterior pelvic-ring fractures Among the strongest applications, particularly for difficult S1/S2 trajectories after satisfactory reduction. A randomized trial demonstrated improved screw-position grading, fewer guidewire attempts, and less fluoroscopy. The entire unstable ring still needs an adequate fixation strategy. Randomized trial Femoral neck fractures selected for head-preserving fixation Useful for placing multiple screws with the intended spread, parallelism, and subchondral depth. Comparative clinical evidence supports better targeting and fewer repeated drilling attempts. Robotic availability should not determine whether fixation or arthroplasty is appropriate, or justify a mechanically inadequate screw construct. Comparative clinical study Selected acetabular anterior- or posterior-column fractures Most suitable when displacement is minimal or satisfactory reduction can be obtained and a safe column corridor exists. Robotics may also guide a supplementary percutaneous screw after open reduction of another component. Evidence is less mature than for posterior pelvic-ring fixation. Combined open and robotic fixation study Robotic assistance may add little value when conventional placement is straightforward, imaging is clear, or direct exposure already permits reliable screw insertion. Setup, registration, cost, and team experience must be weighed against the expected targeting benefit. Better screw geometry does not necessarily mean better healing or function. Reasons to avoid robotic percutaneous placement—or change the surgical plan—include: Unacceptable or unstable reduction: An accurately placed screw cannot compensate for malreduction. No safe bony corridor or inadequate fixation strength: Severe comminution, bone loss, or unfavorable anatomy may require a different construct. Articular injury requiring direct reconstruction: Displaced fragments, marginal impaction, or incarcerated fragments may require open reduction; robotic screws can sometimes supplement that operation. Unreliable navigation: Poor imaging, unstable reference fixation, tracking failure, or movement after registration makes guided placement unsafe until corrected. Urgent damage-control needs: Robotic setup should not delay hemorrhage control, debridement, vascular treatment, or emergency stabilization. These are chiefly limitations of the percutaneous technique or navigation workflow, rather than universal contraindications to robotics. Osteoporosis, obesity, and an open injury require individual assessment; none alone establishes a blanket exclusion. I would remain cautious about claiming that robotics consistently reduces nonunion, femoral-head osteonecrosis, or neurovascular injury—the evidence for those patient outcomes is less secure than the evidence for placement accuracy.

Reduced tactile feedback can make excessive force, cortical breakthrough, and tissue injury harder to recognise—but the premise needs qualification. Some orthopaedic robots provide haptic boundaries: resistance that keeps an instrument within the planned cutting region. That differs from faithfully transmitting the feel of bone or soft tissue. In systems where the surgeon manually drills or inserts screws through a robotic guide, some direct tactile feedback remains. Stryker From a surgical perspective, the consequences are: Task Consequences when tissue-force feedback is absent or reduced Practical implications Osteotomy and bone preparation Reduced perception of changing bone resistance, instrument binding, and completion of the far cortex can delay recognition of breakthrough. Potential consequences include overpenetration, unintended fracture, or injury to adjacent structures. Planned cutting boundaries, depth limits, direct observation, and physical soft-tissue protection become especially important. Experimental force-sensing systems can detect breakthrough and stop advancement, but this capability cannot be assumed for every robot. PMC Drilling and screw placement Subtle changes in resistance that suggest cortical contact, breach, or poor purchase may be less apparent. Excessive applied force can also cause the drill to slide across bone—skiving—or deflect the guide, producing a trajectory different from the plan. The surgeon must reconcile navigation with actual instrument behaviour and verify trajectory and depth when concerned. Clinical studies document soft-tissue pressure, skiving, and drilling pressure as sources of error; these are not all caused by absent haptics. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Soft-tissue dissection and retraction Without force feedback, tension and tissue resistance are harder to judge. Excessive traction or compression may cause tearing, crush injury, bleeding, or nerve injury before visual changes become obvious. The operator relies more heavily on visible tissue deformation, careful incremental movement, and any available force sensing. In a preclinical study, providing force feedback reduced applied forces during retraction, dissection, and suturing; it did not establish lower clinical complication rates in orthopaedic patients. Springer Nature Link Two distinctions are particularly important: Accurate position does not guarantee safe force. A tool can remain on its planned trajectory while exerting excessive pressure. Likewise, a virtual boundary does not necessarily identify or protect a mobile nerve, tendon, or vessel that enters the working region. Thermal injury is a separate issue. Bone cutting and drilling can generate damaging heat, but absent haptic feedback alone does not establish that overheating will occur. Irrigation, tool condition, speed, feed, and cutting duration require attention regardless of robotic guidance. Experimental studies show that drilling parameters materially affect temperature and force. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov In conventional robotic joint replacement and screw-guidance workflows, much of the exposure and soft-tissue dissection is still performed manually. Therefore, the soft-tissue consequences above apply most directly when the robot itself manipulates tissue without adequate force feedback. I am confident about these mechanisms, but cannot give a reliable percentage increase in orthopaedic complications attributable specifically to absent haptic feedback. That risk is difficult to isolate from platform design, navigation accuracy, surgeon experience, and other safeguards.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the joint-registry data and mid-to-long-term follow-up converge on a conclusion that is more restrained than the marketing narrative: robotic assistance has not demonstrated a consistent, clinically meaningful advantage in revision rates or implant survivorship for total knee or total hip arthroplasty, with the possible exception of revision for dislocation in THA and encouraging survivorship data in UKA. The evidence for patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) is similarly modest and inconsistent. Most importantly, the well-documented improvement in alignment accuracy has not been shown to translate into fewer revisions in the registry data that are best suited to answer that question. TKA: Registry Data Show No Survivorship Advantage at 5 Years The strongest evidence comes from large registry analyses, and it is consistently null. A target trial emulation using National Joint Registry data, matching 69,020 conventional TKRs against 17,255 robotic TKRs, reported 5-year implant survival of 98.5% (95% CI 98.3–98.7) in the conventional group versus 98.6% (98.2–99.0) in the robotic group. The hazard ratio for revision was 1.03 (95% CI 0.86–1.26; P = 0.71)—a near-null finding with narrow confidence intervals that exclude a clinically meaningful benefit. The authors explicitly stated that indications for revision and intraoperative complications did not differ between groups. This is corroborated by an analysis from the American Joint Replacement Registry of Medicare beneficiaries, which found that robotic use was not significant for TKA all-cause revision (P = 0.75), mechanical loosening (P = 0.42), or other mechanical complications (P = 0.46) at five years. The authors concluded that “the purported benefits of using this technology to improve component survival are not supported”. A single-center series with longer follow-up for robotic TKA reported 5-year revision-free survivorship of 96.2%, with revision occurring in 3.8% of cases at final follow-up. While these absolute figures are favorable, the study was not designed to compare against a conventional cohort, and the revision rate is within the range expected for conventional TKA. THA: All-Cause Revision Comparable, but a Specific Benefit for Dislocation The THA registry picture is more nuanced: overall revision is not reduced, but a complication-specific benefit has emerged. An AJRR analysis of over 124,000 primary THAs (113,477 conventional, 10,988 robotic) with minimum 2-year follow-up found that all-cause revision did not differ: 1.9% in the robotic group versus 2.1% in conventional (HR 0.9, 95% CI 0.7–1.1; P = 0.42). However, revision for dislocation was significantly lower in the robotic group (0.3% vs. 0.6%; HR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3–0.9; P = 0.03). The authors interpreted this as robotic assistance being “a potentially useful adjunct during THA to decrease the risk of early revision for dislocation,” while cautioning that until a clear improvement in revision-free implant survival is demonstrated, “surgeons should remain cautious of widespread adoption”. A systematic review of robot-assisted THA reinforces this bifurcation: it found that radiographic precision was consistently improved, but these technical advantages were not consistently accompanied by superior functional outcomes, and described this “discrepancy between radiological precision and clinically meaningful benefit” as the principal finding of the review. Some individual studies within that review reported lower revision rates in robotic cohorts, but the authors noted that most included studies had relatively few adverse events and that larger prospective studies with longer follow-up are required. UKA: The Most Favorable Survivorship Data, but with Important Qualifications UKA is where the survivorship signal is strongest. A multicenter series reported 10-year survivorship of 91.7% (95% CI 88.8–94.6) for robotic medial UKA, with high patient satisfaction. Another long-term cohort reported 10-year survivorship of 94.8%, which the authors noted is consistent with other long-term robotic UKA cohorts and “supports the possibility that robotic assistance could play a role in narrowing the historical survivorship gap” between UKA and TKA. However, two qualifications are essential. First, the National Joint Registry analysis found no difference in 5-year revision risk between robotic and conventional UKR (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.75–1.42; P = 0.86), with 5-year survival of 97.8% conventional versus 96.4% robotic. This is a direct comparative finding that tempers the single-arm survivorship figures. Second, the favorable robotic UKA data are largely from high-volume, specialized centers, and the comparison is often against historical manual UKA benchmarks rather than contemporaneous matched controls. The honest interpretation is that robotic UKA achieves survivorship that is at least comparable to, and possibly better than, historical manual UKA, but the registry-level comparative evidence does not yet demonstrate a clear superiority over conventional UKA. Patient-Reported Outcomes: Statistically Detectable in Places, but Inconsistent and Small The PROM data do not show a consistent or clinically meaningful advantage for robotic arthroplasty. TKA. A meta-analysis pooling KSS, OKS, and WOMAC found little difference at short-term follow-up, but a statistically significant difference at medium-term follow-up (MD 5.50, 95% CI 2.19–8.81). Whether a 5.5-point difference on pooled PROM scales exceeds the minimal clinically important difference is debatable and likely domain-dependent. An RCT of imageless handheld robotic TKA reported significantly higher PROMs at 12 months compared with conventional TKA, but this is a single trial with a specific platform. The overall picture is one of small, inconsistent, and platform-specific differences rather than a robust class effect. THA. The evidence is more clearly null. A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs concluded that there was “little to no difference in clinical and functional outcomes” between robotic and conventional THA, including no important difference in medium-term or short-term PROMs. Another systematic review found comparable functional outcomes between robotic and manual THA. The most defensible statement is that robotic THA does not produce a consistent, clinically meaningful improvement in PROMs over conventional THA. UKA. Robotic UKA is associated with high satisfaction (approximately 95%) and clinically meaningful improvements in joint-specific PROMs, with 10-year survivorship exceeding 90%. UKA as a procedure has historically demonstrated superior functional outcomes compared with TKA despite higher revision rates, and robotic assistance appears to preserve these functional benefits while improving survivorship. This is a more coherent value proposition than is observed for TKA or THA. Does Improved Alignment Translate into Fewer Revisions? This is the central question, and the registry evidence provides a clear negative answer for TKA. Robotic TKA reliably reduces alignment outliers. A meta-analysis reported that outliers >3° from neutral were reduced from 25.8% to 10.1% with robotic assistance. Another analysis found a 67% reduction in mechanical alignment outliers (RR = 0.33). The radiographic case is not in dispute. The problem is the causal chain from outlier reduction to revision reduction. A 2025 meta-analysis focused specifically on survivorship “did not find any statistically significant difference in revision rate of RA-TKA and CM-TKA at 2-, 5-, or 10-year post-surgery,” and concluded that “while improved alignment accuracy is well-documented, the translation to reduced revision rates or improved outcomes remains unproven in large cohort studies”. A separate review stated the same conclusion directly: robotic TKA “consistently improves radiographic alignment accuracy compared with manual TKA, yet this precision has not translated into improved long-term functional outcomes or implant survival”. The registry data explain why this might be. Revision after TKA is a relatively rare event with multiple causes—infection, instability, stiffness, periprosthetic fracture, polyethylene wear, and loosening—and alignment is only one contributor. A simulation analysis estimated that a survivorship advantage of 1.4% to 2% at 15 years would be required to detect a difference attributable to alignment technology, which means that even if a true benefit exists, it is too small to be reliably detected in most registry datasets with current follow-up durations. The National Joint Registry analysis with a near-null hazard ratio and narrow confidence intervals is consistent with either no effect or an effect too small to be clinically decisive at 5 years. The situation is different for THA dislocation, where the mechanism is more direct: cup malposition is a well-established contributor to instability, and robotic assistance improves cup positioning accuracy. The AJRR finding of a halved risk of revision for dislocation (HR 0.5) is therefore mechanistically coherent and represents a genuine translation of improved geometric accuracy into a specific, clinically relevant outcome. But this is a complication-specific benefit, not a general survivorship benefit, and all-cause revision remained unchanged. A Surgeon's Synthesis The registry and mid-to-long-term evidence supports the following stratified conclusions: TKA: Robotic assistance does not improve 5-year implant survivorship or reduce all-cause revision. The alignment advantage is real but has not been shown to translate into fewer revisions in large registry datasets. PROM differences are small and inconsistent. The value proposition for TKA is therefore better framed around reproducibility and reduced extreme outliers than around long-term implant survival. THA: Robotic assistance does not reduce all-cause revision but is associated with a halved risk of revision for dislocation, a mechanistically plausible benefit of improved cup positioning. This is a specific, not a general, survivorship advantage. PROMs are not meaningfully improved. UKA: Robotic UKA achieves survivorship exceeding 90% at 10 years with high satisfaction, and may narrow the historical survivorship gap between UKA and TKA. However, direct registry comparisons against conventional UKA at 5 years show no difference, and the favorable data come largely from specialized centers. Alignment to revision: For TKA, the causal link is not established. Improved alignment accuracy has not produced a detectable reduction in revision rates in registry data, and the effect size—if real—is likely too small to detect at current follow-up durations. For THA dislocation, the link is more plausible and supported by registry data, because the mechanism between cup position and stability is direct and the complication is specific enough to detect. The honest caveat is that registry follow-up for robotic arthroplasty is still relatively short, and the technology and its indications are evolving. The absence of a detectable survivorship advantage at 5 years does not preclude a smaller benefit emerging at 10–15 years, but it does mean that claims of improved long-term survival are currently not supported by the highest-quality comparative data. The most defensible clinical positioning is that robotics delivers more predictable execution and, in THA, a specific reduction in dislocation-related revision, while the broader survivorship and functional benefits remain unproven.

骨质量差对机器人辅助内固定的影响，需要拆解为两个性质不同的问题：骨质量直接决定螺钉的“生物学锚定”强度，而机器人系统优化的是螺钉的“几何学位置”。 前者是材料层面的约束，后者是空间层面的执行。机器人无法改变骨密度，但它可以通过选择更好的骨性路径，在给定的薄弱基础上尽可能保留把持力。骨水泥强化的触发点，则在于骨质量已低至几何优化无法代偿、必须引入材料学手段的阈值。 🦴 骨质量如何削弱螺钉把持力：一个可量化的线性关系 骨质量对螺钉固定的影响并非模糊的“把持力下降”，而是具有可测量斜率的关系。生物力学研究显示，骨密度每降低 10 mg/mL，椎弓根螺钉的最大轴向拔出力减少约 60 N。在骨质疏松脊柱中，标准轨迹螺钉的拔出力通常低于 500 N，而非骨质疏松患者可达1000 N 以上；骨质疏松脊柱中螺钉松动率高达 30%–60%，需要腰椎融合的老年患者中骨质疏松患病率约为50%。Kumano 等提出的临床临界值是：轴向拔出力低于 100 N 时，不应直接使用椎弓根螺钉固定，否则极易发生松动脱出。 在髋部，骨质量的影响同样直接。老年转子间骨折的骨质量差、不稳定骨折类型和复位不佳，是早期机械性失败的独立风险因素。骨水泥强化动力髋螺钉可在股骨头内形成骨-骨水泥-螺钉“三结合界面”，减少螺钉切出和切穿的发生率，其逻辑正是弥补骨-螺钉界面本身的力学薄弱。 这一关系对机器人适应证的含义是明确的：机器人不能提高每单位骨密度所能提供的拔出力斜率，它只能影响“螺钉被放置在骨密度相对更高的区域”这一变量。 🤖 骨质量如何重新界定机器人置钉的适应证边界：从“精度增益”转向“路径优化” 在骨质量正常的脊柱中，机器人辅助的核心价值是轨迹执行的几何精度。但在骨质疏松脊柱中，这一价值必须被重新表述：机器人的作用从“把螺钉放得更准”，转变为“在骨量整体不足的椎体内，找到一条骨密度相对更高的可执行路径”。 这一转变有具体的数据支撑。一项 AI 轨迹优化研究显示，在老年骨质疏松患者中，优化轨迹的骨密度和拔出力较标准 AO 轨迹至少提高 2.0 倍；在一个具体病例中，AO 轨迹的拔出力为 326–432 N，而优化轨迹达到 1400–2249 N。关键在于，该研究的作者明确指出，最优轨迹高度个体化，徒手技术难以实现，因此其后续方向正是将 AI 模型与手术机器人和导航技术整合。这意味着，在骨质疏松条件下，机器人的适应证从“需要精确置钉的病例”扩展为“存在一条骨密度更优但几何上仅机器可稳定执行的轨迹的病例”。适应证的门槛不再是单纯的解剖精度需求，而是路径优化的可执行性。 与此同时，骨质量本身构成了机器人精度的一个独立风险因素。一项机器人置钉准确性研究显示，骨密度降低（T ≤ -2.5）是机器人置钉不满意结果的独立风险因素。在严重骨质疏松（T ≤ -3.5）中，风险进一步升高，机制被描述为“骨密度过低降低了螺钉把持力，导致螺钉轨迹偏离”。这揭示了一个在临床决策中容易被忽视的回路：骨质量差不仅削弱最终的固定强度，还可能削弱机器人置钉过程本身的几何保真度——当螺钉在低密度骨内行进时，其实际路径可能偏离规划路径。机器人辅助皮质骨轨迹（CBT）螺钉的数据也从侧面印证了这一逻辑：CBT 螺钉的轴向拔出力比传统椎弓根螺钉高 30%，植入扭矩约为传统螺钉的3 倍，其优势机制正是最大化与皮质骨的接触，而骨质疏松对松质骨的影响远大于对皮质骨的影响。机器人辅助 CBT 置钉的优良率可达 97%，弥补了徒手 CBT 置钉皮质穿透率可高达 20% 的技术瓶颈。换言之，在骨质疏松脊柱中，机器人适应证的一个合理扩展方向，是辅助执行那些依赖皮质骨锚定、但徒手难以稳定完成的轨迹（如 CBT），而非仅仅是在松质骨内追求更高的置钉精度。 💉 第二层：术中阻力与影像学线索。 指南将“置钉过程阻力异常低”与 T 值并列作为触发条件，这具有直接的术中可操作性。在机器人辅助下，术者虽缺乏人手连续力感知，但可以通过观察置钉扭矩的异常低平、或导航界面提示的轨迹偏移，来间接判断骨-螺钉界面已不足以提供有效锚定。此外，椎体骨密度在 CT 上的视觉评估也可作为辅助判断：严重骨质疏松的椎体在规划影像上呈现明显的骨小梁稀疏和皮质变薄。 第三层：骨折类型与力学环境。 在髋部，骨水泥强化的指征不仅取决于 T 值，还取决于骨折稳定性与复位质量。系统综述的结论是，骨水泥强化在骨质量差、不稳定骨折类型（如 AO 31-A2/A3）和复位不佳的高机械失败风险人群中具有明确作用。一项前瞻性研究纳入的正是 T 值 ≤ -2.5 的老年转子间骨折（AO 31-A2 和 31-A3），骨水泥强化被用于防止螺钉切出。因此，髋部骨水泥强化的触发逻辑是骨质量阈值（T ≤ -2.5）与骨折力学脆弱性（不稳定型、复位不理想）的叠加，而非单一的骨密度指标。 第四层：翻修场景中的优先级提升。 在骨质疏松骨中进行翻修时，单纯增大螺钉直径的补救效果有限，甚至可能因椎弓根崩裂而适得其反。尸体研究显示，在翻修条件下，增大螺钉直径反而降低了拔出力，而骨水泥强化螺钉在初次和翻修测试中均持续表现出更优的固定。因此，在骨质疏松患者的翻修手术中，骨水泥强化的适应证应被前置性地考虑，而非等到再次失败后才启用。 💎 从医师视角的判断框架 将上述分析收束为一个分层决策逻辑： 在脊柱，面对骨质疏松患者，机器人辅助的适应证应被表述为：该病例是否存在一条骨密度更优、但仅机器人可稳定执行的轨迹（AI 优化路径或 CBT）？ 如果存在，机器人的价值在于在不引入骨水泥的前提下，通过几何路径优化争取可接受的把持力；如果 T 值已低于 -3.0，或术中阻力提示骨-螺钉界面已无有效锚定，或规划显示所有可执行路径的预期拔出力均处于临界水平，则应将机器人定位为骨水泥强化螺钉的精确置入工具，而非骨水泥的替代方案。在 T 值 -2.5 至 -3.0 的灰区，决策取决于轨迹优化的空间和术中阻力信号，而非单一的骨密度数字。 在髋部，骨水泥强化的触发逻辑是骨质量（T ≤ -2.5）与骨折力学脆弱性（不稳定型、复位不理想）的交集。机器人辅助在髋部骨质疏松骨折中的角色，更多是辅助通道螺钉或髓内钉的精确置入，但骨水泥强化与否的核心判断，应基于骨-内植物界面能否在给定骨折力学环境下维持稳定，而非机器人精度本身。 最需要避免的误判，是将机器人精度优势与骨质量改善混为一谈。机器人可以在骨质疏松椎体内找到一条相对更好的路径，但它不能改变这条路径所经过的骨小梁本身的质量。当几何优化的极限已被触及，骨水泥强化不是对机器人技术的否定，而是对其能力边界的诚实承认。

**对已有常规关节置换经验的术者，机器人全膝置换的流程学习曲线通常以约10～30例作为参考，全髋置换约需十几至三十余例；但不存在“做满某个例数就安全过关”的统一标准。**研究多数衡量的是手术时间趋于稳定，并非罕见并发症风险已经稳定。 1．如何理解学习曲线的例数？ 术式 研究中的参考 不能忽略的前提 机器人辅助全膝置换 一项前瞻性研究在第7例后观察到手术时间转折；近期亚太专家共识概括的熟练阶段约为15～30例，依术式和术者背景而异 “7例”来自特定术者、平台及团队，术者已有传统置换经验，并接受过尸体培训 机器人辅助全髋置换 文献常报告约14～35例；一项三名术者的研究中，高病例量术者约20例出现时间改善，低、中病例量术者未观察到同样明确的转折 病例间隔、团队稳定性和原有髋关节手术经验都会影响进度 来源：全膝前瞻性研究、全髋学习曲线研究、亚太关节机器人专家共识。 这些数字不能用于证明“早期病例没有额外风险”。准确定位、软组织平衡、异常处理和手术效率，可能有不同的学习曲线。 2．新中心应如何起步？ 建议采用以下分阶段方案；这是临床实施建议，不是全国统一准入标准。 阶段 建议安排 进入下一阶段的条件 临床前准备 选择已有相应传统置换能力的术者；完成平台理论、模拟、病例观摩及尸体操作培训 能完整演示装机、配准、验证、关键操作、异常识别和常规器械接替 初始病例 由熟悉该平台、且能接管同一术式的导师现场带教；固定核心手术团队 导师确认关键步骤可靠，团队能完成异常处置 巩固阶段 连续开展适宜病例，逐例复盘；可在累计10、20、30例设置正式评估点 依据实际能力和质量结果决定继续带教或授予独立权限 扩大范围 基础病例稳定后，再逐步加入严重畸形、僵硬、发育不良或复杂翻修病例 对新增复杂情境重新评估，必要时恢复现场带教 **导师带教例数应由能力决定，不能预设“前几例有人在场就足够”。**厂家工程师可以支持设备操作，但不能替代临床导师。尸体培训也应覆盖完整流程和转换演练，而非仅完成一次截骨或磨髋臼。亚太共识支持理论、计算机模拟与尸体操作相结合，并强调传统手术能力是基础。亚太专家共识 3．如何控制早期耗时与并发症？ **先减少同时变化的因素。**初期尽量保持术者、团队、入路、假体和力线策略稳定，避免同时更换多个环节。 **选择适宜病例。**优先初次置换、暴露与活动度较好、风险可控的患者；不要把最复杂病例作为首批病例。 **排程留余量。**依据本中心实际增加的准备和配准时间安排，避免用成熟期台次压缩初期操作。 **设置安全退出规则。**配准反复失败、参考架不稳定、机械臂不可达或导航与解剖不一致时，及时转换，不能为完成机器人病例而坚持。 **同时追踪时间与结果。**记录总手术室占用、配准耗时、转换及返工、假体位置、骨折、感染、神经血管损伤和再次手术，并完成随访。少量病例“零并发症”不能证明安全性已稳定。 最终授权应由例数记录、导师评价、实际操作考核和持续质量审核共同决定。对新中心而言，20～30例可以作为重点评估窗口，但不是自动毕业线；手术时间尚未明显缩短，也不能单独判定培训失败。

From the standpoint of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the central resource-allocation problem is not “robotic or conventional” as a blanket choice. It is when and for whom robotic assistance generates a marginal clinical or economic return that justifies its fixed and variable costs. The evidence supports a selective, value-based case-selection framework rather than either universal adoption or blanket restriction. The primary gate: institutional volume, not individual case complexity The single most consistent determinant of economic viability is case volume at the institutional or platform level. A robot is largely a fixed cost; its per-case economics improve with throughput. For robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA), a middle-income-country analysis concluded that one robot must perform at least 640 TKA cases per year over 12.5 years for the technology to be economically attractive; only maximal utilization (850 cases/year) or the lowest capital-cost scenario achieved cost-effectiveness. A separate cost-effectiveness analysis found robotic-arm-assisted TKA became cost-effective once case volume exceeded 49 cases per year, a much lower threshold that reflects different assumptions about capital cost and downstream savings. A systematic review of minimum caseloads reported thresholds in the range of ≥300 cases per year for cost-effectiveness in some orthopedic robotic programs. These figures are not mutually consistent, but they point in the same direction: below a meaningful volume threshold, the fixed cost dominates and robotic assistance is difficult to justify on efficiency grounds, regardless of how well any individual case is selected. For robotic-assisted unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (rUKA), the economic case is stronger. A systematic review of Markov and clinical studies found incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) ranging from £1,238 to $47,180 per QALY, consistently below country-specific thresholds, particularly in high-volume centers. A five-year randomized cost-utility analysis reported an incremental cost per QALY of £13,078 for a unit undertaking 400 cases per year. A ten-year follow-up analysis similarly supported cost-effectiveness of robotic arm-assisted medial UKA. The mechanism is not primarily the index procedure—rUKA has higher upfront costs—but reduced revision rates and improved outcomes over time, which require volume to be realized. For robotic-assisted total hip arthroplasty (RATHA), the pattern is similar but less pronounced. A systematic review of over 1.3 million patients found that RATHA had higher procedural costs but often lower total 90-day care costs due to shorter stays, fewer readmissions, and reduced rehabilitation needs, with favorable ICERs particularly in high-volume centers. The economic case is therefore conditional on the institution’s ability to capture downstream savings, not simply on the robot’s technical performance. The practical implication is that the first case-selection decision is made at the program level, not the patient level. A low-volume center cannot select its way to cost-effectiveness by concentrating on complex cases; the fixed-cost burden per case remains too high. The defensible starting condition is a credible volume projection—whether through a high-volume arthroplasty practice, shared use across services, or a regional referral model—before robotic acquisition is considered. The second gate: selecting patients for whom the marginal clinical return is plausible Once a volume threshold is met, selection should target patients in whom robotic assistance has a plausible mechanism for improving outcome or reducing costly failure, rather than applying it indiscriminately. In arthroplasty, complexity is the relevant stratifier—not the mere diagnosis of osteoarthritis. A Bayesian decision-tree model designed specifically to prioritize RA-TKA under constrained resources identified coronal deformity ≥ 10° and BMI > 35 as the most influential patient variables, with the posterior probability of benefit ranging from 14.6% to 89.2% depending on complexity and access. This is a useful operationalization: the robot’s value is highest where conventional execution is least reliable—severe coronal deformity, distorted anatomy, prior surgery, or marked obesity—because that is where the precision and planning advantages are most likely to change the clinical trajectory. NICE’s early value assessment similarly noted that older, higher-BMI, multimorbid patients and those with anatomy that makes conventional implantation difficult may benefit most, although it also recognized that complex cases are often performed in lower-volume centers that may not have access to the technology. For UKA, selection is more straightforward: patients with isolated medial compartment osteoarthritis are the population in which rUKA has demonstrated both clinical and economic advantages. Expanding rUKA to patients who would otherwise receive TKA is not a resource-efficient use; the value proposition is specifically in the UKA indication. In spine surgery, the relevant stratifier is surgical complexity and the cost of failure. A meta-analysis of lumbar fusion found robot-assisted placement saved $4,086–$4,865 per patient versus navigation and $7,317–$9,654 versus freehand, driven by reduced hospital stays, fewer revisions, and shorter surgical time. The savings became more significant in patients with more severe complications and in more complex surgical segments.
