This supports prioritizing robotic assistance for multi-level fusions, deformity corrections, revision settings, and cases where screw malposition would carry high clinical and financial consequences—rather than for straightforward single-level procedures in which freehand or navigation may already be adequate. In trauma, selection should target fractures in which the robot’s corridor-screw precision addresses a specific failure mode. For Tile C pelvic fractures, a multicenter study found robotic-assisted navigation with patient-specific implants was most cost-effective in normal-weight, non-osteoporotic patients, while remaining clinically valuable in high-risk subgroups. This illustrates a nuanced selection principle: economic efficiency and clinical necessity may point to different patients. The robot may be most efficient in the straightforward anatomy, but most necessary in the complex or osteoporotic patient in whom conventional precision is inadequate. A resource-allocation policy must decide explicitly which objective it is prioritizing. The third gate: organizational and platform factors that determine whether selection translates into efficiency Case selection cannot compensate for a poorly organized program. The economic literature is consistent that workflow optimization and team integration are not optional refinements—they are determinants of whether robotic surgery achieves per-case cost parity or advantage. High-throughput environments with efficient scheduling, dedicated teams, and optimized turnover achieve reduced per-case costs, while early adopters with steep learning curves and unoptimized workflows incur higher costs that persist longer. A specific organizational lever is case clustering. Scheduling robotic cases sequentially on the same list amortizes setup and breakdown across multiple procedures; when sequencing and team familiarity are optimized, robotic arthroplasty can match or exceed manual throughput. Conversely, a program that scatters robotic cases across the schedule cannot capture this amortization and will show persistently higher per-case costs even if individual case selection is sound. Platform choice also matters for resource efficiency. A cost-effectiveness analysis of computer-assisted versus robotic versus manual THA found computer-assisted THA was the most cost-effective technique in the US setting, with savings of $1,595 versus robotic THA and $949 versus manual THA. This does not mean robotics is always inferior, but it does mean that within a constrained budget, the comparison is not only robotic versus manual—it is robotic versus other enabling technologies, and the marginal benefit of robotics over navigation must be explicitly justified for the selected case mix. A defensible selection algorithm From a practicing surgeon’s perspective, a resource-efficient selection framework can be summarized in four sequential questions: Does the program have the volume to amortize the fixed cost? If not, robotic acquisition is difficult to justify on efficiency grounds, and shared or regional models should be considered before patient-level selection. Does the patient fall into a phenotype in which robotic assistance has a plausible mechanism for improving outcome or reducing costly failure? In arthroplasty: severe deformity, distorted anatomy, high BMI, or isolated medial compartment OA suitable for UKA. In spine: multi-level, deformity, revision, or high-consequence screw placement. In trauma: fracture patterns in which corridor-screw precision addresses the dominant failure mode. Is the robot being used where a cheaper enabling technology would achieve the same marginal benefit? Navigation may be sufficient for many spinal and trauma indications; robotics should be reserved for cases in which its additional capabilities are expected to change the clinical or economic outcome. Is the workflow organized to capture the downstream savings? Without efficient scheduling, case clustering, and team integration, the projected reductions in length of stay and revisions may not be realized, and the economic case for the selected cases collapses. The honest limitation is that these criteria remain probabilistic and context-dependent. The Bayesian model that would allow formal prioritization is still theoretical and awaits institutional validation. The volume thresholds reported in the literature vary widely because they depend on capital cost, reimbursement structure, and assumptions about downstream savings. A resource-allocation policy should therefore treat robotic case selection as an institution-specific optimization problem, not a fixed list of diagnoses, and should build in audit of whether the selected cases are actually delivering the projected clinical and economic returns.

界定机器人辅助脊柱手术的适应证与禁忌证，关键不在于给疾病诊断本身贴上“能做”或“不能做”的标签，而在于区分两个层面：禁忌证主要由“机器人技术前提是否能够被满足”来界定，而非由疾病本身的严重程度来界定；适应证则取决于该病例的核心手术难点，是否恰好落在机器人“在解剖标志不可靠时重建几何路径”的能力射程之内。 你列举的五种情形，恰好分布在这一判断框架的不同位置上。 先确立共同的技术前提禁忌 2024年版《中国机器人辅助胸腰椎手术指南》将禁忌证明确限定为两条：全身性疾病无法耐受机器人辅助手术，以及患者追踪器安放位置无法满足要求，或无法获得满足导航要求的图像。颈椎翻修相关的文献进一步将脊柱严重畸形或结构异常、无法满足手术体位要求、影像学资料不完整列为禁忌。 这一界定的意义在于：它把“禁忌”从对疾病严重程度的判断，转移到了对配准与追踪可行性的判断上。一个Cobb角90°的重度侧凸，如果参考架能够稳定安置、导航图像能够可靠获得，它在技术上就并非禁忌；反之，一个影像条件良好的轻度病例，如果因体位或肥胖导致追踪失效，它反而构成禁忌。机器人手术的禁忌证是“技术条件的禁忌”，而非“病理形态的禁忌”。 重度脊柱侧凸：适应证明确，但“适应证”不等于“精度不受影响” 机器人辅助在重度脊柱侧凸中被列为适应证，这一点在指南层面是清晰的（脊柱畸形项下包含“脊柱侧凸”）。但“列为适应证”与“精度不受解剖复杂度侵蚀”是两个不同的问题。 一项2025年的对照研究提供了关键的分层数据：在平均Cobb角93.69°的严重复杂畸形组中，机器人辅助的完美置钉率仍达到90.60%，与非严重畸形组的92.18%无统计学显著差异；两组的临床可接受置钉率（A+B级）均超过95%，显著优于传统技术下Cobb角>90°时仅60%–80%的可接受率。这证实了机器人在重度畸形中仍能维持可用的精度基线。 但同一研究也划出了一条清晰的边界：当椎弓根直径小于1 mm时，即便有机器人辅助，穿破率仍可高达22.2%。另一项针对Lenke 1A型青少年特发性脊柱侧凸的研究则揭示了另一个被低估的误差来源：术中脊柱震动及椎体旋转本身就会影响机器人的置钉精度，凹侧置钉优良率在未校准条件下仅为88.16%，而术中简易校准可将总体优良率从92.18%提升至97.60%。这意味着，重度侧凸的机器人适应证是成立的，但它是一个需要附加条件来兑现的适应证：极窄椎弓根需要术前规划阶段就判断通道是否具有可执行性，而旋转和震动带来的配准漂移需要术中校准或神经监测来兜底。适应证本身不排除重度侧凸，但重度侧凸中的极端解剖亚型（椎弓根<1 mm）和未被管理的术中漂移，构成了事实上的相对边界。 重度椎体滑脱：适应证覆盖“滑脱”，但机器人的作用靶点在“置钉”而非“复位” 指南将“先天性重度腰椎滑脱”明确列入脊柱畸形适应证，但这并不意味着机器人解决的是重度滑脱的全部核心难题。重度滑脱（Meyerding Ⅲ度及以上，或滑脱>50%）的手术核心挑战，在于复位所需的力学策略和软组织松解，而非单纯的螺钉轨迹精度。文献明确指出，对于滑脱程度>50%的重度椎体滑脱，主流治疗仍以常规切口、椎管减压、神经根松解、椎弓根螺钉固定配合椎间植骨融合为主，以对滑脱椎体进行复位固定。机器人所贡献的，是在这一复杂重建过程中提供更可靠的置钉通道：术前规划可以根据椎弓根的走行和大小确定最佳的进钉点、轨迹、直径和长度，从而增强螺钉把持力，利于术中椎体复位，降低拔钉风险。 因此，对于重度滑脱，机器人是一个有价值的辅助工具，而非复位难题的解决方案。它的适应证定位应是：在该病例需要进行椎弓根螺钉固定的前提下，机器人用于提升置钉的几何可靠性，从而为后续的复位和融合提供更稳固的锚定基础。如果术者期待机器人本身来简化复位操作或降低滑脱复位的技术难度，那是对其能力边界的误判。真正的相对禁忌不在“滑脱度数”本身，而在于骨质疏松严重到螺钉把持力无法通过轨迹优化来代偿，或解剖条件使规划通道本身不可执行。 椎弓根发育不良：机器人价值最直接、证据最一致的场景 在五种情形中，椎弓根发育不良是机器人优势逻辑最清晰、临床共识最一致的一个。儿童脊柱外科的专家笔谈明确指出，手术机器人通过术前规划螺钉路径，尤其适用于椎弓根发育异常或椎体位置异常的患者。其机制是直接的：发育不良的椎弓根本身就是一个几何通道极其狭窄、且骨性标志无法可靠提示通道走向的结构，徒手置钉的精度冗余已被解剖条件压缩至极限。临床报告描述了一个典型情形：患者合并椎弓根和椎体发育畸形，常规透视辅助下“很难精确通过极其狭窄的椎弓根，如有毫米偏差，很容易伤及脊髓和神经根”，而机器人系统提供了可行的路径执行能力。 在这一场景中，机器人的适应证边界与禁忌证边界几乎重合于同一条线：如果发育不良的椎弓根仍存在一条可被规划的安全骨性通道，机器人就是首选工具；如果通道本身已不存在（完全闭锁或直径不足以容纳任何有临床意义的螺钉），那么机器人精确执行一条不存在的通道并无意义，此时应考虑节段融合方式的改变（如跳过该节段、改用椎弓根外固定点），而非执着于置钉。这与前述“极窄椎弓根<1 mm时穿破率仍高”的证据相互印证：机器人扩大的是“可执行通道”的下限，但它不能创造通道。 骨质疏松：机器人改变的是“置钉几何”，而非“骨-螺钉界面生物学” 这是五种情形中最需要澄清定位的一个。骨质疏松的核心问题是骨-螺钉界面的把持力下降，文献报道骨质疏松患者中螺钉松动率可超过50%。机器人本身并不改变骨密度，也不直接增强界面生物学固定。它的作用是在这一薄弱界面上，通过优化几何参数来尽可能保留把持力。 证据支持这一判断，但需要精确表述。一项针对低骨量患者的 multicenter 研究显示，AI规划联合机器人引导提高了A级置钉比例，并降低了螺钉松动率。在骨质疏松性腰椎滑脱中，机器人辅助放置更长、更大直径的双螺纹螺钉，达到了与骨水泥强化螺钉相似的固定效果，同时手术时间更短、辐射更少、后期翻修难度更低。生物力学研究也显示，机器人辅助置钉的Grade A准确率更高（87.3% vs. 75.0%），上位关节突侵犯率更低（9.9% vs. 34.1%），这间接减少了因轨迹偏差导致的初期稳定性丧失。 但必须指出其边界：机器人优化的是螺钉在骨内的几何路径和位置，它不能替代骨水泥强化、可扩张螺钉或皮质骨轨迹螺钉等针对骨质量的固定增强策略。在严重骨质疏松中，机器人辅助置钉的松动率改善是“在薄弱基础上做得更好”，而非“消除了薄弱基础”。机器人不能被视为骨质疏松条件下固定失败风险的独立解决方案；它的合理定位是与其他固定增强技术协同使用，或在骨质量处于临界水平、尚未达到必须骨水泥强化的程度时，通过几何优化来争取更好的初期稳定性。 合并内植物的翻修手术：证据支持“替代性安全通道”，但规划可行性是前提 翻修手术是五种情形中机器人获益机制最独特的一个。正常解剖标志已被瘢痕和既往内置物破坏，松动或断裂的螺钉留下的钉道、原位骨水泥，使“沿原有路径重新置钉”或“在邻近区域寻找新路径”都面临不确定性。一项2025年的前瞻性研究专门评估了这一场景：64例翻修患者、388枚螺钉，机器人辅助置钉的位置不良仅2枚（0.5%），且无临床后果，术中无并发症。该研究的结论精确地描述了机器人的角色：它为翻修手术中“松动/断裂的内置物或骨水泥周围”提供了替代性的安全骨性通道。 这一定位的关键在于，机器人不是“把标准螺钉放得更准”，而是在原有安全通道已被占据或破坏的条件下，基于术前影像重新计算出一条可行的新路径。但这也同时划定了它的前提条件：这条新路径必须在影像上可被识别、在规划中可被避开金属伪影和骨水泥团块、在机械臂工作空间内可被抵达。如果翻修区域被大块骨水泥或金属完全遮蔽，以至于规划系统无法识别出任何可用的骨性走廊，那么机器人所依赖的“重新计算”便失去了输入基础。因此，翻修手术的机器人适应证应被界定为：在术前影像规划阶段能够识别出一条避开原有内植物/骨水泥的可执行通道的病例；术前CT三维重建评估椎弓根完整性和通道可行性，是这一判断的必经步骤。 综合权衡：一条以“核心难点是否被机器人射程覆盖”为轴的分层逻辑 将上述分析收束为可操作的判断框架： 第一层，技术前提筛查（适用于全部五种情形）。 确认追踪器安置、导航图像获取、体位要求能够被满足。这是2024年指南所界定的禁忌证核心，也是所有后续判断的前提。任何情形在这一层被否决，即构成该次手术的机器人禁忌，转为传统技术。 第二层，核心难点匹配。 在通过第一层后，追问该病例的核心手术难点是什么： 如果难点是“在解剖标志不可靠时重建一条可执行的几何通道”（椎弓根发育不良、翻修手术、重度侧凸中的置钉环节），机器人的精度优势有明确的转化路径，属于优势适应证。 如果难点包含机器人无法直接解决的结构性或生物学问题（重度滑脱的复位力学、骨质疏松的界面把持力、极窄椎弓根的通道不存在），机器人是辅助工具而非解决方案，其适应证应被限定为“在完成该病例必要操作（复位、固定增强、通道替代方案）的前提下，用于提升置钉环节的几何可靠性”。 第三层，情形内部的相对边界。 每一种情形内部都存在一个“机器人仍可执行、但精度优势开始递减或需要附加条件”的亚型边界：重度侧凸中的椎弓根<1 mm和未被管理的术中旋转/震动；重度滑脱中骨质量差到几何优化无法代偿；骨质疏松中需要骨水泥强化而非单纯轨迹优化的严重程度；翻修中规划系统无法识别出可用骨性走廊的金属/骨水泥遮蔽程度。这些边界不构成疾病层面的绝对禁忌，但它们要求术者在术前规划阶段主动识别，并在必要时将机器人定位为辅助角色或转为传统技术，而非假定精度优势会在任何解剖条件下自动兑现。

作为一名执业骨科医师，在评估一项技术时，我习惯将其放回具体的解剖与操作场景中去审视。针对你提出的问题，我需要先澄清一个前提：在脊柱与关节的骨性结构核心操作（如椎弓根螺钉置入、截骨、假体安放）中，常规腔镜并非主流的对照技术。腔镜的优势主要体现在软组织间隙的观察与操作（如椎间孔镜、关节镜），而当操作对象是骨性结构、且需要恢复力线与稳定性时，传统上依赖的是开放直视下的解剖标志辨识与C臂透视的二维间接反馈。因此，以下的讨论将主要聚焦于骨科机器人与传统开放/透视引导手术的对比，并在涉及软组织视野时，附带说明其与腔镜逻辑的本质差异。 精准度：从“经验校正”到“计划-执行”的闭环 传统骨科手术的精准度，在很大程度上依赖于术者对二维影像的空间想象能力和手上的“手感”校正。即使经验丰富的脊柱外科医生，徒手或透视辅助下的椎弓根螺钉误置率仍可达到一个不可忽视的水平，皮质穿破的风险始终存在。机器人带来的核心改变，是将精准度的实现方式从“术中反复试探与校正”转变为 “术前或术中三维规划—机械臂刚性执行”的闭环。 在脊柱区域，这种转变的量化体现尤为清晰。一项前瞻性随机对照试验纳入1116枚胸腰椎螺钉，机器人组A级（完美置入）螺钉比例为95.3%，而传统透视组为86.1%；机器人组实际钉道与计划轨迹的平均偏差仅为（1.5±0.8）mm，且无螺钉因误置而翻修。另一项2024年的倾向性评分匹配研究同样证实，机器人组的置钉准确率显著优于徒手开放和C臂引导下的微创技术。这种优势在复杂脊柱畸形中具有特殊价值：当严重侧弯或后凸导致解剖标志完全扭曲时，传统方法赖以定位的“正常解剖关系”不复存在，而机器人基于三维影像规划出的钉道，可以在 distorted anatomy 中提供一条不依赖于肉眼辨识的、可重复的安全通道。 在关节区域，精准度的焦点则从“钉道”转向力线与假体空间位置。传统全膝关节置换中，术者的肉眼判断和器械误差可能导致下肢机械轴线的偏离。机器人辅助系统（如ROSA）的研究显示，术后髋-膝-踝角（HKA）在机器人组为（179.25±2.50）°，传统组为（177.68±2.73）°，机器人组更接近理想的中立位；冠状面股骨组件角也更接近目标值。综述证据进一步指出，机器人辅助TKA的假体对位误差可稳定控制在1°以内，这对于减少因力线不良导致的早期磨损和远期松动具有明确的影像学意义。在复杂关节翻修场景中，骨缺损和金属伪影使传统定位更加困难，而机器人结合三维建模可实现亚毫米级（如0.38 mm）的配准精度，髋臼假体植入角度与计划值的偏差可控制在1°左右。 视野优势：从“二维间接”与“有限直视”到“三维数字空间” 传统骨科手术的“视野困境”是双重的。开放手术虽然提供了直视条件，但在深部脊柱或翻修关节中，肉眼对椎弓根内侧壁、脊髓、神经根或骨缺损三维形态的直接观察仍然是有限的；而C臂透视提供的二维投影，需要术者在脑中完成三维重建，这种间接性在解剖变异或复杂畸形中会显著放大认知负荷与操作风险。常规腔镜虽然能将视野延伸至体腔内并提供放大图像，但其在骨性结构操作中的局限在于：它擅长观察软组织表面，却无法“看穿”骨质内部以规划一条穿过骨性通道的轨迹。 骨科机器人的视野优势，本质上是用数字化的三维空间信息来替代或补充肉眼与二维透视的不足。其核心并非简单地在术野中增加一个摄像头，而是构建了一个可与机械臂共享的、具有空间坐标的手术规划域。在脊柱手术中，机器人系统整合术中三维影像（如O臂或3D C臂），将骨骼的立体形态、规划钉道与机械臂的实时位置统一在同一个坐标系下，术者在屏幕上看到的不是一个平面的透视影像，而是一个可以旋转、缩放、逐层观察的三维数字解剖模型，规划路径与毗邻结构（椎弓根皮质、椎体前缘、关节突）的关系一目了然。这种视野模式使得经皮微创置钉不再依赖于“盲穿”式的反复透视确认，而是在进入人体之前，路径的安全性已经在三维空间中得到了验证。 在关节置换中，这一逻辑体现为三维手术规划与术中实时追踪的结合。传统TKA的截骨与软组织平衡高度依赖术中的机械导向器和术者手感，而机器人系统将术前的下肢力线参数和假体目标位置转化为三维空间中的虚拟边界，机械臂在术中实时受控于这一边界，术者因此获得了一种超越肉眼直视的“空间约束视野”——能够“感知”截骨平面是否偏离了计划的角度。在翻修手术中，面对失去正常解剖标志的关节，这种基于配准的三维视野更是成为定位新假体旋转中心与骨缺损边界的核心依据。 需要向患者坦诚说明的边界 在肯定上述优势的同时，我必须指出当前证据的边界。机器人带来的精准度提升，在多数研究中首先体现为影像学分级和轨迹偏差的改善，而这种影像学优势转化为临床结局（如翻修率、长期功能评分）的显著差异，在现有随访周期内尚未得到一致证实。此外，精准度的获益需要与手术时间延长和显著的成本增加进行权衡，后者是目前限制其广泛常规应用的重要现实因素。因此，在我的临床决策中，机器人并非取代传统技术的“更优解”，而是在特定复杂场景下——如严重脊柱畸形、解剖标志丧失的翻修、对置入精度有苛刻要求的病例——提供一种将不可控的经验误差转化为可计划、可验证的工程精度的工具。

For an experienced arthroplasty surgeon, a reasonable planning allowance is approximately 10–30 robotic TKA cases and 15–35 robotic THA cases to improve operative efficiency. These are working ranges, not certification thresholds. Some teams learn faster; others require substantially more cases. Crucially, a plateau in operating time does not establish competence or safety. Registration, implant positioning, troubleshooting, and the ability to complete surgery conventionally must also be assessed. Procedure Evidence and interpretation Robotic TKA One experienced team reported workflow integration after 7 cases, whereas another platform-specific study identified 20 cases. Implant-positioning accuracy was maintained during the learning phase in those studies. Neither finding guarantees that every new programme will have the same experience. Robotic THA A study of 299 procedures found an approximately 20-case efficiency learning curve for the high-volume surgeon. The lower-volume surgeons did not demonstrate the same clear improvement within the observed series. Sources: Seven-case TKA study, 20-case TKA study, THA volume study. For a new programme, I would recommend the following structure. These are practical recommendations, rather than validated numerical requirements: Train the whole team before clinical launch. Complete platform-specific education, observe experienced users, and rehearse positioning, registration, tracker placement, instrument access, and conversion. Cadaver-based training is particularly useful for exposure and access problems; simulation and dry labs support repeated workflow practice. Existing proficiency in conventional arthroplasty remains essential. Arthroplasty expert consensus Use an experienced, procedure-specific surgeon proctor for initial cases. Continue supervision until performance is consistently satisfactory, including troubleshooting. Manufacturer technical support is valuable but does not replace clinical supervision. Begin with straightforward primary cases. Initially avoid combining robotic adoption with severe deformity, ankylosis, complex hardware removal, revision surgery, or an unfamiliar surgical approach. Keep the operating team and implant workflow consistent. Allow extra theatre time and concentrate experience. Reduce initial list pressure and schedule cases regularly with a small core team. There is no universally validated minimum annual robotic case volume. Published “high-volume” categories should not be treated as credentialing standards. Advance according to audited performance. Review operative and anaesthetic time, registration failures, conversions, positioning accuracy, tracker-related injuries, infection, instability, and early reoperation against the programme’s conventional results. Investigate unexpected injuries or repeated technical failures before expanding complexity. The safest threshold is demonstrated competence, not case count alone. Early studies reporting preserved accuracy or similar complications are reassuring, but generally cannot exclude increases in rare complications. A new programme should therefore earn greater independence and case complexity through observed performance and ongoing outcome review.

从骨科临床应急处置角度看，**已有可执行的机械臂撤离与转常规手术方案，但不能笼统地说，所有医院面对血管、神经损伤时的衔接都已同样成熟。**设备能否撤开、团队能否迅速控制损伤，是两个不同层面的问题。 1．设备层面的转换已有基础，但必须遵循具体机型流程。 例如，ROSA部分膝关节机器人使用手册列有紧急移开机械臂或撤离设备的程序，并要求备有配套常规手术器械，以便机器人无法使用时继续手术。这说明转换应当是术前准备的一部分。厂家使用手册 但急停不等于机械臂已经安全脱离患者。器械是否仍在骨内、导向套筒是否连接、机械臂如何解锁，都需按设备要求处理，不能直接强行移动。 2．多数骨科场景中，转换是“撤开辅助设备、恢复常规操作”，未必需要重新建立整个术野。 关节置换本身通常已有开放切口；不少脊柱机器人主要提供置钉导向，医生也在患者旁操作。因此，其转换方式与腹腔机器人撤机不同。 不过，经皮脊柱或骨盆手术一旦发生深部血管损伤，小切口可能无法完成止血，仍可能需要扩大暴露、改变入路，甚至由血管外科实施开放或介入治疗。撤机顺利并不代表抢救已经完成。 3．成熟的衔接方案应覆盖以下环节。 **立即识别并停止致伤动作：**暂停钻孔、截骨或推进，明确宣布进入应急处置。 **同步开展抢救与撤机：**由指定人员按机型流程处理机械臂，主刀和麻醉团队同时评估损伤、循环状态及救治需求，避免所有人都集中于设备。 **谨慎处理可疑致伤器械：**怀疑器械穿透血管时，不能未经判断就拔除；是否暂时保留，应结合其是否具有压迫作用及后续止血方案决定。 **迅速获得必要暴露和专科支持：**提前准备常规器械、止血与输血资源，并明确血管外科、神经外科或介入团队的响应路径。骨与血管联合损伤指南强调，需要具备出血控制、血管重建及骨创伤能力的团队协作。英国骨科协会标准 **对神经异常先查原因：**神经监测报警并不等于已经发生结构性损伤，应同步排查麻醉、血压、监测技术及机械性压迫等原因，再决定是否需要调整内植物或探查减压。 **判断一家医院的方案是否成熟，关键是有无针对该机型的书面预案、明确分工、常规器械备份，以及经过演练的紧急响应。**不能仅凭“可以随时转徒手”这一表述判断安全性。 目前我没有足够的骨科专门证据，支持给出统一的“多少秒完成转换”或急症转换成功率。更准确的结论是：技术上通常能够转换，实际救治是否及时可靠，取决于具体设备、术式、损伤部位和团队准备程度。

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the comparison in percutaneous sacroiliac (SI) and pelvic ring screw fixation yields a clear hierarchy of evidence. The reduction in fluoroscopy time is the most consistent and largest benefit; the improvement in safe-corridor accuracy is robust but its magnitude varies; and the reduction in neurovascular complications is mechanistically plausible and supported by low rates, but direct comparative evidence remains thin. Fluoroscopy Time: The Most Consistent and Quantifiable Advantage This is the endpoint where the evidence is least ambiguous. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies (642 patients in the 2D fluoroscopy group, 663 in the new navigation group) found that navigation techniques—including robotic—reduced fluoroscopy time by a mean difference of 71.89 seconds (95% CI 51.37–92.41) and reduced fluoroscopy frequency by 17.22 images per procedure (95% CI 7.73–26.70) compared with conventional 2D fluoroscopy. A 2026 meta-analysis of 15 studies (1,247 patients, 2,893 screws) similarly reported a standardized mean difference of −1.84 (95% CI −2.43 to −1.25) favoring robotic assistance for radiation exposure, although this was graded as low-certainty evidence due to inconsistency. Individual comparative studies illustrate the potential magnitude. A 2026 retrospective study reported fluoroscopy time of 55.1 ± 23.1 seconds in the robotic group versus 181.1 ± 104.4 seconds in the fluoroscopy group (p = 0.053)—a difference that did not reach conventional statistical significance in this small sample (25 patients) but is clinically substantial and consistent with the pooled estimates. An earlier TiRobot meta-analysis confirmed significantly less radiation exposure time and fewer fluoroscopic images compared with conventional fluoroscopy. The clinical implication is straightforward: this is a benefit that accrues to both the patient and the entire surgical team, and it is the most reliably reproduced advantage of robotic guidance in this anatomical region. Safe-Corridor Accuracy: A Real Advantage, With Magnitude Dependent on Context The accuracy advantage of robotic guidance over conventional fluoroscopy is statistically robust, but the effect size reported in the literature depends heavily on the comparison made and the anatomical complexity of the screws. The 2025 meta-analysis provides the broadest estimate: accuracy was 82% in the 2D fluoroscopy group versus 92% in the new navigation group (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.53–3.90), with the authors noting that O-arm, 3D CT, and robotic navigation appeared to be even better among the navigated techniques. The 2026 meta-analysis of pelvic channel screws reported a larger apparent effect—excellent/good accuracy of 98.2% with robotics versus 86.4% with fluoroscopy (OR 5.32, 95% CI 3.18–8.89)—but graded this as low-certainty evidence due to risk of bias. The 2026 retrospective study illustrates the variability in study-level estimates: 94% accuracy with robotics versus 62% with fluoroscopy (p = 0.06), a large absolute difference that did not reach significance in a small cohort. A 2022 TiRobot meta-analysis found a statistically significant accuracy advantage (P = 0.011) alongside fewer guide-wire attempts and less intraoperative blood loss. The pattern that emerges is that the accuracy advantage is most defensible as a reduction in severe, clinically consequential breaches rather than in all breaches equally. A 2020 review specifically examining S2 sacroiliac screws—a more demanding corridor than S1—found no screw breaches in the robotic group, compared with breaches in freehand S1 and S2 groups, suggesting the benefit may be amplified in the more complex upper sacral segments. For S2AI screws specifically, robotic series report no intraoperative neurologic, vascular, or visceral complications, with accuracy rates in the 93.8%–97.9% range and only rare moderate breaches. Neurovascular Complications: Low Absolute Rates, Indirect Comparative Evidence This is the endpoint with the weakest direct comparative evidence. The honest position is that robotic guidance is associated with very low neurovascular complication rates, and the mechanism by which it should reduce these complications is sound, but studies have not been adequately powered or designed to demonstrate a statistically significant difference in neurovascular complication rates specifically. The 2025 meta-analysis concluded that complications were “acceptably low” but “poorly reported in both groups” . The 2026 retrospective study stated explicitly that “no major intraoperative complications occurred” in either group. The 2026 pelvic channel screw meta-analysis did find a significant reduction in overall complications (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.30–0.71), but this is a composite endpoint that includes non-neurological complications, and the evidence was graded as low certainty. The mechanistic argument is that more accurate screw placement—specifically the reduction or elimination of severe cortical breaches—translates into fewer opportunities for neurovascular injury. A review of 3D navigation in iliosacral screw placement notes that reported screw malposition rates with conventional techniques can reach 24%, with neurological complications in up to 18% of cases, and concludes that 3D navigation offers superior accuracy and significantly reduces the risk of neurovascular complications. For robotic S2AI screws, multiple series report zero neurologic complications despite the proximity of the lumbosacral plexus and iliac vessels. But these are single-arm observations, not head-to-head comparisons with sufficient event rates to detect a difference. The accurate formulation is therefore: robotic guidance provides a more reliable technical foundation for avoiding neurovascular injury by reducing the severe misplacements that create the anatomical substrate for such injury, but the direct evidence that it reduces the clinical rate of neurovascular complications compared with fluoroscopy is inferential rather than established by adequately powered comparative studies. A Surgeon's Synthesis In percutaneous SI and pelvic ring screw fixation, the value proposition of robotic navigation relative to conventional fluoroscopy is ordered as follows: Fluoroscopy time and radiation exposure: the strongest and most reproducible benefit, with pooled reductions of approximately 72 seconds and 17 images per case, and individual studies suggesting reductions of 60%–70% in selected settings. Safe-corridor accuracy: a clear but context-dependent advantage, with pooled accuracy improving from roughly 82%–86% to 92%–98%, and the greatest clinical relevance in the more demanding S2 corridor and in reducing severe breaches. Neurovascular complications: low absolute rates with a sound mechanistic rationale, but the comparative evidence remains indirect and underpowered. Robotic series consistently report zero or near-zero neurovascular events, but no adequately sized comparative study has demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in these events specifically. The caveat that must accompany this assessment is that the evidence base is dominated by observational studies, with low GRADE certainty for several pooled estimates and a recognized need for higher-quality prospective or randomized comparisons. The advantage is real and clinically meaningful, but it is best characterized as a shift toward a more controlled and verifiable workflow rather than as a proven reduction in the most feared complication.

The best candidates are fractures that already warrant percutaneous screw fixation, can be adequately reduced and held stable, and have a narrow or difficult screw corridor. Robotic guidance helps execute fixation; it does not replace fracture reduction or determine the appropriate implant. Fracture pattern When robotic assistance is most useful Main qualification Sacroiliac disruptions and selected sacral fractures Guiding iliosacral or transsacral screws through narrow corridors, particularly when fluoroscopic interpretation is difficult. This is among the better-supported trauma applications. Reduction must be maintained, and imaging must confirm an adequate bony corridor. Some unstable patterns require additional fixation. Anterior or posterior acetabular column fractures Nondisplaced/minimally displaced fractures requiring fixation, or fractures amenable to satisfactory closed or limited open reduction. Long column-screw trajectories are technically demanding. Displaced articular fragments, marginal impaction, or instability requiring direct reconstruction may make percutaneous screws alone inappropriate. Selected pubic ramus and other pelvic ring fractures Accurate placement of long screws where adequate bone corridors exist. The construct must address the overall pelvic instability; accurately placed screws may still provide insufficient fixation. Femoral neck fractures selected for head-preserving fixation Reproducing planned screw spread, parallelism, and depth, with fewer guidewire adjustments. Reduction quality and implant choice remain decisive. Robotics should not encourage cannulated-screw fixation when arthroplasty or a different fixation construct is preferable. Pelvic and acetabular procedural guidance specifically emphasizes minimal displacement or satisfactory closed/limited open reduction. A randomized sacroiliac study supports improved placement and less fluoroscopy. Femoral neck comparative evidence also supports technical accuracy, although reliable patient-important superiority remains uncertain. Pelvic/acetabular guidance, sacroiliac trial, femoral neck comparative study Robotics may be unnecessary when fixation is straightforward with conventional imaging, when nonoperative treatment is appropriate, or when its setup and cost add little practical benefit. Robot-guided percutaneous fixation is unsuitable when reduction is unacceptable or cannot be maintained, no safe corridor exists, the planned screws cannot provide sufficient stability, or imaging, registration, tracking, or arm access is unreliable. Fracture movement after registration requires reassessment before proceeding. These technical contraindications are also identified in pelvic robotic guidance. Procedural guidance In unstable polytrauma, robotic setup should not delay resuscitation or urgent stabilization. An open injury requiring debridement or a fracture requiring open reduction does not automatically prohibit adjunctive robotic guidance, but it changes the operative priorities and may eliminate the advantage of a percutaneous approach.

As a practicing orthopedic surgeon, I would frame the advantage of orthopedic surgical robots not as a simple “better tool,” but as a shift from surgery that depends heavily on the surgeon’s visual judgment and manual steadiness to a patient-specific, planable, executable, and verifiable process. This matters most in the spine, complex joints, and revision/deformity cases where the margin for error is small. I should note that the evidence is heterogeneous across robotic platforms, surgeons, case selection, and outcome definitions; I cannot claim a uniform advantage for every system or every indication. 1. Precision: from “experienced hand-eye judgment” to sub-millimeter deterministic execution In conventional open or arthroscopic surgery, precision depends on direct visualization, fluoroscopic judgment, hand stability, and spatial imagination. Physiological tremor and subjective estimation cannot be eliminated. A robot does not make the surgeon omniscient, but it can replace or augment human uncertainty with mechanical determinism. Spine: In pedicle screw placement, the robot plans a trajectory from preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging and executes it under navigation tracking. Reported accuracy is often in the sub-millimeter range, with screw accuracy frequently cited at 96–99%+ depending on the system and grading criteria. A systematic review has reported that robot-assisted screws were about 2.24 times more likely to be accurately placed than freehand technique. The clinical value is not just “better screws” but reduced risk of medial wall breach, spinal canal violation, and neurovascular injury. The mechanical arm also eliminates physiological tremor and reproduces the planned trajectory more consistently than freehand or fluoroscopy-assisted methods. Joint replacement: The precision advantage is mainly in repeatable execution of bone cuts and component alignment. Conventional surgery relies on extramedullary/intramedullary guides and visual estimation, with a recognized rate of alignment outliers. Robotic-assisted systems can keep resection angles and component position within predefined ranges, reducing alignment variability and outliers. This provides a more reliable mechanical basis for implant function and potentially long-term survivorship. However, I would be clear: this precision advantage is largely at the execution level. It does not by itself guarantee that the surgical strategy—fusion levels, deformity correction strategy, soft-tissue balance, etc.—is optimal. The robot executes the surgeon’s plan; it does not replace surgical judgment. Also, although accuracy is improved, some studies do not show significant differences in long-term pain, function, or patient-reported outcomes. Precision is important, but it is not the only determinant of outcome. 2. Visualization: from “looking through a keyhole” to “data-driven 3D navigation” Conventional open surgery offers direct visualization but limited global views of deep structures through a small exposure. Conventional arthroscopy is minimally invasive but relies on 2D images, sacrifices depth perception, and has a restricted field of view. Robotic/navigation systems change the visualization paradigm fundamentally. Patient-specific 3D reconstruction: Preoperative CT or intraoperative 3D imaging is used to build a 3D model of the patient’s bone. The surgeon can rotate, inspect, and plan from any angle before making a cut or placing a screw. This is effectively a patient-specific “3D map” that allows planning of safe corridors around nerves, vessels, and the spinal canal—rather than relying on momentary 2D fluoroscopic images and mental spatial reconstruction. Real-time tracked navigation: During surgery, the system tracks instruments relative to the patient’s anatomy and displays their position in real time. Through a small incision, the surgeon can maintain a clear spatial understanding of the instrument tip relative to deep critical structures. This provides something closer to the “direct vision” of open surgery without extensive dissection, and it compensates for the limited depth perception and narrow working space of conventional arthroscopy. In complex intra-articular or spinal work, this can improve confidence and safety during exposure-limited procedures. Reduced fluoroscopic dependence: A practical clinical benefit is fewer intraoperative X-ray shots and lower radiation exposure to the patient and OR staff. Reported reductions vary widely—some series report reductions of more than 30%, others more than 70%—but the direction is generally consistent. This is meaningful for occupational health. Bottom line From my perspective, the specific advantage in complex bone, joint, and spinal regions is that robotics creates a plan–execute–verify loop: 3D patient-specific visualization addresses the “I can’t see or fully imagine the deep spatial relationships” problem, and sub-millimeter mechanical execution addresses the “my hand is not perfectly steady or repeatable” problem. Together they raise the safety and reproducibility of technically demanding steps. But it remains an enabling technology, not a replacement for the surgeon. Its value ceiling depends on indication selection, understanding of the pathology, and surgical strategy. It makes precise execution more reliable; it does not make the direction of that precision correct. And I would emphasize that high-level evidence on long-term functional superiority over conventional techniques is still mixed and indication-dependent.

As a practicing orthopedic surgeon, I would reframe the question. The operative question is not “which cases can be done robotically,” but which cases, given a fixed capital and consumable cost structure, are most likely to generate a downstream clinical or economic return sufficient to justify the incremental cost. The health-economic evidence points to a three-layer filter: institutional volume first, case-specific downstream conversion second, and payment/platform constraints third. Volume is not a secondary consideration—it is the precondition without which case selection becomes economically meaningless. Layer 1: Volume is the gate, not an afterthought The fixed costs of a robotic platform—capital purchase or lease, maintenance, imaging integration, and disposable instruments—mean that per-case cost falls with volume far more than any case-selection strategy can compensate for. The threshold estimates vary by platform, procedure, and health system, but the direction is consistent: For robotic unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (rUKA), a five-year cost-utility analysis found an incremental cost per QALY of £13,078 at 400 cases per year, with a cost per QALY below the £20,000 threshold achieved at ≥300 cases per year; when a single revision for presumed infection was removed from the manual group, cost-neutrality required more than 900 cases per year. For robotic-arm-assisted TKA, a US decision-analytic model found cost-effectiveness at a $50,000/QALY willingness-to-pay threshold only when **hospital volume exceeded 49 procedures per year**; at an average volume of 50 cases, the ICER was $41,331/QALY, and the result was highly sensitive to annual volume. Another analysis estimated that ≥253 robotic TKAs per year per robot would be required for cost-effectiveness. A German single-center analysis reported that case-related technology costs fell 60% (from USD 1,210 to USD 490) alongside volume expansion, and that the per-case cost premium should be calculated at a volume of 125 implantations per year. In spine, modeling suggests that performing 557 thoracolumbar procedures per year with robot assistance could save approximately $608,546 annually, primarily through reduced revisions, shorter stays, and reduced surgical time. These thresholds are not transferable across systems or platforms, but the implication for case selection is direct: if a center's annual robotic volume is far below the relevant break-even range, no amount of case selection will make the program economically efficient. The rational response in that situation is not to “cherry-pick” complex cases, but to cluster cases, standardize workflow, and build team familiarity until volume approaches the threshold. Dispersing a robot across multiple low-volume sites or performing one or two cases per week is the least economically defensible configuration. Layer 2: Above the volume threshold, select cases where the precision advantage is most likely to convert into downstream savings Once volume is adequate, the marginal logic shifts to the probability that improved execution will prevent a costly downstream event—revision, complication, readmission, or secondary surgery. For cases where conventional technique already performs reliably and the precision difference does not produce an observable clinical consequence, robotic use is largely an incremental cost without a corresponding incremental health gain. Joint replacement. Long-term follow-up data show that for routine primary TKA and THA without significant deformity, robotic assistance has not been demonstrated to reduce revision or loosening rates at the population level. The economic case is therefore strongest in subgroups where conventional precision is most challenged and the downstream stakes are highest. A 2026 Bayesian decision-tree model identified coronal deformity ≥10° and BMI >35 as the most influential patient-level variables predicting benefit from robotic TKA; in simulated scenarios, recommendation probabilities ranged from 14.6% to 89.2% depending on complexity and access, with robotic access acting as a binary gatekeeper. Severe extra-articular deformity is another economically coherent indication: conventional TKA in this setting may require staged surgery or additional osteotomy, whereas robotic assistance can enable single-stage TKA, directly avoiding the cost and risk of a second procedure. Revision and previously operated knees are a plausible but less well-evidenced extension of the same logic: distorted anatomy reduces the reliability of conventional alignment guides, and the plan–execute loop has a stronger value proposition, though prospective economic data remain limited. In THA with Crowe III–IV developmental dysplasia, the accuracy advantage in cup placement is more likely to matter clinically, but randomized evidence on long-term revision outcomes is still sparse. Spine. The economic evidence is more guarded. A 2026 Chinese review concluded that current evidence supports robotic improvement in screw accuracy and reduction in surgeon radiation exposure, but the impact on patient outcomes, complications, revisions, and cost-effectiveness remains inconsistent; the explicit recommendation is that robotics be used as an adjunct for “difficult screw placement or complex workflow” cases, with routine use decided in light of case characteristics, team experience, equipment, and cost. The cost savings that have been modeled or observed in spine—$4,086–$4,865 per patient versus navigation and $7,317–$9,654 versus freehand, or roughly $608,546 annually at 557 cases—are driven by avoidance of revisions, shorter stays, and reduced surgical time, and are therefore concentrated in revision, multi-level, anatomically variant, and percutaneous fixation cases where screw failure carries greater consequences and higher probability. They are unlikely to materialize uniformly in every simple single-level lumbar fusion. Trauma. The evidence here is the most nuanced. A 2026 retrospective cohort of valgus-impacted osteoporotic femoral neck fractures found that TiRobot-assisted fixation was associated with significantly lower rates of femoral head necrosis (5.56% vs 25.00%), non-union (8.33% vs 27.78%), and fixation failure (5.56% vs 22.22%) at 24–36 months, alongside shorter operative time, less blood loss, and shorter hospital stay. However, the surgical cost was significantly higher (CNY 28,998 vs CNY 17,654), and the intervention was a combined strategy of manual reduction plus robotic assistance, not robotics alone. In contrast, a Chinese real-world analysis of intertrochanteric fractures found that robotic-assisted nailing between 2019 and 2021 did not significantly reduce postoperative mortality or secondary fracture risk, did not significantly increase QALYs, and did not demonstrate good cost–benefit due to higher overall costs. The defensible trauma selection is therefore periarticular or intra-articular fractures where reduction and fixation precision are decisive for healing, not simple, stable patterns where conventional fixation already performs well. Layer 3: Payment environment and platform choice constrain the feasible set Case selection cannot be separated from how the incremental cost is borne. Under fee-for-service models, additional procedural costs may be partially offset through reimbursement or volume; under fixed DRG payments or global budgets, the additional cost may not be reimbursed, fundamentally changing the economic calculus. In China, volume-based procurement (VBP) and the availability of domestic robotic platforms alter the feasible set: a 2026 real-world study of Beijing municipal hospitals found that for orthopedic procedures, domestic robotic systems were associated with lower total treatment cost and consumable cost by approximately CNY 8,900 and CNY 11,800 respectively, along with reduced blood loss and shorter time to first ambulation, compared with imported systems. This does not mean domestic platforms are clinically equivalent across all indications, but it does mean that platform selection is itself a component of case-level economic efficiency, not a separate procurement decision. Shared robot units across multiple sites can also defray fixed costs, but low-volume centers cannot overcome the structural disadvantage of insufficient volume through case selection alone. A practical selection framework, with its uncertainties stated I would operationalize the evidence as a three-filter allocation framework rather than a static disease list: Filter What it answers Practical implication Institutional volume Is the program above the relevant break-even range? If not, prioritize case clustering and workflow standardization before fine-tuning case mix Downstream conversion probability Is precision failure likely to produce a costly event? Prioritize severe deformity (≥10°), extra-articular deformity, high BMI (>35), revision knees, Crowe III–IV DDH; revision/multi-level/anatomically variant spine; periarticular fractures with healing-critical alignment Payment and platform constraints Who bears the incremental cost, and at what per-case premium? Prefer platforms with lower local incremental cost or coverage; consider shared units where volume is otherwise insufficient I would not default to robotics for routine primary TKA/THA without significant deformity, simple single-level lumbar fusion, or stable intertrochanteric fractures, because the available evidence does not demonstrate that the precision advantage translates into a population-level reduction in revision, loosening, or mortality sufficient to justify the incremental cost in those scenarios. I should be candid about the limits of this framework. The volume thresholds are platform-, procedure-, and health-system-specific and should not be treated as universal mandates. The case-level economic advantages—single-stage surgery for extra-articular deformity, revision avoidance in complex spine, healing improvement in selected femoral neck fractures—are directionally plausible but often derived from modeling studies, single-center retrospective cohorts, or indirect evidence, not from prospective economic trials. The Chinese health-economic evidence base, in particular, is still accumulating. Case selection in robotic orthopedics is therefore best understood as a dynamic optimization under local volume, payment rules, and case mix, not as a fixed set of indication rules already settled by evidence. My own bottom line as a surgeon is this: do not use the robot where conventional technique already achieves the outcome that matters, and do not use case selection to mask a structural volume problem—because in a low-volume program, even the “right” cases will not make the economics work.

从执业视角看，这个问题需要先拆解“智能辅助功能”的具体所指。目前骨科机器人所称的“智能”，并非一个统一的、具备自主认知的能力，而是分布在术前规划、术中执行约束、以及末端感知反馈三个不同层面上的技术集合。它们对安全性的提升作用，证据强度并不均等：在约束“置钉轨迹”这一几何问题上，证据最为确凿；在预防“力相关误操作”这一物理问题上，技术正在成熟但临床验证仍不充分；而在需要判断“何时该停”的软组织邻近区域，当前的“智能”仍存在结构性盲区。 置钉偏差：从“经验容错”到“几何约束”，证据最为坚实 降低置钉偏差是骨科机器人智能辅助功能中证据等级最高、结论最一致的领域。其作用机制并非机器人“更聪明”，而是通过术前三维规划与机械臂的空间约束，将术者从依赖二维透视和徒手感觉的“经验容错”模式中解放出来，置于一个几何上被限定的执行通道内。 多项2025年的高级别证据为此提供了量化支撑。一项纳入42项研究（含22项RCT）的网络荟萃分析显示，配备整合导航的通用型机器人，其Gertzbein-Robbins A级置钉率的汇总比例为93.89%，A+B级（临床可接受）达到99.16%。另一项针对腰椎RCT的荟萃分析给出了效应量：机器人组的A级置钉率显著更高（OR 2.18），同时需要翻修的螺钉比例显著更低（OR 0.21）。在并发症层面，一项纳入13项研究的荟萃分析报告，机器人组的神经损伤发生率（1.9% vs. 4.3%）和翻修手术率（3.1% vs. 5.2%）均显著低于传统徒手技术。一项Cochrane收录的RCT则将精度差距精确到了毫米级：机器人组导针置入的平均偏差为0.86±0.57 mm，而传统透视组为2.55±1.88 mm（P<0.001）。这种从“厘米级经验判断”到“亚毫米级几何执行”的转变，是智能辅助在置钉安全性上最核心的价值。 然而，这种获益并非无差别地适用于所有场景。证据一致指向复杂解剖（如畸形、翻修）和微创经皮置钉是机器人精度优势最能转化为安全收益的领域。在解剖正常的常规腰椎融合中，机器人对临床结局（如VAS评分、融合率）的改善并不显著，其价值更多体现在过程指标（精度、辐射、翻修率） 而非最终的患者报告结局上。这意味着，“智能辅助”降低置钉偏差的能力是真实的，但它转化为可感知的临床获益，需要病例选择与之匹配。 力相关误操作：防误穿预警的“技术承诺”与“证据缺口” 这是“智能辅助”中直接指向“术中误操作”的环节，但其成熟度远低于置钉精度。 理论上，集成力反馈或阻力监测的系统能够在钻头突破骨壁的瞬间，通过捕捉阻力骤降的信号触发报警或自动停止，从而降低损伤下方神经血管的风险。部分商用系统（如具备力反馈功能的TiRobot ForcePro）已将这一机制作为核心安全宣称。在工程层面，相关研究也在推进“超前预测”能力，例如有模型声称能实现超前2秒的钻削力预警，以应对力反馈延迟导致的钉道偏移风险。 但关键问题在于临床证据的层级。目前关于力反馈防误穿效能的描述，主要来自技术说明、厂商资料或离体实验，缺乏在真实手术环境中以“神经损伤发生率”为终点的高质量对照研究来证实其能够独立地、可量化地降低误操作风险。一个必须正视的现实是，力反馈系统捕捉的是工具与骨之间的力学交互，它能够较好地服务于“防止钻透皮质”这一目标，但当操作邻近硬膜囊或神经根时，安全与否取决于对软组织力学属性的实时判断，而这恰恰是当前力感知技术尚未有效覆盖的领域。因此，对于“力相关误操作”，智能辅助提供了一道有理论依据且工程上可行的辅助防线，但宣称其已“有效降低”临床误操作率，尚缺乏足够强度的证据支撑，其实际安全冗余度高度依赖于术者的持续监控与随时接管。 关节置换中的智能规划：减少“离群值”，而非消除“并发症” 在关节置换领域，智能辅助的贡献主要体现在术前规划与术中执行的一致性上，其安全性收益的表述需要更为审慎。 AI与机器人辅助被证实能够提供更优的术前规划和实时导航，从而减少机械轴对齐的离群值。汇总数据显示，机器人AI平台相较于传统技术，可将机械轴对齐离群值降低最高达32%。从逻辑上，对齐精度的提升有助于减少因力线不良导致的远期磨损和松动，并可能降低并发症率。然而，这更多是一种基于过程指标改善的推论，而非直接针对“术中误操作”的临床证据。在关节置换中，机器人智能辅助的核心作用对象是截骨角度和假体位置，而非传统意义上的“术中误操作”（如神经血管损伤）。亚太专家共识同时警示，机器人TKA存在其特有的并发症，如追踪器针道相关并发症（发生率约1.4%，包括感染、骨折、神经血管损伤），这是传统手术中不存在的风险维度。因此，在关节领域，“智能辅助提升安全性”的准确含义是：它降低了与“精度不足”相关的风险，但同时引入了一组低发生率但特异性的新风险，整体安全性的净效应需要权衡，而非单向提升。 临床视角的审慎结论 骨科机器人的智能辅助功能，在降低置钉几何偏差这一维度上，已经获得了高级别证据的支持，其安全价值是确切的。但在预防力相关误操作和软组织邻近区域的安全保障上，当前的“智能”仍处于“感知辅助”而非“决策替代”的阶段，力反馈的防误穿效能尚待真实世界的高质量验证，而对软组织力学属性的“感知真空”仍是结构性局限。因此，对于“能否有效提升手术安全性”的回答应当是分层的、有条件的：在置钉精度和减少辐射暴露上，答案是肯定的；在减少翻修和神经损伤的临床结局上，证据指向积极但强度不一，且高度依赖于复杂病例的选择；在力相关误操作的主动预防上，技术提供了有前景的辅助工具，但将其视为一道已验证的独立安全屏障为时尚早。智能辅助的合理定位，是将术者的经验从“几何判断”中部分解放出来，使其能将注意力更多地投向那些当前机器尚无法感知的领域——力觉判断与软组织决策，而非替代术者成为安全性的最终责任人。

Robotic navigation generally improves radiographic screw placement and reduces fluoroscopy use, but a reduction in neurovascular injuries has not yet been convincingly demonstrated. The strongest direct evidence concerns iliosacral screws in the posterior pelvic ring; evidence for other pelvic screw corridors is less extensive. From an orthopedic surgical decision-making perspective, the findings are: Outcome Comparison with conventional fluoroscopy Safe-corridor placement Generally more accurate, with fewer cortical breaches and guidewire redirections. However, accuracy definitions vary between studies. Fluoroscopy time Usually shorter during screw insertion, sometimes substantially so. The reduction depends on the imaging and registration workflow. Neurovascular complications Uncommon in both groups. Existing studies are generally too small to establish a reliable difference in these rare events. A randomized trial of 30 patients and 45 screws reported excellent/good placement in 100% of robotic screws versus 95% of conventional screws. Median fluoroscopy time after pelvic reduction was 6 versus 36 seconds, approximately 83% shorter. Neither group had reported postoperative complications or revisions. These results support improved technical performance, but the sample was insufficient to establish superiority for preventing nerve or vascular injury. Randomized trial A separate 128-patient retrospective study found cortical penetration in 5 of 62 freehand screws, compared with none of 118 robot-assisted screws. This supports better corridor containment, but a cortical breach is a radiographic outcome and does not necessarily cause clinical injury. Comparative study Results are not uniformly conclusive: a small 2026 comparison found shorter fluoroscopy time and higher accuracy with robotics, but neither difference reached statistical significance. Recent comparative study The practical qualification is that navigation depends on satisfactory reduction and valid registration. Fragment movement after imaging can invalidate the planned corridor, and robotics cannot create a safe bony corridor where anatomy provides none. Also, shorter fluoroscopy time does not necessarily mean proportionately lower total patient radiation when additional three-dimensional imaging is required. I would therefore describe the benefit as better placement consistency and usually less fluoroscopy, with uncertain additional protection against neurovascular injury.

与徒手透视置钉相比，机器人引导对胸腰椎椎弓根螺钉置入准确度的提升是明确的，但幅度需要放在具体的数据参照系中理解。更关键的是，这一优势在脊柱畸形和翻修手术等复杂情形下，确实会变得更加突出，其价值从单纯的“精度数字提升”转向了“在解剖标志失效时重建可执行的置钉路径”。 📊 总体提升幅度：完美置钉率的绝对增益约9个百分点 如果以最严格的“完美置钉”（Gertzbein-Robbins A级，即螺钉完全位于椎弓根皮质骨内）为标准，现有最高级别的证据给出了较为一致的量级。 一项纳入13项研究（含5项RCT）的meta分析显示，机器人辅助脊柱手术（RASS）的完美置钉率为94.2%，徒手透视组为85.1%，机器人组的优势具有统计学显著性（OR 2.41, p < 0.001）。与此同时，显著穿破（>2 mm）的发生率从徒手的11.4%降至机器人的3.8%（OR 0.32）。在临床后果层面，机器人组的神经损伤率（1.9% vs. 4.3%）和翻修手术率（3.1% vs. 5.2%）均显著更低。 具体到胸腰椎骨折这一常见场景，一项前瞻性研究的数据与此高度吻合：机器人组180枚螺钉的置钉准确率为97.2%，徒手组为91.1%；同时，关节突侵犯率从5.6%降至1.7%。另一项研究则以“植钉准确优秀率”为指标，报告了94.6% vs. 84.9%的差异。 因此，就胸腰椎常规置钉而言，机器人引导带来的完美置钉率绝对提升幅度大致在9个百分点左右，并将显著穿破的风险降低了约三分之二。这一增益是真实的，但并非颠覆性的数量级改变——它意味着在每100枚螺钉中，大约能多避免9枚出现任何皮质穿破、多避免7至8枚出现显著穿破。 🌀 脊柱畸形：优势从“精度提升”转向“可行性重建” 在脊柱侧弯等畸形病例中，机器人辅助的价值超出了上述平均数字所能概括的范围，其优势的性质发生了变化。 一项针对脊柱侧弯矫形术的回顾性研究（178例患者）显示，机器人组的置钉准确率为98.51%，徒手组为95.50%。单看数字，差距（约3个百分点）甚至小于总体meta分析中的平均增益。但这恰恰揭示了畸形病例的核心问题：徒手组95.50%的准确率本身，是在一个解剖条件已经极度恶化的人群中取得的，其“不准确”的5%所对应的风险，远高于常规病例中同样的百分比。在该研究中，机器人组的并发症总发生率显著更低（2.74% vs. 11.43%），这提示精度上的微小差异，在畸形病例中被放大为了具有临床意义的并发症差异。 更直接的证据来自前述meta分析的亚组分析：在畸形病例中，机器人相对于徒手技术的优势比值（OR）为2.67，高于总体分析的OR 2.41。针对成人脊柱畸形的综述也指出，机器人引导在畸形手术中可达到97%–99%的A/B级（临床可接受）准确率，并“适度但可重复地优于透视引导徒手技术”。其核心机制在于，畸形椎体的旋转、楔变和解剖标志的丧失，使徒手置钉所依赖的“以骨性标志推断通道”这一基本前提部分失效；机器人的术前三维规划则不依赖于术中肉眼所见的标志，而是基于影像数据重建的骨性几何，从而在“无标志可循”的区域重新建立了一条可执行的通道。 🔧 翻修手术：优势体现为“在废墟中定位” 翻修手术为机器人提供了一个比畸形更为严苛的验证场景。既往内置物、骨水泥、瘢痕组织和已破坏的解剖层次，使正常置钉的“入口”和“路径”都可能不复存在。 一项前瞻性研究专门评估了机器人辅助在翻修胸腰椎融合手术中的表现。在64例患者、388枚翻修螺钉中，仅有2枚（0.5%）出现位置不良，且无临床后果，术中无并发症报告。该研究的结论明确指出，机器人辅助为翻修手术中“松动/断裂的内置物或骨水泥周围”提供了“替代性的安全骨性通道”。这一表述精准地描述了机器人在翻修场景中的角色：它并非简单地“把标准螺钉放得更准”，而是在原有安全通道已被破坏或占据的条件下，重新找到一条可用的、避开金属异物和瘢痕的路径。另一篇针对成人畸形的综述也印证了这一点，指出机器人引导下“位置不良螺钉的翻修率很低，即使在技术要求极高的翻修和解剖条件中也是如此”。 💎 从医师视角的判断 机器人引导对胸腰椎置钉准确度的提升，在常规病例中是一个约9个百分点的完美置钉率增益，其临床意义在于将显著穿破和神经损伤的风险压低了约一半至三分之二。在畸形和翻修病例中，这一优势的幅度可能看起来相近甚至更小，但其意义被解剖条件的恶化所放大：在徒手技术赖以操作的骨性标志已经失真或消失的场景中，机器人的规划与执行能力所提供的，不再仅仅是“锦上添花”的精度改善，而是将一部分原本因解剖条件所限而变得不确定甚至不可行的操作，重新拉回到可预期、可执行的范围内。meta分析中亚组OR的升高（畸形病例OR 2.67）和翻修研究中0.5%的位置不良率，共同支持了这一判断：复杂解剖不是削弱了机器人的价值，而是改变了其价值兑现的方式——从“做得更准”转向“在原本难以做准的地方，提供一条可用的路径”。

从骨科临床操作角度看，**力反馈不足的主要影响，是医生对“接触了什么、用了多大力、是否即将突破组织边界”的判断可能变迟，增加过度推进和组织损伤的风险。**但首先需要修正一个前提：不同骨科机器人差异很大，并非都完全缺乏力反馈。 许多脊柱机器人主要承担定位、导向，钻孔和置钉仍由医生手持器械完成，医生可以保留部分直接触觉；部分关节机器人具有虚拟边界阻力或力感知功能。虚拟边界限制的是器械运动范围，不等于真实还原骨与软组织的触感。脊柱机器人临床操作研究、关节机器人尸体研究 1．截骨：可能削弱对切削阻力和突破瞬间的判断。 截骨时，医生通常会结合手感、声音和视觉判断皮质骨、松质骨及骨边缘。若真实阻力反馈不足，可能不易及时察觉锯片卡顿、偏转或突破骨皮质，导致超出预期的切削或损伤邻近组织。这是基于操作机制的风险判断，不能直接等同于机器人截骨的实际并发症一定更多。 具有运动边界约束的系统可以部分补偿这一问题。一项尸体研究发现，特定机器人辅助膝关节置换的软组织损伤少于手工操作；但这不能推广至所有设备，也不能证明临床上完全没有损伤风险。原始研究 2．钻孔、置钉：可能漏掉滑移、偏转和骨壁突破的早期信号。 在脊柱等狭窄骨性通道内，重要的触觉信号包括钻头是否稳稳接触骨面、是否沿斜面滑走，以及推进阻力是否突然下降。反馈不足时，医生可能较晚发现： 入点滑移，实际通道偏离规划； 软组织侧向压力使套筒或器械偏转； 钻头或导针突破骨壁后继续推进。 因此，**机械臂对准规划轨迹，并不保证器械尖端始终沿该轨迹前进。**临床研究已记录软组织压力、骨面滑移及钻孔压力对机器人辅助置钉精度的影响。原始临床研究 3．软组织剥离：难以判断牵拉强度及组织层次。 如果机械臂直接承担剥离、夹持或牵拉，而反馈又不足，医生可能难以及时辨别组织黏连、张力增加和异常阻力，从而增加过度牵拉、撕裂或压迫损伤的风险。血管、神经等结构发生损伤前，也未必出现明显的视觉变化。 不过，**常见骨科机器人主要辅助骨性操作，软组织显露与剥离往往仍由医生完成。**目前不能把其他外科机器人关于软组织操作的研究，直接当作所有骨科机器人的临床证据；这一部分更应视为机制上的风险分析。 临床上，补偿力反馈不足需要结合直接观察、保留的手持触觉、导航核验，以及必要的影像或骨性通道探查。出现异常阻力、器械偏转，或手感与屏幕位置不一致时，应暂停并查明原因，不能只因导航显示正常就继续推进。 目前无法给出“缺乏力反馈使并发症增加多少”的统一数字：设备、操作方式及反馈能力不同，而且研究往往难以把力反馈的作用，与导航精度、医生经验和学习曲线单独分开。

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the consequences of absent haptic feedback should not be framed as a single, generic “loss of feel.” It is better understood as a switch in the information channels available for a given task: tactile and proprioceptive input is partly replaced by visual tracking, auditory cues, torque-signal interpretation, and geometrically defined virtual constraints. The clinical consequences therefore vary substantially by task, depending on how intrinsically force- or torque-dependent that task is and whether redundant safeguards—navigation, neurophysiologic monitoring, virtual boundaries—are in place. Osteotomy: from “feeling bone quality through resistance” to “executing a planned geometric boundary” In conventional osteotomy, the surgeon uses changes in saw or osteotome resistance to sense bone density, the transition from cortical to cancellous bone, and proximity to a thin region such as the hinge in high tibial osteotomy. When the robotic arm lacks haptic feedback, this information is not directly transmitted. The consequences are twofold. First, there is a relative blind spot for bone quality and local mechanical state. The surgeon cannot adjust feed rate based on resistance or judge whether the opposite cortex is about to be breached, particularly in osteoporotic or heterogenous bone. This can bias execution in either direction: over-advancement in sclerotic bone or under-advancement in cancellous bone. Evidence from robotic bone cutting indicates that systems without force feedback rely predominantly on three-dimensional visual cues to estimate tissue deformation and cutting depth, and visual cues only partially compensate for the missing dynamic information. For osteotomies that depend on preserving a hinge—such as open-wedge high tibial osteotomy—this information deficit is clinically relevant, because hinge fracture risk has traditionally been managed through the “ear–hand conversation” of tactile and vibratory feedback about bone elastic modulus. Second, the mechanism by which cutting accuracy is maintained shifts. In semi-active systems without haptic feedback, accuracy does not come mainly from the surgeon “feeling how much has been cut,” but from preoperatively planned virtual fixtures or haptic boundaries: the robot permits bone removal only within the planned volume and resists or locks motion beyond that boundary. In effect, missing force feedback is partly substituted by geometric constraint. This substitution works reasonably well in standardized osteotomies—such as distal femoral and proximal tibial cuts in total knee arthroplasty—where the correspondence between planned geometry and target anatomy is relatively deterministic. It is less adequate in complex osteotomies with variable bone quality or where intraoperative adjustment of cut volume or hinge tension is required, because geometric constraint cannot fully replace tactile judgment. Screw placement: from “feeling the pedicle with a probe” to “navigated trajectory plus torque-pattern recognition” In pedicle screw placement, the consequences of absent haptic feedback are most concrete and most discussed. The core risk is the loss of tactile warning for skiving and cortical breach. In freehand technique, the surgeon detects a sudden change in probe or drill resistance as an indicator of pedicle breach. Robotic systems use high-speed drills at cortical entry; if the entry point is irregular, the trajectory is steep, or soft tissue obscures the bone surface, the drill can slide along the bone surface and deviate from the planned trajectory. Because the surgeon cannot directly feel this lateral skiving force through the arm, skiving has been reported as one cause of trajectory deviation in robotic spine surgery, particularly in minimally invasive percutaneous procedures where direct visual confirmation is limited. Case series have listed skiving among the error sources requiring intraoperative management during robotic screw placement. Compensatory mechanisms: navigation, neuromonitoring, and torque patterns. Absent haptic feedback does not mean an unmitigated safety loss. Real-time navigation provides visual feedback on trajectory. Neuromonitoring is used in percutaneous or robotic procedures to help avoid neurologic injury when tactile feedback is unavailable. More nuanced compensation comes from drill torque signals: during low-speed automated drilling, periodic fluctuations in resistance—“cyclic insertion torque patterns”—can be observed on the navigation interface and may provide an alternative visual–tactile cue about bone–screw interface engagement, although clinical reproducibility and impact on screw accuracy remain unvalidated. Some systems also preserve or substitute “feel” through oscillating instruments or software alerts, for example warning when the drill deviates. The severity of the consequence therefore depends on the operating mode: it is most direct in non-navigated, purely robotic percutaneous placement without neuromonitoring; it is substantially buffered—but not eliminated—by the redundancy of navigation plus neuromonitoring plus torque monitoring. Soft-tissue dissection: from “tactile tension judgment” to “vision plus virtual no-go zones” Soft-tissue manipulation is the area where the consequences of absent haptic feedback are least fully compensable by geometric planning. In conventional surgery, the surgeon uses touch to judge tissue tension, ligament viscoelasticity, adhesion severity, and proximity to neurovascular bundles. When a robot lacks direct tactile and pressure input, visual cues only partially compensate for the estimation of tissue forces, a limitation repeatedly noted in both laparoscopic and orthopedic robotics. In arthroplasty, soft-tissue balance has traditionally relied on the surgeon’s subjective tactile feedback to assess medial and lateral ligament tension. When the robotic system lacks force feedback, quantification of soft-tissue balance must either shift to gap measurements and robotic-arm position data obtained before or during surgery, or remain manually performed by the surgeon outside the robotic workflow. In the latter case, the precision advantage of the robot does not extend to the soft-tissue side. During osteotomy and exposure, the link between absent haptic feedback and inadvertent soft-tissue injury has been documented. In early robotic total hip and knee arthroplasty experience, the proportion of procedures aborted because of soft-tissue concerns—including actual or potential soft-tissue injury—was reported at 18%–34%. These figures reflect early-system learning and workflow issues and should not be extrapolated as current soft-tissue injury rates, but they illustrate that the soft-tissue consequence of missing force feedback is clinically substantive, not merely a theoretical inconvenience. The main compensatory strategy is the “virtual no-go zone” rather than “tactile sensing.” Semi-active systems use software to restrict the motion range of the cutting tool tip so that it cannot enter predefined vital soft-tissue regions. This strategy converts soft-tissue protection from “intraoperative sensing and avoidance” into “preoperative geometric prohibition.” Its effectiveness depends heavily on consistency between intraoperative soft-tissue position and the preoperative plan; if soft tissue shifts outside the plan because of positioning, retraction, or joint motion, the protective value of the virtual no-go zone decreases. Overall judgment: consequences are task-dependent and partly modified by redundancy From a practicing surgeon’s standpoint, I would summarize the net consequences of absent haptic feedback as follows: In standardized osteotomies with high geometric certainty, the consequence is mainly weakened real-time judgment of bone quality, while virtual boundaries and planning accuracy largely preserve execution precision. The cost is reduced adaptability to unplanned bone-quality variation or hinge mechanical state. In spinal screw placement, the consequence is most concretely the loss of tactile warning for skiving and cortical breach, but navigation, neuromonitoring, and torque-pattern recognition provide partial compensation. Net risk depends on the completeness of redundancy, not simply on the presence or absence of haptic feedback. In soft-tissue dissection and balancing, the consequence is least fully compensable by geometric planning. Virtual no-go zones provide spatial avoidance, not mechanical sensing, so soft-tissue protection still depends on the surgeon’s independent judgment of soft-tissue state outside the plan. An often overlooked consequence is the shift in training and decision-making: surgeons accustomed to freehand technique must recode information previously acquired through touch into interpretation of navigation displays, torque waveforms, and planned boundaries. This learning curve may temporarily increase error risk. A more accurate formulation is therefore not that “absent haptic feedback causes a loss of precision,” but that the absence of haptic feedback changes the information basis on which precision and safety are maintained: in bone procedures, that basis shifts partly from force/torque sensing to geometric constraint plus visual tracking; in soft-tissue procedures, that shift is least adequately compensated, and the consequences are least fully eliminable with current technology.

As a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the short answer is yes on both counts, but the magnitude of the advantage is more clearly established than the claim that it is greater in complex settings. The accuracy benefit is consistent and well-quantified; the "greater in complexity" claim is directionally supported but has important nuances that the data do not fully resolve. The Baseline Advantage: Consistently Higher Accuracy and Fewer Severe Breaches Across meta-analyses and randomized controlled trials (RCTs), robotic guidance demonstrates a statistically and clinically meaningful improvement over freehand fluoroscopic techniques in the thoracolumbar spine. The most robust metric is not average accuracy but the rate of severe violations—Gertzbein-Robbins grade D and E breaches, which are the deviations most likely to cause neurological or vascular injury. A 2025 meta-analysis of 18 studies (1,566 patients) found that freehand fluoroscopic placement had significantly worse accuracy in these high-grade breaches (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.28–0.80), and the robotic group had a lower rate of revision surgery for screw mispositioning (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.17–0.48). For overall accuracy, a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs reported that the robot-assisted group was significantly more accurate than conventional freehand (OR 3.5, 95% CI 2.75–4.45, P<0.0001). A separate RCT-based meta-analysis in the lumbar spine found that robotic guidance was associated with higher odds of achieving a perfect Grade A screw (OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.19–4.01) and a significant reduction in proximal facet joint violation (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06–0.39), alongside a lower revision rate (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.07–0.62). In absolute terms, the accuracy gap is frequently reported in the range of 3 to 9 percentage points. In adult spinal deformity, for example, robotic-guided placement achieved 95% accuracy versus 86% for freehand. The Complex-Setting Claim: Directionally Supported, but Not Uniformly "Greater" This is where the evidence requires more careful qualification. Spinal deformity. The data consistently show that robotics retains an accuracy advantage in scoliosis and adult deformity, which is clinically important because distorted anatomy is precisely where freehand landmarks become less reliable. A 2024 meta-analysis of seven studies in scoliosis surgery found that robot-assisted placement had significantly better clinically acceptable screw results compared with freehand (OR 2.61). A meta-analysis focused specifically on scoliosis reported higher accuracy for robotics relative to both navigation (OR 2.02) and conventional freehand (OR 3.06), alongside a shorter hospital stay. A clinical series in scoliosis correction reported 98.51% accuracy with robotics versus 95.50% with freehand. However, whether the advantage is magnified in severe deformity is less clear. A 2025 retrospective study specifically comparing severe complex deformity with non-severe deformity found that robot-assisted technology achieved a perfect screw placement rate of 90.60% in severe complex deformity versus 92.18% in non-severe deformity, a difference that was not statistically significant (p=0.3997). This suggests that robotics can maintain a high level of accuracy even in severe deformity, but it does not prove that the relative advantage over freehand is larger there—because that study did not include a freehand comparator in the severe group. The defensible interpretation is that robotics preserves its accuracy advantage in deformity, and may be most valuable in cases where freehand reliability would be most compromised, but the "greater advantage" claim is inferential rather than directly quantified across severity strata in the highest-quality comparative data. Revision surgery. The evidence here is smaller in volume but consistent in direction. A retrospective study of 81 patients undergoing posterior lumbar revision surgery—39 with the Renaissance robot and 42 with freehand—found that the robot-assisted technique was statistically superior in screw placement accuracy (P<0.05), with fewer superior-level facet joint violations. A broader systematic review noted that robots tended to be more accurate with fewer reoperations than freehand or fluoroscopic techniques. The clinical logic is compelling: in revision surgery, distorted anatomy, scar tissue, and obscured landmarks reduce the reliability of freehand trajectory estimation, so a plan-execute system with preoperative or intraoperative 3D data has a stronger rationale. But the evidence base in revision is composed of smaller retrospective series, not the large RCTs that underpin the baseline accuracy claim. I would characterize the revision advantage as supported but less robustly quantified than the general thoracolumbar advantage. Important Caveats from Clinical Practice Accuracy does not automatically mean superiority over navigation. A 2025 network meta-analysis based on RCTs found that robotic placement offered no advantage over navigation in terms of pedicle screw accuracy, while navigation itself significantly improved accuracy over freehand. This is a crucial nuance: the advantage is relative to freehand fluoroscopy, which is the comparator in your question, but within the broader ecosystem of image guidance, robotics is not necessarily the most accurate modality—it is one accurate modality among several, with different workflow and cost profiles. The clinical outcome benefit is concentrated in error prevention, not functional improvement. The RCT meta-analyses show reductions in severe breaches and revision rates, but differences in overall complication rates and patient-reported outcomes are often not statistically significant. The value is in avoiding catastrophic misplacement, not in improving average functional scores. The evidence is strongest in the lumbar and thoracolumbar spine. Thoracic screw placement at the upper thoracic or cervicothoracic junction, where the pedicles are smaller and the margin for error is narrower, has less dedicated comparative evidence. The generalizability of the lumbar data to those regions should not be assumed. Bottom Line Robotic guidance does improve thoracic and lumbar pedicle screw accuracy compared with freehand fluoroscopy, with the most consistent benefits being a reduction in severe (Grade D–E) breaches and revision surgery for malposition, and an increase in the proportion of perfectly placed screws. The absolute accuracy gain is typically in the range of 3–9 percentage points, and the odds ratios for accuracy consistently favor robotics. In complex settings, the advantage is directionally supported: robotics maintains high accuracy in scoliosis and revision surgery, where freehand reliability is most challenged, and the clinical rationale for the technology is strongest. But the claim that the advantage is quantitatively larger in complex versus routine cases is not uniformly established by the highest-quality data; the severe-deformity evidence shows robotics maintains its performance, while the direct freehand comparison across severity strata is limited. As a surgeon, I would say robotics is most defensible in complex anatomy and revision, but I would not tell a patient the relative benefit is proven to be larger there—I would say it is the setting where the technology's ability to preserve accuracy is most clinically valuable.

Current evidence shows more consistent implant positioning with robotics, but no established overall reduction in revision rates or improvement in long-term implant survival. Hip registry studies do show a promising reduction in revisions related to malposition or dislocation. From an orthopedic surgical decision-making perspective, the evidence should be separated by procedure and follow-up: Evidence Main finding Interpretation TKA: American Joint Replacement Registry Two-year revision rates were 1.2% in both groups; adjusted odds ratio 1.0. A subsequent five-year analysis also found no survivorship advantage. Better positioning has not demonstrated fewer overall knee revisions over this interval. Two-year study, five-year study TKA: UK National Joint Registry, 2026 Estimated five-year survival was 98.6% robotic versus 98.5% conventional, without a significant adjusted difference. Supports similar early survivorship. Mean follow-up was only approximately 2.5 years, so the five-year estimates require caution. Registry study TKA: long-term randomized trial Fifteen-year survivorship was 98% in both groups, with no significant differences in functional outcome scores. Reassuring durability, but no demonstrated superiority. The older robotic technology studied cannot fully represent current systems. Randomized trial THA: UK National Joint Registry, 2026 Estimated five-year survival was 98.8% in both matched groups. Malposition-related revision risk was lower with robotics: HR 0.53. A possible benefit for particular failure mechanisms, without better overall survival; robotic mean follow-up was approximately 2.5 years. Registry study THA: American Joint Replacement Registry, 2026 Two-year all-cause revision was 1.9% robotic versus 2.1% conventional, without a significant adjusted difference. Revision for dislocation was 0.3% versus 0.6%. A potentially meaningful instability benefit, although the absolute difference is small and the study is observational. Registry study Patient-reported outcomes are less consistently improved than radiographic accuracy. Some studies report better early recovery or scores, but durable, clinically important superiority remains unproven. The long-term knee trial found similar outcomes, while a matched hip study found no greater likelihood of achieving clinically important improvement with robotics. Robust long-term comparative evidence for contemporary robotic THA remains limited. Hip outcomes study Does alignment translate into fewer revisions? Not reliably at the population level so far. Avoiding substantial malposition is valuable, but revision also depends on infection, fixation, soft-tissue balance, instability, fracture, implant design, and patient factors. More accurately executing a plan also does not establish that the chosen alignment target is optimal for that patient. The defensible clinical message is: robotics improves precision; longer implant life and better lasting function should not be promised. Current hip findings suggest fewer selected positioning-related failures, but registry associations cannot prove that alignment itself caused the reduction. Conversely, an absence of statistical difference does not exclude a small benefit that longer follow-up may reveal.

From a practicing surgeon's perspective, under the constraint of high equipment and consumable costs, the core task of case selection is not to "use the robot as much as possible," but rather—conditional on a case volume sufficient to amortize fixed costs—to concentrate the robot's precision gain on those cases where conventional technique is most likely to fail, and where that precision gain therefore has demonstrable clinical relevance. This is a dual filter: first satisfy the volume threshold, then, within that volume, screen for qualitative fit. 📊 First filter: annual case volume as a precondition for economic viability The high fixed cost of robotics (depreciation, maintenance contracts) means that per-case cost is highly sensitive to volume. Systematic reviews report minimum cost-effective volume thresholds ranging from roughly 40 to 300 cases per year, depending on procedure and cost assumptions. In unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA), this threshold has been relatively clearly modeled: a ten-year cost-utility analysis found that when all re-intervention costs are included, robotic-assisted UKA becomes cost-saving once annual volume exceeds 100 cases; when infection is excluded as a stochastic event, the cost-saving threshold rises to 800 cases per year, but even in that conservative scenario the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio is only £757, far below the £20,000 willingness-to-pay threshold, and therefore still cost-effective. A separate Markov model placed the UKA cost-effectiveness threshold at 94 cases per year, with additional conditions of patient age <67 years and a 2-year revision rate ≤1.2%. Taken together, a center performing fewer than roughly 100 robotic UKAs per year will struggle to justify the economics. For total knee arthroplasty (TKA), the threshold evidence is more complex. In the Chinese diagnosis-related-group and volume-based procurement context, Markov modeling supports robotic-arm-assisted TKA as still cost-effective under the new procurement system, but this conclusion is highly sensitive to the changed cost structure after implant price reductions. In middle-income country settings, widespread adoption of robotic TKA is not considered economically attractive. This indicates that TKA case selection cannot be discussed in isolation from the local payment environment and procurement prices. Spine surgery shows a different volume-efficiency relationship. Savings from robot-assisted lumbar fusion derive mainly from shortened length of stay, fewer revisions, and reduced complications: one meta-analysis reported savings of US$4,086–4,865 and US$7,317–9,654 per case versus computer navigation and freehand, respectively; another calculation showed that at 557 thoracolumbar cases within one year, robot assistance saved approximately US$608,546. This magnitude suggests that the economic viability of spine robotics often requires a high annual surgical volume, and that the savings are larger in patients with more severe complications and more complex constructs. Practical implication: Before considering any specific case-selection criteria, an institution should answer a more fundamental question—whether its annual volume for the relevant procedures crosses the cost-effectiveness threshold for that procedure. For centers below the threshold, even if robotic use in an individual complex case is clinically defensible, from the standpoint of medical resource efficiency, concentrating robotic capacity in high-volume centers is the more defensible strategy. 🦵 Joint replacement: within sufficient volume, prioritize the anatomical conditions in which conventional instrument chains are least reliable Once the annual volume threshold is crossed, joint replacement case selection should center on deformity severity and anatomical complexity, not on disease diagnosis as a binary criterion. UKA should be a priority direction. This is not only because its cost-effectiveness threshold is relatively attainable, but because long-term follow-up evidence consistently shows robotic UKA has advantages in aseptic loosening, revision rate, and re-intervention rate—which are precisely the main sources of cost savings. In centers with adequate volume, prioritizing the robot for UKA represents the highest convergence of economic logic and clinical evidence. TKA selection should focus on complex deformity and anatomical conditions that compromise conventional positioning technique. In extra-articular deformity, diaphyseal deformity, and retained intramedullary nails, the reliability of conventional intramedullary referencing or standardized cutting guides declines, whereas CT-based or imageless robotic planning can complete in a single stage a complex TKA that would conventionally require a two-stage approach—and significant cost savings have been reported. This means robotic TKA cost-effectiveness is more readily established in complex knees than in routine primary TKA: single-stage robotic surgery avoids the additional hospitalization, rehabilitation, and surgical costs of a two-stage conventional pathway, so the economic case derives from substituting for a pathway that is itself more expensive, not merely from precision improvement. Conversely, routine, low-complexity primary TKA is the context in which robotic cost-effectiveness is weakest. Current evidence does not support robotic TKA having superior long-term survivorship over conventional technique in routine cases, while the additional per-case consumable and time costs are certain. Under resource constraints, using the robot for this category exchanges a certain cost for an uncertain marginal clinical benefit. Regarding revision and complex acetabular defects, the literature suggests robotic assistance has unique value in complex acetabular defect reconstruction and is cost-effective from a long-term perspective, although operative time may be slightly longer. These cases are few in number and technically demanding conventionally, making them suitable as a high-priority niche indication for robotic capacity—but they should not be the mainstay for maintaining equipment utilization. 🦴 Spine: use "difficult screw placement or complex workflow" as the functional case-admission criterion The core judgment in spine robotic case selection is not the disease diagnosis but whether the screw placement in that case falls within the zone where conventional technique reliability declines. A systematic review explicitly states that robotics can serve as an adjunct for difficult screw placement or complex workflow cases, but that whether to use it routinely should be decided cautiously based on case characteristics, team experience, equipment conditions, and cost. This effectively provides an operational selection principle: prioritize robotics only in "difficult" and "complex" cases, rather than making it the default pathway for all spinal fusion. Specifically, circumstances meeting "difficult screw placement or complex workflow" include percutaneous fixation, anatomical variation, multi-level surgery, and revision surgery—situations that increase screw placement difficulty and team radiation exposure, and where the mechanical guidance value of robotics is clearest. In osteoporotic patients, robot-assisted screw placement is associated with lower screw loosening rates, and screw loosening is precisely one of the most troublesome failure modes of conventional technique in this subgroup; osteoporotic instrumented fusion therefore constitutes a failure-mechanism-driven priority indication. From a cost perspective, the sources of spine robotic savings—fewer revisions, shorter hospitalization, fewer complications—are largest precisely in complex cases. This is economically self-consistent with the "prioritize complex cases" logic: the robot's incremental cost is fixed while its incremental benefit is higher in complex cases, so the cost-effectiveness ratio is better in complex than in simple cases. 🦴 Trauma: use whether the fracture displacement pattern permits "precise corridor creation without open reduction" as the dividing line Trauma case selection criteria are relatively clear and consistent with the indication logic set out in Q2: the value of robotic assistance lies in precise fixation through percutaneous or minimally invasive corridors, not in replacing open reduction. Therefore, priority cases are those in which the degree of fracture displacement permits stable fixation without open anatomical reduction. In pelvic and acetabular fractures, undisplaced or minimally displaced fractures are suitable robotic targets, whereas comminuted, highly displaced fractures requiring open reduction are not. In calcaneal fractures, propensity-score-matched studies have shown robotic assistance reduces intraoperative blood loss, shortens length of stay, and lowers operating costs, suggesting that in appropriate trauma subgroups robotics can improve process metrics without increasing total cost. The cost-effectiveness evidence in trauma is overall weaker than in joint and spine surgery, so case selection should be more conservative, concentrating robotics in the middle ground where conventional percutaneous fixation precision is unreliable but the trauma of open surgery is too great. 🏥 Institutional-level efficiency levers: changing the cost equation more than per-case selection can Case selection is only one layer of the efficiency strategy. Once the equipment is purchased, institutional operational decisions may have a greater impact on per-case cost than case selection itself.
