Axis 2—Failure-mechanism match: Does the dominant risk in this case arise from trajectory geometry (dysplastic pedicles, distorted deformity anatomy, revision with lost landmarks, narrow S2AI corridors) or from biological or soft-tissue factors (severe osteoporosis with poor purchase, extensive scarring, reduction requiring soft-tissue releases)? The robot's benefit is strongest when the former dominates and diminishes when the latter dominates. On this framework, the ranking of indication strength is dysplastic pedicles and revision with altered landmarks at the top, severe scoliosis and high-grade spondylolisthesis as supported but complexity-dependent indications, and osteoporosis as the most conditional, requiring stratification by severity and by whether the clinical problem is registration, purchase, or trajectory. The honest limitation is that the evidence for these complex indications is heterogeneous and often drawn from case series and expert consensus rather than high-certainty comparative trials; the 2024 guideline itself grades its core recommendations at GPS (expert consensus) level. The robot is a powerful tool for the geometric problems of spine surgery, but the decision to use it should be grounded in a clear-eyed assessment of which problem in that specific patient the robot is actually solving.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the learning curve for robotic arthroplasty is real, measurable, and shorter than many surgeons fear—but “time neutrality” and “consolidated proficiency” are two different thresholds, and a new programme must be structured around the second, not the first. The evidence supports a phased implementation model: simulation and cadaver training before any live case, a defined number of proctored cases, and a case-volume plan that concentrates early experience rather than dispersing it. How Many Cases? The Numbers, and What They Actually Mean The literature does not give a single number, because the learning curve depends on the platform, the procedure (TKA vs THA), the surgeon's baseline volume, and whether the metric is operative time, accuracy, or complication avoidance. But the ranges are consistent enough to be clinically useful. Robotic TKA. The most commonly cited figure is a time-neutrality curve of roughly 10 cases, with a CUSUM-defined inflection averaging 7.9 cases in a multicenter analysis of a handheld wireless system. Platform-specific data from a 2026 systematic review of 40 studies and 10,533 procedures show a wider spread: proficiency after a mean of 18.4 cases for NAVIO, 29.5 for ROSA, and 34.2 for MAKO. A separate review of 32 articles reported 32 ± 24 cases for time neutrality (range 3–73) and 16 ± 12 cases for proficiency (range 3–61). A frequently cited single-surgeon series found a 16-case learning curve with a 12-minute increase in operative time during that phase. The clinical interpretation of these numbers matters more than the numbers themselves. Reaching time neutrality at 10 cases does not mean the surgeon has mastered the system. The 2026 THA data make the distinction explicitly: proficiency was achieved at 15–17 cases, but consolidated proficiency required 38–43 cases. Another THA analysis reported a 12–17 case proficiency threshold across platforms, with a 21.5% improvement in computer registration time and a 6.6% improvement in overall surgery time after proficiency was reached. The practical implication is that the first 10–20 cases are the period of workflow acquisition and time stabilization, while the next 20–30 cases are the period of refinement and consolidation. A programme that stops paying attention after case 15 will plateau before it has captured the full efficiency and safety benefit. Robotic THA. The THA curve is slightly longer and more sensitive to baseline volume. High-volume surgeons have a learning curve of roughly 20 cases, while low- and medium-volume surgeons may take longer and, in some analyses, showed no measurable improvement through 20 and 63 cases, respectively. This is not a reason to exclude lower-volume surgeons, but it is a reason to concentrate their early robotic experience rather than spreading it thinly across a low annual case load. One study found that a low-volume surgeon performing approximately 30 cases per year could still achieve surgical time proficiency within a similar number of cases as high-volume surgeons, suggesting that case clustering and focused repetition may matter more than annual volume alone. UKA. The curve is shorter: 6 cases for operating time and team comfort, with no learning curve for implant positioning accuracy or limb alignment. Structuring a New Programme: A Phased, Evidence-Linked Model A new programme should not treat the first live case as the starting point of training. The evidence supports a staged pathway that separates cognitive preparation, technical rehearsal, supervised execution, and graduated independence. Phase 1: Pre-clinical training (before any live case). This should include manufacturer-led training, simulation, and cadaver or sawbone practice. Recommendations from a health-management review include observing at least two cases (including room and instrument setup), simulation and inanimate/cadaver model training, and team-based dry-lab training that includes OR nurses. The cadaver component is not optional decoration; it is the only pre-clinical setting in which the surgeon can rehearse registration, docking, bone preparation, and conversion to manual technique under realistic anatomical constraints. Phase 2: Proctored live cases. The recommended number of proctored cases varies by source and by the surgeon's prior experience, but the range is 3 to 10 cases. A general recommendation is a minimum of three proctored sessions, with the important caveat that if the proctor has to intervene to resolve a problem, that session should not count as completed. The Royal College of Surgeons of England recommends 10 proctored cases for new consultants and 5 for post-fellowship surgeons, with cases reflecting the surgeon's usual practice mix of low and high complexity. It also suggests an early learning curve of at least 20 cases on a dual console (or platform equivalent) before independent practice is considered. These are not identical figures, and that heterogeneity reflects the absence of a single validated credentialing standard. The defensible programme design is to set a minimum of 5 proctored cases, extend to 10 for surgeons without prior navigation or robotic experience, and use the proctor's sign-off as a gate for independent practice, not as a formality. Phase 3: Graduated independence with structured oversight. After proctoring, the surgeon should not simply be released into an unrestricted robotic practice. The RCS England pathway recommends graduated independence in specific procedures agreed with the proctor, with mentorship and departmental support during the learning curve. In practical terms, this means starting with straightforward primary cases (mild deformity, normal BMI, no prior surgery) before moving to the complex indications—severe coronal deformity, fixed contracture, revision, or retained hardware—where the robotic workflow's prerequisites are more likely to be tested. It also means tracking conversion to manual technique, registration failures, and early complications as quality indicators during the first 30–40 cases, not just operative time. Case-Volume Thresholds and the Case-Clustering Principle The evidence on volume is more nuanced than a simple annual minimum. High-volume surgeons reach early learning curves faster, and only surgeons performing more than 51 cases annually demonstrated early learning curves in one analysis, while lower-volume surgeons showed delayed or absent improvement. But annual volume alone is not the whole story: a low-volume surgeon who clusters cases can achieve proficiency within a comparable number of cases. The programme-level implication is that robotic cases should be concentrated into blocks rather than distributed as one case every few weeks. Clustering preserves team familiarity, reduces setup and breakdown repetition, and accelerates the entire team's learning curve, not just the surgeon's. For credentialing, the emerging evidence-based thresholds are approximately 15–20 cases for initial proficiency and 40 cases for consolidated proficiency in THA, and a similar order of magnitude for TKA depending on platform. A new programme should treat 40 cases as the point at which it can reasonably expect stable efficiency and reliable workflow, and should not judge its success or failure on the first 10 cases. Keeping Early Operative Time and Complications Acceptable The early-phase risk is not primarily a risk of worse accuracy; radiographic accuracy tends to remain stable throughout the learning curve. The early-phase risk is prolonged operative time and workflow disruption, which are themselves associated with infection and other complications. The strategies that most directly mitigate this are: Team training, not just surgeon training. The robotic workflow depends on the scrub nurse, circulating nurse, and assistant as much as the surgeon. Interdisciplinary dry-lab and simulation training involving the OR team is recommended specifically because the safest surgeries are performed by teams that have experience working together. Standardized pre-case checklists and parallel setup. Setup should not be strictly sequential with patient preparation. The registration and docking steps should be rehearsed so that they become predictable, and the team should have a verbal plan for what happens if registration fails or the system requires troubleshooting. A low threshold for conversion early in the curve. The programme should explicitly authorize and expect conversion to manual technique when registration is unreliable, the planned trajectory is unreachable, or the workflow is not progressing safely. Early conversion is not a failure of the learning curve; it is a safety mechanism that prevents prolonged operative time from becoming a complication. Bottom Line The learning curve for robotic arthroplasty is short enough to be manageable but long enough to require deliberate programme design. Time neutrality is typically reached in 7–17 cases depending on platform and procedure, but consolidated proficiency takes 30–40 cases, and the evidence does not support stopping structured oversight at the point of time neutrality. A new programme should require pre-clinical simulation and cadaver training, at least 5–10 proctored live cases with sign-off by a proctor, gradual progression from straightforward to complex cases, clustered case scheduling, and team-based training that includes OR staff. The early-phase focus should be on workflow stability, team familiarity, and a low threshold for conversion, rather than on operative speed. The honest caveat is that the proctoring numbers and volume thresholds come from expert consensus and observational learning-curve studies rather than randomized evidence, and different platforms impose different cognitive and technical demands; the programme should be prepared to extend the supervised phase if the surgeon or the team has not achieved stable workflow by the proctor's assessment.

对于机器人导航下经皮骶髂关节与骨盆环螺钉内固定，与传统透视相比，现有证据在置钉准确度和透视时间上指向了明确且一致的获益，而在神经血管并发症发生率上，两者的表现均处于极低水平，差异难以被现有研究样本量检出。机器人导航的核心价值，在于用可规划的几何确定性，替代了传统透视下高度依赖术者经验的手感与反复影像验证。 🎯 安全骨性通道的置钉准确度：机器人优势明确且具有统计学意义 在骨盆这个解剖结构复杂、骨性通道狭窄且毗邻重要神经血管的区域，置钉准确度的提升是机器人导航最核心的获益。 一项2023年发表的TiRobot机器人对比传统透视的回顾性研究提供了直接的分层数据。在术后CT评估中，机器人组54枚螺钉的置钉准确率（Gertzbein-Robbins A+B级）为92.59%，而传统透视组42枚螺钉的准确率为78.57%，差异具有统计学意义（P<0.05）。更重要的是，传统透视组出现了2枚D级（严重穿破）螺钉，而机器人组为零。另一项2026年的回顾性对比研究也观察到了相似的趋势，机器人组的准确率为94%，传统透视组为62%（p=0.06，接近但未达统计学显著性）。一项电磁导航机器人的研究则报告了94% vs 71% 的准确率对比，差异具有统计学意义。 在更精细的偏差度量上，一项2023年的前瞻性研究（针对骶骨脆性骨折）显示，机器人组在螺钉置入角度偏差（1.96° vs 2.87°）和导针偏差（1.92 mm vs 2.91 mm）上均显著小于徒手透视组（p值分别为0.0145和0.0209），从几何层面量化了精度的提升。一项2022年的Meta分析进一步从证据层面确认，TiRobot辅助固定相比传统透视能带来更优的螺钉准确度（P=0.011）。 这一准确度优势的临床意义在于，它直接作用于“皮质穿破”这一上游事件。一项研究明确指出，机器人辅助显著减少了非计划性的皮质或神经孔侵犯。在骨盆后环这个容错空间极小的区域，将严重穿破的风险压低，本身就是对安全骨性通道最实质性的保护。 ⏱️ 透视时间：机器人导航带来了量级上的压缩 在减少患者与术者的辐射暴露方面，机器人导航的优势是所有结局指标中最为悬殊和一致的。 多项研究的数据在量级上相互印证。一项2023年的研究显示，机器人组的术中透视时间为7.25 ± 1.72秒，而徒手透视组为20.93 ± 5.64秒（p<0.0001）。一项中文研究的数据类似，机器人辅助组的透视时间为7.2 ± 1.5秒/次，显著短于传统组的25.7 ± 7.6秒/次（P<0.05）。2026年的回顾性研究虽然绝对数值更高，但组间差异同样巨大：55.1秒 vs 181.1秒（p=0.053）。 透视时间的压缩并非孤立的技术指标。2022年的Meta分析将“更少的术中透视时间”（P=0.000）与“更少的透视次数”（P=0.000）和“更少的导针尝试次数”（P=0.000）并列报告，揭示了一个清晰的因果链条：机器人导航通过术前或术中三维规划，在置钉前即确定了路径，从而避免了传统透视下依赖反复二维影像验证和调整导针所带来的累积辐射。传统透视下经皮骶髂螺钉置入平均需透视约25次，而导航辅助下仅需约12次，辐射暴露减少约一半。这一获益同时作用于患者和手术团队，是机器人技术最无可争议的临床价值之一。 🩺 神经血管并发症发生率：均处极低水平，差异未被现有证据捕捉 在神经血管并发症这一“硬安全终点”上，需要诚实地指出：现有对比研究普遍报告两组均无或极少发生重大神经血管损伤，未能检测到统计学差异。 一项2023年的TiRobot研究在结果部分明确写道：“两组均无血管损伤、伤口感染或尿路感染导致的后果，也没有机器人诱导的神经损伤并发症”。2026年的回顾性研究同样报告“无重大术中并发症发生”。另一项专门评估机器人手臂辅助骨盆骨折固定的研究，其结论中也明确指出“两组均无神经血管损伤”。 这一“阴性”结果需要被正确解读。它并不意味着机器人与传统透视在安全性上完全等效，而是说明：在骨盆后环螺钉固定这一特定操作中，严重神经血管损伤的基线发生率本身极低，以至于在数十例至上百例样本量的对比研究中，不足以产生统计学上可检出的差异。机器人导航的准确度优势，其安全价值恰恰体现在对“皮质穿破”这一更常见、更敏感的替代终点的改善上。皮质穿破是神经血管损伤的必要前置事件，机器人将严重穿破（D级）的风险从传统透视下的存在降至零，逻辑上降低了下游灾难性并发症的概率，只是这种概率的绝对下降幅度在现有样本量下无法被量化。 💎 一个分层的判断 将三个结局放在一起，机器人导航在骨盆后环螺钉固定中的证据图谱是清晰的： 在准确度和透视时间上，优势是真实、一致且具有统计学意义的。 机器人将置钉准确率从传统透视的约78%—80% 提升至92%—94% 区间，同时将透视时间压缩了约60%—70%（从数十秒/次降至个位数至十几秒/次）。这两个获益直接对应了手术的核心质量与安全指标。 在神经血管并发症上，两者均处于极低水平，现有证据未能显示差异。 机器人导航的安全性论证，不应建立在“降低并发症发生率”这一尚未被证实的终点上，而应建立在“通过减少皮质穿破和导针反复尝试，系统性地降低了发生神经血管损伤的前置风险”这一逻辑链条上。 因此，对于骨盆后环损伤这类解剖容错空间极小的手术，机器人导航的价值定位是：用可规划的几何精度，替代传统透视下反复的二维影像试探与手感依赖，在将置钉准确度提升一个层级的同时，显著削减患者与团队的辐射负担。 其安全获益是准确度提升的逻辑延伸，而非一个可独立量化的并发症发生率下降。

〔从执业骨科医师的视角来看，开展骨科机器人手术的门槛，不是一个可以凭个人意愿跨越的“技术选项”，而是一套由国家强制力背书、以机构资质为前提、以个人“持证”为底线、以团队熟练度为上限的复合准入体系。它的核心逻辑是：机器人手术的精度优势，只有在经过系统性验证的人员和流程中，才可能转化为患者安全。 📜 执业资质：以“限制类技术”为框架的硬性门槛 骨科机器人手术在中国首先是一个法规问题，其次才是技术问题。自2022年起，人工智能辅助治疗技术（涵盖骨科机器人）被纳入国家《限制类医疗技术目录》，这意味着开展该技术的机构和医师必须满足特定的法定条件。 对机构的隐含要求：医师个人资质依附于机构资质。医师所在的医疗机构本身必须具备开展限制类技术的相应条件，并作为培训基地或与培训基地建立协作关系。个人无法脱离机构单独获得“机器人手术资质”。部分培训基地在招生时明确要求医师来自三级医院，这反映了限制类技术对机构平台支撑能力的底层要求。 对医师个人的硬性条件：汇总多家省级以上培训基地的招生简章，核心门槛高度一致： 执业资格：必须持有《医师执业证书》，执业范围为外科专业（骨科方向）。 职称与年限：通常要求主治医师及以上专业技术职称。部分基地的要求更为严格，例如西安市红会医院要求副高及以上，或主治医师满5年，且具备三甲医院骨科10年以上临床工作经验；北京友谊医院则要求主治医师具备5年以上骨科或相关外科经验。少数基地（如青岛大学附属医院）对特定亚专业方向（脊柱、关节）的要求相对宽松，从事相关专业2年以上并获主治医师职称即可，但这不是主流。 执业记录：部分基地明确排除近3年发生负完全或主要责任的二级以上医疗事故者。 “持证上岗”是底线：完成培训并考核合格后，医师将获得由省级卫生健康行政部门认证的培训基地颁发的《限制类医疗技术临床应用规范化培训合格证书》。这份证书是合法开展机器人手术的前提，没有“先做再补”的灰色空间。 🎓 专项培训：一个至少6个月、以“病例数”为硬指标的强制过程 培训绝非厂商装机时的几天“操作带教”所能替代。国家规范框架下，一个被普遍遵循的完整培训周期不少于6个月，其结构可以概括为“理论—模拟—动物—临床”的递进链条。 可量化的最低完成标准，在多家基地的招生简章中呈现出高度趋同性： 理论学习：完成20学时以上的课程并通过考核，内容涵盖法律法规、伦理、系统原理与手术规划。 模拟与动物训练：在模拟器上掌握系统装卸、基本控制与精准操作；在动物模型上完成操作训练，部分基地要求动物训练10例以上。 临床实践（核心环节）：在上级医师指导下，参与完成10例以上不同类别的机器人辅助手术，并参与10例以上患者的全过程管理（含适应证评估、风险预案、术后处理）。 考核与认证：完成上述内容后，通过基地组织的理论与实操考核，获得省级认证的合格证书。 值得注意的是，一些培训基地（如北京世纪坛医院）提供“基础培训”（1—2天集中培训，获结业证书）与“完整资质培训”（叠加6个月临床实践，获限制类技术合格证书）的分阶段路径。这实际上区分了“了解”与“合法独立开展”两种不同的目标，对于计划实际开展手术的医师而言，只有后者才具有准入意义。 ⏳ 上手周期：法规的“最低时限”与临床的“熟练拐点”是两回事 6个月的培训周期解决的是合法性与最低能力基线，但一个外科医生真正达到流畅、高效、并发症可控的“熟练”状态，需要的是病例量的积累，而这个数字因部位和系统而异。 关节（TKA/THA）：学习曲线的证据最为集中。机器人TKA达到操作时间平台期所需的病例数，不同系统报道在6—17例之间；CUSUM分析显示，11例即可实现操作时间的优化。一项前瞻性研究显示，每累积30例，平均手术时间有可测量的下降（97.6→86.6→76.7分钟）。对于机器人THA，达到胜任（competency）通常需要15—17例，而达到巩固熟练（consolidated proficiency）则需要38—43例，有研究据此建议将约40例作为技术辅助THA的资质认证病例量参考。 脊柱：脊柱机器人的上手周期涉及设备操作与手术决策两个层面。一项针对手术室巡回护士使用天玑机器人进行模具操作的研究显示，掌握设备操作技能至少需要8例模拟操作。对于外科医生，韩国一项针对神经外科住院医师的试点研究显示，在模型和导师监督下完成28例手术后，其椎弓根螺钉的临床可接受置入率达到96.99%。但这远非“熟练”的终点——脊柱手术的复杂性在于决策与并发症处理，其学习曲线远长于单纯的器械操作。 一个必须诚实的界定：上述“病例数”来自特定系统、特定研究设计和特定术者背景，不能直接等同于“任何医生做满这个数就自动熟练”。它们提供的是排程与认证的参考锚点，而非保证。真正的熟练度取决于病例的连续性与多样性、是否有结构化反馈，以及术者是否主动进行刻意练习。6个月的法定培训期内完成的10例，只是暴露于技术，不足以形成稳定的肌肉记忆与决策直觉。 💎 一个需要放在职业规划里的判断 对于一名计划开展骨科机器人手术的医师，这套体系意味着：你首先需要在一家具备限制类技术开展条件的机构执业，以主治医师（通常）的身份，争取单位同意，脱产或半脱产进入一家省级认证培训基地，完成至少6个月、以20学时理论和10例临床实践为硬指标的系统训练，取得省级合格证书。此后，在独立开展的初期，你仍将经历一个以病例数（关节约11—40例，脊柱视复杂度而定）为标志的、操作时间与决策信心逐步稳定的爬坡期。 这套门槛的严厉程度，本质上反映了一个审慎的临床判断：机器人手术的“精准”是一种系统性的精准，它依赖于术者对规划逻辑的理解、对系统局限的认知（如力反馈缺失的补偿策略），以及在异常发生时（如Q5所述的中转开放）的团队协同能力。缩短或绕过这个训练周期，所冒的风险不是“做得慢一点”，而是在系统给出错误确定性的时刻，术者缺乏识别它的能力。

Yes—limitations in robotic-arm reach and angular range can affect surgery in unusual patient positions and deep orthopedic sites. From an orthopedic surgical perspective, the key issue is whether the instrument can reach the target at the required angle, with adequate clearance and safe exposure. I am not a practicing surgeon; this is an evidence-informed clinical perspective. Patient positioning: Lateral, prone, or markedly tilted positions change the relationship between the patient, operating table, and robot. A feasible trajectory may become obstructed by the table, positioning supports, or the patient’s body. This makes initial setup important: for example, Stryker’s hip workflow explicitly requires checking reamer reach before securing the robotic base. Stryker surgical workflow guide Deep surgical sites: Depth alone does not make robotic surgery unsuitable. The practical concern is the combination of depth, a narrow operative corridor, soft-tissue bulk, and the required instrument angle. A robotic arm may reach the region but lack sufficient clearance to complete the planned movement safely. Robotic guidance does not replace adequate surgical exposure. Clinical response: The team should assess reach and the full instrument path before proceeding, optimize positioning and exposure, and maintain tracking visibility. If safe access remains inadequate, conventional instruments or another suitable technique may be necessary. These are practical implications of the mechanical constraints, rather than evidence that every difficult position produces worse outcomes. The limitation is system- and procedure-specific. I cannot give a universal maximum depth or angular cutoff, or a reliable frequency of access-related conversion, without knowing the robot, instruments, and operation. Standard lateral or prone positioning is not inherently incompatible with robotic assistance.

从骨科临床应急处置角度，**转为常规手术已有明确的技术路径，但不能笼统认为所有设备、医院和复杂急症都能实现“无缝切换”。**撤离机械臂与控制血管、神经损伤是两件事：前者取决于设备和团队训练，后者更取决于损伤部位、暴露条件及救治能力。 1．哪些方面已经比较明确？ 常见骨科机器人主要承担定位、导向或骨切削，医生通常就在患者旁，许多步骤本身仍由医生手工完成。因此，停止机器人辅助后，可以根据情况继续采用常规器械、透视辅助，或扩大切口进行开放处理，并非所有情况都需要重新开始手术。 胸腰椎机器人置钉指南明确要求，术者应具备传统手术经验，并能在机器人无法正常工作时转换为常规手术。不过，这一要求本身并不能证明各中心处理重大血管、神经损伤的能力完全一致。胸腰椎机器人置钉指南 2．真正的应急衔接应包含什么？ **立即停止可能继续造成损伤的操作。**按具体设备流程停机、解除约束并移开妨碍救治的机械臂。急停不等于器械自动安全退出；仍在骨内或组织内的器械必须受控处理。 **救治与设备撤离并行。**术者处理损伤，麻醉团队维持循环、氧合并按需启动输血，指定人员负责机械臂和设备，避免所有人都等待“撤机完成”。 **必要时改变暴露和手术方式。**扩大切口、改用开放入路，或启动血管外科、介入、神经外科等支援。转为“徒手”只是手段，目标是及时控制损伤。 **常规器械和备用影像应能及时使用。**不能发生机器人停用后，才寻找兼容器械、止血设备或透视设备的情况。 3．血管损伤和神经损伤的转换重点不同。 血管损伤首先涉及出血控制与循环稳定。尤其脊柱前方、盆腔或腹膜后的大血管损伤，原有切口可能无法提供有效暴露，可能需要另一入路或介入治疗。不能盲目拔除可能暂时封堵破口的导针、螺钉或器械，应在具备控制出血的条件下制定处理方案。 疑似神经损伤则需立即停止相关操作，同时排查机械压迫、牵拉、血肿及麻醉、生理因素；依据情况进行影像检查、器械调整或减压。并非每一次神经监测报警都代表永久损伤，也并非所有神经损伤都能靠撤除螺钉立即恢复。 4．如何判断一家医院的方案是否成熟？ 比“能否切换”更有意义的是：是否有针对该型号机器人的书面流程、明确分工及模拟演练，是否备有常规手术器械，以及能否及时获得输血、血管修复或介入支援。团队还应分别评估停止危险操作、获得有效暴露、完成止血或减压所需的时间，而不能只统计机械臂撤离时间。 **目前缺乏足够的骨科专属、多中心数据，支持统一承诺“多少秒完成转换”或某一固定抢救成功率。**因此，更准确的结论是：常规转换路径已建立，重大急症中的可靠衔接仍须由具体医院、设备和团队的演练与救治能力来保证。

From the perspective of a practicing spine surgeon, the most useful way to define indications and contraindications for robot-guided spine surgery is not as a static list of diagnoses, but as a continuous assessment of two independent questions: (1) Is the robotic workflow technically feasible—can registration and tracking be achieved reliably? (2) Does the precision advantage carry meaningful marginal clinical value for this specific pathology, compared with what navigation or freehand technique can already achieve? A condition can be a strong indication on the first question and a weak one on the second, or vice versa. The five scenarios you name sit at different points on that two-dimensional map. Severe scoliosis: a feasibility success, with a caveat about marginal value Technical feasibility is well supported. A 2025 retrospective comparative study applied explicit severity criteria—Cobb angle >80°, flexibility <25%, or focal kyphosis >90°—to define severe complex deformity (SCD) and compared robotic-assisted screw placement in SCD versus non-severe deformity (NSD). The results showed no significant difference in perfect screw placement rate (90.60% vs. 92.18%, p=0.3997) or major curve correction rate (66.34% vs. 71.05%), with comparable complication rates (5.88% vs. 4.76%). Other series report robotic screw accuracy of 96.0% (G&R A/B) in adult degenerative scoliosis and 95.7% for S2AI screws, with no placement-related complications. This supports a defensible position: robotics maintains accuracy in severe deformity rather than degrading, which is clinically important because freehand landmark reliability is precisely what is compromised in these cases. The caveat is marginal value, not feasibility. The SCD study showed that patients with severe deformity had significantly longer hospital stays (27.65 vs. 21.19 days) despite comparable operative time and blood loss. This suggests the robotic advantage is in not losing accuracy, rather than in producing a measurable outcome benefit that offsets the broader burden of severe deformity surgery. I would characterize severe scoliosis as a strong technical indication where the robot preserves performance, but not as a condition where the robot has been shown to improve the overall clinical trajectory beyond what expert navigation-assisted technique can achieve. The exclusion criteria in robotic scoliosis trials are also instructive: Scheuermann's disease, active infection or malignancy, primary bone abnormalities such as osteogenesis imperfecta, and medical intolerance of correction surgery are disease-level exclusions independent of the robot. High-grade spondylolisthesis: a focused, anatomy-specific indication The evidence here is narrower but directionally clearer. A 2025 case series of Meyerding III–IV high-grade spondylolisthesis treated with robotic-guided posterior transdiscal (PTD) fixation reported successful screw placement as planned in all cases, with no intraoperative revisions, no perioperative complications, and no neurologic deficits, alongside significant improvements in VAS and ODI at a mean 12-month follow-up and operative times of 60–75 minutes. The authors framed the value as enhancing accuracy and safety "in challenging anatomy" by reducing reliance on fluoroscopy and minimizing trajectory deviation. A separate case series of robotic-assisted Bohlman technique for high-grade L5-S1 isthmic spondylolisthesis similarly described the approach as promising. The indication should be framed precisely: robotic guidance is not indicated for the reduction maneuver itself, and the Chinese expert consensus explicitly notes that for severe slips or difficult reduction, forcing reduction is not mandatory. The robotic value is in reliable transdiscal or pedicle screw instrumentation across a distorted lumbosacral junction, not in solving the biomechanical problem of the slip. High-grade spondylolisthesis is therefore a moderate-strength, anatomy-specific indication: the robot helps place hardware where trajectories are difficult, but the surgeon remains responsible for reduction strategy and fusion biology. The evidence base is preliminary case series, not comparative trials. Dysplastic pedicles: the clearest relative indication in the degenerative spine This is arguably the least controversial of the five. The 2026 Chinese expert consensus on robot-assisted TLIF explicitly identifies "slender pedicles, anatomical variation, and revision surgery" as the settings where robotics offers "great advantages" compared with conventional fluoroscopic TLIF. The consensus lists slender pedicles, spinal variation/deformity, and multi-level fusion as particularly suitable. Published evidence on robot-guided screw placement in anatomically challenging cases such as dysplastic pedicles reports accuracy rates of around 98% within the pedicle or with cortical encroachment <2 mm. One important technical caveat from the pediatric deformity literature: decreased accuracy was noted when the preoperative plan included screw placement directly overlying the pedicle cortex, meaning the planning itself must respect the dysplastic anatomy rather than simply assuming the robot will compensate. Dysplastic pedicles are therefore a strong relative indication on both dimensions: technically feasible with high accuracy, and the marginal value over freehand is highest precisely where the margin for error is narrowest. The limitation is that the evidence is concentrated in case series and expert consensus rather than large comparative trials, and the planning quality remains surgeon-dependent. Osteoporosis: the most nuanced of the five, with two distinct failure modes Osteoporosis is not a single contraindication but a set of related technical and biological risks that must be managed separately. Registration and navigation accuracy. Severe osteoporosis is associated with failure of matching and unsatisfactory robot-assisted screw placement. A risk-factor analysis identified severe osteoporosis (T < −3.5) as an independent risk factor for malposition, along with severe vertebral rotation (Nash-Moe III–IV) and severe facet degeneration; two Grade E screws in that series carried all three risk factors. The mechanism is that poor bone quality can degrade registration fidelity and increase the likelihood of cortical breach even under robotic guidance. Screw purchase and fixation failure. This is a biological limitation that robotics does not solve. The Chinese RA-TLIF consensus states that the procedure is "not suitable for patients with severe osteoporosis with poor screw purchase". A relative contraindication designation for osteoporosis is standard in pedicle screw labeling because it may result in insufficient correction and compromised mechanical stability. The robot improves trajectory accuracy but does not improve bone–metal interface strength. How to manage it rather than simply exclude it. The practical framework is stratification by severity and adjunctive strategy. For T-scores ≤ −3.5, the consensus-aligned approach is preoperative planning for cement augmentation or cortical screws to improve anchorage, combined with intraoperative image guidance and manual adjustment. The RA-TLIF consensus recommends DXA assessment, preoperative anti-osteoporosis treatment, and consideration of bone cement augmentation intraoperatively. Some systems incorporate real-time pressure monitoring that shuts down when abnormal resistance is encountered in osteoporotic bone, reducing the risk of uncontrolled breach. Bone-mounted robotic systems have reported acceptable screw loosening rates in osteoporotic patients compared with normal-BMD controls, suggesting that with appropriate technique the technology is usable. I would therefore define osteoporosis as a severity-graded relative contraindication: mild-to-moderate osteoporosis is not a contraindication and may still benefit from robotic trajectory precision; severe osteoporosis (T < −3.5) with poor predicted purchase is a relative contraindication requiring either cement augmentation, cortical screw strategy, or a decision to avoid instrumentation. The absolute contraindication is not osteoporosis itself but bone so poor that neither standard nor augmented fixation can achieve stable purchase. Revision surgery with existing instrumentation: a strong indication conditional on registration strategy The 2026 Chinese consensus identifies revision surgery as a setting of "great advantage" for robotics, alongside slender pedicles and anatomical variation. A scoping review of robotic assistance in revision spine surgery reported accurate pedicle screw placement in 96.1% to 99.8% of screws, exceeding conventional computer-assisted navigation. A clinical commentary on complex spinal revision similarly notes that robotic technology is "particularly valuable" because it allows careful navigation around existing hardware and previously operated areas. The critical qualification is registration strategy. Existing instrumentation can obscure bony landmarks, generate CT artifact, and interfere with tracker placement or surface registration. The literature describes successful use of synthetic CT (sCT) generated from MRI for preoperative planning and intraoperative navigation in patients with existing instrumentation, yielding results comparable to conventional CT in cadaveric morphometric analysis and robot-assisted lumbosacral screw placement. Newer frameless registration systems report target registration error of 0.61 mm and maximum tool-tip error of 1.40 mm without bone-mounted hardware or intraoperative imaging, which is directly relevant to revision cases where tracker placement is constrained. Revision with instrumentation is therefore a strong indication conditional on a hardware-specific registration plan. The robot does not automatically solve revision anatomy; it requires the team to choose a registration method (sCT, intraoperative 3D imaging, or frameless registration) that can accommodate the hardware. If no reliable registration pathway exists, the case reverts to a navigation or freehand problem. A synthesis: the two-axis framework and the role of general contraindications Scenario Technical feasibility Marginal clinical value over navigation/freehand Net designation Severe scoliosis High (accuracy preserved) Moderate (longer stays; comparable correction) Strong technical indication, outcome benefit unproven High-grade spondylolisthesis High for hardware placement; reduction is surgeon-dependent Moderate (anatomy-specific) Moderate indication, preliminary evidence Dysplastic pedicles High (~98% accuracy) High (narrowest margin for error) Strong relative indication Osteoporosis Reduced at T < −3.5 (registration and breach risk) Variable; purchase is a biological limit Severity-graded relative contraindication Revision with hardware Conditional on registration strategy High (distorted anatomy, existing implants) Strong indication with a registration prerequisite Alongside these condition-specific assessments, there are general contraindications that apply regardless of diagnosis: systemic disease precluding tolerance of robotic surgery, and inability to place the tracker or obtain navigation images adequate for the surgical requirement. Active infection at the operative site, certain metabolic disorders affecting osteogenesis, and severe obesity (BMI >40 as a relative contraindication in the RA-TLIF consensus) are also relevant. These are not substitutes for the condition-specific analysis; they are an additional filter. What I would tell a colleague The honest bottom line is this: the robot's clearest, best-evidenced role is in preserving accuracy where anatomy is distorted or narrow—dysplastic pedicles, revision with hardware, and severe deformity—because that is where freehand and even navigation become least reliable. For osteoporosis, the robot improves trajectory precision but does not solve purchase; the indication must be graded by severity and paired with cement or cortical-screw strategy. For high-grade spondylolisthesis, the robot helps with hardware, not with reduction. And for severe scoliosis, the robot maintains performance but has not been shown to improve the overall clinical trajectory. The evidence behind several of these designations is case series and expert consensus rather than large comparative trials, and I would present it as such. The most important practical principle is that feasibility is not the same as value, and a condition should not be called an indication simply because the robot can be docked and a screw can be placed.

I can frame this from a surgeon’s clinical perspective, although I am not a practicing orthopedic surgeon. The main advantage of orthopedic robots is the ability to translate a patient-specific surgical plan into more consistent bone cuts and implant trajectories, while giving the surgeon a three-dimensional map of anatomy that may be difficult to see directly. The strength of that advantage varies by procedure and platform. More precise planning and execution in complex bone and joint anatomy.
Depending on the system, CT imaging or intraoperative landmark mapping creates a patient-specific model. This allows the surgeon to plan implant size, position, and bone removal rather than relying solely on standard guides and visible landmarks. Some systems provide haptic boundaries—virtual limits that constrain a saw or burr to the planned resection. This can be especially useful when deformity makes conventional landmarks less reliable. These capabilities are platform-specific. AAOS In knee replacement, the practical benefit is fewer deviations from the intended component position. However, improved accuracy is not universal across every measurement: one randomized trial found fewer alignment outliers with robotics, while another found significant advantages mainly in sagittal component alignment. I would therefore describe robotics as improving consistency, rather than guaranteeing a perfect reconstruction. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov More controlled instrumentation in narrow spinal corridors.
For pedicle screws, robotic guidance helps reproduce a planned entry point and trajectory through a narrow bony passage. Clinically, that matters because small deviations can breach the pedicle near neural or vascular structures. In one randomized trial involving 234 patients, 95.3% of robot-assisted screws were completely within the pedicle, compared with 86.1% using conventional fluoroscopy-assisted placement. Those figures describe one system and study; they are not a universal performance guarantee. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Better spatial information, rather than automatically better optical vision.
The established visualization benefit is a registered anatomical model and planned instrument path displayed alongside the operative workflow. This helps the surgeon understand bone geometry and trajectories beyond the exposed surface. Importantly, much of this benefit comes from the accompanying imaging and navigation; the robot adds physical guidance or control. It should not be confused with a live, magnified view of every nerve, vessel, or soft-tissue structure. AAOS Compared with conventional arthroscopy, the advantages are less established.
Arthroscopy already provides magnified views inside a joint. Emerging robotic systems aim to add camera stability, improved depth perception, and more reproducible drilling or bone resection. However, the evidence remains substantially less mature than for joint replacement and spinal instrumentation, with much of the reported work involving preclinical or cadaveric studies. I would not confidently claim that robotic arthroscopy routinely provides superior visualization or clinical outcomes. PubMed From a clinical decision-making standpoint, greater technical accuracy does not necessarily mean less pain, better function, or longer implant survival. AAOS guidance identifies no clear short-term difference in function, outcomes, or complications between robotic and conventional total knee replacement. The surgeon still has to select the appropriate target and judge whether the reconstruction is suitable for the patient. aaos.org

Robotic guidance can improve thoracic and lumbar pedicle screw accuracy, but there is no single percentage improvement that applies to every system or surgical setting. Its usefulness in deformity and revision surgery is supported by evidence; a consistently greater advantage in those settings remains unproven. For surgical interpretation, “accuracy” needs a definition: Gertzbein–Robbins grade A means no pedicle cortical breach; grades A+B include breaches under 2 mm and are commonly classified as clinically acceptable. That classification does not guarantee safety for every individual screw. Representative comparative results are: Study and setting Robotic guidance Freehand with fluoroscopy Absolute improvement Randomized trial: 234 patients, 1,116 thoracolumbar screws—grade A 95.3% 86.1% 9.2 percentage points Same trial—grades A+B 98.7% 93.5% 5.2 percentage points Retrospective study: 80 patients—grades A+B 99.4% 90.1% 9.3 percentage points These are study-specific results, rather than a pooled estimate. Randomized trial, retrospective comparison. Results also depend on robot generation and technique: an early randomized lumbar/sacral trial actually favored freehand placement, demonstrating that robotic superiority is not universal. Earlier randomized trial In spinal deformity, the clinical rationale is strong: rotated vertebrae and abnormal pedicles make conventional landmarks harder to interpret. However, difficulty alone does not establish a larger robotic benefit. A prospective study found comparable robotic accuracy across surgeons with differing experience, but this does not directly prove that deformity increases the advantage over freehand placement. Prospective study In revision surgery, a retrospective comparison of 81 patients reported grade-A placement in 93.6% versus 87.2% of screws, favoring robotics by approximately 6.5 percentage points. Grades A+B were approximately 98.5% versus 96.9%, a smaller difference of 1.6 points. This supports usefulness in revision surgery, but does not establish a greater benefit than in primary surgery. Revision-surgery study From a surgical decision-making perspective, robotics is particularly attractive when landmarks are distorted. Nevertheless, I would not promise a larger accuracy gain in complex cases, or an equivalent reduction in neurological injury. Thoracic and lumbar results should also be assessed separately where possible; combined thoracolumbar figures can conceal important differences in anatomy and baseline risk.

Improved alignment has not yet translated into a consistent reduction in all-cause revision or better long-term patient-reported outcomes. Robotic arthroplasty generally executes the surgical plan more precisely, but the clinical evidence differs by joint, procedure and robotic generation. Evidence Main finding Surgical interpretation Total knee arthroplasty: US registry Among 142,550 TKAs, linked two-year revision rates were 1.2% in both groups; adjusted odds ratio 1.0 (95% CI 0.8–1.3). No demonstrated early revision advantage. The population was aged ≥65 years. Revision for dislocation was lower: 0.3% versus 0.6%, adjusted hazard ratio 0.5. A potentially meaningful, cause-specific benefit, but not proof of improved overall implant survival or causation. The long-term TKA trial found no functional advantage, and the contemporary multicentre RACER-Knee randomized trial found no clinically meaningful patient benefit at 12 months. RACER-Knee trial From an orthopaedic surgical perspective, alignment is one contributor to success alongside soft-tissue balance, fixation, implant design, infection risk and patient factors. Furthermore, accurately achieving a planned alignment does not establish that the selected target was optimal for that patient. I would counsel patients that robotics offers more reproducible execution, with a possible reduction in selected failure mechanisms, but cannot currently promise a longer-lasting implant. Robust comparative 10–15-year evidence for today’s platforms remains limited. Registry associations also retain potential confounding from surgeon experience, implant choice and patient selection.

Compared with free-hand fluoroscopic techniques, robotic guidance consistently and significantly improves the accuracy of thoracolumbar pedicle screw placement, and this advantage is not merely statistically significant but magnified in complex settings such as spinal deformity and revision surgery, precisely where anatomical landmarks are distorted and the consequences of misplacement are most severe. 📊 The Baseline Advantage: Fewer Critical Breaches and Revisions The most robust evidence comes from a 2025 meta-analysis of 18 studies (1,566 patients) comparing robot-assisted surgery (RS) with fluoroscopy-assisted surgery (FS). The key finding is not simply that robots are “more accurate” in a binary sense, but that they specifically reduce the most dangerous errors: Major cortical violations (Gertzbein D–E grades): FS had significantly worse accuracy for these severe breaches, with an odds ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.28–0.80) favoring robotics. In practical terms, the robot roughly halves the odds of a screw deviating far enough outside the pedicle to threaten neural or vascular structures. Revision surgery due to screw mispositioning: This is the hard clinical endpoint that matters most to a surgeon. The need for revision was significantly lower in the robotic group, with an OR of 0.28 (95% CI 0.17–0.48). This means that when a screw is placed with robotic guidance, the likelihood that it will need to be taken back to the operating room for repositioning is roughly one-quarter of that with free-hand fluoroscopy. A separate network meta-analysis of thoracolumbar fracture surgery reinforced the safety signal, finding that robot-assisted percutaneous fixation had the lowest overall complication risk (SUCRA 94.9%) among all techniques compared, including free-hand and conventional fluoroscopy. 🦴 The Complex-Setting Amplification: Deformity and Revision The question of whether the advantage is greater in complex settings is clinically critical, because these are the cases where free-hand fluoroscopy is least reliable. The evidence supports a clear “yes,” with an important nuance about which complexity matters most. Spinal Deformity (Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis and Adult Degenerative Scoliosis). In deformity surgery, normal pedicle anatomy is rotated, and the safe corridor is often narrowed. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of posterior spinal fusion in scoliosis found that robot-assisted (RA) placement had significantly greater odds of accurate screw placement compared with conventional free-hand (CF) technique, with an OR of 3.06 (95% CI 1.79–5.23). The same review showed RA was also superior to navigation (OR 2.02 vs. NS). A narrative review of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis quantified the absolute misplacement rates: 0.4–7.2% for robotics, compared with 1.5–50.7% for free-hand technique. The upper bound of the free-hand range (50.7%) is striking and reflects the reality that in severe deformity, free-hand placement without navigation can be exceptionally unreliable. The review explicitly recommends dedicating robotic and computed navigation to complex deformities or revisions with altered landmarks, precisely because these are the scenarios where the technology’s relative benefit is largest. Revision Surgery. The evidence here is more nuanced. A 2026 review of robotic lumbar fusion notes that the literature supports robotics as an adjunct for “difficult screw placement or complex workflow” cases, which includes revision surgery, but it also cautions that the impact on outcomes like revision rates and cost-effectiveness is inconsistent. A specific study of 81 revision patients found that the robotic group achieved 250/267 Grade A screws versus 251/288 in the free-hand group—a difference that is not as dramatic as the deformity data. This suggests that while robotics is useful in revision, the accuracy advantage may be less pronounced than in primary deformity cases. The likely reason is that in revision surgery, the primary challenge is often soft-tissue exposure and altered bony anatomy from previous hardware, rather than the pure trajectory geometry that robotics excels at controlling. ⚠️ An Important Clinical Caveat: Accuracy Does Not Automatically Equal Superior Outcomes As a practicing surgeon, I must add a critical qualifier. The meta-analyses show a clear process advantage—fewer cortical breaches and fewer revision surgeries for misplacement. However, a 2026 Chinese review concluded that while the evidence supports improved screw accuracy and reduced surgeon radiation exposure, the impact on overall patient-reported outcomes, complication rates beyond screw revision, and cost-effectiveness remains inconsistent. In other words, the robot helps you place the screw correctly, but whether that translates into a measurably better functional result for every patient is not yet definitively proven in the literature. Furthermore, the robotics advantage in deformity comes with a documented trade-off: significantly longer operative time compared with both navigation and free-hand techniques. 💎 Bottom Line Yes, robotic guidance meaningfully improves thoracolumbar pedicle screw accuracy versus free-hand fluoroscopy, and this advantage is amplified in complex deformity surgery. The most defensible quantification is a halving of the odds of major cortical breach and a reduction to roughly one-quarter of the odds of revision for screw mispositioning in the general thoracolumbar population. In scoliosis deformity, the accuracy odds ratio in favor of robotics versus free-hand rises to 3.06, with absolute misplacement rates dropping from a free-hand range that can reach 50% down to under 7%. In revision surgery, robotics remains a valuable adjunct for difficult workflows, but the accuracy advantage is more modest and the evidence on downstream outcomes is less consistent. The technology’s value is therefore best framed not as a universal upgrade for every pedicle screw, but as a targeted precision tool whose return on investment is highest precisely in the complex, distorted anatomy where free-hand technique is most likely to fail.

There is no single reliable “extra time” figure: the additional time depends on the procedure, robotic platform, team experience, and whether setup is performed in parallel with other work. Registration is usually intraoperative; preoperative imaging and planning should be counted separately from time under anaesthesia. The following published examples provide useful benchmarks, but they are not interchangeable or additive: Component Reported time Interpretation Robotic-arm setup for knee replacement Median 10 minutes, range 6–19 minutes, in one early-adoption study. This is setup duration, not necessarily an equivalent increase in surgical time if performed before patient arrival or alongside other preparation. Bone registration for knee replacement Approximately 4–5 minutes in one series; another reported about 2 minutes per bone. Tracker placement, planning adjustments, and verification may be counted separately. Total additional surgical time for knee replacement One multicentre randomized trial reported 111.9 versus 85.0 minutes, approximately 27 minutes longer with robotics. This measures the overall difference, not just registration and setup. Other platforms and experienced teams may achieve smaller differences. Hip replacement learning effect One fluoroscopy-based robotic series decreased from 44.3 to 38.0 minutes after its initial learning phase. This is a 6-minute improvement within robotic cases, not a robotic-versus-manual comparison. Spinal robotic setup/registration One study reported setup decreasing from 24 to 17 minutes; another reported mean registration/system setup of 27.7 minutes. Definitions differ. These figures cannot be interpreted as the net additional duration of the complete spinal operation. Sources: knee setup and registration studies, the knee randomized trial, and procedure-specific hip and spine workflow studies. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Troubleshooting is the least predictable component. There is insufficient consistently reported evidence to assign a dependable average “debugging allowance.” In one knee study, femoral registration took 23 minutes in a case requiring repeated registration because the tracker was moving. This illustrates an occasional substantial delay, rather than a typical registration time. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov From an operating-room management perspective, I would optimise workflow in six ways: Complete preparation before the operating list. Confirm imaging quality, correct patient and side, uploaded plans, compatible implants, instruments, and equipment readiness. Resolve missing data before anaesthesia. Standardise room layout and team roles. Establish reproducible positions for the robot, imaging equipment, tracking camera, patient, and instrument tables. Assign responsibility for setup, registration support, and troubleshooting. Perform independent tasks in parallel. Where staffing, sterility, and device instructions permit, prepare equipment while anaesthetic and patient preparation proceed. This reduces elapsed room time without rushing surgical steps. Prioritise reliable first-pass registration. Secure reference arrays, maintain tracking visibility, acquire landmarks carefully, and verify accuracy. Repeating an unreliable registration is necessary; preventing the initial failure is the efficiency opportunity. Train the whole team and maintain continuity during adoption. Published series found operative-time learning milestones at approximately 16–30 knee cases, 12 hip cases, and 25 spine cases. These are study-specific efficiency milestones—not universal competence thresholds. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Audit each stage and establish a conversion pathway. Record room entry-to-exit, incision-to-closure, setup, registration, repeat imaging, troubleshooting, and turnover separately. Keep conventional instruments available and define when unresolved technical problems warrant conversion; there is no universally appropriate minute-based cutoff. For scheduling, I would use a conservative initial allowance and then replace it with local, procedure-specific timing data—including delays, not just averages. Faster cutting or screw insertion does not necessarily mean a shorter operating-room episode, and efficiency should never come from omitting registration checks or necessary imaging.

From the perspective of a practicing arthroplasty surgeon, the question of who benefits most from robotic assistance and which conditions remain relative contraindications is fundamentally the same question viewed from two directions. The patients who derive the greatest benefit are those in whom the conventional instrument chain is most likely to fail to restore alignment, balance, or component position reliably—and the conditions that remain relative contraindications are those in which the robot's geometric precision is overmatched by a more fundamental biomechanical or soft-tissue problem that precision alone cannot solve. The robot addresses "placing it accurately"; it does not address "getting it in," "balancing it," or "restoring a competent soft-tissue envelope." 🦵 Total Knee Arthroplasty: Who Benefits Most Severe coronal deformity (marked varus or valgus) is the group with the most consistent evidence of benefit. A 2026 systematic review of robotic-assisted TKA in complex primary and revision cases found that robotic assistance consistently restored coronal alignment, with the greatest improvements observed in moderate-to-severe varus and valgus deformities. Comparative studies specifically in these deformity strata showed that robotic-assisted TKA produced fewer coronal alignment outliers compared with conventional techniques. The same review noted that robotic systems reduced the need for extensive soft-tissue releases and enabled reliable early functional recovery—a clinically meaningful advantage, because extensive releases in severe deformity are themselves a source of morbidity and instability. One systematic review of moderate-to-severe coronal deformity quantified the residual limitation honestly: only 64% (82/129) of severe varus knees achieved neutral alignment within ±3°, while all 7 severe valgus knees were corrected to neutral—a reminder that robotic assistance improves but does not guarantee correction at the extremes. Flexion contracture ≥10° is a second group in which robotic TKA with functional alignment has demonstrably offset the historical disadvantage. A comparative study of robotic TKA using functional alignment principles stratified patients by intraoperative flexion contracture ≥10° versus <10°. Patients with contracture achieved comparable mid-term outcomes and early survivorship to those without contracture; aseptic survivorship was 100% in the contracture group versus 99.32% in controls (p = 0.59), and all-cause revision rates were similar. A separate study demonstrated that image-based robotic TKA preserves the knee joint line level even in advanced fixed flexion deformities when combined with functional alignment, minimizing joint-line displacement and bone loss. This matters because the conventional management of flexion contracture—extensive posterior release and distal femoral recut—carries its own risks, including mid-flexion instability and excessive resection when deformity exceeds 20°. Retained hardware and prior surgery around the knee is a third category of potential benefit, but the evidence is weaker. A 2026 scoping review describes robotic TKA in post-traumatic and previously operated knees as differing substantially from routine primary TKA, because retained implants, extra-articular deformity, distorted landmarks, bone defects, scarred soft tissues, and infection risk may all compromise standard instrumentation and implant positioning. CT-based or imageless planning can define deformity, anticipate implant–hardware conflicts, guide bone resection, and quantify gap balance, and the current literature supports technical feasibility and potential workflow advantages in carefully selected cases, particularly when landmarks are distorted. But the same review states plainly that the available evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, consisting mainly of case reports, small case series, and early retrospective cohorts, and that current data do not establish improved survivorship, lower infection risk, better patient-reported outcomes, or cost-effectiveness. For prior high tibial osteotomy specifically, robotic TKA has been associated with fewer lateral releases (30% versus 54%) and comparable short-term outcomes, but this is a process advantage rather than a proven outcome advantage. 🦵 TKA: Relative Contraindications and Conditions Requiring Caution Fixed flexion deformity beyond the range that functional alignment can compensate, and collateral ligament insufficiency, are the most clearly articulated relative contraindications. A review of functional alignment in valgus knees states that the strategy should be applied cautiously when valgus deformity is associated with medial collateral ligament incompetence, severe fixed lateral contracture, major bone loss, extra-articular deformity, neuromuscular imbalance, patellar instability, or a requirement for constrained fixation. The critical limitation is stated directly: "A robot can quantify the deformity but cannot restore a deficient ligament.". This is the cleanest statement of the boundary between what robotics solves and what it does not: the robot provides geometric control of bone cuts and component position, but it cannot reconstruct a incompetent ligament or substitute for a constrained implant when the soft-tissue envelope is fundamentally deficient. Severe stiffness should not be treated as an absolute contraindication, but the learning curve is a genuine risk modifier. A large propensity-matched study of 25,611 primary TKAs found that robotic-assisted TKA had a numerically higher but non-significant trend toward manipulation under anesthesia (OR 1.24, P = 0.12). However, learning-curve analysis identified a breakpoint at case 11.8, with MUA rates of 5.2% before the learning phase versus 2.9% after (P = 0.042); the learning phase was independently associated with a 2.13-fold increase in MUA risk (95% CI 1.02–4.45, P = 0.043). After excluding early cases, robotic TKA showed no increased risk (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.74–1.29). The implication is that stiffness risk is concentrated in the surgeon's early robotic experience, not in the technology itself; for a patient with pre-existing stiffness, the relevant question is not "robotic or manual" but whether the surgeon has progressed beyond the adoption phase. Ankylosis and bony fusion of the knee are rarely addressed in the robotic TKA literature specifically. The more relevant principle comes from the hip literature: when conventional bony landmarks are absent or fused, registration itself becomes the technical challenge, and the procedure must be evaluated on a case-by-case feasibility basis rather than by diagnosis. 🦴 Total Hip Arthroplasty: Who Benefits Most Crowe type III–IV developmental dysplasia is the group in which the evidence for robotic THA is most consistent, with an important evidence caveat for Crowe IV. A retrospective comparison of robotic versus conventional THA in Crowe 3–4 DDH (45 patients, 52 hips) found that robotic THA achieved more precise acetabular inclination (37.11° ± 3.37° versus 41.13° ± 6.49°) and anteversion (17.59° ± 1.78° versus 21.87° ± 1.71°), alongside lower postoperative VAS pain (1.35 versus 2.41) and higher modified Harris Hip Score (92.34 versus 79.68), at the cost of longer operative time (117.06 versus 79.71 minutes). A systematic review of robotic-arm-assisted THA in dysplasia found significantly lower errors in cup inclination and anteversion for Crowe I–III compared with both conventional and navigated THA, and greater accuracy in restoring the center of rotation for Crowe I–III—but no difference was observed in Crowe IV hips, where the evidence remains limited and the accuracy advantage is unclear. This is a crucial nuance: Crowe III–IV dysplasia is often described as a single "severe DDH" category, but the robotic advantage is best established for Crowe I–III, while Crowe IV remains an evidence gap rather than a proven indication. Post-traumatic arthritis with retained hardware around the hip is a second category of potential benefit, supported largely by case series. A report of simultaneous hardware removal and conversion to robotic THA describes robotic assistance as helping improve preoperative planning and implant position and alignment in cases made difficult by previous hardware and bone loss. A separate case series of complex primary robotic THA including post-traumatic arthritis with hardware noted that these cases present challenges from heterotopic ossification, acetabular protrusion, abductor deficiency, prior infection, and retained hardware, and that robotic-arm assistance may be considered especially in the absence of conventional bony landmarks. The evidence is feasibility and technique description, not comparative effectiveness. 🦴 THA: Relative Contraindications and Conditions Requiring Caution Ankylosing spondylitis and bony ankylosis of the hip constitute the clearest "technically feasible but risk–benefit must be individualized" category. Early case reports of robotic-arm-assisted THA in complex primary cases including ankylosing spondylitis described poor postoperative Harris Hip Scores in the ankylosing spondylitis patient, despite good scores in the dysplasia and post-traumatic cases. More recent work has developed lateral acetabular registration techniques specifically for arthrodesed hips, because the standard three pelvic landmarks used in initial registration may be unavailable or unreliable in the fused pelvis. One study reported that robotic THA in AS patients significantly reduces dislocation rates and improves patient satisfaction, and improves the likelihood of cup positioning within the target zone. But the honest interpretation is that robotic assistance solves the registration and cup-positioning problem in the ankylosed hip, not the soft-tissue release problem: obtaining exposure and mobility in a fused hip requires extensive soft-tissue dissection, with attendant blood loss and rehabilitation burden, and the robot does not offset that dimension of risk. A report of robotic THA in an arthrodesed hip noted that dislocation was achieved in all cases except one with bony ankylosis, in which en bloc registration was performed—a technical workaround that illustrates the feasibility but also the anatomical constraint. 💎 The Practical Framework Greatest benefit: TKA patients with moderate-to-severe coronal deformity (fewer alignment outliers, reduced need for extensive releases) and flexion contracture ≥10° managed with functional alignment (comparable survivorship and joint-line preservation). THA patients with Crowe I–III dysplasia (more accurate cup position and center-of-rotation restoration). Retained hardware around the knee or hip is a plausible but evidence-limited indication where CT-based planning can define deformity and anticipate implant–hardware conflict. Relative contraindications and caution zones: TKA with collateral ligament incompetence, severe fixed contracture beyond functional alignment's compensatory capacity, major bone loss, or a requirement for constrained fixation—because the robot can quantify deformity but cannot restore a deficient ligament. Severe stiffness is not a contraindication per se, but the learning-curve phase carries a measurable increase in MUA risk. THA with ankylosing spondylitis or bony ankylosis is technically approachable with modified registration, but the soft-tissue and exposure burden remains a traditional surgical problem that precision does not solve. Crowe IV dysplasia should be recognized as an evidence gap rather than a proven robotic indication. The unifying clinical question is not "is this a robotic case?" but "is the core problem one of accurate placement, or one of exposure, soft-tissue competence, and biological healing?" Robotics systematically addresses the former; for the latter, it provides useful information but does not substitute for surgical judgment.

As a practicing orthopedic surgeon, I have to begin with a candid qualification: the premise of the question—that “long-term follow-up data” exist in a form sufficient to answer it definitively across all procedures—is only partly true. The evidence base is uneven. It is strongest for joint replacement, moderate for certain fracture subtypes, and comparatively thin for spine surgery. And where high-quality long-term data do exist, the answer is largely consistent: robotic assistance has not been shown to confer a general advantage in the hard endpoints you have named. The demonstrated advantage remains concentrated at the intraoperative, execution level—accuracy and alignment—and this has not reliably translated into fewer long-term complications, less implant loosening, or better fracture healing across the board. Total Knee Arthroplasty: high-quality long-term data show parity, not superiority This is the area with the most mature evidence, and it is unambiguous. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 20 comparative studies (2,599 robotic TKAs, 2,804 conventional TKAs) found pooled survivorship rates of 98.3% vs. 97.9% at 2 years, 97.1% vs. 96.8% at 2–5 years, and 97.8% vs. 96.9% at 10 years, with no significant differences at any time point (P=0.3 at 10 years). The authors concluded that conventional TKA is non-inferior to robotic TKA in implant survival, complications, and pain scores. This is corroborated by registry data. A 2025 analysis of the American Joint Replacement Registry linked to Medicare, following patients aged 65 and older for 5 years, found robotic use was not significant for all-cause revision (P=0.75), mechanical loosening (P=0.42), or other mechanical complications (P=0.46). The authors stated explicitly that “the purported benefits of using this technology to improve component survival are not supported”. The 10-year RCT data point the same way. A randomized trial with minimum 10-year follow-up found no differences between robotic and conventional TKA in functional scores, aseptic loosening, overall survivorship, or complications. A separate 15-year follow-up report noted identical 98% implant survivorship in both groups. The one nuance is a small improvement in the proportion of knees within ±3° of neutral mechanical axis in the robotic group, but this difference disappeared at a ±5° outlier threshold and—critically—did not translate into any difference in aseptic loosening or survival. Simulation modeling suggests a potential survivorship advantage of only 1.4% to 2.0% at 15 years would require impractically large studies to detect, which itself indicates the effect size, if real, is small. Total Hip Arthroplasty: the evidence is even more clearly null For THA, a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs concluded there is “little to no difference” in clinical, functional, and radiological outcomes between robotic-assisted and conventional THA, with effect sizes for major complications and revision rate described as relatively small and accompanied by very large confidence intervals. The pooled revision risk estimate was imprecise (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.08–22.74) and based on evidence rated “very low certainty” due to high risk of bias and inconsistency. A 10-year randomized trial specifically comparing robotic milling versus manual stem implantation found no difference in outcome scores or rates of aseptic loosening or revision. A broader review of 14 comparative studies found that while robotic THA achieved more frequent placement of the acetabular cup in the safe zone, there was no difference in overall complication rate or functional outcomes. In other words, the alignment precision advantage is real but has not been shown to reduce long-term loosening or revision at the population level in randomized evidence. Spine: the short-term data show accuracy, not long-term clinical superiority For spine, the “long-term” label is harder to apply. A propensity-score-matched cohort study comparing robot-assisted, fluoroscopy-guided, and freehand pedicle screw fixation in lumbar degenerative disease—with a mean follow-up of 2.2 years—found higher screw accuracy in the robotic group (p<0.01) but no significant differences in radiological adjacent segment disease, mechanical failure, clinical ASD rates, or patient-reported outcomes among the three groups. Survival analysis for clinical ASD also showed no difference. This is a crucial finding: the accuracy advantage of robotic screw placement is well established, but in this matched cohort it did not translate into fewer adjacent segment problems, less mechanical failure, or better clinical outcomes at short- to mid-term follow-up. A review of robotic and computer-assisted systems in pelvic and spinal surgery noted that while accuracy and reduction precision can be improved, “there is still no evidence for long-term clinical outcomes” for many of these applications. I would emphasize that 2-year data on ASD are insufficient to judge a phenomenon that often takes 5–10 years to manifest; the honest statement is that long-term spine data on these endpoints are lacking, not that robotic surgery has been proven equivalent. Trauma: a signal of benefit in a specific fracture subtype, but not generalizable This is the one area where some data point toward a reduction in hard adverse outcomes, but the evidence requires careful qualification. A 2026 retrospective cohort study of valgus-impacted osteoporotic femoral neck fractures in elderly patients compared manual reverse closed reduction plus robotic-assisted cannulated screw fixation (n=36) with conventional in-situ freehand fixation (n=36). At 24–36 months, the robotic-assisted group had markedly lower rates of: femoral head necrosis: 5.56% vs. 25.00% non-union: 8.33% vs. 27.78% fixation failure: 5.56% vs. 22.22% These are striking differences. However, I would not generalize them. This is a retrospective, single-center study of a specific fracture phenotype (valgus-impacted, osteoporotic femoral neck fractures) in which the intervention was a combined strategy—manual reverse reduction plus robotic assistance—not robotic assistance alone. The authors themselves frame the conclusion as showing “a positive tendency” within the limitations of the cohort. For long bone shaft fractures and other trauma applications, the literature still describes non-union and malunion as persistent issues and notes that long-term clinical outcome evidence remains limited. The fair reading is that robotic assistance may improve healing-related outcomes in technically demanding periarticular fractures where reduction and fixation precision are decisive, but this has not been established as a general trauma principle. What this means clinically The pattern across these data is consistent and important: the accuracy and alignment advantages of robotic surgery are real, but they have not been shown to produce superior long-term implant survival, lower loosening rates, or better fracture healing in the general patient population. For TKA and THA, the highest-quality evidence—RCTs and registry analyses with 5- to 15-year follow-up—shows parity, not superiority, on these endpoints. For spine, the accuracy advantage is clear but the long-term clinical translation remains unproven, and the follow-up in most comparative studies is too short to judge ASD or late mechanical failure. For trauma, a specific fracture subtype shows a promising reduction in non-union and fixation failure, but this is low-certainty, retrospective evidence for a combined technique, not a generalizable claim. I would not tell a patient that robotic surgery will make their implant last longer or their fracture heal more reliably based on current long-term data. I would say that it improves the precision of execution, and that in selected complex cases—severe deformity, challenging anatomy, specific fracture patterns—that precision may plausibly matter for the mechanical environment and healing. But the burden of proof for long-term superiority has not been met, and the evidence that does exist leans toward equivalence at the population level rather than advantage.

**与传统二维透视置钉相比，机器人导航通常能提高骶髂螺钉的置入准确度，减少导针反复调整及置钉阶段的透视时间；但对神经血管并发症发生率是否显著降低，目前证据仍不足。**证据主要集中于骨盆后环骶髂螺钉，不能直接推广到所有骨盆环通道。 1．安全骨性通道内的准确度：总体有改善，但不是“零穿破” 一项小型前瞻性随机试验中，机器人组置入23枚螺钉，传统组22枚，研究定义的置钉优良率分别为 100%和95%；导针尝试次数的中位数分别为 1次和7次。这些结果支持机器人减少反复调整，但样本较小，不能将100%理解为普遍保证。随机试验 另一项对照研究中，机器人组54枚螺钉仍有4枚被评为骨皮质穿破，说明导航和机械臂不能消除偏差。对照研究 还需注意：不同研究的“准确”“优良”“可接受”定义并不一致，骨盆螺钉分级不能直接套用上一题胸腰椎螺钉的分级标准。 2．透视时间：通常减少，但必须看统计范围 上述随机试验中，骨盆复位后置钉阶段的透视时间中位数，机器人组为 6秒，传统组为 36秒，减少约83%；但机器人组另外需要术中轨迹规划时间，不能据此认为整台手术时间也减少83%。随机试验全文 **透视时间、拍片次数与辐射剂量不是同一个指标。**比较患者总辐射负担时，还必须计入定位、配准及三维扫描等影像采集，结合设备参数和患者体型判断；不能仅凭透视次数下降，就认定总剂量同比下降。 3．神经血管并发症：有降低风险的合理机制，但尚难量化 减少骨皮质穿破和导针反复穿刺，理论上有助于降低神经血管损伤风险。但这类损伤相对少见，小样本研究即使机器人组没有损伤，也不足以证明风险更低。 例如，上述随机试验两组均未报告术后并发症或翻修，因此它能支持技术可行性，却无法可靠回答“神经血管损伤降低了多少”。随机试验 从临床判断看，机器人安全获益的前提仍是：**CT确认存在安全通道、先获得满意复位、置钉过程中维持骨块与参考架稳定，并核验实际导针位置。**导航不能创造不存在的骨性通道；复位丢失或骨块相对移动后，原规划也可能失效。AO 骨盆导航置钉技术参考 因此，目前最稳妥的表述是：准确性和减少透视使用的优势较明确，严重神经血管并发症的下降幅度尚不能给出可靠统一数字。

以中国大陆医疗机构为背景，开展骨科机器人手术应同时满足三方面要求：**合法执业、获得相应手术及机器人技术的院内授权、完成针对具体系统的培训与能力评估。**厂家培训证书不能替代执业资格和医院授权。 1．执业资质：首先应具备原手术的能力与权限。 术者应依法取得医师资格并完成执业注册，在相应执业范围内开展工作，同时具备拟开展的关节置换、脊柱内固定或创伤固定等手术的权限。 国家《医疗机构手术分级管理办法》要求，医院根据手术级别、专业特点、术者岗位、临床能力和培训情况综合授予权限，并进行动态评估。因此，不能仅凭职称或机器人培训结业证判断能否独立主刀，也不能把所有机器人手术统一认定为同一级别。国家卫生健康委规定 尤其重要的是：术者应能够识别机器人定位错误、判断何时停止使用，并具备转常规手术及处理相关并发症的能力。 2．专项培训：既要学会操作设备，也要学会发现设备“不可信”的情况。 从临床安全角度，培训和考核至少应覆盖： 培训内容 应达到的能力 病例选择与规划 掌握适应症、影像要求、规划原则及设备适用范围 装机与定位配准 正确安装追踪器、校准器械，完成独立精度核验 实际操作 掌握截骨或置钉流程，识别滑移、偏转和异常阻力 故障与急症处理 熟悉急停、器械安全脱离、机械臂撤离及转常规手术 团队协作 与麻醉、护理、影像等人员明确分工并完成演练 较合理的培训路径是：**理论学习与模拟操作—跟台观摩—指导下完成病例—能力考核—获得授权后独立开展。**这是临床培训建议；具体培训时长、指导病例数及考核标准，应核对当地要求、医院制度和相应机型规范，不能把建议当作全国统一硬性标准。 医院也应按医疗技术管理要求，完成相应技术准入、质量控制和动态评估。《医疗技术临床应用管理办法》 3．上手周期：必须区分“操作熟悉”与“能够安全独立开展”。 目前没有适用于所有骨科机器人、所有术式的统一病例数。 **关节置换：**一项研究报告约7例后手术流程趋于熟练；另一种七轴机器人系统的研究报告约20例进入熟练阶段。这些主要反映特定团队的时间学习曲线。7例研究、20例研究 **脊柱置钉：**一项125例单中心研究发现，最初25例的装机、配准和置钉等环节耗时较长，此后趋于稳定。原始研究 **这些数字不是独立执业门槛。**研究中的术者通常已有相应常规手术经验；操作时间稳定，也不能证明已经掌握罕见急症、复杂畸形或翻修病例的处理能力。 临床上，是否允许独立开展，更应看术者能否稳定完成规划与精度核验、识别并纠正偏差、安全转换手术，以及连续病例的质量表现。换机型、换术式或进入更复杂病例时，也应重新评估。 **不确定之处：我目前无法确认存在一套全国统一、专门覆盖所有骨科机器人的“必须某职称、培训多少天、完成多少例”标准。**具体人员是否符合要求，还需结合所在地区、医院及设备型号核实，不能套用其他专科机器人的准入标准。

From a practicing arthroplasty surgeon's standpoint, the registry and long-term follow-up evidence supports a clear but procedure-specific conclusion: robotic assistance has not demonstrated a population-level reduction in all-cause revision or a consistent improvement in patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) in either TKA or THA, but there is one mechanism-specific exception in THA—a significantly lower risk of revision for dislocation—and a more favorable, though still contested, signal in UKA. The question of whether improved alignment translates into fewer revisions is answered by the current evidence as: not yet demonstrated at the registry level, and the reasons for that null finding are informative rather than dismissive. Registry Data: No All-Cause Revision Advantage in TKA or THA The two largest matched registry analyses converge on the same finding. The National Joint Registry (NJR) target trial emulation, published in the BMJ, matched 69,020 conventional TKAs with 17,255 robotic TKAs at a mean follow-up of 2.5 years. Five-year implant survival was 98.5% versus 98.6%, with no significant difference in revision risk (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.86–1.26, P=0.71). The E-value analysis indicated that an unmeasured confounder with a hazard ratio association of at least 1.60 would be required to shift the confidence bound toward a significant benefit or harm, indicating a stable, near-null finding rather than a power failure. The American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) linked to Medicare data reached the same conclusion: robotic use was not significant for TKA all-cause revision (P=0.75), mechanical loosening (P=0.42), or other mechanical complications (P=0.46) at five years. For THA, the AJRR analysis of 113,477 conventional and 10,988 robotic THAs found no difference in all-cause revision at two years (1.9% versus 2.1%, HR 0.9, 95% CI 0.7–1.1, P=0.42). The NJR THA analysis similarly reported five-year survival of 98.8% in both groups with no revision risk difference (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.75–1.22, P=0.73). The Mechanism-Specific Exception: Revision for Dislocation in THA The one registry endpoint where robotics shows a statistically significant and mechanistically coherent advantage is revision for dislocation in THA. In the AJRR analysis, revision for dislocation was 0.3% (35/10,988) in robot-assisted THA versus 0.6% (689/113,477) in conventional THA, corresponding to a hazard ratio of 0.5 (95% CI 0.3–0.9, P=0.03)—a halving of the risk. This is the finding that most directly answers the "does precision translate into outcomes" question: the robot's core competence is three-dimensional acetabular cup positioning, and cup malposition is a principal modifiable cause of dislocation. When the outcome is specified to match the mechanism, the precision advantage becomes detectable. The authors themselves frame the clinical implication narrowly: robot-assisted THA might be considered a means to mitigate early dislocation risk in scenarios where that risk is a concern, but until it demonstrates clear superiority in broader outcomes, its role remains adjunctive. UKA: A More Favorable Signal, With an Important Follow-Up Caveat UKA is where the survivorship evidence is most favorable, but the registry and meta-analytic data are in tension because of follow-up duration. The NJR UKA analysis at 2.5 years mean follow-up found no difference in revision risk (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.75–1.42) and five-year survival of 97.8% conventional versus 96.4% robotic. However, mid- to long-term evidence points in a different direction: a 10-year robotic UKA survivorship of 94.8% has been reported, consistent with other long-term robotic UKA cohorts, and the authors interpret this as potentially narrowing the historical survivorship gap between UKA and TKA. A meta-analysis reported a revision odds ratio of 0.28 (95% CI 0.12–0.67, P=0.004) favoring robotic UKA. The most defensible reading is that the registry null result reflects a follow-up window too short to capture the dominant UKA failure mode—aseptic loosening—which typically manifests beyond five years, whereas the long-term cohort data suggest a durability advantage that the registries have not yet had time to observe. Patient-Reported Outcomes: No Consistent Advantage, With One Nuanced Exception The PROMs evidence is the most consistent null finding in the literature. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies encompassing approximately 5,800 patients concluded that across KSS, OKS, KOOS, WOMAC, HSS, VAS pain, and range of motion, there was no consistent statistically or clinically meaningful difference between robotic and conventional TKA at final follow-up. The authors stated explicitly that the documented radiographic precision advantage "has not translated into superior patient-reported functional recovery or pain relief at short-, mid-, or long-term follow-up" , with most pooled effect sizes falling below the minimal clinically important difference threshold. A 2026 narrative review synthesizing RCTs, meta-analyses, and registry data reached the same conclusion for both TKA and THA: robotic arthroplasty "consistently improves component positioning precision but has not demonstrated improvements in patient-reported outcomes, complication rates, or implant survivorship" . The one nuanced exception is joint awareness, measured by the Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12). A meta-analysis of 39 studies and 13,289 joints found that robotic TKA achieved higher FJS-12 across all follow-up periods (long-term MD 8.37, 95% CI 0.86–15.89), and robotic THA consistently outperformed manual THA (within one year MD 6.60, 95% CI 3.47–9.74; one to two years MD 7.19, 95% CI 1.21–13.17; beyond two years MD 1.92, 95% CI 0.46–3.39). Whether these differences reach the MCID for FJS-12 and whether they replicate in broader populations remains uncertain, but this is the one PROM domain where a consistent signal exists. Does Improved Alignment Translate into Fewer Revisions? The evidence answers this question in the negative at the current time, and the reasons are clinically instructive rather than simply a failure of the technology. The alignment improvement itself is robust. Robotic TKA reduces mechanical axis outliers beyond 3° from 25.8% to 10.1%—a 67% relative reduction. But multiple reviews state directly that "this precision has not translated into reduced revision rates or improved outcomes in large cohort studies" . Three explanations are supported by the data, and each has practical implications: Follow-up duration is mismatched to the failure mode that alignment should influence. The dominant long-term failure modes—aseptic loosening and wear—typically require a decade or more to manifest, whereas the NJR data have a mean follow-up of 2.5 years and the AJRR five years. Modeling studies estimate that a survivorship advantage from improved alignment may only become detectable at 15 years, and even then may be on the order of 1.4% to 2%—a difference requiring very large cohorts and long follow-up to detect. The registry null result is therefore not evidence that alignment is irrelevant; it is evidence that the observation window has not yet captured the failures alignment is meant to prevent. Alignment is only one determinant of revision among many. Implant design, fixation, patient factors (BMI, activity, bone quality), and soft-tissue balance all contribute. A population-level all-cause revision endpoint dilutes the contribution of alignment precision.
