When Cement-Augmented Screws Are Required: Hip The hip evidence is less mature than the spine evidence, and the two fracture types must be separated. Intertrochanteric fractures. Cement augmentation of the cephalocervical component has biomechanical support—increased rotational stability and pullout force—and is considered for pertrochanteric fractures with severe osteoporosis to increase primary stability. A consensus process identified elderly patients with severe osteoporosis as candidates for cement-augmented fixation. Dynamic hip screw augmentation has been used to prevent screw cut-out in osteoporotic intertrochanteric fractures. The indication is therefore severe osteoporosis in an unstable or cut-out-prone intertrochanteric pattern, not all intertrochanteric fractures. Femoral neck fractures. The evidence here is poor and does not support routine augmentation. A dedicated review of hip fracture augmentation concluded: “Femoral neck: evidence poor for augmentation”, and noted that calcium phosphate cement augmentation did not improve results after internal fixation of displaced femoral neck fractures; arthroplasty is listed as a good alternative to fixation in this setting. This is an important asymmetry: in the femoral neck, the biological problem of head–neck healing and the availability of arthroplasty as a reliable alternative outweigh the mechanical argument for augmentation. A Surgeon's Synthesis The organizing principle is that robotic precision and biological purchase are separate problems. The robot solves the first; cement augmentation addresses the second. In practice: Osteoporosis does not contraindicate robotic spine insertion, and robotic accuracy remains high (≈97%) even in osteoporotic bone, but severe osteoporosis (T ≤ −3.5) raises the risk of trajectory deviation as well as post-operative loosening. Cement augmentation should be planned—or at least immediately available—when the interface is expected to fail: severe osteoporosis with anticipated poor insertional torque, osteoporotic fracture fixation, osteolytic tumor, or intraoperative evidence of inadequate purchase. The benefit is a marked reduction in hardware loosening; the cost is a meaningful rate of asymptomatic cement leakage and a small but real risk of symptomatic embolism. In the hip, augmentation is more clearly indicated for severe osteoporotic intertrochanteric fractures to prevent cut-out, while femoral neck fracture augmentation is not supported by the evidence and should not be performed routinely. The honest limitation is that high-quality comparative evidence directly comparing cemented versus uncemented screws within a robotic workflow is limited; most augmentation evidence comes from conventional or mixed surgical series. The decision therefore remains individualized, driven by bone density, fracture pattern, intraoperative purchase, and the patient's physiological reserve rather than by a rigid threshold.

There is no single reliable “extra time” figure across robotic orthopedic surgery. The time depends on the procedure, platform, team experience, and whether one measures incision-to-closure time or total operating-room occupancy. A useful clarification: preoperative imaging and planning occur before surgery, but registration—matching the patient’s anatomy to the computer model—is generally performed in the operating room, often after exposure. From a surgeon’s workflow perspective, the published figures should be interpreted as follows: Component Representative reported time What the figure means Robotic-arm setup for knee replacement Median 10 minutes, range 6–19 minutes, in one early-adoption study. Setup duration, not necessarily an equivalent increase in operative time; some tasks can overlap with other preparation. Tracker mounting and landmark registration for knee replacement Median 7 minutes, with bone-surface registration approximately 2 minutes per bone, in the same study. Separate robotic workflow steps; not all studies define these intervals identically. Troubleshooting or repeat registration One problematic femoral registration took 23 minutes because the tracker was moving. An example of an outlier, not an expected routine allowance. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Early versus established robotic knee workflow Approximately 12 minutes longer during the learning phase: 90.3 versus 78.4 minutes in one study. This compares early and later robotic cases, not robotic versus conventional surgery. PMC Spinal robot setup One study reported 37–44 minutes initially, decreasing to 8–15 minutes with experience. A platform- and institution-specific setup estimate, not the net additional duration of the entire spinal operation. mdpi.com These figures should not be added together to produce a universal time penalty. Tasks may overlap, and robotic guidance replaces some conventional steps. Preoperative planning also adds staff workload without necessarily extending anesthesia time. I cannot confidently give a general average for “debugging”: its frequency and duration are inconsistently reported. How I would optimise the workflow Complete imaging and plan checks before the operating day. Confirm image quality, correct side, implant compatibility, and availability of the approved plan. This prevents avoidable delays from missing data or repeat imaging. Standardise room layout and assign roles. Predetermine robot, camera, imaging equipment, and instrument positions. Assign responsibility for startup checks, draping, tracker preparation, and troubleshooting. Perform independent preparation tasks in parallel. Equipment preparation can overlap with other appropriate room activities, provided this does not compromise sterility, patient access, or anesthesia care. Prevent registration failures. Secure trackers, maintain camera visibility, and verify accuracy according to the platform’s protocol. Time spent obtaining reliable registration is preferable to repeated registration or discovering an error during instrumentation. Train the whole team and maintain continuity. The learning curve involves nursing, radiography, and technical support as well as the surgeon. Studies reported improvements after approximately 16–30 knee cases and 25 spinal cases, but these are workflow observations—not universal thresholds for clinical competence. PMC Establish a troubleshooting and conversion pathway. Keep conventional instruments available and define when unresolved technical problems warrant abandoning robotic assistance. Persistent attempts to rescue a malfunctioning workflow can consume more time than conversion. Audit total room time and delay causes. Measure setup, registration, surgical execution, troubleshooting, and turnover separately. Compare similar procedures and case complexity, and track unusually prolonged cases as well as averages. For scheduling, I would use an initial platform-specific allowance, then replace it with the team’s own measured times. The objective is predictable efficiency while preserving registration accuracy and surgical checks—not simply faster robot setup.

Yes—limitations in robotic-arm reach and angular movement can affect surgery in unusual patient positions and deep orthopedic sites. From an orthopedic surgical workflow perspective, the key question is whether the instrument can reach the target at the required angle, through a safe surgical corridor, without collision. I am not a practicing orthopedic surgeon; the following reflects published evidence and surgical guidance. Patient positioning can restrict access. Lateral positioning, table tilt, and supports can place the target outside the arm’s usable workspace or cause interference with the table. A clinical report of robotic spine surgery in the lateral position specifically describes positioning the patient to prevent the table edge from obstructing robotic-arm adjustment. Such positions are therefore feasible, but require deliberate setup. Clinical report Deep sites require both adequate reach and the correct trajectory. At the acetabulum or along a spinal screw trajectory, reaching the entry point alone is insufficient: the instrument must also align correctly and advance to the necessary depth. As a mechanical and clinical inference, thick soft tissues, a narrow exposure, or an obstructing bony structure can further restrict this corridor. In many orthopedic systems, the arm positions a guide or holds an instrument outside the body; the instrument enters the deep site. These limitations can change the operative workflow. The team may need to adjust robot placement, table height, patient position, or exposure. Stryker’s hip workflow guide explicitly recommends checking reamer reach before fixing the robot’s position and angling the robot to increase its available range of motion. Persistent access problems may require completing the affected step with conventional instruments. Manufacturer workflow guide The limitation is platform and procedure specific. Mechanical joint limits also differ from deliberately programmed safety boundaries. Restricted access does not automatically mean reduced accuracy, but it can prevent execution of the planned trajectory. I cannot give a universal maximum depth, angle, or complication rate: these depend on the robot, instruments, anatomy, and positioning.

**最值得考虑机器人辅助的，是已经具备置换指征、常规解剖定位或重建较困难，同时仍能可靠完成配准和器械操作的患者。**但目前还不能确定某类复杂患者“获益最大”：证据对假体定位精度的支持，通常强于对长期功能、松动或翻修减少的支持。 1．全膝置换：哪些患者可能更有价值？ 情况 机器人可能提供的帮助 判断边界 重度内翻、外翻畸形 量化截骨、假体位置及屈伸间隙，辅助个体化调整 仍需判断畸形来源、可矫正性及韧带功能；不能替代必要的松解、截骨或限制型假体 屈曲挛缩 显示伸直间隙与截骨调整之间的关系，帮助避免盲目增加截骨 不能直接解除后关节囊挛缩，也不能保证恢复正常活动度 关节外畸形、骨折后畸形愈合 在髓内定位受限时，提供其他定位与规划方式 严重关节外畸形仍可能需要额外矫形，不能全部通过关节内截骨补偿 既往钢板、髓内钉存留 部分系统可避免使用髓内定位杆，可能减少不必要的取出操作 必须排除感染，并确认内固定不干扰截骨、假体、追踪钉及配准 需要特别区分证据类型：一项研究发现，屈曲挛缩≥10°的患者接受机器人全膝置换后，可获得与无明显挛缩者相近的部分随访结果；但两组均使用机器人，因此不能据此证明机器人优于传统手术。屈曲挛缩研究 2．全髋置换：髋发育不良是较有针对性的应用场景。 机器人三维规划可帮助评估髋臼骨量、旋转中心及杯体位置。一项机器人与手工全髋置换各147例的回顾性比较研究显示，机器人改善髋臼组件定位精度，Crowe II、III型患者的旋转中心重建尤其体现出优势。但这并未证明长期松动或翻修一定减少。髋发育不良比较研究 对于Crowe IV型高脱位、严重骨缺损或明显股骨畸形，机器人可辅助部分规划和操作，但不能替代骨缺损重建、必要的股骨截骨及神经保护。还应核对具体系统是否仅辅助髋臼侧，不能默认它同样控制股骨侧。 3．严重僵硬、内植物存留、关节强直，是否属于相对禁忌？ 这些更适合视为需要逐项评估的技术难点，而非跨所有设备通用的禁忌。 **严重僵硬：**若活动范围不足以完成系统要求的标志采集、间隙评估或器械进入，就可能无法使用该流程；但没有适用于所有系统的统一活动度下限。 **内植物存留：**本身不一定是禁忌，有时反而增加导航的价值。已有保留内固定完成机器人全膝置换的病例报告，但证据有限，不能保证所有钢板、髓内钉或原有关节假体均可保留。病例报告 **关节强直：**可能需要先松解或解除骨性融合，才能完成配准和后续操作，风险明显高于常规置换。已有机器人处理强直膝的个案，但只能证明特定条件下可行，不能作为常规推荐依据。强直膝病例 **严重骨质疏松或骨缺损：**可能影响追踪钉固定和假体稳定性；若无法可靠固定追踪装置，或所需重建假体不受系统支持，应改用其他方案。 此外，**活动性关节感染、无法耐受手术等属于置换本身的限制；配准不可靠、器械无法到达、所需术式超出设备批准范围，则属于机器人辅助的限制。**最终应结合影像、活动度、韧带与骨量、既往内植物位置，以及具体设备说明书决定，而不是仅凭“畸形重”或“关节僵”作判断。

**机器人引导通常能提高胸腰椎椎弓根螺钉的影像学准确度，但提升幅度不是固定值。**以一项较有代表性的随机试验为例，“完全位于椎弓根内”的比例提高约 9个百分点，“临床可接受”的比例提高约 5个百分点。对于畸形、翻修病例，其辅助价值可能更大，但尚不能确定优势必然比普通病例更突出。 1．具体能提高多少？首先要统一准确度标准 常用 Gertzbein–Robbins 分级中： **A级：**螺钉完全位于椎弓根骨皮质内。 **A＋B级：**完全在骨内，或骨皮质突破不足2毫米，研究中常称“临床可接受”。但这一名称不代表任何方向、任何部位的轻微突破都绝对安全。 Han等开展的随机试验纳入234例患者、1116枚胸腰椎螺钉，对比TiRobot引导与徒手透视辅助置钉： 指标 机器人组 徒手透视组 绝对差值 A级：完全位于骨皮质内 95.3% 86.1% 提高9.2个百分点 A＋B级：研究定义的临床可接受 98.7% 93.5% 提高5.2个百分点 C—E级：突破≥2毫米 约1.3% 约6.5% 降低约5.2个百分点 后两行根据论文公布的各级百分比计算，存在四舍五入误差。这是按螺钉统计的结果，不是患者神经损伤率或再次手术率；研究主要涉及退变、创伤病例，也不能代表所有机器人平台。随机试验原文摘要 因此，临床上更适合说“特定研究显示提高若干个百分点”，不宜笼统宣传“准确率提高数倍”。与二维透视徒手置钉相比的优势，也不能直接套用到与现代三维导航的比较中。 2．畸形病例：有优势信号，但未证明优势一定更大 椎体旋转、椎弓根狭窄或发育异常，会增加依赖常规解剖标志置钉的难度。三维规划与机械臂导向在这些情况下具有明确的技术价值。 一项青少年特发性脊柱侧弯对照研究报告，机器人组与徒手组的研究定义准确率分别为 89.5%和79.1%，相差 10.4个百分点。但其患者、评价方法和研究设计不同，不能与上述普通胸腰椎随机试验直接横向比较，进而断言“畸形病例增益更大”。侧弯置钉对照研究 3．翻修病例：临床理由充分，定量证据仍有限 既往融合骨块、解剖标志缺失和原螺钉通道，会增加翻修置钉难度。机器人可辅助规划新通道，并减少对表面标志的依赖。一项腰椎翻修对照研究支持机器人组具有更高置钉准确性及更少上位关节突侵犯，但还不足以给出适用于所有翻修情境的统一提升幅度。腰椎翻修对照研究 **我的判断是：复杂病例更有理由考虑机器人辅助，但“更需要辅助”不等于“已证实获益幅度更大”。**严重畸形还可能同时增加配准、机械臂到达和器械滑移的困难；若没有安全骨性通道，机器人也不能创造通道。最终仍应以术中核验和具体平台、团队的实际结果为依据。

Cases should be selected according to the expected additional benefit of robotic assistance—not simply to keep an expensive machine occupied. From a surgeon’s clinical perspective, efficient resource use requires both appropriate patient selection and an efficient service. 1. Establish the indication for surgery independently The patient should first meet the usual criteria for replacement, fixation, or spinal instrumentation. Robot availability should not lower the threshold for surgery, expand an otherwise inappropriate indication, or delay urgent treatment. For each eligible patient, the practical question is: What clinically important problem will the robot help solve, compared with the best available conventional or navigated technique? Case category Resource-conscious approach Complex primary arthroplasty with distorted landmarks, extra-articular deformity, or retained hardware Consider robotics when planning and guidance could simplify reconstruction or avoid an additional procedure. Confirm platform suitability; complexity alone does not establish value. Selected spinal instrumentation with difficult trajectories Consider robotics when it offers a meaningful advantage in trajectory execution. Compare it with available navigation, not only freehand surgery. Routine primary hip or knee replacement Reasonable within an efficient established programme, but a substantial cost premium is harder to justify without demonstrated patient benefit or episode-of-care savings. Fracture fixation Select cases with a specific guidance benefit, adequate reduction, and suitable anatomy. Do not assume robotics will improve union or justify delaying definitive care. Unsupported procedures or technically unsuitable cases Prefer an established alternative; restrict investigational applications to an appropriately governed research pathway. These are selection principles, not validated cost-effectiveness rules. For example, a small series of complex knee replacements suggested savings when robotic single-stage surgery replaced a projected staged pathway, but only seven cases underwent economic analysis. That is encouraging rather than definitive evidence. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov 2. Calculate the full additional cost The assessment should include: Equipment purchase or lease, maintenance, software, and training. Consumables, additional imaging, and any implant-price commitments. Operating-room time, staffing, sterilization, and troubleshooting. Rehabilitation, readmissions, complications, and revisions. The opportunity cost of occupying theatre time that could treat other patients. Cost-effective does not necessarily mean cost-saving. One 200-patient study found shorter hospital stays with robotic knee replacement, but total in-hospital costs remained higher once robotic costs were included. PMC 3. Use sufficient appropriate volume—but avoid volume targets that drive unnecessary surgery Concentrating suitable cases in experienced teams can spread fixed costs and improve workflow. However, there is no universal break-even caseload: separate economic models estimated thresholds of roughly 50 and 253 knee cases per robot annually, reflecting different assumptions, prices, and expected benefits. These are model outputs, not clinical eligibility standards. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov For a low-volume institution, referral to an established centre or shared access may provide better value than purchasing a separate system, provided travel and access burdens are considered. 4. Require demonstrated benefit rather than assumed future savings As discussed in Q7, a general long-term reduction in loosening or revision has not been established. Economic models that assume such reductions may therefore overstate value. I would test the business case under a conservative scenario of no long-term revision advantage, then examine whether measured recovery benefits and workflow savings still justify the expense. Some published models explicitly depend on lower revision rates and post-acute care costs. PubMed 5. Audit outcomes and preserve fair access A programme should compare similar patients receiving robotic and conventional surgery, tracking patient-reported outcomes, complications, reoperations, total costs, and theatre capacity. Selection should reflect clinical need and expected benefit, rather than insurance status, ability to pay, or marketing appeal. My recommendation is selective use within an experienced, adequately utilised programme, with regular review of actual outcomes and costs. Younger age, obesity, or severe deformity alone is insufficient to establish economic value, and current evidence cannot reliably identify a universally “most cost-effective” patient subgroup.

在经皮骶髂关节与骨盆环螺钉固定这一高风险领域，机器人导航与传统透视的差异是明确且具有临床意义的。核心结论是：机器人导航在提升置钉准确度和大幅缩短透视时间方面证据充分，而在神经血管并发症发生率上，现有数据表明其风险极低，但与传统透视的直接比较受限于并发症本身的低发生率与文献报告质量，其优势更多体现为通过提升精度来“规避”风险，而非在统计数据上呈现出显著的并发症率下降。 🎯 置钉准确度：从“可接受”到“精准”的跨越 螺钉误置是经皮骨盆螺钉固定最主要的风险来源，因为骨盆复杂的解剖和毗邻的神经血管结构，使可接受的骨性通道极为狭窄。机器人导航提升的不仅是“可接受率”，更是“完美置钉率”。 一项2025年发表于《BMC Surgery》的系统综述与meta分析（纳入19项研究，共1305例患者）提供了最高级别的汇总证据。结果显示，以机器人导航为代表的新型导航技术，其置钉准确率的合并优势比（OR）为2.44，显著优于传统2D透视。在绝对数值上，新型导航组的平均准确率为92%，而传统2D透视组为82%，相差10个百分点。该分析进一步指出，在各类导航技术中，3D CT与机器人导航的表现“似乎更优”。 具体到机器人系统的对比研究，数据同样支持这一优势。一项2026年的回顾性研究显示，机器人辅助组的置钉准确率为94%，而传统透视组为62%（p=0.06，未达统计学显著，可能与样本量较小有关）。针对天玑（TiRobot）系统的研究则报告了更为精细的精度指标：机器人组的A级（完美置钉）比例为82.8%，显著高于透视组的66.7%；临床可接受率（A+B级）达到96.1%。在角度和导针控制的微观层面，一项2023年的研究显示，机器人组的螺钉角度偏差（1.96° vs. 2.87°）和导针偏差（1.92 mm vs. 2.91 mm）均显著更小。 这些数据说明，机器人导航的价值在于将置钉结果从传统透视下较大比例的“可接受但并非完美”，系统性地推向“精准”区间，从而为安全骨性通道的维持提供了更可靠的几何保障。 ⏱️ 透视时间：具有统计学与临床双重意义的显著缩短 缩短术者与患者的辐射暴露，是机器人导航在此类手术中最一致且效应量最大的获益之一。 2025年的meta分析给出了精确的汇总估计：新型导航组的透视时间平均缩短了71.89秒（95% CI 51.37–92.41），透视次数平均减少了17.22次（95% CI 7.73–26.70），差异均具有统计学显著性。这意味着在每一台手术中，患者和整个手术团队所受的电离辐射剂量都获得了可观的削减。 单项研究的数据进一步印证了这一趋势，且不同机器人系统的绝对缩短幅度可能因对照组的基线操作习惯而异： 一项2026年的研究中，机器人组透视时间为55.1秒，传统组高达181.1秒（p=0.053），前者仅为后者的约30%。 一项2023年针对骶骨脆性骨折的研究中，机器人组每枚螺钉的透视时间仅为7.25秒，而传统徒手组为20.93秒（p<0.0001）。 国内针对天玑系统的多项研究也报告了类似量级的缩短，机器人组的透视时间常被控制在10秒上下，甚至更短。 在骨盆手术中，清晰的透视影像是置钉成功的前提，传统技术依赖反复的多角度透视来确认导针和螺钉位置。机器人导航将这一“术中反复试错”的过程，前移并替换为“术前/术中一次性规划与机械臂精确执行”，从而在根本上压缩了对实时透视的依赖。 🛡️ 神经血管并发症：低发生率下的“预防性”优势 直接比较两组神经血管并发症发生率的最大障碍，在于这类严重并发症的绝对发生率本身就很低，以至于在多数单项研究中，即便机器人组一例未发生而传统组发生数例，也极难达到统计学显著性。 现有最高级别的汇总证据对此的描述是审慎的。2025年的meta分析结论是，两组的并发症发生率都“可接受地低（acceptably low）”，但同时也指出，这些并发症在两组中的报告质量都不佳（poorly reported），因此无法就并发症率本身的差异得出确切结论。在个别研究中，确实观察到了机器人组并发症更少的趋势。例如，一项2026年的研究中，机器人组未发生主要术中并发症，而对照组的情况在摘要中未详细展开。一项2023年的中文meta分析则报告，机器人辅助组可降低患者术后总体并发症发生率。 这种“低报告率、低发生率”的现实，要求我们从另一个角度理解机器人导航对安全性的贡献：其核心机制并非在并发症发生后进行更有效的“抢救”，而是通过前述的精度提升，从源头上降低了螺钉突破骨性边界、侵及邻近神经血管结构的概率。 一篇OTA International的述评对此的总结是，机器人技术的主要优势在于提高经皮螺钉的准确度，而这“可能在降低经皮骨盆骨折手术神经血管损伤风险方面发挥作用——尤其是在手术量较少的术者中”。换言之，机器人系统通过标准化和机械化的精度执行，为经验曲线不同阶段的术者提供了一个更可靠的安全基线，其价值在高风险解剖区域和低手术量的场景中可能被进一步放大。 💎 从医师视角的综合判断 综合来看，在经皮骶髂关节与骨盆环螺钉固定中，机器人导航相对于传统透视的获益是非对称性的。在准确度和辐射暴露这两个可精确量化的维度上，优势明确且效应量可观：完美置钉率获得系统性提升，透视时间被压缩至传统方法的三分之一甚至更低。在神经血管并发症这一最终临床结局上，机器人导航的价值是“预防性”和“基线保障性”的，它通过将置钉过程从依赖术者个人手感与反复透视确认的经验性操作，转变为规划驱动的精确执行，来降低风险事件的发生概率。但其优势的统计学证明，受限于这类并发症固有的低发生率与文献报告的不充分性，尚无法在汇总数据中呈现为显著的并发症率下降。对于术者而言，这意味着机器人导航提供的是一套提升操作确定性、减少对辐射依赖、并为复杂骨盆解剖提供可预期安全路径的系统性工具，其最终的安全收益，需要在个体化的术前规划与严格的适应证选择中持续兑现。

Independent robotic orthopaedic practice requires competence in the underlying operation, training on the specific robotic platform, and approval through the hospital’s credentialing process. Completing a manufacturer’s course alone does not establish readiness for independent practice. Exact requirements vary by country, institution, procedure and device; there is no universally applicable minimum case number. aaos.org From a surgical-practice perspective, I would separate the requirements into the following areas. Area What should be required Professional credentials A valid medical licence, recognised specialty training and privileges for the underlying procedure. Board certification, specialist registration or equivalent requirements depend on jurisdiction and hospital policy. Conventional surgical competence Ability to perform the operation without robotic assistance, recognise complications and manage conversion. Robotics must not substitute for knowledge of anatomy, exposure, implant selection or fixation principles. Platform-specific training Training in the particular robot, software, instruments, imaging requirements, registration, tracking, safety limits and troubleshooting. Experience with one platform does not automatically establish competence with another. Supervised clinical introduction Appropriate initial case selection, supervised or proctored cases, documented assessment and formal approval before independent practice. Maintenance of competence Review of outcomes and technical performance, continuing education, training after material platform changes and reassessment when experience or activity is insufficient. AAOS identifies licensure, specialty training, experience and current competence as core considerations for hospital privileges. Current Royal College of Surgeons guidance additionally supports structured robotic training, proctored cases and competency assessment. These are professional standards and recommendations; their implementation as binding requirements remains local. aaos.org Specialised training should cover the complete procedure, including failure scenarios. The essential components are: Planning and judgement: patient selection, image interpretation, implant positioning and recognition of an unsuitable or incorrect computer-generated plan. Practical skills: laboratory or simulation training, tracker placement, registration verification, robotic bone preparation or trajectory guidance, and protection of surrounding structures. Troubleshooting and rescue: tracking loss, inaccurate registration, tracker movement, equipment failure, emergency access and conversion to conventional surgery. Team coordination: the scrub team, assistants, anaesthesia staff and imaging personnel need training relevant to their roles. The BOA’s musculoskeletal robotics guidance specifically recommends cadaveric training for surgeons and team simulation covering setup, registration, troubleshooting and surgical or medical emergencies. A manufacturer’s technical specialist can support equipment use but does not replace clinical supervision or the surgeon’s responsibility. boa.ac.uk The learning curve is usually measured by operating time—and that is not the same as competence. Procedure Examples from published studies Interpretation Robotic total knee replacement Individual studies reported workflow improvement or proficiency thresholds around 7, 16 or 30 cases. Useful for planning an introductory period, but not a universal credentialing threshold. Robotic total hip replacement One series identified an initial learning phase of 14 cases, with substantial subsequent reduction in operative time. The result reflects one surgeon, platform and workflow. Robotic spinal instrumentation Clinical series reported improvement after approximately 14–25 cases. Setup, screw placement and overall operating time may improve at different rates. Complex anatomy and rescue skills require separate assessment. These figures come from individual clinical studies rather than mandatory training standards. link.springer.com A surgeon can reach a stable operating time without yet demonstrating reliable management of unusual anatomy or equipment failure. Conversely, some studies found good implant-positioning accuracy from the earliest cases even while efficiency continued to improve. Neither speed nor accuracy alone is sufficient for sign-off. link.springer.com I would therefore favour competency-based approval supported by case experience, assessing planning, registration checks, technical execution, judgement, communication and emergency conversion, followed by outcome monitoring. General robotic-surgery credentialing research has found wide variation between hospitals and cautions against using a small number of proctored cases as the sole proxy for proficiency; that research is not specific to orthopaedics. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Without a specified country, hospital and robotic system, I cannot state an exact compulsory course, examination, supervised-case count or annual minimum. Those must be checked against the applicable credentialing policy and device training requirements.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the question of haptic feedback in robotic surgery needs to be unpacked carefully, because the premise—that robotic arms categorically lack haptic feedback—is not uniformly true across all platforms. Semi-active haptic systems (such as the MAKO platform) are specifically designed to provide force feedback and constrain the surgeon's hand within a predefined safe zone, and the surgeon can feel resistance and adjust movements accordingly. The problem is more accurately framed as a spectrum: fully active or teleoperated systems and many spine robotic platforms provide diminished, altered, or absent direct tactile feedback, whereas semi-active orthopedic systems attempt to preserve or simulate it. With that caveat, I will address the consequences where haptic feedback is genuinely compromised or absent, as this is where the clinically meaningful risks lie. 🦴 Osteotomy: losing the "feel" of bone density and cut-through In conventional freehand osteotomy, the surgeon continuously integrates tactile information—changes in bone density, the resistance of cortical versus cancellous bone, and the sudden drop in force that signals the blade has breached the far cortex. This is not a marginal sensory channel; it is central to controlling depth and avoiding over-penetration into neurovascular structures. Consequence 1: impaired force modulation and depth judgment. Robots achieve high positional accuracy but have poor tactile response and are not good at assessing the forces required to apply to a cutter while resecting bone, whereas surgeons can sense changes in bone density and adjust cutting forces accordingly. In a teleoperated bone-cutting paradigm, bone cutting further reduces any sort of feedback, because unlike soft tissue, bone does not deform to provide a visual cue of applied force. The operator must instead rely on end-effector movement, auditory cues, and system data—none of which reliably signal the moment of cortical breach. The lack of force feedback increases the difficulty of judging whether the blade has cut through the target, and the reduced ability to judge depth may pose a risk to soft tissue underneath the bone structures. This is not a theoretical concern: the clinical literature explicitly recognizes that robotic bone cutting can be associated with inaccurate osteotomy angles and poor prosthesis positioning when visual judgment alone must substitute for tactile control. Consequence 2: prolonged cutting time and incomplete cuts. Because the operator cannot feel the completion of a cut, additional cutting time may result from not appreciating that a particular section has been completed, and the lack of force feedback is associated with frequent instrument stalls in ultrasonic bone-cutting systems. The mitigating design response: This is precisely why semi-active haptic systems exist. The MAKO-type platform provides haptic feedback that limits instrument movement within predefined boundaries, effectively creating a virtual fixture that prevents the saw from exiting the planned resection volume. Haptic virtual fixtures have been shown in controlled tasks to improve precision and reduce cognitive load, and in fibula osteotomy specifically, AR combined with haptic virtual fixtures improved task precision. The consequence of absent haptics is therefore not an unavoidable flaw of robotics per se, but a design-dependent vulnerability that is addressed by semi-active architectures and virtual fixtures rather than by the robot autonomously "feeling" the bone. 🔩 Screw placement: the skiving problem and the loss of pedicle "feel" Pedicle screw placement is the procedure in which the loss of haptic feedback has been most explicitly characterized, because freehand surgeons rely on "feel" when cannulating or probing a pedicle—the tactile transition from cancellous to cortical bone is a primary feedback signal for trajectory control. Consequence 1: skiving at the entry point. The most concrete mechanical consequence is skiving: when a high-speed drill contacts the cortical bone at the entry point, the bit can slide along the irregular surface rather than penetrating, deviating from the intended trajectory. Skiving is explicitly listed among the poor haptics and sensory feedback limitations of robotic and navigated percutaneous screw systems. In a series of robot-assisted cases, skiving accounted for 3 of the recorded deviations, with an irregular bony surface causing lateral deviation from the planned trajectory. The clinical significance is that a skived entry hole propagates: the subsequent tap and screw follow the wrong trajectory, and the error is not necessarily corrected by the navigation display once the physical channel has been created. Consequence 2: diminished surgeon confidence and reliance on visual surrogates. The absence of direct haptic feedback in robot-assisted spine surgery remains a concern, particularly in minimally invasive procedures where direct visual confirmation is limited. The loss of haptic and sensory feedback has been described as reducing surgeon confidence and procedural efficacy due to the lack of direct interaction with tissue. In response, the field has developed visuohaptic surrogates: a cyclical insertional torque (CIT) pattern can be observed both visually on the navigation interface and haptically through the handheld drill during slow-speed automated drilling, potentially offering a cue for bone engagement where tactile feedback is reduced. Newer systems also incorporate oscillating instruments that allow surgeons to maintain "feel" and mechanisms that alert the surgeon to drill-bit misalignment or smooth the bone before drilling to prevent skiving. Some surgeons adopt a hybrid approach, using navigation to confirm the pedicle pathway while retaining the haptic "feel" of a gearshift probe to cannulate the pedicle. These workarounds are themselves evidence that the haptic deficit is real and clinically consequential. 🩸 Soft-tissue dissection: the most direct patient-safety consequence Soft-tissue dissection is where the absence of tactile feedback translates most directly into patient harm, because soft tissues are precisely the structures that force feedback is best suited to protect. Consequence 1: unintended soft-tissue damage. The lack of tactile and haptic sensation in robotic-assisted surgery can result in tissue damage and comorbidities, and visual cues can only partially compensate for the reduction in kinetic feedback. Early experience with robotics in total hip and knee replacement reported having to abort the procedure in 18–34% of cases, with soft-tissue issues and concerns over actual and potential soft-tissue damage among the reasons; these injuries caused significant morbidity, negating the desired advantages of precision and reproducibility. The absence of touch impairs tissue characterization, complicates diagnostics, and elevates the risk of unintended damage. Consequence 2: compromised tissue identification. Beyond gross injury, the haptic deficit impairs the surgeon's ability to distinguish tissue types by stiffness—a capability that freehand surgeons use to identify abnormal tissue such as tumors and to avoid fragile structures. Current systems largely rely on visual input, lacking tactile feedback and autonomy, which increases training demands and limits scalability. The mitigating design response: The risk of soft-tissue damage in robotic joint replacement can be mitigated by haptic software prohibiting the cutting tip from striking vital soft tissues and by the surgeon ensuring a clear workspace path for the cutting tool. This is the core rationale for semi-active haptic-guided systems in arthroplasty: rather than restoring natural tactile sensation, they impose a software-defined boundary that prevents the end effector from entering a protected volume. Handheld robotic burrs take a different approach, controlling speed and exposure to protect against iatrogenic ligament injury in the absence of a haptic interface. These are compensatory strategies, not solutions to the underlying sensory deficit—they protect against the most severe consequence (striking a vital structure) but do not restore the surgeon's ability to palpate tissue or judge force. 💎 The bottom line The consequences of diminished haptic feedback are real, procedure-specific, and clinically documented, but they are not uniform across robotic platforms. In osteotomy, the loss is primarily one of force and depth judgment, with risks of over-cutting, soft-tissue injury beneath the bone, prolonged cutting time, and—in the absence of haptic constraint—inaccurate resection. In screw placement, the dominant mechanical consequence is skiving at the cortical entry point, which can propagate into trajectory error, compounded by reduced surgeon confidence and reliance on imperfect visual or torque-based surrogates. In soft-tissue dissection, the consequence is the most direct: unintended tissue damage and impaired tissue identification, which historically contributed to procedure abortion in early robotic arthroplasty experience. The field's response has been architectural rather than sensory: semi-active haptic constraints, virtual fixtures, oscillating instruments, and visuohaptic torque patterns are all attempts to substitute for, rather than restore, the surgeon's hand. As a practicing surgeon, I would state clearly that the safety of robotic orthopedic surgery depends less on whether the robot "feels" and more on whether the platform design ensures that the absence of natural haptics is compensated by a constraint that makes the dangerous trajectory physically impossible—and on the surgeon maintaining the anatomical judgment to recognize when that constraint is not functioning as intended.

The surgeon needs competence and privileges for the underlying operation, additional training on the specific robotic system, and demonstrated ability to use it safely—including conversion to conventional surgery. A manufacturer’s course certificate alone should not establish readiness for independent practice. There is no universal international “robotic orthopaedic surgeon” credential or mandatory case number. Exact requirements depend on the jurisdiction, hospital, procedure, and platform. Area Requirements or appropriate competency standard Professional credentials Valid medical registration/licensure, recognised specialist training, and eligibility to practise the relevant surgery. Board certification or its local equivalent may be required by the institution. Procedure-specific experience Demonstrated competence in the conventional operation—arthroplasty, spinal instrumentation, or fracture fixation—including patient selection and complication management. Fellowship training may be required for complex procedures, but is not a universal robotics requirement. Hospital privileges Explicit institutional authorisation for the robotic application, with review of training, experience, and initial clinical performance. Privileges for robotic knee replacement should not automatically establish competence in robotic hip or spine surgery. Platform-specific training Training in planning software, imaging, registration, tracking, instrument calibration, robotic constraints, safe operating modes, and technical limitations. A different platform or substantial application change warrants assessment of additional training needs. Supervised clinical introduction Observed and supervised/proctored cases, followed by documented assessment before independent practice. The required number should reflect both local policy and demonstrated performance. Maintenance of competence Continuing education, review of outcomes and complications, appropriate refresher training after prolonged inactivity, and reassessment when introducing substantially different technology. These principles align with American College of Surgeons guidance on introducing new technologies. That guidance supports didactic and laboratory training, supervised/proctored practice, and outcome review; it does not prescribe a universal minimum case volume. It is general surgical guidance, not an orthopaedic-specific licensing rule. ACS Specialised training should cover more than operating the robotic arm. In a practical orthopaedic curriculum, I would expect: Planning and judgment: choosing appropriate patients, recognising unsuitable anatomy, reviewing segmentation, and selecting clinically appropriate alignment or fixation targets. Hands-on technical skills: safe tracker placement, registration and independent verification, instrument handling, and recognition of tracking loss, skiving, or inaccurate guidance. Failure and emergency management: safe disengagement, manual conversion, and coordinated responses to bleeding or neurological concerns. Team performance: communication with nursing, anaesthesia, radiography, and technical support personnel. Manufacturer programmes can provide platform instruction, case observation, and cadaveric practice. For example, published Mako training descriptions include preoperative planning, workflow, and faculty-guided cadaver procedures. Completion documents training exposure; independent clinical competence still requires assessment. stryker.com The learning curve must be defined by what is being learned. Time efficiency, accurate execution, sound decision-making, and emergency competence are different outcomes. Procedure Illustrative published learning milestone Important limitation Robotic total knee replacement Individual studies identified operative-time milestones at approximately 16 cases and 30 cases. These are study-specific estimates, not mandatory credentialing thresholds. Robotic total hip replacement One fluoroscopy-based system study reported an efficiency learning curve of 12 cases. This cannot be transferred directly to other platforms or approaches. Robotic spinal instrumentation One 125-patient series found improvements in setup, registration, and screw-insertion times after the first 25 cases. This does not establish competence for every spinal region, deformity, or emergency. These figures come from procedure-specific clinical studies. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov For independent practice, I would favour observed proficiency over a case-count-only rule: reliable registration, appropriate decisions, accurate execution, recognition of misleading guidance, and safe conversion, supported by review of clinical outcomes. Broader robotic credentialing consensus likewise favours objective performance benchmarks and ongoing monitoring. PubMed I cannot specify the legally required certificates, proctored-case count, or annual maintenance volume without the country, institution, and robotic application. Any precise universal number would be misleading.

**截至目前，机器人改善假体定位和部分力线指标的证据，比“减少翻修、延长假体寿命”的证据更充分。**大型登记研究尚未显示全膝、单髁或全髋置换的全因翻修率一致下降；但全髋置换已出现减少定位不良相关翻修的信号。患者报告结局也未呈现稳定、具有临床意义的全面优势。 这里将“注册研究”理解为关节登记数据库研究；它与随机对照试验提供的证据有所不同。 1．翻修率与假体存留率：应按术式分别看。 术式 代表性结果 临床解读 全膝置换 英国NJR登记研究中，传统与机器人组估计5年假体存留率为98.5%和98.6%，调整后翻修风险无显著差异 尚未证明机器人降低全因翻修 单髁置换 同一研究中，两组估计5年存留率为97.8%和96.4%，调整后翻修风险同样无显著差异 不能仅看存留率点估计就判断机器人更差；机器人组估计的不确定性较大 全髋置换 英国NJR研究中，两组估计5年存留率均为98.8%；机器人组定位不良相关翻修风险较低，但全因翻修无显著差异 可能减少特定失败原因，尚未证明整体假体寿命延长 上述英国研究平均随访约2.5年，“5年存留率”是生存分析估计，并非每位患者都完成5年随访；还不能视为充分的长期结论。膝关节登记研究、髋关节登记研究 美国AJRR也发现，全膝置换2年全因翻修风险无显著差异。其全髋研究则发现，机器人组因脱位翻修约0.3%，传统组约0.6%，但全因翻修仍无显著差异。这属于观察性关联，不能直接认定由机器人单独造成。AJRR全膝研究、AJRR全髋研究 2．真正的中长期随访与患者报告结局如何？ **全膝：**一项平均随访13年的随机试验中，两组无菌性松动率均约2%；以翻修或无菌性松动为终点，15年存留率均约98%，功能与WOMAC等评分没有显著差异。但这是较早期机器人系统，不能完全代表现代平台。长期随机试验 **单髁：**一项5年随机试验未发现患者报告结局明显不同，机器人组再次干预较少；不过，再次干预不等同于更换假体的翻修，而且两组假体设计不同，不能把全部差异归因于机器人。5年随机试验 **全髋：**一项3年对照研究中，机器人组部分评分统计学上更好，但差值未达到最小临床重要差异，即未证明患者能够感受到有意义的额外改善。现代系统的长期比较仍不足。3年对照研究 3．力线与平衡改善，是否已经转化为翻修减少？ **尚未被普遍证实。**更准确地执行计划，不代表该计划对每位患者都是最优；术中测得的间隙或松弛度，也不完全等于负重活动时的动态稳定性。翻修还受感染、骨质、固定方式、假体设计、软组织及患者因素影响。 要证明“机器人通过改善力线／平衡减少翻修”，需要在可比较的假体和治疗条件下，长期追踪这些指标与失败原因之间的联系。登记研究可发现风险关联，但通常无法单独验证这条因果链。 因此，临床告知应是：**机器人有助于提高重建的一致性，全髋的特定定位相关失败可能减少；目前仍不能承诺整体翻修更少、假体更耐用或患者长期感受一定更好。**未发现显著差异，也不等于证明两种方法完全等效。

Robot-assisted percutaneous fixation is best suited to fractures that can be reduced adequately and stabilized with screws through a narrow, clearly identifiable bone corridor. Its main contribution is accurate trajectory execution; it does not compensate for inadequate reduction or an unsuitable fixation construct. From an orthopaedic surgical selection perspective: Fracture pattern When robotic assistance is most useful Main limitation Sacroiliac disruptions and selected sacral fractures Iliosacral or transsacral fixation after satisfactory reduction, particularly when the corridor is narrow or difficult to visualize with conventional fluoroscopy. A safe corridor must exist, and reduction must remain stable during imaging and insertion. A small randomized trial supports improved placement and reduced insertion-stage fluoroscopy. Trial Femoral neck fractures selected for head-preserving fixation Nondisplaced fractures, or displaced fractures after satisfactory reduction, when precise screw spread, parallelism and depth are important. Robotics should not determine whether screw fixation is appropriate. A comparative study demonstrated technical improvements without a significant difference in healing rate or final hip scores. Comparative study Selected acetabular anterior- or posterior-column fractures Minimally displaced fractures, or fractures reducible by closed or limited-open techniques, with a suitable extra-articular screw corridor. Significant residual displacement, articular impaction or comminution requiring direct reconstruction may make isolated percutaneous screws inappropriate. Pelvic and acetabular guidance Selected anterior pelvic ring fractures Percutaneous ramus screws when operative stabilization is indicated and a safe corridor is available. Not every ramus fracture needs surgery; the indication depends on the overall ring injury and stability. Guidance Robotic assistance may be unnecessary when nonoperative treatment is appropriate, when conventional imaging permits straightforward safe fixation, or when setup adds little practical benefit. Routine use for every eligible fracture is not supported by evidence. It should be avoided or abandoned when: Adequate reduction cannot be obtained or maintained. No safe screw corridor exists, or screws alone cannot provide the required stability. Imaging, registration or tracking is unreliable. Patient positioning or equipment prevents safe instrument access. These technical exclusions are described in published pelvic fixation guidance. Indications and contraindications In an unstable trauma patient, resuscitation and timely hemorrhage control also take precedence over robotic setup. A fracture requiring open reduction does not automatically exclude robotic assistance: guidance may still help place selected screws after reduction. The important distinction is between suitability for percutaneous fixation and suitability for robotic guidance. Evidence is strongest for technical accuracy and workflow benefits; I cannot confidently rank these fracture groups by proven long-term clinical benefit.

从骨科医师的视角来看，机器人辅助关节置换的“患者选择”，本质上是在寻找“精度需求”与“技术可及性”能够精确匹配的群体。它并非适用于所有患者，其价值在解剖畸形使传统工具的可靠性下降时最为凸显；而在软组织条件严重受损或解剖标志完全失效的场景中，它可能从工具变为挑战。 🎯 最能获益的患者：当“手感”和“标准工具”的局限性被放大时 机器人辅助的价值，在于用可规划的几何确定性，去替代或补充传统技术所依赖的、在复杂解剖中可能失效的触觉与视觉反馈。以下几类患者是这一价值最清晰的体现者。 重度冠状面畸形（内翻/外翻）：证据最坚实的获益群体 这是机器人辅助全膝关节置换（RA-TKA）证据等级最高、方向最一致的适应人群。一项2026年的系统综述（纳入8项研究，1274膝）明确指出，RA-TKA在中度至重度冠状面畸形中能可靠地达到目标放射学对线，并带来良好的患者报告结局。其优势有具体的量化支撑： 力线偏差显著更小：与传感器引导的TKA相比，RA-TKA在重度内翻或外翻膝中，髋-膝-踝角（HKA）和股骨胫骨角（LTC）的绝对偏差显著更小，意味着力线矫正的精确度更高。 畸形越大，获益越明显：一项2024年的研究显示，在大角度畸形患者中，100%的患者术后1年力线偏差控制在3°以内（平均0.54°），而在外翻组中这一比例为92%。系统综述也确认，力线矫正的改善在中重度内翻和外翻畸形中最为显著。其逻辑在于，畸形越重，传统依赖髓外或髓内导向器所累积的对线误差风险越大，而机器人基于三维规划的截骨则能规避这一累积过程。 屈曲挛缩/僵硬膝：从“相对禁忌”向“可管理挑战”转变 传统上，严重僵硬（活动度<90°或严重屈曲挛缩）被视为关节置换的相对禁忌或高难度场景。机器人辅助正在改变这一局面，但需要谨慎区分“技术可行”与“优于传统”。 技术可行性已被证实：一项2026年的病例系列（25膝，术前平均活动度仅38.7°）显示，使用无影像CORI系统辅助TKA，术后平均活动度恢复至110.2°，且无神经血管并发症、髌腱损伤或需手法松解的病例。该系统通过精确截骨和实时软组织平衡，减少了为获得平衡所需的软组织松解，从而可能降低僵硬膝中软组织损伤的风险。 获益的性质需被准确界定：机器人在此类病例中的价值，更多在于通过精准的骨性操作来减少对已处于脆弱状态的软组织的依赖和干扰，从而在实现平衡的同时降低并发症风险。它并未被证明能“治愈”僵硬，而是提供了一条在僵硬条件下仍能安全执行手术的路径。 髋关节发育不良（DDH）：Crowe分型的显著分层效应 在机器人辅助全髋关节置换（RA-THA）中，DDH的获益呈现清晰的Crowe分型梯度。 Crowe I–III型：精度优势明确。一项2026年的系统综述显示，在Crowe I-III型髋中，RA-THA相比传统THA，髋臼杯外展角和前倾角的误差显著更低，并且更好地恢复了旋转中心。一项针对Crowe II-IV型的回顾性研究（115例）也证实，RA-THA组的髋臼假体位置不良率（15%）显著低于传统组（40%）（P=0.01），且无脱位发生（传统组2例），翻修手术为零。 Crowe IV型：获益更具条件性。对于最严重的Crowe IV型（高位脱位），证据存在张力。尽管有病例报告显示RA-THA能成功处理此类高难度病例并实现双下肢等长，但系统综述指出，在Crowe IV型髋中，RA-THA在恢复旋转中心方面并未显示出与传统技术的差异。另有研究认为，对于Crowe 3-4型DDH，机器人与传统THA在短期至中期随访中结果相当。这意味着，在Crowe IV型中，机器人的主要价值可能不在于“精度超越”，而在于作为一个能够处理复杂解剖、辅助实现可靠固定的工具之一，其必要性不如在Crowe I-III型中那样具有明确的精度增量优势。 既往内植物存留的膝关节：一个流程优势大于结局优势的场景 当膝关节周围存在既往骨折内固定物（钢板、髓内钉）或经历过胫骨高位截骨术时，传统TKA面临髓内导向杆无法置入、内固定物干扰截骨导向器等难题。 核心价值是“避开”而非“超越”：机器人辅助的核心优势在于，基于CT的三维规划能够精确预判内固定物与计划截骨面及假体之间的空间冲突，从而在不拆除内固定物的情况下完成手术，避免了二次手术的创伤和风险。这被明确描述为一种流程上的优势，在髓内工具无法使用或标志点不可靠时尤为突出。 必须正视的证据局限：一篇2026年的综述在肯定其技术可行性的同时，做出了关键的限定：现有数据并未表明该技术能提高患者生存率、降低感染风险、改善主观预后或提升成本效益。因此，在此类病例中，机器人应被视为一种规划和执行的辅助手段，而非一个已被证实能带来更优远期结局的解决方案。 ⚠️ 仍属相对禁忌或需极度审慎的场景 这些情况的核心矛盾在于：机器人所依赖的规划-执行链的某一环节，被病理状态从根本上削弱了。 严重僵硬/关节强直：从“手术难点”到“系统可行性挑战” 需要明确区分“僵硬膝”（活动受限但仍有一定活动度）与“关节强直”（骨性或纤维性融合，几乎无活动度）。后者构成更严峻的挑战。 显露与操作的物理限制：在强直性脊柱炎继发髋关节骨性融合的病例中，髋关节完全无活动度，呈固定畸形，导致手术消毒、解剖显露和截骨操作都极为困难，臼杯安放的角度和深度控制难度极大。机器人系统（尤其是机械臂和示踪器）需要在有限的空间内完成对接和操作，其外部几何包络可能成为限制因素。 注册与配准的潜在风险：严重僵硬或强直可能伴随软组织挛缩和骨性标志的变形，这可能影响基于影像的注册精度，或使术中参考架（array）的稳定固定变得困难。尽管有病例报告显示机器人可用于此类患者，但这更多体现的是在极端条件下技术上的“可行性”，而非一个被证据支持的“优势适应症”。将其视为相对禁忌，是出于对系统失效风险的审慎考量。 既往内植物存留：从“优势”到“禁忌”的条件性转变 如前述，内植物存留可以是机器人辅助的优势场景，但也可能转化为相对禁忌，关键在于内植物的位置和性质。 当内植物是“障碍”而非“路标”时：如果内固定物（如髓内钉）占据了计划使用的髓腔通道，或严重遮挡了关键的骨性标志（如股骨外髁、胫骨平台），导致注册和配准无法可靠完成，那么机器人系统的前提——“基于可靠影像的精确规划与执行”——就不成立了。此时，传统方法（可能需要先移除内固定物）可能更为直接。 感染风险的考量：既往手术史本身是围手术期感染的危险因素。虽然机器人手术不改变无菌原则，但在一个瘢痕化、血供可能受损的术野中进行复杂的机器人系统装机和无菌套安装，需要额外的审慎。综述也提及，感染风险是此类复杂病例决策中需要考虑的因素之一。 关节强直：作为严重僵硬谱系的终点 关节强直（尤其是骨性融合）是上述“严重僵硬”挑战的极端形式。它不仅仅是活动度的丧失，更意味着解剖平面的完全消失和软组织弹性的彻底丧失。在这种条件下，机器人辅助所依赖的间隙平衡评估、软组织张力判断等核心功能，其输入信号本身已严重失真或不可用。因此，它应被视为相对禁忌中的高风险端，仅在具备极端丰富经验的中心，作为个体化决策下的最后选项之一进行审慎评估。 💎 一个分层的判断 将获益人群与禁忌场景并列，可以得出一个清晰的决策框架： 机器人辅助关节置换的“最佳适应症”，是那些“解剖畸形使传统工具的精度可靠性下降，但软组织条件和骨性标志仍足以支撑系统完成规划与执行”的患者。 重度冠状面畸形和Crowe I-III型DDH是这一逻辑的典型代表，其精度优势有明确的量化证据支持。僵硬膝和内植物存留则属于 “有条件获益” 的范畴，其价值更多体现在流程可行性和风险规避上，而非已被证实的远期结局优势。 相对禁忌的核心，是“系统赖以工作的前提被病理状态所破坏”。 严重僵硬/关节强直威胁的是操作空间与配准可靠性，而某些位置不佳的内植物威胁的是规划的几何基础。在这些情况下，医生需要诚实地评估：机器人系统是否还能提供其所承诺的“确定性”？如果答案是否定的，那么选择传统技术、或转换手术策略，比坚持使用一个可能失效的工具更为安全。最终，这一决策的责任，仍然在于术者对具体患者解剖条件与自身技术边界的独立判断。

From a surgical decision-making perspective, the indication should first be established for the operation, and then separately for robotic assistance. Arthritis, a fracture classification, or a spinal deformity does not, by itself, indicate robotic surgery. There is no single universally accepted disease-by-disease classification for robotic eligibility. A precise decision must combine clinical need, anatomy, the specific robot’s authorised application, and whether its guidance can be used reliably. Disease or injury group When robotic assistance may be appropriate Contraindications or important boundaries Knee osteoarthritis requiring total knee replacement Symptomatic moderate-to-severe disease with substantial pain or functional limitation despite appropriate nonoperative treatment, when replacement is otherwise indicated. Robotics may assist bone preparation, alignment, and balancing. Mild radiographic disease or minimal symptoms do not become indications because a robot is available. Active joint infection generally precludes routine elective replacement. Major bone loss or ligament insufficiency may require implants or reconstruction beyond the platform’s supported application. Isolated compartment knee arthritis Robotic partial replacement is reasonable when disease is genuinely confined to the intended compartment, with suitable ligament function and correctable deformity. Disease elsewhere in the knee, inflammatory arthritis, significant stiffness, or ligament dysfunction may make partial replacement inappropriate. Robotics cannot compensate for selecting the wrong operation. Exact ligament and deformity criteria depend on the implant and operative strategy. Hip arthritis, osteonecrosis, dysplasia, or post-traumatic degeneration When total hip replacement is clinically justified, robotic assistance may support acetabular preparation and component positioning. Complex anatomy may increase its planning value. Early osteonecrosis without collapse or secondary arthritis should not automatically lead to replacement. Severe dysplasia, retained hardware, or major bone defects require individual assessment of reconstruction needs, image quality, and platform compatibility. Degenerative spinal disease or deformity When instrumented stabilisation or fusion is independently indicated, robotic guidance may assist compatible screw placement. A diagnosis such as stenosis or disc degeneration alone does not establish a need for fusion. Screw-guidance robotics does not itself treat neural compression, establish the indication for fusion, or replace decompression. Thoracolumbar fractures Classify morphology using AO Spine, and document neurological status and relevant modifiers. Robotics can assist fixation once operative stabilisation has been selected. AO type B and C injuries generally favour operative treatment; selected type A injuries can be managed nonoperatively. Neither category automatically determines robotic eligibility. Urgent decompression or stabilisation must not be delayed for robotic setup. Pelvic-ring and acetabular fractures Selected injuries needing fixation, particularly where adequate reduction permits a safe percutaneous screw corridor. Tile B/C injuries have been studied, but eligibility depends on the actual displacement, reduction, and available corridor. Haemodynamic instability, uncontrolled contamination, an unreduced fracture without a safe corridor, or inability to obtain reliable imaging makes planned robotic screw fixation inappropriate at that stage. An acetabular classification alone cannot establish suitability for percutaneous fixation. Arthroscopic sports procedures, tumour reconstruction, osteotomies, and revision surgery Consider only a specifically supported application with appropriate expertise and evidence, or an appropriately governed investigational pathway. Do not extrapolate indications from primary robotic joint replacement or spinal screw placement. Evidence and regulatory status differ substantially by procedure and system. The arthroplasty distinctions above follow ACR/AAHKS guidance, AAOS partial-knee selection criteria, and manufacturer descriptions of hip applications. Inflammatory arthritis, for example, may argue against partial knee replacement while still being an indication for total joint replacement. Wiley Online Library The spinal and pelvic distinctions are supported by specialist guidance and clinical pelvic-fixation studies; they should not be interpreted as universal robotic eligibility rules. media.aofoundation.org I would separate contraindications into three practical categories: Reasons not to perform the proposed operation: no adequate clinical indication, unacceptable operative risk, or—for routine elective arthroplasty—active infection. These are not uniquely robotic contraindications. Infection may itself require a different operation. Reasons not to use the robot for that operation: inability to obtain or verify registration; insecure tracking or reference fixation; inadequate imaging; no safe instrument trajectory; inaccessible anatomy; or incompatible instruments or implants. These can justify proceeding conventionally even when surgery remains necessary. Device guidance explicitly depends on identifiable rigid bony anatomy and compatible equipment. strykermeded.com Factors requiring individual assessment: osteoporosis, obesity, severe deformity, previous surgery, retained metalwork, and restricted positioning. These should not be labelled universal absolute contraindications. They matter when they compromise fixation, imaging, access, or the planned reconstruction. I cannot specify a defensible universal BMI, bone-density, age, or deformity cutoff across robotic platforms. For a clinical protocol, I would document: diagnosis and classification → reason surgery is needed → intended robotic task → device/implant eligibility → verified technical feasibility → criteria for conversion to conventional surgery. The current, locally applicable instructions for the exact robot, software version, and implant must determine the final device-specific limits.

**会影响。机械臂存在工作空间、关节角度和器械通道限制，特殊体位及深部术区可能出现“影像上能规划，实际无法安全到达”的情况。**但限制程度取决于具体型号、器械配置、患者体型及手术室布局，不能一概而论。 1．特殊体位：主要影响轨迹可达性和设备避碰。 俯卧、侧卧等体位会改变机械臂与患者的相对关系。肩部、胸廓、髂嵴，以及手术床、头架、体位支架等，都可能阻挡机械臂或器械。某条轨迹即使没有骨性障碍，也可能因机械臂关节接近活动极限而无法执行。 一项颈椎置钉尸体研究中，部分已规划轨迹无法完成，原因包括颈部体型限制，以及机器人安装位置过近。这证明可达性确实可能成为瓶颈，但该研究规模小，不能据此推算所有系统的临床失败率。颈椎尸体研究 2．深部术区：机械臂到位，不代表器械通道足够。 深部骨盆、髋臼及部分脊柱区域，还需要同时满足： 器械有效长度足够，导向套筒能够获得合适支撑； 进针或切削角度可行，不受骨性结构及周围软组织阻挡； 通道受力可控，避免软组织侧向推力或长器械弯曲导致偏移； 能够观察和保护邻近结构，不能仅依赖导航屏幕。 因此，深度本身不是统一禁忌，但深度与狭窄通道、陡斜角度共同存在时，操作难度会增加。 3．机器人不能消除手术入路本身的解剖限制。 例如，部分侧方腰椎入路受到肋笼和髂嵴限制，某些高位或低位节段可能不适合该入路；机器人定位并不能让这些结构“让路”。已有单体位机器人辅助腰椎融合的技术研究，也明确提示这些限制。技术研究 另一方面，特殊体位并不意味着无法使用机器人：已有侧卧单体位完成腰椎融合及机器人辅助置钉的病例系列，但这只能说明在特定设备、患者和团队条件下具有可行性。病例系列 4．临床上如何应对？ 术前应同时评估骨内轨迹、体表进入路径和设备摆位；术中在关键操作前核验机械臂能否无碰撞到位、器械能否安全进入。调整患者、手术床或参考架后，应按设备要求重新核验定位，必要时重新配准。 若仍无法安全到达，应调整入路、扩大必要暴露，或改用导航辅助、透视辅助及常规操作。**不能为了迁就机械臂的角度而接受不安全的置钉轨迹。**目前也没有适用于所有骨科机器人的统一“最大可操作深度”或“安全角度”，必须依据具体设备说明书和患者解剖判断。

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, my answer is: the general framework for converting from robotic to manual surgery is maturing, but protocols specifically for intraoperative vascular or nerve injury are not yet sufficiently mature, and maturity is uneven across subspecialties and platforms. What exists is stronger at the level of generic emergency principles and system-failure response than at the level of a validated, step-by-step, orthopedic-specific “robot-to-open” pathway for a named crisis such as major arterial bleeding or loss of neurophysiologic signal. What is relatively mature: generic rescue principles The core principles are now reasonably well articulated: recognize the error, classify it as recoverable or non-recoverable, rapidly undock, convert to manual/open surgery, control bleeding, resuscitate, and use closed-loop team communication. These are sound and should be part of every robotic program. A 2026 review of emergency rescue strategies in robotic surgery proposed a structured system-based framework including rapid undocking, conversion, hemorrhage control, and resuscitation, with simulation and team situational awareness. However, that framework is not orthopedic-specific; it draws heavily on general robotic and laparoscopic experience. The 2026 Asia-Pacific expert consensus on joint replacement also states that true robotic competency should include the ability to convert safely to conventional surgery and to recognize when system inconsistency or interruption requires abandoning the robotic workflow. That confirms conversion competence as a required surgeon skill, but it does not provide a crisis-specific checklist for vascular or nerve injury. What is not mature: orthopedic-specific, crisis-specific protocols Vascular injury is a real, not theoretical, risk. Case reports describe deep circumflex iliac artery branch injury from reference-pin placement in robotic THA, femoral artery injury during MAKO-assisted THA, and popliteal artery injury in early adoption of robotic TKA (two cases in 35). The management in these reports was conventional vascular intervention—embolization or vascular repair—not a predefined seamless robotic-to-manual conversion protocol. In practice, “conversion” means abandoning robotic operation and activating the hospital’s open vascular or interventional rescue pathway. The maturity of that pathway depends on the institution’s vascular surgery capability, not on the robot itself. For nerve injury, published crisis-conversion protocols are even scarcer. Much of the risk is associated with reference-pin or tracker placement rather than active robotic motion, which suggests prevention—avoiding pins in dangerous zones—may be more actionable than a post-injury conversion algorithm. That does not remove the need for a conversion plan if a neurologic deficit or signal loss occurs, but it means the evidence base for a nerve-specific robot-to-manual protocol is thin. The weak link: undocking time and team performance The first step in any emergency conversion is undocking. Reported routine undocking takes 2–3 minutes, while emergency undocking targets 1 minute or less. However, a resuscitation review found that untrained teams averaged about 146 seconds—close to 2.5 minutes—which would delay control of major bleeding or initiation of high-quality resuscitation. This is the central problem: the existence of a protocol is not the same as its effectiveness. Some institutions have rapid-undocking protocols with trigger phrases such as “Emergency undock” and simulation drills, but orthopedic-specific, high-fidelity-simulation-validated team workflows that seamlessly link robotic undocking to immediate manual hemorrhage control are not yet widely standardized. A generic “emergency conversion to open” checklist is better than nothing, but its actual execution efficiency and outcomes in vascular or nerve injury scenarios have not been systematically evaluated. My maturity assessment Generic rescue framework: relatively mature. Rapid undocking, conversion, hemorrhage control, and team communication are recognized and should be institutionalized. Orthopedic-specific and crisis-specific protocols: not mature. There is a lack of stepwise, simulation-validated conversion pathways tailored to spine, joint, and trauma surgery and to specific crises—arterial bleeding versus loss of neuromonitoring, for example. Current practice relies more on the surgeon’s open-surgical skill and the hospital’s emergency response system than on a validated fail-safe built into the robotic workflow. Effectiveness validation: seriously insufficient. Undocking time data show that an under-rehearsed conversion is itself a source of delay. Team simulation and outcome assessment for vascular/nerve injury conversion remain a clear gap in orthopedic robotics. My practical bottom line Before starting any robotic orthopedic case, I assume conversion is possible and require the team—scrub nurse, circulating nurse, anesthesia—to verbally confirm a shared plan: if major bleeding occurs now, how do we expose the field and begin open control within one minute? That plan includes who calls vascular surgery, where open instruments and vascular repair trays are, how the patient is positioned to allow rapid conversion, and who performs the undocking. The reliability of that plan currently depends more on team preparation and experience than on a widely validated standardized robot-to-manual protocol. I would not tell a patient or an OR director that the conversion protocol is fully mature; I would say the principles are sound, the orthopedic-specific execution pathways are still being built, and the evidence for their effectiveness in vascular or nerve injury is limited.

**机器人引导通常能够提高胸腰椎椎弓根螺钉置入准确度，但提升幅度没有统一数值。**在畸形、翻修等复杂病例中，其辅助价值可能更大；不过，“复杂病例获益一定更大”目前尚不能作为确定结论。 1．提升多少，首先取决于“准确”的定义。 常用Gertzbein–Robbins分级中，A级指螺钉未突破骨皮质；A＋B级通常指无突破或突破不足2毫米，常被作为影像学“可接受置钉”。后者不代表绝对安全，还应考虑突破方向及邻近神经、血管。 一项机器人与传统透视辅助置钉的胸腰椎随机对照试验，结果如下： 评价指标 机器人组 传统透视组 绝对提升 A级：完全位于骨性通道内 95.3% 86.1% 9.2个百分点 A＋B级：影像学可接受 98.7% 93.5% 5.2个百分点 这些是按螺钉统计的结果，不能解释为每位患者的并发症风险下降相同比例，也不是所有机型都能达到的固定增幅。随机对照试验 2．脊柱畸形：部分研究显示较大差距，但不能直接证明增益更突出。 畸形患者常有椎体旋转、椎弓根细小和解剖标志异常，三维规划与导向因此具有较强的临床合理性。 一项纳入106例脊柱侧弯患者的回顾性研究，报告机器人导航、O-arm导航和徒手组术后置钉准确率分别为96.7%、93.0%和80.4%。机器人与徒手相差16.3个百分点，但与O-arm导航仅相差3.7个百分点。侧弯对照研究 这说明比较对象很重要：机器人相对徒手的优势，不能全部归因于机械臂，也包含三维影像与导航的贡献。该研究与普通胸腰椎试验的病例、分级和流程不同，不能把16.3与9.2个百分点直接比较，进而断言畸形患者获益更大。 3．翻修手术：有潜在优势，可靠的增幅估计仍不足。 翻修时，既往截骨、融合骨块、原钉道及内植物可能破坏正常定位标志，机器人可辅助重新规划入点与通道。已有回顾性比较研究支持其应用价值，但尚不足以给出适用于所有翻修病例的准确度提升数字。腰椎翻修比较研究 同时，金属伪影、骨缺损、器械受原钉道引导偏移，以及术中骨段位置改变，都可能削弱导航优势。 因此，临床上可表述为：**特定胸腰椎随机试验显示，A级准确率提高约9个百分点、A＋B级提高约5个百分点；复杂病例可能更需要这种辅助，但其增益大小仍取决于具体解剖、对照技术、设备和团队。**准确率提高也不能直接等同于神经、血管损伤或再次手术率同比下降。

从骨科临床与医院管理角度，**合理筛选的核心，是将机器人用于“有明确手术指征、能够可靠实施、预期增益值得额外成本”的病例，而不是为了摊薄设备成本增加手术量。**成本效益并不等于单台手术更便宜，也不等于医院能够盈利。 1．按预期临床增益筛选，不能只按“复杂程度”筛选 以下可作为病例讨论框架，并非已经验证的统一评分标准： 优先级 病例特征与判断 优先评估 已有明确手术指征；常规定位困难；机器人能帮助完成具体关键步骤。例如部分解剖标志不清的脊柱翻修、畸形置钉，以及复位满意且存在安全通道的骨盆经皮固定 个体化选择 常规初次关节置换、解剖条件较好的短节段脊柱固定等。应比较本团队传统手术结果、机器人额外耗时及患者费用，不能默认人人都能获得有意义的额外收益 不宜使用或暂缓 无明确手术指征、无安全操作通道、无法可靠配准、超出设备适用范围，或准备设备可能延误紧急救治的病例 **复杂病例可能更需要辅助，也可能更难安全使用机器人。**因此，不能把“最复杂的病例”直接当作“最划算的病例”；开展初期还应选择适合带教、风险可控的病例。 2．核算完整治疗成本，避免只看耗材价格 至少应纳入设备折旧、维护与软件、专用耗材、影像、培训、额外手术室时间，以及住院、康复、再入院和再次手术费用。比较时还要校正病情复杂程度，避免将患者选择或康复流程带来的差异全部归功于机器人。 经济学研究的结论受年手术量、当地价格和远期效果假设影响很大。例如，一项美国模型在年手术量50例时，机器人全膝置换达到成本效益的概率仅约一半；这一结果依赖其支付意愿阈值及模型假设，不能作为中国医院的采购或使用门槛。成本效益模型研究 尤其不能把“机器人将显著减少远期翻修”作为确定收益计入预算——这一点尚未在所有术式中得到证实。 3．通过团队和流程提高利用效率 **集中在具备相应病例量和救治能力的团队开展。**减少设备闲置与反复培训；区域协作应建立在转诊获益足以抵消患者交通、等待等成本的基础上。 **固定核心团队、集中排程、提前规划。**减少装机、配准和器械准备中的重复等待。 **按季度审查真实结果。**同时看准确性、并发症、转换率、手术室占用、患者功能与总费用，不能只看机器人完成例数。 **将患者负担纳入选择。**说明额外费用、替代方案及获益的不确定性，不把机器人包装成获得优质治疗的必要条件。 对单个病例，最实用的问题是：**“机器人具体解决了什么困难？如果不用，风险或结果会差多少？额外成本由谁承担？”**如果无法清楚回答，就不足以仅凭技术先进或设备已经购入来推荐使用。

From the perspective of how indications and contraindications should be precisely defined, the honest answer is that current definitions are uneven across subspecialties. In spine and trauma, classification-linked criteria are beginning to emerge; in joint replacement, the boundary is more often drawn by patient factors and deformity phenotype than by a formal disease classification. A precise definition therefore requires a multidimensional structure rather than a single “robots are indicated for X” list. The organizing principle: three layers, not one A clinically usable definition should operate at three layers simultaneously. Layer 1 — Disease/injury classification. This answers what pathology is being treated and at what morphological severity. This is where classification systems enter. Layer 2 — Technical eligibility for robotic registration and execution. This answers whether the robot can actually be used safely and accurately in this patient. It is distinct from disease severity. Severe obesity or osteoporosis may make accurate registration impossible, independent of the underlying diagnosis. The 2024 Chinese thoracolumbar guideline captures this directly: contraindications include systemic disease precluding tolerance of robotic surgery, and tracker placement or navigation image acquisition that cannot meet surgical requirements. Layer 3 — Relative value versus conventional technique. This asks whether robotics adds enough to justify its costs, workflow burden, and learning curve for this specific indication. This layer is where most controversy sits, because radiographic precision advantages have not consistently translated into superior long-term functional outcomes across all indications. A precise definition must keep these layers separate. Conflating “the robot can be used” with “the robot should be used” is the most common source of imprecision in current discourse. Spine: the most classification-linked area Thoracolumbar. The 2024 Chinese guideline defines indications by disease category and includes specific injury/condition subtypes: traumatic (thoracolumbar burst fracture, osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture), degenerative (spondylolisthesis, disc herniation, thoracic/ lumbar stenosis), deformity (congenital severe spondylolisthesis, scoliosis, kyphosis), tumor (vertebral and intraspinal), and infection. This is a disease-category definition, not a severity-graded one. It does not specify, for example, a Cobb angle threshold or a Meyerding grade cutoff for spondylolisthesis. Cervical. The 2024 cervical guideline includes indications and contraindications as its first two recommendations, but the detailed severity thresholds require reading the full recommendation text; the publicly indexed abstract confirms the structure but not the full classification criteria. This is a place where I would flag uncertainty rather than infer thresholds. Deformity severity. For spinal deformity, severity classification does affect the robotic discussion. A commonly used research threshold defines severe complex deformity as Cobb angle >80°, flexibility <25%, or focal kyphosis >90°. In severe and rigid deformities, the argument for navigation/robotic assistance is stronger because anatomical landmarks are distorted and freehand accuracy degrades. But this is a relative enrichment of indication, not an absolute threshold codified in a guideline. Revision and distorted anatomy. Robot-assisted TLIF consensus explicitly notes advantages in thin pedicles, anatomical variation, and revision surgery. Again, this expands the relative indication rather than creating a clean absolute criterion. Revision surgery also appears as a contraindication in some implant-specific documents, which illustrates the need to separate patient-level from platform-level contraindications. A practical formulation for spine: indication = a condition within a guideline-listed disease category + anatomical feasibility for registration/tracking + a clinical rationale for precision in a high-risk trajectory (deformity, revision, distorted pedicles, cervicothoracic junction). Contraindication = inability to tolerate surgery/anesthesia, inability to obtain usable navigation images or tracker fixation, active local infection precluding hardware, or anatomy so distorted that the planned trajectory cannot be safely executed even with navigation. Joint replacement: classification helps, but phenotype and patient factors dominate TKA. Robotic TKA trials commonly use Kellgren-Lawrence grade III–IV as the radiographic inclusion criterion, often combined with coronal deformity limits (e.g., <20° varus) and flexion contracture limits (<15°). These are trial eligibility criteria, not universally accepted clinical indications. They tell us what has been studied, not necessarily what should be done. The more defensible current position is that robotic TKA is selectively valuable in knees where alignment precision and reproducible execution are likely to matter—severe deformity, post-traumatic arthritis, extra-articular deformity—while acknowledging that platform-specific evidence remains limited. THA and DDH. The Crowe classification is the most useful classification-linked framework here. Robotic arm-assisted THA has been shown to improve cup placement accuracy in Crowe I–III dysplasia, and studies also report feasibility and benefit in Crowe IV cases. This is a good example of a classification-graded indication: the more severe the dysplasia and the more distorted the acetabular anatomy, the stronger the relative rationale for robotic assistance. Absolute contraindication remains active hip joint infection, and severe abnormal anatomy that prevents navigation software from functioning is cited as a practical exclusion. UKA. The classification picture is less settled. Traditional contraindications included patellofemoral osteoarthritis and varus ≥15°, but modern evidence and robotic alignment capabilities have led some authors to argue for expanding indications. This is a domain where a precise, universally accepted classification-based boundary does not yet exist. Trauma: AO/OTA classification is the cleanest example For femoral shaft fractures, robot-assisted closed reduction trials explicitly define inclusion by AO/OTA classification 32-A, 32-B, or 32-C, while excluding open fractures, pathological fractures, polytrauma requiring priority management, active infection, and severe medical comorbidity. This is the most transparent classification-linked definition in the orthopedic robotics literature: the injury morphology is named, the exclusions are listed, and the boundary is testable. Pelvic ring injuries represent an emerging indication, with robot-assisted reduction described as feasible for “most patients with unstable pelvic fractures,” but the classification-specific boundaries are still being defined. How to make the definition precise: a proposed structure Instead of asking for a single list, I would define indications and contraindications as a matrix for each disease/injury category: Dimension What must be specified Example Pathology + classification Named diagnosis and classification grade/stage AO/OTA 32-A/B/C; Crowe I–IV; K-L III–IV; Cobb >80° Anatomical eligibility Registration/tracker feasibility; image quality; trajectory accessibility Tracker site usable; navigation image adequate Patient tolerance Medical fitness for anesthesia/surgery; active infection status Uncontrolled infection = absolute contraindication Relative value threshold Whether precision advantage is clinically meaningful for this phenotype Stronger in severe deformity/revision; weaker in routine primary cases Platform/team constraints Surgeon experience, system-specific evidence, OR workflow Steep learning curve; platform heterogeneity A contraindication is absolute when it makes robotic execution unsafe or technically impossible (active infection at the operative site, inability to tolerate surgery, inability to obtain usable navigation). It is relative when it merely reduces the marginal benefit (obesity, osteoporosis, routine primary osteoarthritis without deformity). Much of what is called a “contraindication” in current practice is actually a relative limitation. The honest caveat The strongest classification-linked definitions exist where robotic systems have been studied under trial protocols with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria—femoral shaft fractures and thoracolumbar disease categories are the clearest examples. In joint replacement, the classifications (K-L, Crowe) are useful but the evidence base is heterogeneous across platforms, and patient selection still depends substantially on clinical judgment and local context. A truly “precise” definition across all diseases and injury classifications does not yet exist in a uniform, evidence-graded form; what exists is a set of category-specific frameworks at different stages of maturity. The clinical task is to use the classification systems that do exist, while explicitly separating technical eligibility from relative clinical value—and to be candid with patients that for many routine indications, the robotic advantage is in execution precision rather than proven long-term superiority.

从执业创伤骨科医师的视角看，机器人辅助经皮内固定的适应证与禁忌证，其分界线并不落在“哪个骨折名字”上，而落在两个更根本的追问上：第一，骨折能否通过闭合或微创方式获得满足置钉要求的复位？第二，复位后的骨性通道，能否在三维影像上被规划并可靠执行？ 机器人精于“在既定复位上精准执行固定”，但它本身不解决复位问题。因此，凡是复位环节超出闭合或微创能力、或规划所依赖的骨性参考系已不存在的场景，机器人辅助的临床增益便迅速衰减，甚至沦为多余。 股骨颈骨折：适应证明确，但被“闭合复位成败”一刀切分 股骨颈骨折是机器人辅助经皮空心钉或FNS固定的成熟适应证。临床研究界定的纳入标准通常包括：年龄18~65岁、新鲜骨折（受伤至手术<2周）、拟行经皮3枚空心钉固定。其获益逻辑在于，股骨颈内三枚螺钉的平行度、分散度与深度，传统上依赖术者手感和反复透视校准，机器人通过三维规划将这一“经验依赖”过程转化为可执行的几何通道，减少导针调整次数和X线暴露。 但这一适应证的边界，恰恰由排除标准本身所定义。在Holosight机器人的研究中，“因闭合复位困难改行切开复位者（如部分难复的Garden Ⅳ型患者）”被明确排除。这一排除条款的临床含义是：机器人辅助的起点，是闭合复位已经成功或至少已达到可接受的对位。如果骨折类型决定了闭合复位本身即难以实现而需要切开，那么后续的置钉环节完全可以在直视下完成，再引入机器人进行经皮规划，其增量价值便大幅缩水。此时机器人辅助并非“错误”，而是“多余”——它增加了一套装机、注册和规划流程，却未解决该病例真正的瓶颈（复位）。 骶髂关节与骨盆后环损伤：适应证最宽，获益最稳定的领域 骶髂关节螺钉固定是机器人辅助经皮内固定中证据最一致、适应证界定最清晰的场景之一。其解剖基础决定了机器人的优势几乎是“结构性”的：骶髂螺钉需要在髂骨、骶骨之间一条狭窄的骨性通道内穿行，毗邻骶神经根、髂血管和骶管，传统透视下二维影像对通道边界的呈现本身就不充分。 明确的适应证覆盖：累及骨盆后环的骨折，包括脆性骨盆骨折（FFP）的Ⅱ型、Ⅲ型和Ⅳ型，以及高能量骨盆后环损伤。对于FFP，经皮骶髂螺钉已被视为Ⅱ型和Ⅲ型损伤的首选方案之一。一项纳入141例患者（平均年龄82岁，FFP Ⅱ型占75%）的研究显示，机器人辅助骶髂螺钉固定中，无螺钉出现松动或移位的迹象，中位住院时间12天，单侧骶髂螺钉的中位手术时间仅26分钟。 这一领域的禁忌证相对“纯粹”，主要指向患者整体条件不适合手术（如无法耐受麻醉、严重凝血障碍、局部感染），而非某一特定骨折分型。换言之，只要患者能接受手术，且术前CT能规划出贯穿通道，机器人辅助的获益逻辑基本成立。需要额外讨论的是明显移位的骶髂关节脱位：机器人本身不完成复位，但如果复位能够通过微创复位技术或骨牵引等闭合手段达成，后续固定仍属于机器人辅助的合理范畴。真正的“多余”场景在于：如果移位程度决定了闭合复位无法达成而需切开，固定环节便可在直视下完成。 髋臼柱骨折：适应证最窄，禁忌边界最锐利 髋臼骨折是三种类型中机器人辅助适应证最为局限的。髋臼的关节面平整度要求极高，而经皮螺钉固定对骨折块间的对位容错空间极小。 现有证据对适应证的界定高度一致且严格。对于累及后柱的髋臼骨折，适应证为外伤所致、轻度移位后能够闭合复位者，其中最佳适应证为低位后柱骨折或横形骨折。对于髋臼骨折的经皮固定总体而言，适应证被限定于无移位或仅有轻微移位的骨折。 与此对应，禁忌证也最为清晰和“硬性”：粉碎性骨折、高度移位骨折、股骨头突入盆腔需要切开复位者，以及缺乏术中导航条件者，均被列为禁忌。此外，骨折移位导致螺钉通道错位无法获得满意复位者，以及进针点皮肤感染者，也不适于该治疗方法。这些禁忌的本质是同一个：闭合或微创复位已无法重建可供规划螺钉通道的骨性解剖。当骨折块粉碎或移位严重到需要切开直视下复位时，置钉操作在直视下完成本身并不比机器人规划困难多少，机器人辅助的增量获益被复位的“不可闭合性”所彻底稀释。此时使用机器人，不仅“多余”，在某些情况下甚至可能诱导术者为了“用上机器人”而勉强尝试闭合复位，从而在复位质量上做出妥协，这背离了髋臼骨折治疗以关节面复位为核心目标的基本原则。 综合判断：一条以“复位”为前置条件的决策原则 将三种骨折类型并置，一个分层的决策图景浮现出来： 骨折类型 机器人获益逻辑 核心适应证 禁忌/“多余”场景 骶髂关节/骨盆后环 骨性通道狭窄，透视判读困难，几何规划不可替代 FFP Ⅱ–Ⅳ型；高能量后环损伤 患者不适合手术（非骨折特异性） 股骨颈骨折 螺钉平行度/分散度依赖手感，规划可减少反复调整 新鲜、闭合复位成功的经皮空心钉固定 闭合复位失败需切开者（如难复性Garden Ⅳ型） 髋臼柱骨折 关节面容错极小，仅适用于复位已可接受的病例 无/轻微移位，或轻度移位后可闭合复位的低位后柱/横形骨折 粉碎性、高度移位、需切开复位、股骨头突入盆腔 贯穿三者的核心原则可以凝练为一句话：机器人辅助经皮内固定的合理适应场景，是“复位已不成问题，精度才是问题”的病例；而它的禁忌或“多余”场景，是“复位本身就是问题，且必须通过开放手段才能解决”的病例。 在临床筛选中，比骨折分型名称更优先的决策节点应当是：这个骨折，在闭合或微创条件下，能否获得一个允许规划并置入螺钉的、几何上可接受的复位？ 如果答案是否定的，那么无论骨折位于股骨颈、骨盆环还是髋臼，机器人辅助经皮固定的窗口便尚未打开，术者应当将决策重心放回复位策略本身，而非固定工具的选择上。

Limitations in the reach and angular range of robotic arms do affect surgery, and the impact is most tangible in exactly the scenarios you identify: special patient positions and deep, confined orthopedic sites. However, the clinical significance is not uniform—it depends on the specific site, the robotic platform's kinematics, and whether the system was designed with that anatomical constraint in mind. Spine: Position-Dependent Reach Failures Are Documented The clearest evidence of a practical reach limitation comes from lumbar spine surgery in the lateral position. In a prospective comparison of single lateral positioning versus lateral-prone positioning for robotic-assisted pedicle screw placement at L2–L5, two patients with high pelvic incidence in the single lateral group had to be converted to the lateral-prone position because the robotic arm could not obtain a safe trajectory at L5. This is a direct, procedure-level demonstration that arm reach and angular range can determine whether a planned minimally invasive approach is executable in a given body position. The underlying issue is kinematic. Surgical robots with limited degrees of freedom cannot be adjusted to all necessary operating postures, which can reduce control accuracy or make certain trajectories unreachable. In lateral spine surgery specifically, the robot may also collide with the operating table if the patient is not positioned sufficiently close to the table edge. These are not theoretical constraints; they are workflow realities that shape patient positioning and approach selection. Pelvis and Acetabulum: Deep Workspace Is the Core Constraint The deep pelvis and acetabulum represent the most demanding test of reach and dexterity. Rigid-link robotic systems, by design, have limited access to confined spaces such as the region behind an acetabular implant or deep within the pelvic ring. Quantitative cadaveric data make this limitation concrete. In a model of debridement for osteolysis behind an acetabular component, a conventional rigid tool covered only 54% of the workspace. A robotic system that combined a rigid-link arm with a continuum manipulator—a flexible, articulating extension—raised coverage to 91%. This comparison is instructive: it shows both that the standard rigid robotic arm has a meaningful reach deficit in deep acetabular work, and that the deficit is addressable through a different mechanical design rather than being an immutable property of "robotics" as a category. For percutaneous screw fixation of posterior column acetabular fractures, the reach problem manifests differently. Positioning must be adjusted specifically to avoid the thigh blocking the robotic arm's movement and screw insertion—for example, flexing the hip 30° with a pillow under the iliac crest in the prone position. The robot's reach envelope, in other words, imposes constraints on how the patient is positioned, not just on where the tool can go. Arthroscopy and Confined Joint Spaces: Instrument Design Interacts with Arm Reach In hip arthroscopy, cadaveric feasibility work has shown that a robotic system can reach most regions accessible in standard arthroscopy, but with significant instrument-dependent limitations. A 5-mm instrument was limited in movement because of its long articulation section, whereas an 8-mm instrument with a shorter articulation section exhibited a full range of motion inside the joint. Even so, the posterior part of the femoral head and the posteroinferior portion of the acetabular labrum could not be observed because of the rigidity of the equipment. This illustrates a compound limitation: arm reach, instrument articulation length, and instrument rigidity interact to determine what is actually accessible, and the limiting factor may be the end-effector rather than the arm alone. Beyond Reach: The Force Ceiling in Deep Pelvic Work There is a related but distinct limitation that becomes relevant in the deep pelvis: force output. In pelvic reduction surgery, the force required can exceed 200 N, while the force limit of commonly used medical robotic arms is approximately 160 N. This is not a reach or angular-range problem in the kinematic sense, but it is a workspace limitation in practice: the robot may be able to reach the target yet be unable to perform the required manipulation there. For fracture reduction in the deep pelvis, this force ceiling can be the binding constraint. How These Limitations Are Being Addressed The trajectory of robotic design is toward mitigating these constraints rather than accepting them as fixed. Continuum manipulators extend reach into confined spaces beyond what rigid links can achieve. Bilateral or multi-arm systems are being developed to provide large operating volumes, with each arm responsible for its ipsilateral side, which is particularly relevant in spine surgery where trajectories may span both sides of the midline. Base extensions can be used to reach locations outside the standard workspace. These are engineering responses to a recognized clinical problem. A Surgeon's Assessment The limitations are real and clinically consequential, but they are site-specific and platform-specific rather than a blanket indictment of robotic surgery. In lateral lumbar spine surgery, reach constraints at L5 in high-PI patients can force a change in positioning. In the deep acetabulum, rigid robotic arms leave a substantial portion of the periprosthetic workspace inaccessible, which is why continuum manipulators and flexible instruments are being developed. In hip arthroscopy, instrument design can limit motion even when the arm itself can reach the region. And in pelvic reduction, the force ceiling of current arms can be the operative bottleneck. The practical implication is that preoperative planning must include a reach and access assessment, not merely a trajectory plan. The surgeon needs to know, before committing to a position or approach, whether the robot can physically achieve the required trajectory and whether the end-effector can perform the intended task at that depth. When the answer is uncertain, the documented precedent is to change the patient's position—as in the L5 conversion from single lateral to lateral-prone—rather than to force an unreachable trajectory.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the selection of fracture patterns for robot-assisted percutaneous fixation follows a clear logic: the technology is most valuable when a screw must traverse a narrow, anatomically constrained "safe corridor" in bone, and when conventional fluoroscopic guidance makes that traversal unreliable.
