Conversely, it is unnecessary when the corridor is wide or easily visualized, and contraindicated when the preconditions for navigation fail or when the fracture's primary challenge lies outside the domain of screw trajectory precision. Best-Suited Fracture Patterns: Where Precision Trajectory is the Bottleneck These are the indications with the clearest rationale and the strongest supporting evidence. Femoral Neck Fractures (Undisplaced, or Reducible in Young Patients)
Percutaneous cannulated screw fixation is the standard treatment for undisplaced femoral neck fractures in the elderly and for femoral neck fractures in young adults, where the goal is preservation of the native hip. The technical challenge is that freehand screw placement has a high malposition rate, which compromises biomechanical stability and can damage the remaining blood supply to the femoral head. Robot-assisted placement addresses this by enabling precise, parallel screw configuration through a minimally invasive approach, with reported benefits including shorter surgical time, reduced radiation exposure, and reduced incidence of femoral head necrosis. The evidence supports its use in patients under 65 with sarcopenia, where precision and soft-tissue preservation are particularly consequential. Even for Garden IV fractures in young and middle-aged adults—the most severe displacement pattern—robot-assisted fixation combined with additional compression screw augmentation has been reported as a viable option. Sacroiliac (SI) Joint Disruptions and Posterior Pelvic Ring Injuries
This is among the most established indications. The SI corridor is narrow and surrounded by the lumbosacral plexus, iliac vessels, and sacral foramina. A 2024/2025 technique description explicitly lists pelvic fractures involving the posterior pelvis as the indication for 3D robot-assisted SI screw fixation, and characterizes it as a technique for safe fixation of dorsal fragility fractures of the pelvis with fewer complications. A Chinese institutional protocol specifies SI joint dislocation with displacement >1 cm, particularly when there is horizontal or vertical instability, high neurologic risk, or unfavorable anatomy, as an indication where robotics can achieve zero neurologic injury. The pooled evidence from earlier analyses supports improved accuracy and substantially reduced fluoroscopy time in this region. Acetabular Column and Associated Fractures (Minimally Displaced, Reducible)
For the acetabulum, the indication is more constrained than for the SI joint. The consensus is that robot-assisted percutaneous fixation is appropriate for nondisplaced or only minimally displaced acetabular fractures. A Chinese series on posterior column involvement specifies the indication as fractures involving the posterior column that are minimally displaced and can be closed reduced, with the best indication being low posterior column fractures or transverse fractures. For anterior column fractures, robotic percutaneous screw fixation has been combined with posterior plating for transverse with posterior wall fractures, and for both-column fractures, robot-assisted percutaneous fixation has been described as a minimally invasive alternative to ORIF. The common thread is that the fracture must be reducible to a configuration in which a screw corridor exists; the robot then executes the trajectory with sub-millimeter accuracy. Other Corridors Where the Same Logic Applies
The same principle extends to pubic symphysis disruptions and pubic ramus fractures requiring percutaneous fixation, LC-II corridor screws in pelvic ring injuries, and retrograde elastic intramedullary nailing for displaced midshaft clavicle fractures, where a safe extra-articular corridor must be identified and followed. Situations Where Robotic Assistance Is Unnecessary These are scenarios in which the fundamental value proposition of the robot—traversing a difficult corridor with high accuracy—does not apply, either because the corridor is uncomplicated or because the procedure is already reliably performed with conventional technique. Wide-Corridor, Easily Palpated or Fluoroscopically Visualized Fixation
Procedures such as standard intertrochanteric fracture fixation with a cephalomedullary nail, where the entry point and lag screw trajectory are large and readily confirmed on fluoroscopy, do not derive a meaningful accuracy benefit from robotic guidance. The same applies to lateral malleolus or distal radius fractures fixed percutaneously under direct or easily obtainable fluoroscopic views. The robot adds setup and registration time without changing the technical difficulty of the trajectory. Fractures Requiring Open Reduction as the Primary Objective
When the binding constraint is articular surface reconstruction, impaction reduction, or soft-tissue management, rather than screw trajectory, the robot does not address the core problem. A displaced intra-articular calcaneus fracture, a pilon fracture with metaphyseal comminution, or a tibial plateau fracture requiring direct articular visualization and elevation are examples where the surgical priority is reduction, not corridor precision. Robot assistance may still be used adjunctively, but it is not the defining technology and may not justify the added workflow. Simple, Single-Screw Fixations in Superficial Bone
For medial malleolus fractures, patellar fractures, or olecranon fractures that are treated with a single screw or tension band through a small incision with direct visualization, the marginal precision benefit of robotics is small relative to the setup burden. Contraindications: When Navigation Preconditions Fail or the Fracture Defeats the Screw Strategy The contraindications are not judgments about whether the robot is "good" for trauma, but statements that the technical prerequisites for safe navigation cannot be satisfied, or that the fracture morphology makes corridor screw fixation itself inappropriate. Absolute or Technical Contraindications Inability to obtain adequate intraoperative navigation imaging or to position the patient tracking array. This is the fundamental precondition for any robotic procedure; without it, the system cannot register or track. Lack of intraoperative navigation capability in the treating facility or setting. Local infection at the planned pin or screw entry site, which precludes percutaneous instrumentation through that skin. Fracture-Specific Contraindications (Where the Corridor Strategy Itself Fails) Comminuted or highly displaced acetabular fractures in which a screw corridor cannot be defined or cannot be reduced to a navigable configuration. The Chinese posterior column series explicitly states that patients whose displacement makes the screw corridor unrecognizable and prevents satisfactory reduction are unsuitable for this method. Femoral head protrusion into the pelvis requiring open reduction for acetabular fractures; percutaneous fixation cannot address the central dislocation. Severe bilateral comminution, delayed irreducibility, or inadequate pin purchase are described as important cautions in the pelvic literature, reflecting situations in which neither the reduction nor the fixation can be reliably achieved through a percutaneous corridor. Patient and Systemic Contraindications Open contamination, hemodynamic instability, or severe soft-tissue swelling are relative or absolute contraindications derived from the principles of conventional percutaneous surgery; they apply equally to robotic percutaneous fixation. Patients not medically suited for surgery is the broadest and most general contraindication listed in the SI screw technique descriptions. A Surgeon's Synthesis The organizing question is not "which fracture diagnosis is on the list," but "does this fracture require a screw to follow a narrow, anatomically constrained trajectory that conventional fluoroscopy makes unreliable, and can that trajectory be achieved percutaneously?" If the answer is yes—as with SI disruptions, minimally displaced or reducible acetabular column fractures, and undisplaced or reducible femoral neck fractures—robotic assistance has a clear and evidence-supported role. If the corridor is wide, the fracture requires open reduction as its primary objective, or the navigation preconditions cannot be met, the robot adds burden without addressing the binding constraint. The most honest limitation is that the evidence base for many of these indications remains observational or derived from technique descriptions rather than large randomized comparisons, so the boundaries are best applied with attention to the specific fracture morphology and the institution's navigation infrastructure.

从骨科医师的视角来评估，目前骨科机器人的智能辅助功能，在“降低置钉偏差”这一特定、可量化的终点上，证据是充分且一致的；但在“降低术中误操作”这一更宽泛的安全命题上，它的作用是真实的，却是有条件的、有边界的，不能被简化为一个笼统的“更安全”标签。 智能辅助的本质，是将一部分安全责任从术者的实时手部控制与经验判断，转移到了术前规划、术中配准与内置安全约束的可靠性上。这既创造了新的安全冗余，也引入了新的失效模式。 🎯 置钉偏差：智能辅助最坚实的证据所在 在脊柱椎弓根螺钉置入中，智能辅助（自动规划、机械臂导向、实时追踪）对精度的提升，是目前整个骨科机器人领域证据等级最高、方向最一致的部分。 随机对照证据：一项2026年发表于Cochrane图书馆的多中心RCT（70例）显示，机器人辅助组导针置入的平均偏差为0.86 ± 0.57 mm，显著低于传统透视组的2.55 ± 1.88 mm（P<0.001）。更关键的是，机器人组的通道调整次数（0.06 vs 0.28，P=0.014）显著更少，这意味着智能规划与机械导向从源头上减少了“需要中途纠偏”的置钉尝试。 大样本回顾性证据：一项纳入218例患者的队列研究显示，机器人辅助组的Gertzbein-Robbins 0级（最优）置钉率为93.33%，传统透视组为78.76%（p=0.002），优势比（OR）为3.78；每治疗6.9枚螺钉，即可多获得1枚最优置钉（NNT=6.9）。另一项前瞻性RCT（234例，1116枚螺钉）的数据与此一致：机器人组A级螺钉比例为95.3%，透视组为86.1%，且透视组有2枚螺钉因误置需要翻修，机器人组为零。 这些数据共同支持一个结论：在“将螺钉按计划轨迹精确置入”这一操作层面，智能辅助的精度优势是真实、可重复且具有统计学与临床意义的。 它直接作用于置钉偏差这一上游环节，而非泛泛地宣称“减少并发症”。 🛡️ 术中误操作风险：内置安全机制的真实作用与失效模式 智能辅助降低误操作风险的机制，主要体现在两个层面：内置的安全约束与对高风险亚组的保护效应。但这两个层面都有明确的边界。 内置安全约束：从“持续监控”到“自动阻止” 传统手术中，防止误操作完全依赖术者的持续注意力与手眼协调。智能辅助系统引入了两重不依赖术者注意力的“自动刹车”： 空间安全边界（虚拟约束）：系统围绕规划的操作区域建立数字“边界墙”。以MAKO系统为例，如果切割工具试图超出预设的安全区，机械臂会立即产生物理阻力（如撞上一堵墙）或锁定，并瞬时停用切割动力。这种“故障安全（fail-safe）”设计，将一部分防止几何偏差的责任从人转移到了机器。 碰撞保护：2023年实施的行业标准（YY/T 1901-2023）明确要求，机械臂在受到非预期的碰撞力或力矩时，应发出警示并立即停止运动。这防止的是机械臂在术中因意外接触而对患者或术者造成的直接机械损伤。 这些功能的逻辑是清晰的：它们用不依赖于人注意力的机械/软件约束，去覆盖人手操作中因疲劳、分心或反应延迟可能产生的偏差。这是智能辅助对“误操作”最直接的干预。 对高风险亚组的保护效应：以神经损伤为例 置钉偏差的临床后果，最终体现在神经血管损伤等严重并发症上。2025年的一项Meta分析提供了关键数据：机器人辅助脊柱手术相比传统技术，神经损伤发生率从4.3%降至1.9%（OR 0.45, p=0.001），翻修手术率从5.2%降至3.1%（OR 0.59, p=0.02）。在成人脊柱畸形手术中，机器人辅助组的脊髓功能障碍发生率也显著更低（1.2% vs 3.4%）。 这一获益的因果链条是明确的：精度提升（偏差更小）→ 皮质穿破减少 → 对邻近神经结构的机械侵扰减少 → 神经损伤发生率下降。 智能辅助并非直接“保护了神经”，而是通过减少上游的置钉偏差，间接实现了这一保护。 ⚠️ 必须正视的残余风险：智能辅助不能消除的失效模式 智能辅助的安全收益是真实的，但它并未消除术中误操作的风险，而是将其转移和变形了。2025年的一篇系统综述明确识别了机器人辅助脊柱手术的三类残余误差来源：注册误差、轨迹不准与干扰误差（skiving）。其中注册误差可能通过高分辨率影像和稳定的患者体位来减少，但并未被消除。 这意味着，当以下前提条件被破坏时，智能辅助的安全冗余会迅速收窄甚至消失： 配准漂移：如果术前规划与患者实际解剖的对齐出现偏差（例如因体位变化、示踪器松动或影像质量不佳），系统所“认为”的安全轨迹与真实解剖位置之间就会出现错位。此时，机械臂会精确地执行一个错误的计划。术者如果因为“系统显示准确”而放松了对解剖标志的实时核对，风险反而可能被放大。 解剖变异超出规划覆盖：智能规划基于术前影像，对于术中才发现的、影像上不显著或未充分建模的解剖变异（如椎弓根内壁的隐匿性破损、异常走行的神经根），系统的安全边界是基于错误的解剖假设建立的。 Skiving（器械滑移）：即使在规划通道内，器械尖端仍可能因骨面硬度不均而发生非预期的滑移。系统提供了空间边界，但力反馈的缺失（如Q3所述）使术者难以在滑移发生的瞬间通过手感感知并纠正，系统也无法自动识别这种“在边界内但方向错误”的运动。 此外，MAKO等系统的触觉引导是一种边界性的力反馈（到达边界时感到阻力），这与徒手操作中通过阻力变化实时感知骨皮质突破的连续性力觉存在本质区别。对于软组织保护，系统的逻辑是“禁止进入危险区域”，而非“感知正在被牵拉的组织承受了多大力量”。因此，对于神经、血管等软组织结构的直接保护，智能辅助的作用仍然是被动和预设性的，而非主动和感知性的。 💎 一个需要放在术者决策框架中的判断 因此，对于“智能辅助能否有效降低置钉偏差与术中误操作风险”这一问题，我的判断是分层的： 对于置钉偏差，答案是肯定的，且证据坚实。 智能规划与机械导向在脊柱椎弓根螺钉置入中，系统性地将偏差压缩到了亚毫米级，并显著减少了需要术中纠偏的尝试次数。这一精度优势在Meta分析层面已转化为神经损伤与翻修率的下降，是当前骨科机器人最具临床说服力的安全获益。 对于广义的“术中误操作”，答案是“有条件的、被转移的风险削减”。 智能辅助用内置的空间约束与碰撞保护，替代了术者的一部分持续注意力，在常规、规划覆盖良好的场景中，确实减少了因人手抖动或判断延迟导致的几何偏差。但它同时创造了一个新的依赖：安全性现在高度依赖于术前规划与术中配准的可靠性。当配准出现漂移、解剖变异超出规划假设、或发生边界内的滑移时，术者如果因为“有机器人在”而弱化了对解剖标志的独立核实和对力觉替代信号的警惕，那么被削减的风险可能以另一种形式重新出现。 一个审慎的临床立场是：将智能辅助视为一套为术者提供“冗余安全网”的工具，而不是一套可以替代术者独立安全判断的“自动驾驶系统”。 它的价值最大化，发生在术者主动理解其失效模式，并在每一次使用中持续用解剖标志、影像和替代性力觉信号去独立验证系统所呈现的“确定性”之时。

**有可能，但目前不能认定机器人辅助脊柱手术普遍能够“靠减少翻修抵消成本”，也没有通用的年手术量回本门槛。**需要区分：具有成本效果，可以意味着增加费用但获得值得的健康收益；医院收支平衡，则要求实际收入与可兑现的节省覆盖全部投入。 1．现有经济学研究为什么结论不同？ **部分模型预测可以回本。**一项西班牙预算影响模型预测，约3.83年、累计712例机器人手术后回收投资。但模型采用了误置相关再手术率从5%降至0.5%等假设，并依赖住院时间缩短；这是预测，并非实际完成712例就一定回本。研究有厂商资助及相关利益关系，外推时应审慎。预算影响研究 **实际病例研究也发现费用增加。**一项匹配队列研究显示，机器人腰椎固定的初次诊疗费用高于透视徒手组，提示新增手术室与耗材成本未必能被抵消。不过，该研究也不能完整回答多年后的总成本。匹配队列研究 因此，不能把国外模型的病例量直接用于国内采购决策，也不能把住院时间缩短全部归因于机器人——微创入路、康复流程及病例选择可能同时发生变化。 2．减少椎弓根穿破，为什么不一定带来足够的经济节省？ **影像学穿破减少，不等于同等数量的再手术减少。**部分穿破没有症状、不需要翻修；同一患者多枚螺钉出现偏差，也不能重复算作多次再手术。 应按患者计算： 每例预期减少的翻修成本＝翻修风险的绝对下降幅度×一次翻修的平均增量成本。 例如，仅作假设：若翻修风险绝对下降1个百分点，一次翻修增量成本10万元，平均每例节省为1000元，而不是10万元。是否足以覆盖机器人耗材、额外影像和手术时间，仍需另算。 感染、假关节、邻近节段病等也不能全部计入“机器人可避免的翻修”；成本项目之间还要避免重复计数。 3．年手术量达到多少才能收支平衡？ 可先用简化模型估算： 所需年病例数＝（初始总投入÷目标回收年限＋年度固定支出）÷每例增量净贡献 其中，每例增量净贡献＝额外实际收入＋医院实际节省－新增变动成本。只计算相对于传统方案的差额，不能把原本就能获得的整台手术收入全部算成机器人收益。 下面全部是演算假设，不是设备报价或临床预测：初始总投入1000万元，计划10年收回，每年维护等固定支出50万元，则每年需覆盖150万元；假设每例新增变动成本8000元，没有额外收入。 每例实际节省 扣除新增成本后的净贡献 简化模型所需年病例数 8000元或以下 ≤0元 增加病例量也无法覆盖固定投入 10000元 2000元 750例 13000元 5000元 300例 这里的病例数是实际使用机器人的手术量，不是科室全部手术量。正式预算还需加入学习期、故障停机、融资与折现、设备更新及配套影像投入。 4．医院应如何判断是否值得开展？ 应使用本院同类病例的真实数据，至少比较传统透视、导航与机器人三种方案，并分别测算： 初次手术成本及90天、1年以上的再入院和翻修成本； 耗材、影像、手术室时间及住院的实际可避免成本； 当地支付政策下医院真正获得的收入； 悲观情景：翻修率不下降、住院时间不缩短时，项目能否承受。 尤其要注意，少住一天院不一定能节省完整的“平均床日成本”，节省也不一定归购买设备的医院所有。导航本身可能已提供较好的价值，不能只以徒手作为唯一对照。导航与机器人经济模型 **目前无法负责任地给出“年做200例或300例必然回本”的结论。**高病例量只有在每例增量净贡献为正时，才有助于回收固定投入；不能为达到回本例数而扩大手术指征。

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the distinction between patients who benefit most and conditions that remain relative contraindications is not drawn along simple diagnostic lines. The organizing principle is whether the intrinsic limitations of conventional technique—unpredictable alignment restoration, difficulty localizing in distorted anatomy—represent the dominant bottleneck to a good outcome, and whether robotic planning and execution can specifically relieve that bottleneck. Conversely, a condition is a relative contraindication when the technical preconditions of robotic navigation fail, or when the core surgical challenge lies outside the domain that robotic precision can address. Robotic-Assisted TKA: Benefit Centered on Predictability of Deformity Correction For TKA, the value of robotics is most defensible in converting complex deformity correction from an intraoperative, experience-dependent negotiation into a planned, geometrically defined execution. Severe coronal deformity (varus or valgus, approximately >10°–15°). This is the most evidence-supported beneficiary group. A 2026 systematic review of complex primary and revision TKA reported that in severe deformity, robotic assistance produced significantly fewer mechanical axis outliers >3° compared with conventional technique (3.2% vs. 41.0%, p < 0.001) and fewer HKA angle outliers (5.1% vs. 44.7%), alongside improved postoperative HKA in the severe deformity subgroup (2.09° vs. 3.57°). In valgus deformity specifically, robotic TKA consistently restored alignment toward the neutral mechanical axis, with correction within ±3° of neutral in 96% of cases in one series and 86.2% achieving a defined safe zone in another. A comparative study in severe varus knees found improved coronal alignment, fewer radiographic outliers, and reduced need for soft-tissue release. The mechanism is that robotic planning defines the deformity independently of the distorted mechanical axis and surface landmarks that make conventional intramedullary or extramedullary referencing unreliable in severe deformity. Fixed flexion contracture (≥10°). This is a second clearly defined beneficiary group, with the important nuance that the benefit depends on the alignment philosophy used. A 2026 comparative study of 190 robotic TKAs using functional alignment found that patients with preoperative flexion contracture ≥10° achieved comparable mid-term outcomes and early survivorship to those without contracture: aseptic survivorship was 100% in the contracture group versus 99.32% in controls (p = 0.59), and there were no significant differences in Knee Society Scores, Forgotten Joint Score, or early revision rates. The authors concluded that these findings support functional alignment as a strategy to manage complex deformities without reliance on extensive soft-tissue releases. A separate 2026 analysis similarly suggested that within a robotic workflow, flexion contracture can be managed without large distal recuts or substantial tibial modification. The distinction matters: the flexion contracture benefit is not a generic property of “robotics” but is tied to a planning strategy that uses collateral ligament balance to guide resections rather than a fixed measured-resection target. Severe stiffness and ankylosis: a challenging indication, not a categorical contraindication. The evidence here is fundamentally different in grade and should not be presented as equivalent to the deformity data. Successful robotic TKA has been reported in a knee ankylosed for 10 years in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, with the authors noting that accurate bony registration was difficult because of altered morphology, but that with careful preparation robotic TKA “can be an effective option in complicated situations like ankyloses”. A case series of stiff knees using an imageless robotic system reported ROM improving to 110.2° ± 6.2° at two years, with KSS improving from 32 to 84. However, these are case reports and small series, not comparative evidence. The binding constraint in severe stiffness is not the robot’s geometric accuracy but the soft-tissue exposure, extensile approach, and release strategy—domains in which robotic precision offers no direct solution. Some manufacturer labeling explicitly lists “severely limiting range of motion” as a contraindication for specific robotic knee systems. The defensible position is therefore that severe stiffness/ankylosis is a challenging indication requiring specific expertise and consent regarding higher complication risk, not an absolute prohibition, but also not a routine beneficiary group. Retained hardware: an individualized extended indication, not a contraindication. Robotic TKA has been performed without removal of retained hardware, with the argument that CT-based planning allows the surgeon to define resections and component positions that avoid existing implants. A 2026 review proposed a practical decision-making workflow for post-traumatic and previously operated knees with retained hardware, integrating patient selection, imaging, hardware retention-versus-removal strategy, and robotic execution. The key point is that retained hardware is not a contraindication in itself; the decision is whether the hardware can be safely retained without compromising component alignment or fixation, and this is a planning question that CT-based robotics can inform. The evidence base, however, remains limited to case reports and proposed workflows rather than comparative outcomes. Robotic-Assisted THA: Benefit Concentrated in Crowe I–III DDH; Crowe IV Remains Uncertain For THA, the beneficiary signal is anatomically focused on developmental dysplasia, where distorted acetabular anatomy makes conventional cup positioning less reproducible. Crowe I–III DDH is the evidence-supported beneficiary group. A 2026 systematic review of 11 studies and 1,150 hips (641 robotic, 383 conventional, 126 navigation) found that among Crowe I–III hips, robotic arm-assisted THA achieved significantly lower errors in cup inclination and anteversion compared with both conventional and navigational THA, and greater accuracy in restoring the center of rotation. Another comparative study reported that across all Crowe subtypes, robotic assistance significantly increased the proportion of cups within the 5° safety zone. The mechanism is that robotic planning defines the true acetabular center independently of the distorted native landmarks, and the mechanical arm constrains reaming and impaction to the planned orientation. This is a genuine precision advantage in the specific anatomical problem that makes DDH THA difficult. Crowe IV: an extended indication with uncertain incremental benefit. The same systematic review found no difference in center-of-rotation restoration for Crowe IV hips, and concluded that “the accuracy of Crowe IV hips remains unclear, with limited evidence available”. Case reports describe successful use of robotic THA in Crowe IV with excellent early radiographic and functional results, including combined short stature and Crowe IV DDH. But Crowe IV should be positioned as an extended indication at specialized centers, not a routine beneficiary group, because the dominant challenges—femoral shortening, soft-tissue contracture, sciatic nerve tension, and achieving stable fixation in dysplastic bone—are not primarily cup-orientation problems. Relative and absolute contraindications in THA: failure of navigational preconditions. The contraindication profile for robotic THA is more directly defined than for TKA because it hinges on whether the system can register and track reliably. A published exclusion criteria set for robotic THA explicitly lists ankylosed hip joint, deformities of the femoral or pelvic bone affecting accurate placement of the device arrays, patients requiring trochanteric osteotomy, and pre-existing hardware affecting component orientation. The logic is transparent: an ankylosed hip compromises array placement and registration; severe deformity or hardware that distorts array placement defeats the tracking system; and trochanteric osteotomy changes the surgical approach and exposure strategy beyond the standard robotic workflow. These are not judgments about whether the robot is “good” in ankylosis—they are statements that the technical prerequisites of the technology cannot be satisfied. Case reports of robotic THA in fused hips from ankylosing spondylitis exist and describe the robot as providing useful real-time positional information, but the authors also identify positioning, exposure, femoral neck osteotomy, and true acetabular identification as the core difficulties—none of which are solved by robotic arm precision alone. Synthesis: The Logic and Its Evidence Asymmetry The beneficiary and contraindication categories can be summarized as follows: Procedure Strongest beneficiary group Challenging/extended indication Relative/technical contraindication Basis for the distinction TKA Severe coronal deformity (>10°–15°); fixed flexion contracture ≥10° under functional alignment Severe stiffness/ankylosis; retained hardware Manufacturer-specific exclusions such as severely limited ROM for some systems; active infection Benefit = predictability of deformity correction; limitation = soft-tissue challenge outside the domain of geometric precision THA Crowe I–III DDH Crowe IV DDH (specialist centers) Ankylosed hip; deformity/hardware preventing array placement; need for trochanteric osteotomy Benefit = cup positioning accuracy in distorted acetabular anatomy; limitation = failure of registration/tracking preconditions or core challenge in exposure and soft tissue The critical caveat is an asymmetry in evidence quality. The TKA deformity and flexion contracture benefits are supported by systematic reviews and comparative cohorts with quantified alignment and survivorship outcomes. The THA Crowe I–III benefit is supported by a systematic review with pooled comparative data. By contrast, the “challenging indication” categories—TKA stiffness/ankylosis and retained hardware—rest largely on case reports and proposed workflows, and the THA contraindications are exclusion criteria from device studies rather than prospectively validated contraindication endpoints. This asymmetry should shape how these categories are presented to patients: the deformity and DDH benefits can be described with reasonable confidence, while stiffness, ankylosis, retained hardware, and Crowe IV should be framed as situations of elevated technical demand and thinner evidence, where the decision is individualized and the surgeon’s experience with the specific complexity is as important as the robot itself.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the answer has two parts: the overall accuracy advantage of robotic guidance over free-hand fluoroscopy is statistically robust and consistent, but its clinical magnitude is moderate, and the advantage is not uniform. The benefit appears most pronounced in deformity surgery, where anatomical landmarks are distorted, while evidence in revision surgery is supportive but derived from smaller, primarily retrospective studies. Quantifying the Overall Accuracy Advantage Across the broader literature, robotic guidance consistently outperforms free-hand fluoroscopic techniques on screw accuracy grading. A 2025 meta-analysis of 18 studies and 1,566 patients found that free-hand fluoroscopy was associated with significantly worse accuracy in cases of major cortical violations (Gertzbein grade D–E) , with an odds ratio of 0.47 favoring robotics—meaning the odds of a major breach were roughly halved with robotic guidance. This same analysis reported a corresponding reduction in the need for revision surgery due to screw malposition (OR 0.28). An earlier meta-analysis of 13 RCTs reported an even larger pooled accuracy advantage, with an OR of 3.5 for accurate screw placement favoring robotics, along with significantly lower rates of facet joint invasion (OR 0.06) and revision (OR 0.19). In a meta-analysis focused on thoracolumbar fractures, robotic-assisted minimally invasive surgery achieved significantly higher rates of perfect (GR A) placement (OR 3.58) and satisfactory (GR A+B) placement (OR 3.86) , alongside a significantly lower incidence of severely misplaced (GR D+E) screws (OR 0.26). However, the advantage is not absolute across all contexts. A 2026 RCT of 49 patients with thoracolumbar fractures found no statistically significant difference in clinically acceptable accuracy (GR A+B, 96.1% vs. 96.5%, p = 0.828) between robotic and free-hand fluoroscopy, although the robotic group had a dramatically lower frequency of intraoperative fluoroscopy (5.2 vs. 37.0 exposures). This suggests that in straightforward, acute fracture cases, the baseline accuracy of free-hand technique may already be high, and the robotic advantage is more about reducing radiation exposure and improving consistency than dramatically altering accuracy rates. Is the Advantage Greater in Complex Settings? The evidence supports a qualified yes, with the strongest data coming from deformity surgery. Spinal Deformity (Scoliosis): The Advantage is Most Pronounced In scoliosis, distorted pedicle anatomy and rotational deformity make free-hand placement substantially more challenging. This is where robotic guidance demonstrates a clear and amplified benefit. A 2026 retrospective study of 178 scoliosis patients reported accuracy rates of 98.51% with robotics versus 95.50% with free-hand (P < 0.05) , alongside a significantly lower total complication rate (2.74% vs. 11.43%) and higher screw placement satisfaction. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies and 584 scoliosis patients found that robotic assistance offered significantly better clinically acceptable screw placement compared with free-hand (OR 2.61) , with shorter hospital stays, though at the cost of longer operative duration. Another meta-analysis comparing robotic, navigated, and free-hand techniques in scoliosis confirmed that robotic assistance had significantly greater odds of accurate placement relative to both navigation (OR 2.02) and free-hand. The mechanism is intuitive: in a deformed spine, the “safe corridor” for a pedicle screw is narrower and less predictable. Robotic planning based on preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging provides a trajectory that is independent of distorted surface landmarks, which is precisely where free-hand technique is most vulnerable to error. Revision Surgery: Supportive Evidence, But a Weaker Evidence Base In revision lumbar surgery, the challenge shifts from deformity to altered anatomy, scar tissue, and obscured landmarks from prior instrumentation. The evidence here supports an advantage, but the studies are smaller and predominantly retrospective. A retrospective study of 81 patients undergoing posterior lumbar revision surgery found that the robot-assisted group had statistically superior screw placement accuracy (P < 0.05) compared with free-hand, along with fewer violations of the superior-level facet joint. The authors concluded that the Renaissance robot offered higher accuracy and safety in the revision setting. The evidence for revision is therefore directionally consistent with the deformity data—robotic guidance appears to help when anatomy is hostile—but it lacks the larger pooled analyses available for scoliosis or primary thoracolumbar procedures. A 2026 review on cervical revision surgery noted that reported perforation rates for robotic systems in revision contexts ranged from 15.9% to 17.3% , which, while not directly comparable to lumbar data, underscores that revision anatomy remains demanding even with robotic assistance. A Surgeon's Synthesis The overall picture is that robotic guidance halves the odds of a major cortical breach and substantially reduces the risk of revision for malposition compared with free-hand fluoroscopy. In straightforward primary cases, this translates into a meaningful but not always statistically detectable difference in clinically acceptable accuracy, with the most reliable benefit being reduced radiation exposure. The advantage becomes more clinically decisive in complex anatomy—particularly scoliosis and deformity correction, where the accuracy gap widens and the downstream consequences of malposition are greater. In revision surgery, the available evidence points in the same direction, but the evidence base is thinner, and the hostile anatomy means that robotic assistance reduces, rather than eliminates, the technical challenge. The honest caveat is that the strongest complex-case data come from scoliosis, and the revision literature, while supportive, would benefit from larger prospective or randomized studies to confirm whether the magnitude of benefit matches that seen in deformity correction.

Poor bone quality reduces screw purchase even when insertion is perfectly accurate. Robotic guidance can improve trajectory and implant positioning, but it cannot restore bone strength. Cement augmentation is therefore a separate fixation decision—not an automatic requirement for osteoporosis or robotic insertion. Osteoporosis weakens the bone–implant interface, increasing the risk of screw loosening, pull-out, fracture collapse and, in the proximal femur, cut-out or cut-through. Reduction quality, fracture pattern, implant selection and load sharing remain essential. AO guidance on trochanteric fixation Setting Role of robotic insertion When to consider cement augmentation Osteoporotic spinal fractures requiring instrumentation Helps execute planned trajectories, provided imaging, registration and tracker fixation remain reliable. Severe osteoporosis may compromise these prerequisites. When unaugmented screws are unlikely to provide adequate anchorage—for example, severe osteoporosis with weak purchase, previous loosening, or a mechanically demanding reconstruction. Alternatives or additions include more fixation points and implants designed for poor bone. DGOU recommendations support cement augmentation or special screw designs, rather than mandatory cement for every patient. DGOU recommendations Osteoporotic trochanteric hip fractures Accurate cephalic screw or blade positioning may help, but robotics does not correct an unstable reduction or inadequate construct. Selected patients with severely osteoporotic femoral-head bone and high anticipated fixation-failure risk, using an implant designed for augmentation. AO advises considering PMMA augmentation in this setting; it is not routine for all cases. AO guidance Osteoporotic femoral neck fractures Guidance may assist screws when head-preserving fixation is appropriate. Cement-augmented cannulated screws are not a standard response to osteoporosis. The more fundamental decision may be fixation versus arthroplasty. A cemented arthroplasty stem is a different intervention from screw augmentation. “Required” is too categorical without assessing the individual construct. Cement becomes justified when adequate stability cannot reasonably be achieved with the planned unaugmented fixation and its expected benefit outweighs the risks. There is no universally accepted bone-density threshold that mandates augmentation across hip and spine procedures. Cement also adds risks: leakage into the spinal canal, neural foramina, veins or hip joint; embolic complications; and greater difficulty with later revision. Robotic positioning does not eliminate these risks, so cement delivery requires separate imaging surveillance and implant-specific precautions. DGOU recommendations From a surgical perspective, the priorities are appropriate reduction and construct, accurate insertion, and sufficient anchorage. Bone-health treatment should accompany fixation planning. I would not claim that robotic insertion alone prevents osteoporotic fixation failure or removes the need for augmentation when purchase is inadequate.

As a practicing spine surgeon, I would answer the cost-effectiveness question not with a single break-even number, but with a conditional statement: robot-guided spine surgery can be cost-effective, but only under a specific combination of high annual volume, case-mix skewed toward complexity, and a payment environment that allows the institution to capture the downstream savings from fewer revisions and shorter stays. The published economic evidence is not unanimous, and the most rigorous real-world analysis is actually the most pessimistic. The honest position is that the modeled break-even thresholds (roughly 158–168 cases per year) are plausible under favorable assumptions, but a recent analysis incorporating real-world adverse events found that no scenario achieved financial break-even within a 7-year robot lifespan, with even optimal conditions requiring 33.8 years to recover the initial investment. This discrepancy is the central issue a surgeon or hospital must confront. 💰 The Cost Side: Capital, Consumables, and Hidden Operational Drag The upfront and per-case costs are substantial and highly variable. Capital acquisition ranges from roughly $500,000 to $1.5 million per system, with annual maintenance often exceeding $150,000**. Per-case disposables run **$800–$1,200**, and can reach **$1,500–$2,000 depending on the platform and contract. In the Chinese context, some systems are priced around ¥1.5 million, with consumables adding ¥3,000–¥4,000 per case. Crucially, the modeled savings often assume smooth workflow and no robot-related disruptions. A 2025 analysis of 1,346 FDA-reported adverse events found a mean procedural delay of 58.1 minutes, with precision issues accounting for 66.4% of complications and robot abandonment in 34.4% of cases. When these real-world delays are incorporated into the economic model, the break-even case volume becomes effectively unreachable within the system's useful life. This is not a theoretical concern; it is a direct challenge to the optimistic volume thresholds derived from cleaner registry or modeling data. 💸 The Savings Side: Where the Money Actually Comes From The savings are real but concentrated in specific mechanisms, and the magnitude depends heavily on the comparator and the case mix. Revision reduction is the largest theoretical lever, but its economic impact is uncertain. A meta-analysis of navigation data (not robotics specifically) estimated that reducing the revision rate from 6% to 0.8% would save enough to justify the system at more than 168 cases per year, based on a reoperation cost of $27,768**. A more recent meta-meta-analysis reported robot-assisted placement saving **$4,086–$4,865 per patient** versus navigation and **$7,317–$9,654 per patient versus freehand, but these figures aggregate multiple cost components and are sensitive to the local cost of revision and the baseline complication rate. Length of stay and complications provide measurable but smaller per-case savings. A Spanish budget impact analysis found robot-assisted surgery saved €1,011 per patient, driven by reductions in revision surgeries (€793), complications (€261), and length of stay (€1,523), with the initial investment recovered within 3.83 years and cumulative 10-year savings of €2.54 million. A Singapore study estimated SGD 1,500 in savings per two-level OLIF procedure from reduced operative time, with savings increasing for multi-level cases. These are meaningful sums, but they are an order of magnitude smaller than the capital outlay and require high volume to aggregate into a positive return. Not every comparison favors robotics. In pediatric idiopathic scoliosis, a cost-utility analysis found navigation was more cost-effective than robotics; robotics provided greater clinical benefit but required an additional $255,518 per QALY** compared with navigation. Another study reported an ICER of **$22,572 for robotic-assisted surgery overall, which fell to $16,980 for one- or two-level instrumentation, placing it within conventional willingness-to-pay thresholds in some systems but not others. 📊 The Break-Even Volume: 158–168 Cases in Models, but Real-World Viability Is Contested The most widely cited break-even figures are 168 cases per year (from the navigation-based revision-reduction model) and 158 cases per year (from a separate 3D-navigation cost-benefit analysis at 0% private-payer reimbursement for revisions). These thresholds assume that the system is used efficiently, that the revision-rate reduction is realized, and that the institution captures the savings. However, the evidence base is fragile. A 2026 review of cost-effectiveness studies concluded that evidence remains limited and methodologically heterogeneous, that estimates are highly sensitive to procedural volume, institutional efficiency, and whether capital and maintenance costs are included, and that large administrative database studies often report higher hospital charges for robotic cases rather than savings. The Spanish analysis and the Singapore time-saving study show that savings can be achieved, but the adverse-event analysis shows that they can be erased by operational failures. The truthful synthesis is that 158–168 cases per year is a modeled threshold under favorable assumptions, not a robust empirical constant; the actual break-even volume for a given program depends on its complication profile, case mix, contract terms, and local reimbursement. 💎 Bottom Line Robot-guided spine surgery is not cost-effective as a default technology across all spine procedures; it is a volume-dependent and case-mix-dependent investment whose economic case is strongest when the program can concentrate the robot on complex, revision-prone, or deformity cases where the downstream savings from avoided reoperations and shorter stays are largest. The modeled break-even volume of roughly 160 cases per year is achievable for a high-volume tertiary center, and the Spanish and Singapore data demonstrate that per-case savings of €1,000–SGD 1,500 are possible. But the most rigorous real-world analysis—incorporating the frequency and cost of robot-related delays and abandonments—found that no scenario achieved break-even within the system's useful life, a finding that should temper any business case built solely on modeled revision reductions. As a practicing surgeon, I would frame the decision for a hospital or program as follows: the robot is financially defensible only if the institution can sustain at least ~150–170 relevant cases annually, select cases where the precision and revision-reduction benefits are most likely to be realized, negotiate consumable pricing aggressively, and treat the technology as one component of a value-based pathway rather than a stand-alone revenue generator. Outside those conditions, the capital and per-case expenses are more likely to exceed the realized savings than the optimistic models suggest.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the answer is nuanced and depends heavily on the specific procedure, the technology used, and—critically—what is being measured. The narrative that “robotics reduces radiation” is an oversimplification. The more accurate statement is that robot or navigation assistance generally and reliably reduces radiation exposure to the surgeon and operating room staff, but its effect on the patient's cumulative dose is variable and can, in some workflows, be higher than with conventional fluoroscopy. The protective and surveillance framework for high-volume surgeons is well-defined in principle but inconsistently implemented in practice. 📊 Radiation Exposure: A Divergence Between Surgeon and Patient The effects on the surgeon and the patient must be analyzed separately, as the evidence points in different directions. For the Surgeon and OR Staff: A Consistent and Clinically Meaningful Reduction
This is the most robust finding across the literature. The mechanism is straightforward: robotic and navigation systems rely on preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging to plan trajectories, which reduces or eliminates the need for iterative, real-time fluoroscopic guidance during screw insertion or instrument positioning. Spine Surgery: A prospective randomized controlled trial comparing the TiRobot system to conventional fluoroscopy in thoracolumbar surgery found that surgeon radiation exposure was significantly lower in the robotic group (21.7 ± 11.5 μSv) than in the fluoroscopy group (70.5 ± 42.0 μSv; p < 0.01), even though the total fluoroscopy time was not significantly different between groups. This illustrates a key point: fluoroscopy time and surgeon dose are not always synchronized, because the robot changes the geometry of exposure—the surgeon is no longer positioned near the beam during active imaging. Arthroplasty: A study of direct anterior total hip arthroplasty (THA) demonstrated that a CT-based robotic system allowed for zero intraoperative fluoroscopic images in the robotic cohort, whereas conventional THA required an average of 21 ± 8.9 fluoroscopic shots, delivering over twice the radiation exposure to the surgeon, staff, and patient. Trauma and Pelvis: A 2025 meta-analysis in orthopedic trauma confirmed that robotic guidance was associated with significantly shorter radiation time compared with manual fluoroscopy, supporting a safety advantage for the surgical team. For pelvic fragility fractures, 3D computer-assisted navigation reduced fluoroscopy time by 59% (from 190.3s to 78.4s). For the Patient: A Variable and Sometimes Paradoxical Effect
The patient's cumulative dose is a different matter. While intraoperative fluoroscopy time is often reduced, the preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging (CT or O-arm) required for registration adds a substantial dose that must be counted against the savings. Spine Surgery: A meta-analysis of RCTs found that while radiation time was reduced by 39.6% in robot-guided spinal fusion, the estimated cancer risk and hereditary disorder risk were reduced by 40.2% in the robotic group, suggesting a net patient benefit in this specific context. However, a 2026 systematic review of 3,205 patients concluded that robotic-assisted surgery was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in overall radiation dose or fluoroscopy time compared with freehand techniques, with substantial heterogeneity across studies. The Critical Caveat—Spinal Deformity: The most important counterexample comes from adolescent idiopathic scoliosis surgery. A study comparing freehand (FH) to robotic-assisted navigation (RAN) found that while RAN had a 1.5-fold decrease in intraoperative radiation, the requirement for a perioperative CT scan resulted in a 25-fold greater total radiation dose to the patient (12.5 ± 4.7 mSv vs. 0.5 ± 0.2 mSv). This is a decisive finding: for a young patient with a long life expectancy, the stochastic risk from a 25-fold increase in total dose is not a trivial trade-off for a reduction in intraoperative fluoroscopy alone. A Surgeon's Synthesis on Dose: The reduction in surgeon dose is the most reliable and reproducible benefit. The effect on patient dose is procedure- and protocol-dependent. In straightforward spinal fusion or trauma, the net effect may be favorable. In complex deformity surgery requiring a dedicated perioperative CT, the patient's total dose can be substantially higher. The choice of technology must therefore be informed by which risk (occupational vs. patient stochastic) is being prioritized. 🛡️ Protective Measures for High-Volume Surgeons The framework for protecting the high-volume surgeon is well-established and centers on the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle, but compliance is a persistent weak point. Primary Protection: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
The core PPE for orthopedic surgeons using fluoroscopy includes: Lead apron: Typically 0.25–0.5 mm lead equivalent. Regular use is reported by about 67.6% of surgeons in some surveys, but poorly fitted aprons can increase exposure by up to 30%. Thyroid shield: Protects the thyroid, a highly radiosensitive organ. Use is inconsistent and often poor; one survey found 83% of respondents never used a thyroid shield. Leaded eyeglasses: Critical for protecting the lens of the eye, which is vulnerable to radiation-induced cataracts. Usage is very low; in one survey, none of the respondents used leaded eyewear. The lens dose can be significant, with surgeons working in high dose-rate ranges of 10 μGy/min or higher, making protection advisable. Lead gloves or ring dosimeters are not standard PPE but are relevant for hand protection, which is a concern for radiation-induced skin cancer and dermatitis. Secondary Protection: Technique and Technology Pulsed fluoroscopy: Using pulsed rather than continuous modes (e.g., 4–15 fps) reduces exposure time. Collimation: Narrowing the beam to the region of interest reduces scatter. Distance and shielding: Increasing distance from the source and using mobile lead barriers are effective. One study found that with low-dose O-arm settings and lead shielding, radiation exposure to personnel was reduced to near-zero levels. Choice of technology: The use of navigation or robotics is itself a protective measure, as it reduces the surgeon's proximity to the beam and the number of fluoroscopic images required. 🩺 Health Surveillance for High-Volume Surgeons Surveillance is the most under-implemented component of the safety framework. Dosimetry: The Foundation of Surveillance Personal dosimeters (badge and ring) are essential for quantifying cumulative whole-body and extremity dose. However, 80.4% of surgeons in one survey did not use dosimeters to monitor their dose. The absence of dosimetry data makes it impossible to correlate exposure with health outcomes or to enforce dose limits. Regulatory limits provide a benchmark: the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) recommends an effective dose limit of 20 mSv/year averaged over 5 years, with no single year exceeding 50 mSv. National surveys suggest most orthopedic surgeons receive 0.5–3.5 mSv/year, but these figures are likely underestimates in the absence of universal monitoring. Health Outcome Monitoring: Beyond Dosimetry Skin surveillance: Radiation-induced skin injury (chronic dermatitis) is a recognized occupational hazard. A 5-year longitudinal study found a 34.9% prevalence of dermatologist-graded skin injury at baseline, which declined to 25.6% after an educational campaign emphasizing ALARA and PPE. This demonstrates that surveillance combined with education can produce measurable health improvements. Ocular surveillance: Given the risk of cataracts, lens dose monitoring using dedicated dosimeters (e.g., at the forehead or temple) and periodic ophthalmologic examination are advisable for high-volume surgeons. Biodosimetry: Emerging evidence suggests that chromosomal damage (e.g., increased chromosomal aberrations in lymphocytes) can be detected in orthopedic surgeons despite self-reported compliance with dose limits. The study authors recommend integrating routine biodosimetry assessments into occupational health monitoring to detect early biomarkers of exposure. This is not yet standard practice but represents a direction for more sensitive surveillance. The Implementation Gap
The most important caveat is that knowledge and intention do not equal practice. Surveys consistently reveal major gaps: formal radiation safety training was provided to only 3.9% of surgeons in one study, and basic awareness of ALARA was only 7.8%. The protective measures are well-defined; the challenge is mandatory training, enforced monitoring, and a culture of compliance that treats the high-volume orthopedic surgeon as a radiation worker entitled to the same protections as any other occupationally exposed professional. 💎 A Surgeon's Final Assessment The radiation story in robotic and navigation-assisted orthopedics is one of divergent effects and uneven implementation. For the surgeon, the benefit is real and mechanistically sound—reduced proximity to the beam and fewer iterative fluoroscopic checks. For the patient, the benefit is conditional: it depends on whether the additional 3D imaging required for registration outweighs the intraoperative fluoroscopy saved, a calculus that can tip unfavorably in procedures like deformity correction. The protective framework—ALARA, PPE, and dosimetry—is well-articulated but poorly executed, with unacceptably low rates of thyroid and eye protection and dosimeter use. The path forward requires treating radiation safety not as an individual surgeon's responsibility but as a system-level occupational health mandate, with mandatory training, universal dosimetry, and surveillance for the deterministic (skin, ocular) and stochastic (carcinogenic) consequences of a career-long exposure.

从骨科临床证据看，**目前还不能笼统认定，机器人手术在远期并发症、假体松动或骨折愈合方面全面优于传统术式。**比较明确的优势仍是部分操作的定位与执行精度；这种技术优势是否转化为长期获益，需要按术式分别判断。 1．关节置换：长期假体生存率尚未显示一致优势。 一项至少随访10年的全膝关节置换对照研究，机器人组与传统组的假体生存率分别为98.8%和98.5%，差异无统计学意义。另一项平均随访13年的随机对照研究，也未发现机器人组在长期功能、疼痛及假体生存方面明显优于传统组。10年以上随访研究、13年随机对照研究 这意味着：**不能仅凭假体放置更准确，就承诺更少松动或更晚翻修。**同时，长期研究多涉及较早期系统，其结果也不能直接代表所有新一代机器人。 单髁置换已有良好的10年机器人随访结果，但“机器人组长期表现好”与“优于传统组”是两个结论；没有合适的同期对照，不能确定获益来自机器人本身。单髁置换10年随访 2．脊柱手术：有减少螺钉松动的信号，但长期结论仍不稳固。 部分回顾性研究提示，机器人辅助置钉可能降低螺钉松动率。不过，骨密度、螺钉尺寸与轨迹、融合节段、矫形方案等都会影响结果，现有证据不足以证明机器人普遍降低长期松动、假关节、邻近节段病或再次手术风险。螺钉松动对照研究 还需警惕随访口径：有研究标题中的“5年”指连续5年的病例收集期，患者最低随访实际上只有90天，不能当作每位患者随访5年的证据。研究原文 3．骨折固定：尚不能确认普遍提高愈合率。 机器人能够辅助导针和螺钉布局，但骨折愈合还取决于复位质量、血供、固定稳定性、感染、吸烟及基础疾病。置钉更准确，不能弥补复位不良或血供破坏。 以股骨颈骨折为例，一项至少随访2年的小样本研究未发现两组骨折愈合率有显著差异。对于不愈合、股骨头坏死等结局，仍需要更大样本和更长随访确认；这里的“两年”也不能等同于关节置换领域的十年以上远期观察。股骨颈骨折研究 临床告知时，我会明确表述：**机器人有助于把部分骨性操作做得更准确，但目前不能保证假体更耐用、骨折更易愈合或远期并发症更少。**现有研究未显示显著差异，也不等于证明两者完全等效；低发生率并发症、小样本、失访，以及机器人组同时采用微创入路等因素，都可能影响比较结果。

**最适合机器人辅助经皮内固定的，是已有手术指征、能够获得并维持满意复位、存在安全骨性通道，而置钉定位又比较困难的骨折。**不能仅凭“股骨颈骨折”或“骨盆骨折”这一名称决定使用，更不能因为机器人能精准置钉，就放宽经皮固定的适应证。 骨折或损伤 适合考虑机器人辅助的情况 必须守住的边界 股骨颈骨折 已决定保头内固定，骨折无明显移位，或复位后位置满意且能稳定维持；需要精确布置导针、螺钉 移位型骨折并非一律不能使用，但必须先解决复位和固定方案问题。高龄移位型骨折若更适合关节置换，不能为了使用机器人改做内固定 骶骨骨折、骶髂关节脱位等后环损伤 需要手术稳定，复位满意，S1或S2等通道足够容纳计划螺钉 骶骨变异、通道狭窄时可能更需要辅助，但没有安全通道就不能强行置钉 髋臼前柱、后柱骨折 无明显移位且确需固定，或经闭合／有限切开复位后关节面与柱结构恢复满意，可用通道螺钉稳定固定 明显关节面压陷、游离骨块或复杂粉碎，若需要直视重建，单纯经皮螺钉通常不够 部分耻骨支及其他骨盆环骨折 已确认需要固定，存在合适通道，经皮螺钉能满足整体稳定要求 不能仅固定容易置钉的部位，而忽略后环不稳定或整体固定不足 相关骨盆、髋臼及股骨颈机器人操作指导，都强调“轻度移位，或能够闭合／有限切开复位，并适合经皮螺钉固定”这一前提。这些文件主要提供技术选择原则，并不能证明所有此类骨折使用机器人都更优。骨盆髋臼指导、股骨颈骨折指导 哪些情况下可能属于多余？ 骨折本身适合非手术治疗，没有必要因设备可用而增加内固定。 通道宽、定位简单，熟练团队用常规透视即可稳定完成，而机器人增加的准备、费用与等待没有明确收益。 已需充分开放显露，机器人对计划中的关键步骤没有额外帮助。但“开放手术”本身不等于机器人一定无用。 设备准备会延误时间敏感的救治。尤其血流动力学不稳定的骨盆创伤，应优先复苏、止血与必要的临时稳定。WSES骨盆创伤指南 哪些情况应避免经皮机器人固定，或停止当前机器人操作？ **经皮固定方案不成立：**复位不满意、无法维持复位，或螺钉构型不能提供足够稳定性。此时应调整复位、入路或固定方案；并不是所有后续操作都不能再用机器人。 **路径不安全：**不存在足够骨性通道，或无法避开重要神经血管结构。 **定位不可信：**影像不清、配准核验失败、参考架固定不牢，或骨块相对参考架移动后未能可靠更新定位。 **器械无法安全到达：**机械臂、套筒或器械与体位、手术床、软组织相冲突，且无法妥善调整。 **超出设备用途或不兼容：**拟用植入物、器械或术式不受该系统支持。技术限制与禁忌说明 还应避免将严重骨质疏松、开放骨折或粉碎骨折一概列为机器人绝对禁忌：它们首先影响清创、复位、固定强度与治疗时机；若这些问题未解决，精准定位也无法补偿。 目前缺少足够的直接比较证据，为不同骨折排出统一的“机器人获益榜”。实际选择应回答一个具体问题：机器人是否能在不牺牲复位、稳定性和救治时效的前提下，解决该患者真正存在的定位难题？

**开展骨科机器人手术，需要同时满足合法执业、相应术式的院内授权，以及针对具体设备的培训与能力考核。培训结业证不能代替手术授权，完成一定病例数也不等于可以独立主刀。**以下以中国大陆为背景。 1．执业资质与手术授权 术者应依法取得医师资格并完成执业注册，在符合其执业范围和机构管理要求的条件下开展诊疗；同时，取得医院对相应手术级别、具体术式的授权。国家规定，医疗机构应根据医师专业能力和培训情况授予或取消手术权限，并进行动态管理。《医疗技术临床应用管理办法》、《医疗机构手术分级管理办法》 **不能笼统规定“必须是副主任医师以上”或“拿到机器人证即可主刀”。**具体职称、既往病例量和带教要求，需要核对当地规定及医院准入制度。我未查到适用于所有骨科机器人、全国统一的独立操作证书或最低病例数规定。 术者还应具备相应传统手术能力，能判断导航是否可信，并处理并发症、转换为常规手术；这也是胸腰椎机器人置钉指南明确提出的要求。相关指南 2．专项培训应覆盖什么？ 针对具体型号、软件版本和拟开展术式，合理的培训与考核应包括： **理论与规划：**适应症、禁忌症、影像要求、轨迹或假体规划，以及系统误差来源。 **设备实操：**装机、无菌准备、配准、精度核验、器械使用和故障排查。 **模拟与应急：**识别配准漂移、参考架移位、器械滑移，完成急停、安全撤机和常规手术转换。 **带教病例与评估：**先观摩、参与，再在有资质人员指导下完成病例，考核通过并获得授权后逐步独立开展。 厂商培训主要解决设备使用问题，临床决策、手术能力和独立授权仍由医疗机构负责。护理、麻醉和工程人员也需参与流程训练。 3．上手周期有多长？ 必须区分“会操作设备”“操作时间趋于稳定”和“能够独立安全完成手术”。 层次 可参考的时间或病例量 应如何理解 设备基础操作 取决于具体培训项目 没有可通用于所有系统的固定天数 膝关节置换流程熟练 部分研究约 10～25例 通常针对已有置换经验的术者，且多以操作时间为指标 脊柱机器人置钉熟练 部分研究约 20～30例 受设备、既往经验、病例复杂度及考核指标影响 独立开展复杂病例 无统一周期 应依据实际能力与授权，不能按病例数自动升级 例如，特定膝关节机器人研究报告约16例的时间学习曲线；一项脊柱置钉研究采用约20～30例作为熟练度参考。这些是研究观察，不是法定准入门槛，也不代表完成后就掌握复杂畸形、翻修或上颈椎手术。膝关节研究、脊柱研究 判断能否独立开展，关键应看：能否正确选择患者、可靠完成规划与核验、识别异常并及时停止，以及在机器人停用后继续安全完成手术。获得授权后，仍需结合定位准确性、并发症、转换情况及随访结果持续评估。

Robotic navigation generally improves radiographic screw-placement accuracy and reduces fluoroscopy during percutaneous sacroiliac fixation. Evidence that it reduces actual neurovascular injury is much less certain. From an orthopedic trauma perspective, these outcomes should be assessed separately. Outcome Comparison with conventional fluoroscopy Safe-corridor placement A small randomized trial involving 30 patients and 45 screws reported excellent/good CT placement in 100% of robotic screws versus 95% of freehand screws. This grading endpoint should not be interpreted as every screw being perfectly centered. Fluoroscopy time In the same trial, median fluoroscopy time after pelvic reduction was 6 versus 36 seconds, approximately an 83% reduction. This excludes imaging used for reduction and is not a whole-procedure radiation-dose comparison. Neurovascular complications Neither group had postoperative complications or revisions. With only 30 patients, this cannot establish that robotics lowers the rate of rare nerve or vascular injuries. These figures come from a prospective randomized sacroiliac screw trial. Another comparative S2 iliosacral study reported fluoroscopy times of 8.1 versus 27.4 seconds, supporting a reduction in repeated imaging, although the magnitude varies with the workflow. S2 fixation study The clinical advantage is more reproducible targeting with fewer guidewire redirections. Accurate reduction and confirmation of an adequate bony corridor remain essential: robotic guidance cannot compensate for an unsafe planned trajectory, loss of reduction, registration error, or guidewire bending. Fluoroscopy time also does not directly equal radiation dose, particularly when a workflow includes CT or 3D imaging. I would therefore describe robotics as offering better placement consistency and usually less fluoroscopy, with a plausible but not reliably quantified reduction in neurovascular risk. The strongest direct evidence concerns posterior-ring S1/S2 iliosacral screws; the same numerical benefits should not automatically be applied to every anterior-ring or transsacral screw configuration.

Reduced tactile feedback removes an important warning signal: the surgeon may know where an instrument is intended to go without fully feeling how the tissue is responding. Its consequences differ between bone cutting, screw insertion, and soft-tissue handling. First, the premise needs qualification. Not all orthopedic robots eliminate tactile feedback. Some provide haptic boundaries that resist movement outside a planned cutting region, and many spinal systems guide instruments that the surgeon still holds. These features are different from faithfully transmitting tissue resistance, texture, or insertion torque back to the surgeon. PMC From a clinical surgical perspective: Task Information lost or diminished Potential consequences Osteotomy and bone preparation Changes in cutting resistance when moving between dense cortex, cancellous bone, and the far cortex; unexpected binding or breakthrough. More difficult recognition of breakthrough or abnormal loading, potentially allowing unintended penetration or injury beyond the bone. Virtual boundaries help control the planned cutting volume, but do not fully reproduce tissue sensation or compensate for an inaccurate anatomical registration. Screw placement Resistance during drilling and tapping, cortical contact, and the rise or sudden loss of insertion torque. Less immediate recognition of a drill slipping across the bone surface—“skiving”—a cortical breach, poor screw purchase, or thread stripping. A satisfactory navigation display can be falsely reassuring if the bone has moved or registration is inaccurate. Soft-tissue dissection Tissue compliance, tension, and the resistance that helps distinguish a natural dissection plane from adherent tissue. Excessive grasping or traction, tissue crushing or tearing, and difficulty judging safe manipulation near nerves and vessels. Visual deformation provides useful information, but may not reveal excessive force before injury occurs. These are mechanistic risks, not proof that robotic procedures have higher complication rates. Experimental drilling and milling studies distinguish the benefits of spatial guidance from those of actual force feedback. Clinical spinal reports also document skiving, movement, registration errors, and soft-tissue interference as failure mechanisms; they do not isolate absent haptics as the sole cause. PubMed For osteotomy, thermal injury deserves separate attention. Accurate cutting does not guarantee temperature control: tool characteristics, irrigation, feed rate, and time spent cutting remain important. A robotic porcine-bone study demonstrated that changing the cutting motion substantially affected temperature. However, I cannot confidently attribute an increased clinical rate of thermal necrosis specifically to absent haptic feedback; touch itself is not a reliable temperature monitor. Clinical Biomechanics For screw insertion, the practical response is to retain independent checks of trajectory and bone engagement, rather than relying exclusively on the screen. Where the system permits it, manual insertion can restore more direct torque sensation. That sensation remains supplementary—it cannot by itself establish that a screw is safely contained within bone. PMC For soft-tissue dissection, the concern applies most directly when the robot actually manipulates tissue. If exposure and dissection are performed manually and the robot only guides bone preparation, this particular sensory limitation does not apply to the manual dissection. Animal experiments show that providing tactile feedback can reduce grasping forces and tissue damage, but the size of that benefit in orthopedic patients remains uncertain.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the learning curve for robotic arthroplasty is shorter than many expect but is not uniform across procedures or platforms. The more important insight is that the curve can be actively compressed and made safer through deliberate programme design—structured pre-clinical training, proctoring, case clustering, and a protected early phase—rather than simply accepting that the first several cases will be slower and riskier. How Many Cases to Overcome the Learning Curve? The number depends on what endpoint is being measured and which procedure and platform are involved. A critical distinction must be made between operative-time proficiency and complication-specific proficiency, because they do not occur at the same case number. Robotic TKA: a short operative-time curve, but a longer safety-relevant curve. For operative time, the evidence converges on a relatively early plateau. A prospective study of 115 robotic TKAs using the ROSA system with the anatomic-functional implant positioning technique found that 11 cases were required to achieve optimal operative time, with mean duration of 108 minutes, and that this learning period did not compromise alignment accuracy, ligament balance, or complication rate. A separate analysis of the ROSA system reported an initial learning curve of 6–11 cases for operative time, with similar 90-day complication rates to manual TKA and improved implant alignment. A NASA-TLX workload analysis found that operative time showed a breakpoint at 9 cases, with workload scores stabilizing after approximately 8 cases. A group learning-curve study showed mean operative time decreasing from 97.6 to 86.6 to 76.7 minutes with every 30 cases, with no difference in complication rate. However, when the endpoint is complication-specific, the curve is longer. A large propensity-matched analysis of RA-TKA across ten surgeons identified a learning-curve breakpoint at approximately the twelfth case for the rate of manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) , which fell from 5.2% in the pre-learning phase to 2.9% after proficiency (P = 0.042). After adjustment, pre-learning cases had a 2.13-fold higher odds of MUA. This is a clinically important finding: operative time may stabilize within 10–12 cases, but a measurable safety-relevant outcome may require a similar or slightly longer window before it normalizes. For time neutrality against a surgeon’s own manual TKA—a more demanding benchmark than mere improvement—the literature reports a wider range. A 2026 review estimated 32 ± 24 cases for time neutrality (range 3–73) and 16 ± 12 cases for proficiency (range 3–61). A 2026 study of the ROSA system found that 30 cases were needed for a senior surgeon to balance operative time between manual and robotic TKA, while other series report time neutrality after approximately 20 cases or, for some platforms, 40 cases. The most defensible summary is that operative-time proficiency is typically achieved within 10–20 cases, but time neutrality against manual technique may require 20–40 cases depending on the platform, the surgeon’s manual volume, and team familiarity. Robotic THA: proficiency at approximately 12–17 cases, with a longer curve for consolidated performance. The evidence for robotic THA is more consistent. A CUSUM-derived analysis of an advanced imageless navigation system found proficiency at 15–17 cases for competency and 38–43 cases for consolidated proficiency. A scoping review of robotic THA learning curves reported a weighted mean of 16.4 cases to reach proficiency, with a median of 13 cases. Specific platform studies report 14 cases for the MAKO system, 13 cases for a seven-axis system, and 11 cases for the MAKO system in another series. A study using the ARTHROBOT system reported a learning curve of approximately 20 cases. The important nuance for THA is the distinction between early proficiency and consolidated proficiency. Early proficiency (12–17 cases) is sufficient to achieve acceptable operative times and component positioning. Consolidated proficiency (38–43 cases) reflects sustained, consistent performance and may be the more appropriate threshold for credentialing or independent practice decisions. Furthermore, surgeon volume modifies the curve: high-volume surgeons (>51 cases annually) demonstrated early learning curves, while low- and medium-volume surgeons showed no improvement through 20 and 63 cases, respectively. How Should a New Programme Be Structured? The evidence supports a phased, competency-based structure rather than a fixed case count alone. The organizing principle is to move the steepest part of the learning curve out of the operating room and away from patients, and then to protect the early clinical phase with supervision and deliberate case selection. Phase 1: Pre-clinical training—plastic bone, cadaver, and simulation. A structured pre-clinical phase is identified in the implementation literature as a key strategy to reduce the length of the learning curve and decrease adverse events. The recommended sequence begins with training on plastic bones, followed by cadaveric specimens, before moving to the initial clinical phase. Cadaver training is specifically identified as a factor that can profoundly affect the learning curve, and at least one high-volume surgeon’s rapid progression with the ROSA system was attributed in part to cadaver-lab training prior to first clinical use. Virtual reality and synthetic models are also described as training tools that can be combined with cadaver work. The purpose of this phase is to achieve familiarity with registration, system setup, instrument exchange, and the robotic-specific steps before a patient is involved. Phase 2: Proctored clinical introduction with deliberate case selection. The early clinical phase should be proctored, with an experienced robotic surgeon or a manufacturer-certified proctor present for the initial cases. The evidence supports structuring mentorship and supervision around the identified learning phases rather than applying a uniform level of supervision throughout. A practical structure is: Proctor present for the first 5–10 cases, focusing on registration accuracy, workflow sequencing, and troubleshooting. Proctor available remotely or on-site for cases 10–20, as the surgeon transitions to independent execution. Independent practice after demonstrated competency, ideally benchmarked against the 12–17 case proficiency threshold for THA and the 10–12 case threshold for TKA operative time and early safety outcomes. Case selection during this phase matters. Straightforward primary cases—moderate deformity, reasonable bone quality, no prior hardware—should be prioritized. Complex deformity, revision, and severe stiffness should be deferred until after proficiency is established. Phase 3: Case clustering and team continuity. The learning curve is not solely a surgeon phenomenon; it is a team phenomenon. Low-volume, sporadic robotic cases increase the duration of the operating room team learning curve. The evidence strongly supports case clustering—scheduling multiple robotic cases sequentially—and keeping the operating department team together during the learning curve. A group learning-curve study showing improvement every 30 cases reflects, in part, team familiarization rather than surgeon skill alone. The practical threshold is to cluster at least 2–3 robotic cases per operating list during the learning phase, so that setup, registration, and workflow are rehearsed repeatedly within a short interval rather than relearned after gaps. Phase 4: Volume thresholds and institutional readiness. The evidence distinguishes between surgeon-level proficiency and institutional proficiency. A study of institutional surgical volume found that institutional proficiency required 300–550 cases, far exceeding the 12–35 cases reported for individual surgeons, emphasizing the complexity of system-wide learning. This means that a programme cannot assume that a single trained surgeon is sufficient; the entire perioperative system—scheduling, sterile processing, room turnover, and troubleshooting—must accumulate experience. For credentialing, the evidence supports a threshold of approximately 40 cases for technology-assisted THA, reflecting consolidated rather than minimal proficiency. For a new programme, a defensible volume target is at least 50–100 robotic arthroplasty cases in the first year, with a concentration of cases among a small number of surgeons and a stable team, to ensure that both individual and institutional learning curves are traversed rather than repeatedly restarted. Keeping Early-Phase Operative Time and Complications Acceptable The evidence suggests that early-phase safety can be maintained even while operative time is longer, provided that the programme is structured correctly. The 115-case ROSA TKA study is instructive: perioperative complications remained constant at 3.5% and were not associated with case sequence (P = 0.89), and alignment accuracy was stable throughout the series (ΔHKA = 2.0° ± 1.0°). This indicates that the learning curve primarily affects efficiency, not accuracy or safety, when the system constrains bone resection to the planned geometry and the surgeon follows a structured protocol. The MUA finding, however, shows that some safety-relevant outcomes do improve after the early phase, which is precisely why proctoring and case selection during the first 10–15 cases are important. The practical safeguards that emerge from the evidence are: Do not sacrifice planning for speed. The robot constrains execution to the plan; inaccurate planning during the learning phase is the most likely source of error. Prolonged registration time should prompt reassessment of planning parameters before component positioning. Use the robot’s built-in safety constraints. The finding that alignment accuracy did not degrade during the learning phase, while operative time did, suggests that the system’s geometric constraints are protective. The goal during early cases is to complete the planned procedure accurately, not to match manual operative time. Monitor complication-specific endpoints, not just operative time. The MUA data show that a procedure can appear “efficient” by operative time while still carrying an elevated risk of a clinically meaningful complication. Early-phase audit should include MUA, readmission, and revision, not only minutes in the room. Protect the team. A stable, dedicated team and clustered scheduling reduce the institutional learning burden and prevent sporadic cases from repeatedly resetting the team’s familiarity. A Surgeon’s Synthesis The learning curve for robotic arthroplasty is short for operative-time proficiency—typically 10–20 cases for TKA and 12–17 cases for THA—but longer for consolidated proficiency and some safety-relevant outcomes, with 38–43 cases for THA and a measurable MUA benefit after approximately 12 TKA cases. The curve is volume-dependent and team-dependent, not solely a function of surgeon skill; low-volume surgeons and fragmented teams have demonstrably longer curves. A new programme should be structured as a phased competency pathway: plastic-bone and cadaver training before clinical use; proctored introduction over the first 10–20 cases with straightforward case selection; case clustering and team continuity to compress the institutional curve; and credentialing thresholds aligned with consolidated rather than minimal proficiency (approximately 40 cases for THA, with a first-year programme volume target of 50–100 cases). The most important caveat is that the evidence for complication-specific learning curves is still emerging, and most studies are single-centre or platform-specific; a programme should build its own early-phase audit of operative time, alignment accuracy, and complication-specific endpoints rather than relying solely on published case thresholds.

从执业资质、专项培训到真正“上手”，骨科机器人手术的要求可以概括为：资质是法定的准入门槛，培训是结构化的能力构建过程，而上手周期则是一个因亚专科和平台而异、但可被大致量化的学习曲线。三者共同构成一个从“有资格做”到“能安全做好”的递进链条。 执业资质：法定门槛清晰，但具体准入标准存在基地间差异 骨科机器人手术在中国被纳入国家限制类医疗技术管理（自2022年起），这意味着它并非任何骨科医师可自行开展的技术，必须满足法定的前置条件。 核心的法定要求是：必须在省级以上卫生健康行政部门备案的培训基地完成系统培训并考核合格，方可开展。这一“培训基地认证”是资质链条的起点，而非终点。 在医师个人条件上，各培训基地的招生简章呈现出高度一致的基本框架，但也存在值得注意的差异： 条件 普遍要求 部分基地的更高要求 执业证书 已取得《医师执业证书》，执业范围为外科专业 — 职称 主治医师及以上 西安市红会医院要求副高及以上，或主治医师满5年 临床经验 通常未设硬性年限 北京友谊医院要求5年以上骨科或相关外科经验；红会医院要求三甲医院骨科10年以上 单位同意 需所在单位出具推荐/证明材料 — 执业地点 — 友谊医院明确要求三级医院 这一差异本身反映了当前准入体系的一个现实：国家层面划定了“限制类技术”的底线，但具体谁有资格进入培训、进而获得操作资质，在很大程度上仍由各培训基地根据自身定位和病例复杂度来界定。对于创伤骨科等复杂场景，部分基地显然倾向于将培训资源投向已有相当年资和经验的医师。 专项培训：不是“学开机器的课”，而是一套分阶段的能力验证体系 培训的结构化程度，是判断一个术者是否真正具备机器人手术胜任力的关键。从多家基地的课程设计来看，完整的培训路径通常分为基础准入与完整资质两个阶段，后者以可量化的操作产出为结业标准。 以首都医科大学附属北京世纪坛医院的方案为例，完整资质培训的硬性要求包括： 理论学习：完成20学时以上并通过考核； 动物训练：完成10例以上； 临床实践：在导师监督下，参与完成10例以上不同类别的机器人辅助手术； 全过程管理：参与10例以上患者的术前评估、适应证判断、手术方式选择、风险预案及术后处理。 这一“20学时+10例动物+10例手术+10例全流程管理”的框架，在多份招生简章中反复出现，可视作当前完整资质培训的基准量级。培训周期方面，友谊医院明确为6个月，世纪坛医院在基础培训（1—2天集中授课）之外，完整资质同样需要6个月的临床实践。 但培训的内涵正在被专家共识推向更深层。2026年亚太关节置换共识明确批评了“培训重点局限于‘会操作设备’”的倾向，指出真正的机器人胜任力应包括：正常流程操作、异常识别、故障处置，以及必要时安全转换为传统手术的能力。共识还强调了一个容易被准入制度忽视的维度：不同机器人平台在影像依赖、注册方式、机械臂控制和故障处理流程上并不相同，一种平台上的熟练经验不能替代另一平台的专项培训。这意味着，资质证书所证明的是“完成了某一平台的培训”，而非“获得了跨平台的通用操作权”。 上手周期：学习曲线的“熟练”与“巩固”是两个不同阶段 “上手周期”不宜用一个笼统的病例数来回答，因为不同亚专科、不同术式、不同评价终点（手术时间稳定 vs. 操作精度达标 vs. 并发症率可控）对应的阈值差异显著。从现有学习曲线研究中，可以提炼出有参考价值的量级区间。 关节置换：短周期可达“时间中性”，但“巩固熟练”需要更长的积累。 机器人辅助全膝关节置换（TKA） 的学习曲线文献报道范围较宽，大致在6至43例之间。较为一致的模式是：早期即可获得显著效率提升，但手术时间的稳定平台期出现较晚。一项2026年的前瞻性研究显示，与最初10例相比，手术时间的显著缩短出现在第41—50例区块，此后稳定在约90分钟的水平。另一项研究则发现，达到与徒手TKA相当的手术时间，在单一术者序列中约需20—40例。 机器人辅助全髋关节置换（THA） 的曲线形态有所不同。基于CUSUM方法的研究一致报告，达到基本胜任的阈值在12—17例；但一项更精细的分析引入了“持续稳定熟练”的补充标准（连续5例低于目标绩效），据此提出的资质认证参考病例数约为40例。这提示，“能做下来”和“稳定做好”之间的差距，在THA中大约是一倍左右的病例积累。 脊柱：椎弓根螺钉置入的基线能力门槛约20—30例。 脊柱机器人学习曲线的研究结论相对集中：多数文献支持约20—30例可达机器人辅助椎弓根螺钉置入的基线胜任力。对于脊柱外科的高年资住院医师，有研究倡导至少30例的机器人操作经验。值得注意的是，这一周期对于手术团队中的辅助角色可能更短：一项针对巡回护士掌握Ti-机器人脊柱手术设备操作的研究显示，个体学习曲线的拐点出现在3—11例，总体曲线在8例后开始下降。这提示，术者与团队的非术者成员的上手节奏并不同步，流程效率的改善可能先于术者操作精度的完全巩固而出现。 创伤骨科：缺乏专属的“上手周期”共识，资质门槛实际上更高。 在现有文献中，机器人辅助创伤骨科（如骨盆通道螺钉、关节内骨折）的专属学习曲线研究远少于关节和脊柱。部分培训基地对创伤方向申请者的资质要求（如红会医院的副高/主治满5年+三甲10年）实际上构成了一种前置性的经验筛选，以弥补学习曲线证据的不足。这意味着，在创伤领域，“上手周期”在相当程度上被转化为“准入前的年资要求”，而非一个在培训后可被明确量化的病例数阈值。 需要明确指出的几点局限 第一，“资质证书”与“独立开展能力”之间仍存在间隙。 培训基地的结业标准（如10例手术参与）是最低准入量级，而学习曲线研究提示，达到稳定的效率平台往往需要30—40例以上的独立或主导操作积累。证书赋予的是开展权限，而非熟练度的保证。 第二，学习曲线数据高度依赖于“单术者、单一平台、特定病例组合”的研究设计。 当团队由多名术者轮转、或手术室辅助团队不稳定时，学习曲线可能显著延长。有研究明确指出，异质性团队的学习曲线比单术者导向的培训更长，“达到熟练的速度取决于每位术者个体的接纳速度”。这意味着，科室层面的整体上手周期，不能简单等同于个别术者的病例数。 第三，现有学习曲线研究几乎全部来自关节置换和脊柱椎弓根螺钉置入，创伤、骨肿瘤、复杂翻修等领域的“上手周期”在学术文献中仍缺乏可引用的量化标准。 对于这些场景，当前更可靠的判断依据是培训基地的准入筛选强度和导师监督下的渐进式授权，而非一个通用的病例数阈值。

**与传统二维透视相比，机器人导航辅助骶髂螺钉置入通常能改善螺钉位置、减少导针反复调整和置钉阶段的透视；但对神经血管并发症，目前尚不足以确认发生率显著降低。**证据主要来自骶髂螺钉，不能直接推广至所有骨盆环螺钉通道。 1．安全骨性通道内的置钉准确度：总体有改善，但应看具体分级。 一项30名患者、45枚骶髂螺钉的随机对照试验中，机器人组23枚、传统组22枚，术后CT评估的螺钉位置优良率分别为100%与95%。这是小样本结果，而且“优良率”并不等于“全部完全位于骨内”。随机对照试验 临床评价时，应进一步看完全骨内率、皮质穿破的方向和程度，以及是否进入骶孔或骶管。即使只有少量穿破，其意义也取决于与神经血管的具体关系，不能仅凭一个“准确率”判断安全性。 2．透视时间：通常减少，但不能直接等同于总辐射剂量下降。 上述试验中，骨盆复位完成后的透视时间中位数为6秒对36秒，机器人组约减少83%；但这一口径排除了复位阶段，不能解释为整台手术总透视减少83%。随机对照试验 另一项91名患者的非随机比较研究，报告机器人组与传统组平均透视次数为8.49次对18.67次，也支持减少重复透视，但存在患者选择等偏倚。比较研究 尤其需要区分： 透视次数、透视时间和实际辐射剂量是不同指标。 使用术中CT或三维扫描时，应计入扫描和重复采集，不能只统计置钉阶段。 患者与术者的受照情况不同；术者能在扫描时离开或加强屏蔽，并不代表患者剂量按同样比例降低。 3．神经血管并发症：有减少风险的合理机制，但临床证据仍有限。 减少骨外穿破和导针反复进退，理论上有助于保护神经血管。然而，上述30人随机试验两组均未报告术后并发症或翻修，只能说明该研究未观察到事件，不能证明两组风险相同，也不能证明机器人降低了风险。低发生率事件需要更大的样本和规范随访。试验结果 此外，置钉准确也不能完全避免进针路径上的血管损伤。机器人辅助仍以复位满意且稳定、存在足够骨性通道、配准可靠为前提。骶骨变异、狭窄通道或复位丢失时尤其需要谨慎；前述91人研究排除了骶骨形态异常患者，其结果不能直接套用于这一高难度人群。研究纳排标准 因此，临床上可以较有把握地说机器人有助于提高置钉可控性、减少反复透视；对于“能降低多少神经血管损伤”，目前没有可靠的统一数字，也不能承诺零风险。

从执业脊柱外科医师的决策视角看，界定机器人辅助脊柱手术的适应证与禁忌证，核心不在于背诵一份疾病清单，而在于判断一个具体病例的技术前提是否成立，以及机器人的几何确定性是否恰好落在传统技术的薄弱环节上。机器人手术最根本的约束条件，是能否建立可靠的空间配准——即把术前影像与患者实体解剖精确对齐。2024年《中国机器人辅助胸腰椎手术指南》将“患者追踪器安放位置无法满足要求或无法获得满足要求的导航图像”列为明确的禁忌证。因此，面对你列出的五种情况，权衡的焦点各不相同：有的属于优势被放大的适应证，有的属于前提被动摇的相对禁忌，有的则需要区分“疾病”与“技术”两个层面来分别判断。 重度脊柱侧凸：适应证的核心群体，优势随畸形程度放大 重度脊柱侧凸是机器人辅助脊柱手术证据最一致、获益逻辑最清晰的适应证之一。2024年中国指南明确将“脊柱侧凸、脊柱后凸”列为适应证。其根本原因在于，畸形使徒手置钉所依赖的解剖标志和“手感”系统性失效。文献数据显示，在青少年特发性脊柱侧凸（AIS）中，机器人置钉准确率可达92%–98%，显著高于徒手技术的精度区间。更关键的是，机器人解决的是一个确定性问题：在解剖本身失去确定性的场景中，提供一条不依赖于肉眼辨识的、可重复的几何通道。因此，对于重度侧凸，机器人并非“可选项之一”，而是当畸形严重到传统技术精度瓶颈无法可靠覆盖时，重建安全边界的核心工具。其禁忌权重极低，除非患者因全身状况无法耐受手术，或畸形导致追踪器无法在髂嵴等骨性标志上稳固安放。 重度椎体滑脱：适应证明确，但“重度”本身引入技术审慎 椎体滑脱是机器人辅助TLIF（RA-TLIF）的明确适应证，2024年指南将“腰椎滑脱”以及“先天性重度腰椎滑脱”均列入其中。机器人的价值在于，滑脱节段的椎弓根轨迹因位移和旋转而偏离常规解剖轴线，徒手置钉的容错空间收窄，而三维规划可以在滑脱后的实际解剖上重新定义一条安全的骨性通道。 但“重度”滑脱需要引入一层额外的审慎。共识文献指出，对于重度滑脱或复位困难者，不强行复位是一个可接受的策略。这意味着，机器人擅长的是“在既定位移下精准置钉”，而滑脱的复位本身——尤其是高度滑脱的复位——依赖于术者的策略选择、软组织松解和力学判断，这是机器人几何精度无法替代的决策维度。此外，Ⅲ度以上的重度滑脱在临床实践中常被视为需要更审慎评估的场景，其挑战更多在于整体力线重建和神经减压，而非单枚螺钉的轨迹。因此，重度滑脱的适应症判断应拆分为两个问题：置钉环节，机器人优势明确；复位与整体重建环节，机器人的贡献有限，需依靠术者经验。这并不构成禁忌，但要求术者不能将“机器人辅助”等同于“全流程精度保障”。 椎弓根发育不良：机器人优势最“纯粹”的场景之一 椎弓根发育不良（纤细、缺如或形态异常）是机器人辅助脊柱手术的强适应证。当椎弓根皮质骨管腔狭窄到徒手置钉几乎完全依赖“手感”和术中透视反复确认时，机器人提供的术前/术中三维规划，能够在一个肉眼无法直接观察的微小骨性空间内，定义一条不依赖于实时触觉反馈的轨迹。共识文献明确指出，RA-TLIF“尤其适用于椎弓根纤细”的病例，机器人技术在“解剖变异”中具有巨大优势。在Marfan综合征等伴有椎弓根发育不良的病例中，机器人导航被证实能够有效应对常规椎弓根螺钉技术难以处理的解剖挑战。这一场景中，机器人的获益逻辑最为“纯粹”：它弥补的不是“精度不够好”，而是人手在物理上难以可靠触及和判断的解剖约束。禁忌权重很低，除非发育不良伴随的畸形导致追踪器无法安放或影像无法配准。 骨质疏松：一个需要拆解为两个层面来判断的复杂指征 骨质疏松是五种情况中禁忌证据最直接、但适应证证据同样在演进的一个。不能笼统地将其归为“禁忌”或“适应证”，而必须区分“机器人能不能做” 与 “螺钉能不能把持住”。 从技术前提层面，严重骨质疏松被多项来源视为相对禁忌或注册风险因素。脊柱机器人手术的失败原因中，注册误差约占60%，而严重骨质疏松是导致注册不准确或参考架松动的已知原因之一。其机制在于，追踪器或参考架需要锚定在骨性结构上，骨质量过差时锚定稳定性下降，配准所依赖的骨性界面也可能因骨小梁稀疏而变得模糊。 但从置钉精度层面，近期证据指向一个更积极的方向。一项2026年的多中心研究显示，在低骨量患者中，AI辅助的椎弓根螺钉轨迹规划联合机器人引导，提高了置钉A级比例并降低了螺钉松动率，同时加速了骨融合。这意味着，机器人可以通过规划一条在骨质疏松骨中力学上更优的轨迹（如利用皮质骨通道），部分弥补骨质量本身带来的把持力缺陷。2026年RA-TLIF共识也明确指出，对骨质疏松患者需先进行抗骨质疏松治疗，术中可考虑骨水泥强化等技术，而非简单地将骨质疏松等同于机器人禁忌。 因此，骨质疏松的合理定位是：它是一个需要前置评估和术中辅助策略来管理的“相对困难”场景，而非自动排除的绝对禁忌。术前骨密度评估（DXA）是必要的决策节点；严重骨质疏松（如T值显著偏低）应触发对配准可靠性的额外验证，并预先规划骨水泥强化或皮质骨通道螺钉等补救方案。将其简单列为“禁忌”会剥夺一部分低骨量患者从精准规划中获益的机会，而将其轻率列为“适应证”则忽视了注册失败的真实风险。 合并内植物的翻修手术：优势与风险并存，关键在“伪影管理” 翻修手术是机器人辅助脊柱手术中获益逻辑最强、但技术风险也最集中的场景之一。其获益在于：翻修手术的正常解剖标志已被瘢痕和既往内植物破坏，徒手置钉所依赖的视觉和触觉参考系在很大程度上失效。范围综述和临床报告一致认为，翻修手术是机器人技术的理想适应证，因为机器人用三维规划所定义的几何坐标，替代了已被手术改变的现实解剖标志。此外，机器人辅助的皮质骨通道螺钉技术已被报告可作为螺钉松动导致融合失败后的补救策略，在翻修中提供传统椎弓根螺钉之外的替代固定方案。 然而，合并内植物这一具体条件引入了翻修场景中最核心的技术障碍：金属伪影。机器人系统的配准和分割需要识别清晰的骨性界面，而既往的钛笼、螺钉等金属内植物产生的伪影，可能严重干扰这一过程，使规划所依赖的骨性轮廓变得不可辨识。此外，翻修节段的椎间运动也可能增加注册漂移的风险。因此，合并内植物的翻修手术，其禁忌权重不取决于“翻修”本身，而取决于内植物伪影对关键注册标志点的遮蔽程度。如果伪影局限在非关键区域，且术者可以通过多模态影像融合或更换配准策略来规避，则机器人优势仍然可及；如果伪影恰好覆盖了需要置钉节段的骨性参考面，则配准的可靠性将无法保证，此时应视为相对禁忌，需审慎评估是否转为导航或徒手技术。 综合判断：一个以“配准可靠性”为轴心的决策框架 将五种情况并置，一条清晰的决策轴线浮现出来：机器人辅助脊柱手术的适应证强度，与“解剖对传统技术的不友好程度”正相关；而其禁忌权重，与“配准前提被动摇的程度”正相关。 场景 机器人获益逻辑 主要风险/限制 临床定位 重度脊柱侧凸 畸形使解剖标志失效，几何确定性重建安全边界 极低（除非追踪器无法安放） 强适应证 椎弓根发育不良 弥补人手在微小骨性通道中的物理约束 低 强适应证 合并内植物的翻修 解剖标志被破坏，规划替代现实标志 金属伪影干扰配准 获益明确，但取决于伪影管理 重度椎体滑脱 滑脱后轨迹偏离常规，规划重新定义通道 复位与整体重建仍需术者决策 置钉适应证明确，整体重建需综合判断 骨质疏松 精准轨迹可部分弥补骨质量缺陷 注册失败风险升高，螺钉把持力有限 需前置评估与辅助策略管理的相对指征 这一框架的实践含义是：面对一个具体病例，比“诊断是什么”更关键的追问是：这个患者的骨性解剖，能否为机器人提供一套它能够可靠“理解”的空间坐标？ 如果答案是肯定的，且解剖的复杂性恰好落在传统技术的精度薄弱区间，那么机器人就是合理的工具。如果配准的前提因骨质量、伪影或追踪器安放而被动摇，那么即使疾病本身是“好适应证”，技术上也应保持审慎——机器人的精准，是对“可配准的计划”的精准，而非对“不可配准的现实”的精准。

Yes—current navigation and robotic guidance can reduce screw-placement deviation, particularly in spinal pedicle screw fixation. However, evidence for improved placement accuracy is stronger than evidence for fewer serious clinical complications. From an orthopaedic surgical perspective, these functions provide an additional safety layer, while requiring continued surgical verification. Preoperative trajectory planning, image registration, instrument tracking and robotic guide positioning help the surgeon reproduce the intended entry point and direction. In a multicentre randomized trial involving 70 patients, robotic assistance reduced mean guide-pin deviation from 2.55 mm to 0.86 mm and required fewer trajectory adjustments. However, adverse-event rates did not differ significantly. These measurements concern guide-pin accuracy and should not be interpreted as proof of equivalent reductions in nerve injury or final screw-placement errors. Randomized clinical trial Three qualifications matter clinically: The comparison matters. Benefits over conventional fluoroscopy-guided placement do not establish the same advantage over modern 3D navigation or an experienced surgeon using it. Errors can still occur. Inaccurate registration, reference-array movement, instrument deflection and drill slipping can cause deviation despite apparently correct guidance. Tissue pressure and steep trajectories are documented contributors to drill slipping. Cervical pedicle-screw study “Intelligent assistance” covers different technologies. Evidence supporting navigation and robotic trajectory guidance cannot automatically be extended to every AI planning tool, warning system or autonomous function. The practical judgment is that these systems can improve placement precision and support surgical safety when registration, tracking and instrument behavior are checked reliably.
