文献中记录的一个骨科案例具有代表性：在一例机器人辅助下颈椎手术中，因椎动脉出血，团队被迫改为徒手置钉以处理危机。这一转换的决定性因素是出血本身，但转换后能否迅速获得有效的血管控制，取决于术者对微创切口快速延长的规划，以及血管外科或介入团队的可及性。这意味着，骨科成熟的应急方案不能仅止于“脱机”，还必须包含针对特定术区（如颈椎、骨盆）的快速暴露路径和多学科激活机制（如呼叫血管外科、准备介入栓塞）的预设内容。目前这些内容在文献中多以个案经验的形式呈现，尚未被系统化为可推广的方案。 从医师视角的判断：准备是充分的，但“成熟”的标准尚未达到 如果以“是否存在一个经过骨科专科验证、包含明确决策标准与操作序列、并被学术共同体广泛接受的书面方案”作为“成熟”的标准，那么答案是否定的。骨科机器人术中血管/神经损伤的应急转换，目前更多是一种基于原则的准备状态，而非一个标准化的执行程序。 但这并不意味着临床实践是空白的。负责任的做法，是在开展机器人手术的术前阶段，就将以下要素作为团队能力的一部分进行确认，而非期待术中临时寻找方案： 术前规划中包含“转换预案”：对于毗邻大血管或高风险神经的术区（如颈椎、骨盆、翻修脊柱），术前即应明确：若发生特定类型的出血或神经信号丢失，计划的手术入路将如何被快速延长或改变。 团队角色与物品的“闭环节”：血管器械包、合适的牵开器、以及紧急呼叫血管外科/介入放射科的流程，应在切皮前即处于可即刻启用的状态，并由团队在术前简报（briefing）中确认。 将IONM警报纳入转换标准：骨科团队应与神经电生理监测团队预先约定，何种程度的信号变化构成需要暂停机器人操作、重新评估或直接转换的明确指征。 总结而言，骨科机器人急症中转的“方案成熟度”，其短板不在于“脱机”这一物理动作本身，而在于“脱机之后”的专科化衔接：如何以最快速度获得对深部血管的有效控制、如何将神经监测信号转化为清晰的行动阈值、以及如何将多学科资源前置性地整合进手术计划。在这些专科环节上，现有证据尚以原则性共识和个案经验为主，距离一个骨科专属的、可复制的成熟方案，仍有明确的距离需要跨越。

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the impact of robotic or navigation-assisted fixation on cumulative radiation exposure is highly procedure- and platform-specific, and the evidence contains an important paradox: intraoperative fluoroscopy time is consistently reduced, but this reduction does not always translate into a lower cumulative radiation dose to the patient once the additional imaging required by these technologies is counted. For the surgeon, the occupational benefit is more consistently favorable but is contingent on equipment choice, technique, and—critically—on compliance with protective measures that survey data show is often poor. 📊 The Effect on Patient Radiation Dose: Reduced Fluoroscopy Time, but Not Always Reduced Cumulative Dose The most robust finding across the literature is that robotic and navigation assistance reduces intraoperative fluoroscopy time and the number of fluoroscopic exposures. In a randomized controlled trial of robot-assisted pedicle screw fixation using biplane fluoroscopic positioning, the robotic group had significantly fewer cumulative exposures (4.56 ± 1.70 vs. 13.38 ± 19.01, P = 0.003) and a significantly lower total radiation dose (7.35 ± 3.33 μSv vs. 30.28 ± 97.41 μSv, P = 0.024). A meta-analysis of robotic guidance in orthopedic trauma found significantly shorter radiation time with robotic guidance, with a robust effect size. In direct anterior approach total hip arthroplasty, robotic assistance was associated with a 6.5-fold reduction in fluoroscopic radiation dose (0.4 mGy vs. 2.5 mGy) and a 4.0- to 5.0-fold shorter fluoroscopy time compared with manual technique. However, the cumulative picture is more nuanced, and the key distinction is between intraoperative fluoroscopy alone and total surgery-related radiation including preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging. A study in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis directly quantified this trade-off. Intraoperative fluoroscopy time was indeed lower with robotic navigation than with freehand technique (49.7 ± 13.8 seconds vs. 66.5 ± 25.6 seconds, p < 0.001). But when preoperative CT dose was included, freehand technique had a significantly lower mean total radiation dose (7.6 ± 4.5 mGy) than navigation (21.9 ± 3.3 mGy). The CT required for planning, or the intraoperative 3D scan required for registration, can dominate the total dose. A 2026 meta-analysis of 28 studies and 3,205 patients in spine surgery reinforced this uncertainty. Compared with freehand surgery, robotic assistance did not significantly reduce radiation dose (SMD −0.81; p = 0.07) or fluoroscopy time (SMD −0.56; p = 0.06), with substantial heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses revealed lower exposure with specific robotic systems (e.g., Tianji®) and in degenerative and trauma indications, while no differences were observed between robotic-assisted and navigation-assisted techniques. The practical implication is that the radiation benefit is platform-dependent and indication-dependent, not a universal property of "robotics." 🩺 The Effect on Surgeon Occupational Exposure: A Consistent Reduction in the Dominant Source For the surgeon, the primary source of occupational exposure is scatter radiation from intraoperative fluoroscopy, and reducing fluoroscopy time and exposures directly reduces this source. The randomized trial data and the THA data above therefore translate into a genuine occupational benefit. A Chinese review of spine robotics explicitly states that multiple studies show robotic-assisted spine surgery significantly reduces radiation exposure to the surgical team. The magnitude of the occupational benefit depends on the baseline exposure, which is not trivial. A UK survey found that orthopedic surgeons face annual effective doses ranging from 0.5 to 3.5 mSv, and poorly fitted lead aprons can increase exposure by up to 30%. The international occupational whole-body limit is 20 mSv per year averaged over five years (100 mSv cumulative) , with a lens-of-eye limit of 150 mSv per year and a skin/extremity limit of 500 mSv per year. A high-volume surgeon working at the upper end of the 0.5–3.5 mSv range is already a meaningful fraction of the annual limit, and reducing fluoroscopy time by half or more can materially lower that fraction. The occupational benefit is also site-specific. Lead aprons attenuate 90–95% of scatter radiation at orthopedic energies but do not protect the head, arms, or lower legs. The lens of the eye is a critical organ with a low threshold for deterministic effects (cataract), and the thyroid and hands are also exposed. A reduction in fluoroscopy time reduces exposure to all of these unprotected sites, which is why the occupational argument for robotic or navigation assistance is stronger than the patient-dose argument in procedures where the patient dose is dominated by a single planning CT. 🛡️ Protective Measures for High-Volume Surgeons The survey data on protective practices are sobering and indicate that the gap between recommended and actual protection is large. In a Saudi cross-sectional study, only 67.6% of orthopedic surgeons regularly used lead aprons; leaded eyeglasses and thyroid shields were used less frequently or rarely; and 80.4% did not use dosimeters. A UK survey found that only 2% of residents and 12% of consultants had custom-fitted lead aprons; 64% of consultants never used radiation protection glasses; and 36% of consultants never wore thyroid collars. Only 32% of consultants and 6% of residents had access to a dosimeter, and even fewer received feedback on their annual dose. Given this baseline, the protective measures a high-volume surgeon should insist on are: Primary personal protective equipment (PPE). A custom-fitted lead apron of at least 0.5 mm lead equivalence is the cornerstone; poorly fitted aprons increase exposure by up to 30%. Leaded eyeglasses are essential for lens protection, given the 150 mSv/year lens limit. A thyroid shield should be routine. Ceiling-suspended leaded shields and table-mounted drapes should be used to block scatter at the source. Dosimetry and feedback. A personal dosimeter worn under the lead apron at waist level is the primary monitor. Pregnant surgeons should wear a second badge inside the apron over the abdomen to monitor fetal exposure. A ring badge is advisable for the hands in procedures involving prolonged fluoroscopy. Crucially, dosimetry is only useful if the surgeon receives and reviews the dose feedback; the survey data show that access to feedback is a major gap. Technique and technology choices. Adherence to the ALARA principle (as low as reasonably achievable) remains fundamental: minimizing fluoroscopy time, using pulsed fluoroscopy and low-dose protocols, maximizing distance from the source, and using collimation to reduce the irradiated field. Platform selection matters: the meta-analysis subgroup finding of lower exposure with specific systems (e.g., Tianji®) suggests that choosing a system with favorable dosimetry should be part of the purchasing and protocol decision. 3D navigation coupled with low-dose cone-beam CT protocols has been shown to reduce radiation dose and is recommended in the navigation literature. 📋 Health Surveillance for High-Volume Surgeons The surveillance literature is less prescriptive than the protection literature, but several principles are defensible. Dosimetry-based monitoring is the foundation. The UK's IRR17 framework allows local risk assessment to determine whether dosimetry is necessary, with dosimeters potentially not mandated if estimated exposure remains below 1 mSv/year. For a high-volume surgeon performing fluoroscopically guided procedures regularly, estimated exposure is likely to exceed this threshold, and classified-worker status with mandatory dosimetry is appropriate. The HSE/IRR17 limits of 20 mSv/year averaged over five years, with no single year exceeding 50 mSv, provide the regulatory benchmark. Lens and thyroid surveillance deserve specific attention. The 150 mSv/year lens limit and the association of radiation with cataracts, thyroid cancer, and brain tumors in interventionists make periodic slit-lamp ophthalmologic examination and thyroid examination reasonable components of a health surveillance program for surgeons with cumulative occupational exposure. The European Society for Vascular Surgery 2023 guidelines affirm that skin injuries (erythema, dermatitis, hair loss) are common deterministic effects and markers of inadequate shielding, and should prompt review of protective practices. Monitoring should intensify when techniques or roles change. The literature advises ongoing monitoring, especially when new surgeons incorporate image-guided procedures or when novel techniques are introduced. A surgeon transitioning from freehand to robotic or navigation-assisted practice may actually experience a reduction in exposure, but the transition period—and any change in platform or protocol—warrants renewed dosimetry review. There is no national standardized approach to reconciling cumulative dose for surgeons rotating between institutions, and a single wearable dosimeter with cross-compatible recording has been proposed as a practical solution for surgeons who move between sites. For a high-volume surgeon practicing at multiple hospitals, this is a material logistical consideration. 💎 The Bottom Line Robotic and navigation assistance reliably reduce intraoperative fluoroscopy time and the number of exposures, and this translates into a consistent occupational benefit for the surgeon by reducing the dominant source of scatter radiation. For the patient, however, the cumulative dose benefit is not guaranteed: when the preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging required by these technologies is included, total patient dose may be higher than with freehand fluoroscopy, as the scoliosis study demonstrated (total dose 21.9 mGy with navigation vs. 7.6 mGy with freehand). The 2026 meta-analysis finding of no statistically significant overall reduction in radiation dose or fluoroscopy time across 3,205 patients, with benefit concentrated in specific platforms and indications, means the radiation advantage should be verified for the specific system and procedure in use, not assumed. For high-volume surgeons, the protective priorities are custom-fitted 0.5 mm lead aprons, leaded eyeglasses, thyroid shields, ceiling-suspended shields, and consistent personal dosimetry with feedback—all of which survey data show are underused. Health surveillance should be dosimetry-driven, with attention to the lens (150 mSv/year limit), thyroid, and skin, and should be renewed whenever techniques, platforms, or institutional roles change. The occupational radiation risk in orthopedic surgery is real but manageable; the principal threat is not the absence of protective technology, but the documented gap between available protection and its consistent use.

缺乏力反馈，在骨科机器人手术中不是一个抽象的“手感变差”问题，它在不同操作中会转化为性质不同的具体风险。按临床影响从直接到间接来梳理，截骨和置钉的核心问题是安全边界的确认被延迟或外化，软组织操作则面临触觉信息近乎完全缺失的困境。 截骨/磨削：骨性“底线”的感知被替换，而非被消除 在脊柱椎板切除或关节置换截骨中，术者传统上依靠阻力变化来判断磨钻或锯片是否接近内层皮质骨或软组织边界。机器人系统目前对这一信息的处理，呈现出一种技术路线决定风险形态的分化。 “截骨导板”路线的风险最为直接。机械臂仅将导板定位到规划位置，随后由术者手动操作摆锯在导板槽内切割。系统无法感知也无法阻止摆锯越过骨边界，对后交叉韧带、腘动脉等后方结构的保护，与传统手工手术处于同一水平，完全依赖术者本人的手感与判断。这意味着，这一技术路线在“精准定位”与“安全感知”之间并不对等：定位是机器人的，边界感知仍然是人的，而人的感知在导板限制下反而可能被削弱。 “一体化摆锯/触觉约束”路线看似提供了解决方案，但其本质需要辨析。Mako等系统的“触觉反馈”，是在锯片接近预设的虚拟安全边界时，机械臂施加反向阻力，必要时切断动力。这是一种基于空间位置的边界约束，而非基于组织阻力的力学感知。它有效的前提是：虚拟边界本身被正确设定，且真实解剖结构与术前规划之间没有超出配准精度的偏差。一旦发生注册误差或术中解剖移位，系统并不会因为“感觉到了异常阻力”而做出反应——它只是在忠实地执行一条可能已经偏离现实的几何约束。从这个意义上说，力反馈的缺失并没有被真正补偿，而是被转移到了规划与配准环节的可靠性上。 在椎板切除这一具体场景中，风险更为集中。磨钻穿透内层皮质骨后，下方的硬膜与脊髓几乎不提供任何有临床意义的阻力缓冲。机器人目前“难以判断骨磨削状态”，若不能在内层皮质骨被穿透前及时停止，损伤将是直接的。现有研究尝试用六轴力/扭矩传感器融合振动信号来识别骨磨削状态，识别率可从86.1%提升至96.86%，但这仍处于方法学研究阶段，尚未成为标准配置。 置钉：力信息的“延迟”本身构成风险 椎弓根螺钉置入中，术者传统上通过开路器或钻头阻力的变化来判断是否仍在松质骨通道内。这一触觉信号的价值在于实时性——阻力异常意味着即将或已经发生皮质突破，术者可以在毫米级的推进过程中即刻调整。 机器人系统的力反馈问题，核心不在于“完全没有信号”，而在于信号的时序特征与人手感知不匹配。有研究明确指出，机器人辅助置钉中“力反馈延迟”可导致钉道偏移风险。当系统采集到阻力变化并做出响应时，钻头可能已经推进了足以造成皮质穿破的距离。这种延迟在骨质疏松或解剖变异病例中被放大：骨密度降低使阻力信号本身变得模糊，而解剖变异则使“正常阻力”的基线难以预先设定。 更具临床意义的是，即便在具备力传感的系统中，术者也无法获得人手通过器械传递的那种连续、多维的力学信息。近期有研究描述了一种“周期性置入扭矩模式”，即在低速自动钻削时，导航界面和手持钻上可观察到节律性的阻力变化，被推测为骨-螺钉界面粘滑效应所致，或可作为触觉反馈减弱时的一种替代性视觉-触觉线索。但该现象的作者也明确表示，其临床相关性、可重复性及对置钉准确率的影响尚未被验证。这恰恰说明，当前临床对力反馈缺失的应对，在很大程度上仍停留在寻找替代性间接线索的阶段，而非恢复了可靠的直接力感知。 软组织剥离与通道建立：触觉缺失最难以补偿的领域 在需要经肌肉和软组织层建立工作通道的微创脊柱手术中，力反馈缺失的后果最为严重。微创入路本身已经牺牲了开放手术的直接触觉，机器人系统若再缺乏力感知，术者在器械穿过不同层次组织时，对“遇到了什么结构、施加了多大力量”的判断能力会进一步下降。已有文献明确指出，触觉感知的减弱会增加对神经或血管结构造成意外损伤的可能性。 这一风险在靠近椎管或椎间孔区域时尤为突出，因为该区域的组织阻力差异并不像骨与软组织之间那样鲜明——瘢痕、粘连、硬膜囊与神经根周围的阻力变化可能是细微且渐进的。有综述直言，脊髓神经周围的粘连松解、硬膜囊下减压、血管的精细处理等操作，高度依赖触觉反馈和精细手感，目前仍完全由医生手动完成，机器人尚无法胜任。换言之，在这些软组织操作中，力反馈的缺失并非一个可以通过“更好的视觉导航”来弥补的缺陷，它构成了机器人能力边界的一个刚性限制。 现有补偿策略的定位与未解决的问题 目前的补偿路径大致有三条，各自的局限需要被清晰认识： 其一，视觉替代。 依靠导航界面上的三维位置信息来推断力状态。但视觉信息是离散的、间接的，无法提供力信号那种连续的变化率信息。有文献指出，视觉线索只能部分补偿动力学感知的减少。 其二，力传感与算法预测。 在器械末端集成力/扭矩传感器，或通过算法对钻削力进行超前预测（如前述可提前约2秒预警、平均绝对误差0.14 N的方法），理论上可以缓解延迟问题。但这些方法目前多处于实验或早期临床验证阶段，且传感器集成会引入工具尺寸、消毒兼容性和成本等工程约束。 其三，主动触觉约束系统。 如前所述，一体化摆锯的虚拟边界约束在预设范围内是有效的，但其有效性完全依附于规划与配准的准确性，并不构成独立的力感知安全层。 有meta分析显示，具备触觉反馈的机器人系统在降低术中作用力、缩短任务时间和提高准确性方面显著更优，术者也更偏好这类系统。但这恰恰反证了当前广泛部署的许多系统，在这一维度上仍处于“有限触觉反馈”状态。 从医师视角的总结 缺乏力反馈的影响，不能笼统地表述为“风险增加”。更准确的判断是：它改变了风险的分布形态。在截骨中，它将边界判断的责任从术者的实时触觉转移到了规划与配准的静态可靠性上；在置钉中，它将一个本应是连续闭环的控制过程，变成了一个存在固有延迟的开环或半闭环过程；在软组织操作中，它则暴露了一个目前尚无满意补偿方案的能力真空。机器人系统在几何精度上的优势是真实的，但力反馈的缺失意味着，这种精度优势的安全兑现，在相当程度上仍然依赖于术者在系统之外所维持的独立判断与手动干预能力。

As a practicing orthopedic surgeon, my assessment is that robotic navigation offers a clear and consistent advantage over conventional fluoroscopy in safe-corridor placement accuracy and fluoroscopy time for percutaneous sacroiliac (SI) and pelvic ring screw fixation. The evidence on neurovascular complication rates is more difficult to quantify precisely because these events are rare, but the available data suggests robotic assistance is at least as safe, with a strong mechanistic rationale for reducing severe misplacement. 🎯 Safe-Corridor Placement Accuracy The evidence consistently shows that robotic assistance improves the proportion of screws placed entirely within the desired osseous corridor, which is the definition of safe-corridor accuracy. A 2026 retrospective comparative study directly compared robotic-assisted and freehand fluoroscopy-guided SI screw fixation. It reported a screw placement accuracy of 94% in the robotic group versus 62% in the conventional group, a difference that approached statistical significance (p=0.06) in this small cohort. A larger 2026 study on Tile type C pelvic ring injuries found a significantly higher excellent-and-good screw placement rate with robotic assistance: 97.96% versus 86.36% (p=0.042). Other studies reinforce this pattern. A 2022 study on S2 iliosacral screws reported a 100% excellent-and-good rate in the robot-assisted group compared to 85.7% for freehand (p<0.001). A 2023 study on sacral fragility fractures found significantly smaller deviations in both screw angle (1.96° vs. 2.87°) and guide-needle position (1.92 mm vs. 2.91 mm) with robotic guidance. A review of S2 screw fixation noted that screw penetration occurred only in the freehand groups and not in any robot-assisted cases. A 2024 study combining 3D printing with robotic assistance reported that 88.5% of screws did not penetrate bone in the robotic group, versus 63.3% in the control group. In summary, the absolute improvement in safe-corridor accuracy appears to be in the range of approximately 10 to 15 percentage points, with some smaller studies showing a larger but non-significant trend. This is a clinically meaningful difference in a procedure where a misplaced screw can violate the narrow safe corridor and injure adjacent neurovascular structures. ⏱️ Fluoroscopy Time The reduction in fluoroscopy time with robotic navigation is the most dramatic and statistically robust finding across the literature. Robotic systems allow for planning and execution based on preoperative or intraoperative 3D imaging, dramatically reducing the need for repeated, real-time 2D fluoroscopic shots to guide the screw. The magnitude of the reduction varies by study design and the specific metric measured (total time versus time per screw), but the direction is consistently and significantly in favor of robotics: A 2023 study reported intra-operative fluoroscopy time of 7.25 ± 1.72 seconds with robotics versus 20.93 ± 5.64 seconds with freehand (p=0.0000). A 2022 study on S2 screws found fluoroscopy time of 8.06 ± 3.54 seconds in the robotic group compared to 27.37 ± 8.82 seconds in the freehand group (p<0.001). A 2026 study on Tile C injuries reported significantly fewer fluoroscopy exposures: 8.2 ± 2.1 in the robotic group versus 18.6 ± 4.5 in the conventional group (p<0.001). The 2026 comparative study found a large absolute difference in total fluoroscopy time (55.1 s vs. 181.1 s), though it did not reach statistical significance due to the small sample size (p=0.053). This reduction has direct benefits for both patient and operating room staff safety, lowering cumulative radiation exposure. 🩺 Neurovascular Complication Rates Directly comparing neurovascular complication rates is challenging because these are rare events, and most individual studies are underpowered to detect a significant difference. The available evidence, however, does not show an increased risk with robotics and often shows a trend toward improved safety. The 2026 comparative study reported no major intraoperative complications in either group. The 2026 Tile C study found no severe complications in the robot-assisted group. A 2022 study on S2 screws noted no screw-related complications or revision surgery in any group. One Chinese-language source cited a complication rate of 5.00% in a robotic group, significantly lower than the control group, though the specific complications were not detailed in the abstract. The more compelling evidence for safety is indirect but mechanistically sound: the significant improvement in safe-corridor accuracy and the dramatic reduction in guide-wire adjustments (e.g., 1.3 vs. 4.2 adjustments in one study) directly reduce the number of times a sharp instrument is passed near critical structures. Fewer severe breaches and fewer needle passes logically translate to a lower risk of catastrophic neurovascular injury, even if the rare event rate itself cannot be precisely quantified in small comparative series. 💎 Bottom Line As a surgeon, I would tell a patient or colleague that for percutaneous SI and pelvic ring fixation, robotic navigation offers a meaningful and well-documented improvement in the precision of screw placement and a dramatic reduction in radiation exposure compared to conventional fluoroscopy. The technology allows you to execute a pre-planned, 3D trajectory with a level of consistency that freehand techniques struggle to match. The evidence on neurovascular complications is reassuring but less definitive due to their rarity; the safety benefit is best understood as a downstream consequence of improved accuracy and fewer needle passes, rather than a directly measured reduction in a common adverse event. The primary trade-off remains the capital and consumable cost of the technology, but from a clinical safety and precision standpoint, the data support robotic assistance as a superior alternative in this technically demanding procedure.

Cases should be selected according to the expected additional clinical benefit of robotics relative to its additional cost—not simply to maximise robot utilisation. High case volume can spread equipment costs, but it does not make an unnecessary operation or an unsuitable robotic procedure good value. The economic evidence remains uncertain. NICE’s early assessment found that robotic knee replacement may not be cost-effective, while some hip platforms may be cost-effective; these conclusions were highly sensitive to uncertain assumptions about patient benefit. NICE From a surgical service perspective, I would use the following selection framework. These are practical recommendations, not a validated economic scoring system. Selection question Implication for resource use Is the operation itself clearly indicated? Apply the same clinical threshold as for conventional surgery. Robot availability should not lower the threshold for replacement, fusion or fixation. What specific problem will robotic assistance solve? Give consideration to cases where accurate execution is particularly challenging—for example, distorted anatomy or difficult screw trajectories—provided the platform can safely address that problem. Complexity alone does not establish cost-effectiveness. Could a less expensive method achieve the same result? Compare robotics with experienced conventional surgery and, where appropriate, navigation or other available guidance. The relevant comparison is with the best realistic alternative. Can the team deliver the procedure efficiently and safely? Consider registration feasibility, imaging needs, staff experience, expected additional theatre time and the likelihood of conversion. Is the expected benefit supported by evidence? Avoid assuming that better alignment necessarily prevents revision or that more accurate fixation necessarily improves union. Those assumptions can make economic models look more favourable than the clinical evidence warrants. NICE recognises both the potential benefit in complex cases and the economic advantages of higher-volume centres, but also identifies substantial evidence gaps. There is not yet a reliable list of diagnoses for which robotic assistance is proven to provide the greatest economic return. NICE Routine cases and complex cases require different reasoning. In a mature, efficient service, routine arthroplasty may be reasonable if negotiated costs and measured outcomes support its use. During programme introduction, relatively straightforward cases can support supervised learning, but that training cost should be explicit. Conversely, the most complex cases should not automatically become the first robotic cases merely because their theoretical benefit is greatest. Costs should be measured across the whole episode of care. Include acquisition or lease costs, maintenance, software, training, consumables, imaging, implant prices and additional theatre time, alongside any demonstrated changes in hospital stay, rehabilitation, readmissions or reoperations. Platform-specific implant commitments also matter: an apparently inexpensive robot contract can still increase the total cost of treatment. NICE For perspective, one UK randomised-trial-based economic analysis found robotic knee replacement cost approximately £1,829 more per patient at one year, with a small, uncertain quality-of-life gain. Its favourable ten-year cost-effectiveness estimate depended on extrapolation, rather than ten years of observed benefit. That distinction should be explicit in purchasing and case-selection decisions. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov At the service level, efficient use means: Concentrating expertise and appropriate cases, through coordinated lists or referral networks, while protecting equitable access. Negotiating the complete procedure cost, including implants and consumables, rather than focusing on the equipment price. Accounting for opportunity cost: additional theatre time may displace other beneficial operations. Auditing comparable patients: track total costs, patient-reported outcomes, complications, revisions, conversions and theatre throughput, adjusting for case complexity. Reassessing use when benefits are not demonstrated. Once equipment has been purchased, the purchase itself is not a reason to use expensive disposables in every subsequent case. There is no universal annual case-volume threshold that guarantees value; it depends on local prices, staffing, utilisation and actual clinical benefit. Nor should age, BMI, insurance status or ability to pay substitute for an assessment of likely benefit. The defensible aim is to allocate robotic assistance where it offers a credible advantage, while preserving access to effective conventional care.

From the perspective of a practicing orthopedic surgeon, the boundary between indication and contraindication in robotic TKA and THA is not a static list of diagnoses. It is better understood as a question of whether conventional technique is likely to be precision-fragile for this specific patient, and whether the robotic workflow's prerequisites—reliable registration, stable tracker fixation, and predictable trajectory reach—can be met. Where both conditions are satisfied, the robot's value proposition is strongest. Where the second condition fails, the technology is not merely less useful; it may be inapplicable. Robotic TKA: Greatest Benefit and Relative Contraindications Patients Who Derive the Greatest Benefit The clearest beneficiaries are patients in whom conventional alignment guides and landmark-based resection are least reliable, and in whom the precision of bone resection and gap management is most consequential for the mechanical result. Severe coronal deformity (varus or valgus ≥10°). This is the most consistently supported indication. Severe angular deformity demands specific attention to bone resections and soft-tissue balancing, and conventional instrumentation has been associated with increased surgical time in this setting. Robotic-assisted TKA has been shown to correct severe coronal deformities consistently to within 3–4° of neutral, with postoperative alignment in severe valgus and severe varus groups comparable to or only marginally different from mild-deformity controls. A systematic review of complex primary and revision cases identified severe coronal deformity as a core complex indication and reported that robotic-assisted TKA consistently restored coronal alignment, with the greatest improvements observed in moderate-to-severe varus and valgus deformities. The mechanism is straightforward: a CT-based or imageless plan defines the deformity in three dimensions and constrains execution, bypassing the limitations of intramedullary or extramedullary guides in distorted anatomy. Fixed flexion contracture (≥10°). A retrospective comparative study of 190 robotic-assisted TKAs using functional alignment found that patients with preoperative flexion contracture ≥10° achieved comparable mid-term outcomes and early survivorship to those without contracture: all-cause revision rates were 97.67% versus 98.64% (p=0.66), and aseptic survivorship was 100% versus 99.32% (p=0.59). The contracture group required greater lateral tibial and posterior medial femoral resections, but this was managed within the functional alignment strategy without a requirement for additional soft-tissue releases. This is clinically meaningful because fixed flexion contracture has historically been a driver of additional distal femoral resection and joint-line elevation; the robotic plan-execute loop allows the surgeon to address the contracture through precise, graded bone resection while preserving the joint line. Revision and previously operated knees with retained hardware. The evidence here is technically supportive but lower in certainty. A 2026 scoping review of robotic-assisted TKA in post-traumatic and previously operated knees concluded that current literature supports technical feasibility and suggests potential workflow advantages in carefully selected cases, particularly when landmarks are distorted, because CT-based planning can define deformity, anticipate implant-hardware conflicts, guide bone resection, and quantify gap balance. However, the same review emphasized that the evidence consists mainly of case reports, small case series, and early retrospective cohorts, and remains limited and heterogeneous. A separate case report demonstrated robotic-assisted partial revision using a well-fixed retained femoral component as the registration reference, with favorable short-term outcomes. The practical implication is that retained hardware is not an absolute contraindication, but it changes the workflow: the hardware must be assessed for compatibility with registration and for whether it will obstruct planned resections or tracker placement. Relative Contraindications and Conditions Requiring Caution Severe stiffness with markedly limited range of motion. This is a relative contraindication in the sense that it does not prevent the robot from executing bone cuts, but it diminishes the marginal value of that execution while increasing the technical demand on the soft-tissue side. A case series of 25 stiff knees with preoperative range of motion <50° treated with an imageless robotic system reported significant improvement in range of motion (mean preoperative 38.7° to mean final follow-up 110.2°) and knee scores, with no neurovascular complications or manipulations under anesthesia. This suggests that robotics can be used in stiff knees, but the outcome is driven substantially by soft-tissue management and the surgeon's ability to achieve balance, not by the robot's geometric precision alone. The robot does not solve the biological problem of a contracted capsule; it provides more controlled bone resection within that constrained envelope. I would characterize severe stiffness as a condition of heightened technical demand and reduced marginal benefit, not a contraindication in principle. Ankylosis. The evidence here is thin and should be presented as such. A single case report describes robotic-arm-assisted TKA in a knee ankylosed for 10 years in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, with the authors noting that accurate bony registration was difficult because of the changed morphology, but concluding that with careful preparation the technique can be an effective option in complicated situations. This is a single case, not a series, and it does not establish ankylosis as a routine robotic indication. The more defensible position is that ankylosis is a relative contraindication or a highly selective indication, because the registration difficulty is a direct challenge to the robot's functional prerequisite, and the soft-tissue and biological considerations of ankylosis are not addressed by improved bone-cut precision. Some device labeling lists "severely limiting range of motion" as a contraindication, which reflects the manufacturer's risk framing rather than a universal clinical consensus. "Bad bone" as a functional contraindication. This is not a named disease, but it is a practical threshold that experienced robotic surgeons recognize. Poor bone quality—severe osteopenia, large lytic defects, or bone that cannot reliably hold a tracker pin—undermines the registration and fixation on which the entire robotic workflow depends. The concise formulation from a high-volume robotic arthroplasty practice is "BAD BONE = BAD IDEA FOR ROBOTICS." This is not a formal contraindication in the literature, but it is an honest description of the point at which the technology's prerequisites fail. Robotic THA: Greatest Benefit and Relative Contraindications Patients Who Derive the Greatest Benefit Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Crowe I–III. This is the strongest evidence-supported indication. A 2026 systematic review of 11 studies (1,150 hips) found that among Crowe I–III hips, robotic-arm-assisted THA achieved significantly lower errors in cup inclination and anteversion compared with both conventional and navigation THA, and greater accuracy in restoring the center of rotation. For all Crowe subtypes, robotic assistance increased the proportion of cups within the 5° safety zone. The clinical logic is that dysplastic acetabular anatomy distorts the landmarks on which conventional freehand or imageless navigation depends, and a CT-based plan with robotic execution provides a more reproducible reference. The important caveat is Crowe IV. The same systematic review found no difference in center-of-rotation restoration for Crowe IV hips, and concluded that the accuracy of Crowe IV remains unclear, with limited evidence available. A separate comparison of robotic versus conventional THA in Crowe 3–4 reported a higher proportion of cups within the Lewinnek safe zone in the robotic group (90% vs 77%), but this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.302). The defensible position is that the benefit is best established for Crowe I–III and plausible but unproven for Crowe IV; severe dysplasia with major bone stock deficiency and distorted anatomy may still be a setting where the robot is useful, but the evidence base is not strong enough to call it a proven advantage. Arthrodesed or fused hips (including ankylosing spondylitis). This is a more surprising but increasingly supported indication. A 2025 retrospective cohort of 120 patients with ankylosing spondylitis (60 robotic, 60 manual) found that robotic-assisted THA achieved a significantly lower dislocation rate (1.7% vs 5.0%), a higher proportion of cups within the safety zone (93.3% vs 55.0%), a lower overall complication rate (3.3% vs 8.3%), and a higher one-year Harris Hip Score (77.9 vs 70.4). The operative time was not significantly different, and fluoroscopy use was lower in the robotic group. The mechanism is that in a fused hip, the native acetabular anatomy and the plane of the pelvis are difficult to define by landmarks alone; a preoperative plan and intraoperative registration provide a spatial reference that manual technique lacks. I would frame this not as "the robot solves ankylosis," but as the robot provides a spatial navigation solution in a setting where conventional landmark-based orientation is unreliable. Relative and Absolute Contraindications Active infection remains an absolute contraindication to any arthroplasty, robotic or conventional. Device labeling for robotic TKA similarly lists active local infection as a contraindication, and this principle is not altered by the technology. Severe anatomical distortion that prevents registration or planning. This is the closest thing to a functional absolute contraindication specific to robotic THA. If the acetabular or femoral anatomy is so distorted—by fracture, prior surgery, bone loss, or hardware artifact—that the navigation software cannot segment the bone, acquire usable registration points, or generate a plan, the robotic workflow cannot proceed. A case series of robotic-arm-assisted THA reported loosening of the iliac assembly that made registration impossible and required conversion to conventional THA, and separate cases of acetabular registration error leading to cup malposition. In revision acetabular reconstruction, the overall registration success rate has been reported at 98.5%, but this reflects a selected, experienced workflow; when registration fails, conversion to manual technique is the necessary fallback. This is distinct from DDH, where the anatomy is distorted but plannable; the contraindication is anatomy that is unplannable or unregistrable. Retained pelvic hardware as a relative contraindication. Hardware can obscure registration surfaces, generate artifact on CT, or obstruct tracker pin placement. Robotic-arm assistance has been used in complex primary THA with retained hardware, but the same series describes these as "challenging cases" in which distorted anatomy, bone loss, and previous implants complicate positioning. Hardware is therefore not an absolute contraindication, but it converts the case into one requiring a hardware-specific registration and pin-placement strategy, and it increases the probability that the robot's prerequisites may not be satisfiable. A Practical Framework, With Its Evidence Stated Dimension Greatest benefit Relative contraindication / high caution Robotic TKA Severe coronal deformity (≥10°); fixed flexion contracture (≥10°); revision/previous surgery with retained hardware in selected cases Severe stiffness (outcome driven by soft tissues); ankylosis (registration difficulty, single-case evidence only); poor bone stock that cannot support registration ("bad bone") Robotic THA DDH Crowe I–III; arthrodesed/fused hips including AS Active infection (absolute); anatomy so distorted that registration/planning is impossible (functional absolute); retained pelvic hardware requiring individualized registration strategy I would be explicit with a colleague or patient about the level of evidence behind each row. The severe coronal deformity and flexion contracture indications for TKA are supported by comparative series with mid-term follow-up. The Crowe I–III advantage in THA is supported by a systematic review, while the Crowe IV claim is not. The fused-hip indication is supported by a single retrospective cohort with one-year follow-up. The ankylosis indication for TKA rests on a case report, and should be presented as such. The "bad bone" and "unregistrable anatomy" limitations are not formal evidence-graded contraindications; they are practical descriptions of the point at which the robot's prerequisites fail, and they are arguably more important for safe case selection than some of the named diagnoses. My bottom line as a surgeon is this: the robot is most valuable where conventional precision is most fragile and the anatomy is still plannable. It is least valuable—or inapplicable—where the soft-tissue or biological problem dominates the outcome, or where registration and tracking cannot be reliably achieved. The named conditions in your question fall along that continuum, not into a binary list of indications and contraindications.

As a practicing orthopedic surgeon, I would frame the answer around a distinction that is often blurred in practice: formal credentialing requirements are relatively well-defined in some jurisdictions, but the evidence-based case thresholds for true proficiency are more variable and subspecialty-specific. The requirements operate at three levels—regulatory gatekeeping, institutional privileging, and the individual learning curve—and a surgeon needs to satisfy all three, though the specific numbers differ by country, platform, and procedure. The regulatory gate: China's restricted-technology framework In China, robotic surgery—including orthopedic robotic surgery—is classified as a national restricted medical technology under the 2022 National Health Commission catalog. This is not a voluntary designation; it imposes mandatory training and credentialing requirements. Physicians must complete systematic training at a provincial-level or higher training base and pass an assessment before performing robotic procedures independently. At least one source describes the requirement as a minimum of 6 months of systematic training at a NHC-recognized base. The practical entry criteria for these training programs are instructive. A representative orthopedic robotic training program lists: a valid physician license in surgery, attending physician rank or above, and for some programs, at least 5 years as an attending or associate chief physician rank plus 10 years of orthopedic clinical work at a tertiary A hospital. The training content is structured: no less than 20 hours of theoretical study, no less than 10 animal or model training cases, and participation in no less than 10 supervised clinical robotic cases before assessment. There is also a national technical standard, T/ZGCIT 060-2025, that specifies institutional and personnel requirements for orthopedic robotic clinical application, though the detailed personnel provisions require access to the full standard text rather than the public summary. This framework means that in China, the question is not merely “has the surgeon done enough cases,” but “has the surgeon completed a state-recognized training pathway and been credentialed by a recognized base.” That is a more structured gate than exists in many other jurisdictions. Institutional privileging: the Mazor model as a concrete template In the United States and other systems without a single national robotic-surgery credential, hospital privileging criteria fill the gap. The Mazor robotic spine privileging criteria provide an unusually transparent example of how institutions operationalize this. The baseline requirement is not robotic experience per se; it is privileges for the equivalent conventional procedure—open, minimally invasive, or percutaneous. A surgeon must be board-certified or board-eligible in the relevant specialty and must already be competent in the non-robotic version of the operation. Robotic privileges are then specifically delineated and are not automatically included in the privileges for the underlying procedure. For a surgeon new to the platform, the training pathway includes online modules, an industry-certified program, a bioskills lab certificate, and at least one of live case observation, a surgeon-led course, or a proctor for the initial two cases. Surgeons with ≥20 verified cases as primary surgeon follow a different pathway, but even they must complete the platform-specific training requirements. After initial privileging, a Focused Professional Practice Evaluation (FPPE) requires four cases with chart review within one year before full privileges are confirmed. Ongoing evaluation includes conversion from robotic to open as a monitored quality signal. This is a useful model because it separates platform-specific training from underlying surgical competence, and it builds in a probationary period rather than granting privileges on the basis of a course certificate alone. The learning curve: numbers that matter, and their limits The learning curve literature is more consistent for joint replacement than for spine, and more consistent for operative time than for accuracy or clinical outcomes. For robotic TKA, multiple 2025 studies converge on a short initial learning phase. A VELYS robot study across five surgeons found the learning curve reached after 4 to 11 cases, with the number varying by surgeon volume; the robotic operating time was 57.1 minutes versus 54.1 minutes for navigation, and the increase was statistically significant for only one low-volume surgeon. A MAKO study using CUSUM analysis defined three phases: initial learning (cases 1–11), competence (cases 12–51), and optimized performance (cases 52–90). Total surgical time stabilized around 65 minutes after 50 cases, but the robotic workflow component continued to improve without clear stabilization until the end of the series. The practical implication is that 11 cases may be enough to become safe and functional, but the refinement of workflow and efficiency takes considerably longer, and the component of the operation that continues to improve is not the bone cut but the patient-specific robotic workflow. For robotic spine surgery, the curve is shaped differently. A Chinese CARN training study found that novice surgeons reached proficiency after 70 screws in the robotic group versus 92 screws in the traditional training group, with competency at 121 versus 138 screws and higher pedicle screw accuracy (88.2% vs. 79.6%). A South Korean resident training study using phantom models and supervised live cases achieved a 96.99% clinically acceptable placement rate over 28 cases and 166 screws. However, early robotic spine cases are consistently characterized by longer setup and registration times—30 to 40 additional minutes in the first 10 to 15 cases—and the learning curve involves not just the surgeon but the assistant, radiology technician, scrub nurse, and OR team. A survey of spine surgeons identified concerns about complexity and the learning curve (46.5%) and fear of skill degradation through over-reliance on technology (26.8%) as barriers to adoption. These are not irrational concerns; they point to the fact that the learning curve is not solely about technical facility with the robot, but about maintaining the judgment to recognize when the robot is not helping and to convert or abandon it. What “competence” should mean: beyond operating the device The 2026 Asia-Pacific expert consensus on robotic hip and knee arthroplasty makes a point that I think is clinically essential: robotic competence is not the ability to operate the device. It includes normal workflow operation, recognition of anomalies, fault management, and the ability to safely convert to conventional surgery when registration fails, a tracker loosens, the system is interrupted, or screen information is inconsistent with actual anatomy. The consensus explicitly states that conventional arthroplasty skill is the safety net in these situations, and that experience on one robotic platform does not fully substitute for platform-specific training on another, because registration methods, imaging dependence, arm control, and failure modes differ. For China, the consensus recommends a phased, competency-oriented pathway that incorporates theory, simulation, supervised patient cases, anomaly management, and team coordination into the assessment, with ongoing monitoring of learning-curve-related complications and conversion events. This is more ambitious than a simple case-count requirement, and it aligns with the broader finding that simulation—particularly VR and high-fidelity models—can shorten the learning curve but requires standardized integration and certification pathways that do not yet uniformly exist. The honest limitations The requirements are not uniform across platforms, procedures, or countries. China has a national restricted-technology gate and structured training bases; the U.S. relies on hospital privileging and specialty society guidance, which produces more variability. The case numbers for “proficiency” in the literature are derived largely from operative time and radiographic accuracy, not from long-term clinical outcomes or complication avoidance. A surgeon may reach a time-based learning plateau at 11 TKA cases, but the ability to manage a registration failure or a vascular complication under robotic conditions is not established by that number. And the evidence on whether simulation-based credentialing actually reduces patient harm, as opposed to improving simulator performance, remains limited. My practical bottom line is this: the regulatory and institutional boxes can be checked—training hours, supervised cases, proctored initial cases, FPPE—and in China the restricted-technology framework makes those boxes relatively explicit. But the substantive requirement is broader than any case count: it is conventional surgical competence in the same procedure, platform-specific training that acknowledges the differences between systems, a probationary period with oversight, and a demonstrated ability to recognize system failure and convert safely. The learning curve for efficiency may be 4–11 cases in TKA or roughly 70 screws in spine; the learning curve for safe independent judgment under robotic conditions is longer, less well quantified, and should not be assumed to have plateaued simply because operative time has stabilized.

**可以降低部分置钉偏差和操作风险，但目前不能认为它能全面防止误操作，或保证严重并发症更少。**从骨科临床角度，应把机器人视为增加安全保障的辅助工具，最终判断仍由术者完成。 首先，“智能辅助”不一定意味着人工智能自主决策。当前常用功能主要包括三维规划、导航追踪、机械臂导向，以及部分系统具备的运动边界、偏差报警或力感知；各机型能力不同。 1．对置钉准确性的改善，已有临床证据。 一项胸腰椎随机对照试验中，机器人组螺钉完全位于椎弓根内的比例为95.3%，传统透视组为86.1%。这支持特定系统能够减少骨性通道偏差，但该指标按“螺钉”统计，并不等于患者神经损伤风险按同样幅度下降。随机对照试验 结果也并非所有研究一致：另一项随机试验未发现两组椎弓根内置钉准确性存在显著差异。因此，不能将一种系统的优势推广至所有机器人、所有术者和所有部位。另一项随机试验 2．不同辅助功能，防范的是不同类型的错误。 功能 主要价值 关键边界 三维规划 提前评估入点、方向、长度和骨性通道 规划本身仍可能不合理，必须由医生审核 导航追踪与机械臂导向 帮助维持规划方向，提高操作一致性 配准失准、骨段移动或器械偏转仍可能造成误差 虚拟边界与运动约束 在支持该功能的系统中，限制部分越界动作 边界依赖影像和配准准确，不能保护所有软组织 偏差、碰撞或力感知报警 提示部分异常状态，促使医生暂停核查 并非所有设备具备，也不能识别所有危险 3．“减少置钉偏差”不能直接等同于“减少所有严重并发症”。 血管、神经损伤属于相对少见事件，需要足够大的样本才能可靠判断差异。此外，感染、血肿、麻醉事件及部分减压损伤，也不是置钉导航能够直接防范的。因此，目前更有把握的结论是部分系统提高了置钉准确性；对严重并发症及整体安全性的改善，仍需按设备和术式分别评价。 机器人还可能引入新的风险，例如错误规划被准确执行、追踪器移动后仍沿用原导航，以及术者过度相信屏幕而忽略异常手感。安全使用需要坚持：术前审核规划、术中独立核验精度，出现影像与实际接触不一致时立即暂停，必要时转为常规操作。 所以，机器人能够成为有效的安全辅助，但其作用取决于可靠定位、合适病例和受训团队，不能替代解剖判断、常规核查与应急能力。

**机器人或导航通常更有利于降低术者的职业辐射暴露，但患者的总剂量不一定同步下降。**关键不在是否使用机器人，而在影像流程：是否需要术前CT、术中三维扫描，是否减少了反复透视，以及曝光时工作人员能否撤离或有效屏蔽。 1．患者与术者的剂量，应分别评价。 对象 相比传统反复透视的常见变化 需要注意 术者及手术团队 导航建立后可减少近距离透视操作；三维扫描时人员可撤离或进入屏蔽区域，职业剂量往往下降 若仍在患者旁曝光、屏蔽不足，或手术量大幅增加，年度累积剂量仍可能较高 患者 减少反复调整导针及透视，可能降低剂量 额外CT、三维扫描、重复配准扫描可能抵消收益，部分流程总剂量可能增加 一项小样本随机研究发现，传统非导航腰椎置钉中，术者部分测量位置的累积剂量最高约为导航组的10倍；这说明导航可能明显降低职业照射，但不能将这一比例推广至所有系统和术式。随机对照研究 **透视次数、透视秒数和实际剂量不是同一指标。**患者评价应尽可能记录透视剂量面积乘积、参考点累积空气比释动能，以及CT相关剂量指标，并由医学物理人员按需评估；不同指标不能直接相加。术者则应依靠个人剂量计，不能用患者剂量或手术例数代替。 2．高手术量术者应采取哪些防护？ **先优化曝光流程：**在满足操作安全的前提下，使用低剂量、脉冲透视、合理限束及末帧保存，减少重复曝光；三维扫描时，非必要人员撤离或进入有效屏蔽区。 **重视距离与屏蔽：**使用合适的移动屏风、床旁防护设施，正确穿戴防护衣、甲状腺护领和有侧方防护的铅眼镜；定期检查防护用品完整性。 **手不要进入主射线束：**不能依靠防护手套“允许”手留在束内；手套进入自动曝光控制区域，反而可能触发设备增加输出。IAEA防护建议 **按实际工作量监测：**高负荷近台术者宜由放射防护人员评估双剂量计方案——防护衣内躯干部一个、衣外领口一个；必要时增加眼晶状体或手部剂量计。衣内低读数不能代表眼睛和双手同样低剂量。ICRP职业防护建议 多院执业者还应汇总各机构的职业照射记录，避免每家医院分别看都不高，全年合计却被低估。 3．健康随访应如何安排？ 以中国大陆管理要求为背景，纳入放射工作人员管理者应接受个人剂量监测及上岗前、在岗和离岗职业健康检查。规定的在岗检查间隔不应超过2年；发生事故照射或疑似过量照射时，应及时开展剂量调查、医学评估及必要随访。《放射工作人员职业健康管理办法》 高手术量术者尤其应关注眼晶状体检查，并按职业健康机构要求完成血液、皮肤等相关评估。检查频率应结合个人剂量趋势、岗位及异常情况决定；目前没有依据仅凭“每年做多少台”就统一增加CT、肿瘤标志物等筛查。 实际管理的重点是：**逐期审查个人剂量，发现异常即查原因、改流程，而不是等体检异常后再处理。**机器人可以帮助减少曝光，但不能替代持续的剂量监测和防护。

The ability to convert to manual surgery is established, but I would not describe emergency conversion protocols as uniformly mature or equally validated across all orthopaedic robots and hospitals. The key distinction is between a device that permits conversion and a team that can perform it safely during haemorrhage or suspected neurological injury. BOA guidance emphasises robust local protocols, while NICE requires platform-specific safety training for the entire surgical team. boa.ac.uk From the clinical perspective used in these answers—not personal operative experience—I would assess readiness in three parts: Aspect Assessment Technical ability to stop robotic assistance and use conventional instruments Established in commonly used arthroplasty and spinal workflows. However, release, disengagement and instrument-removal procedures are platform-specific. Clinical management of vascular or neurological injury Established emergency principles and specialty pathways exist, regardless of whether the initial operation was robotic. Evidence that every team can convert rapidly and reliably during a catastrophe Insufficient to make a blanket assurance. Routine conversion for registration failure is not equivalent to emergency rescue during uncontrolled bleeding. Published spinal series document conversion to manual instrumentation, but these largely demonstrate technical fallback rather than validate emergency vascular or nerve-injury protocols. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Conversion is often simpler in orthopaedics than the phrase “emergency undocking” suggests. In robot-assisted hip or knee replacement, the surgeon is already at the operative field through an open exposure. Conversion generally means discontinuing robotic assistance, safely clearing the equipment and continuing with conventional instruments. In percutaneous spinal or pelvic surgery, obtaining adequate exposure for emergency treatment may be more demanding. Console-based abdominal robotic undocking procedures should therefore not be assumed to apply directly to orthopaedic systems. NICE For the emergencies you mention, the priorities differ: Vascular injury: haemorrhage control, resuscitation and appropriate specialist help must proceed immediately alongside any necessary conversion. An instrument or implant that may be tamponading bleeding should not be withdrawn reflexively. Equipment removal must preserve haemorrhage control and access to the patient. General robotic emergency checklists explicitly assign someone to maintain tamponade during conversion. aorn.org Suspected nerve or spinal-cord injury: stop the potentially injurious manoeuvre and assess the cause. For a spinal neuromonitoring alert, this includes surgical, anaesthetic and monitoring-system factors; an alert does not automatically prove direct injury. Implant revision, decompression or wider exposure may be needed according to the findings. AO Spine–PRAXIS guidance provides a structured response, although the evidence supporting the protocol recommendation is rated very low quality. PMC A credible local protocol should demonstrate readiness, not merely exist on paper. I would expect: A platform-specific emergency checklist with clearly assigned roles. Conventional instruments and appropriate emergency equipment immediately accessible. A surgeon competent in the conventional procedure and an established route to vascular or other specialist assistance. Rehearsed scenarios involving bleeding, neurological deterioration, power failure and an instrument that cannot be released normally. Review of actual events and simulations, measuring time to patient access and effective treatment—not just time to move the robot. These are practical readiness criteria consistent with surgical guidance and emergency checklists; they are not a universally validated orthopaedic accreditation standard. aorn.org I cannot support a universal claim that conversion is always achievable within a specified number of seconds or without added risk. The defensible position is that emergency conversion is feasible and should be planned for every case, but its reliability depends on the exact platform, surgical exposure, team rehearsal and rescue resources.

与传统透视相比，机器人或导航辅助固定对辐射暴露的改变并非一个简单的“全面降低”，而是一个高度依赖于技术路线和评价对象的分化图景：对于术者，辐射暴露的降低是显著且一致的；对于患者，则取决于导航所依赖的影像采集方式——基于术前CT或术中3D扫描的机器人系统，可能在降低术中透视的同时，增加患者的总累积剂量。 👨‍⚕️ 对术者：辐射暴露的显著且一致的降低 这是机器人/导航技术最稳健的获益之一。多项研究一致显示，术者的职业辐射暴露获得了实质性削减。 一项系统综述与meta分析提供了具体的量化对比。在胸腰椎融合术中，每枚螺钉对应的术者辐射剂量为：传统透视6.0×10⁻³ mSv，机器人辅助2.0×10⁻³ mSv，而术中CT导航则接近于0 mSv（因术者在扫描时离开手术室）。这意味着，机器人辅助可将术者剂量降至传统透视的约三分之一，而术中CT导航则几乎消除了术者的直接暴露。 具体研究的数据与此方向一致。在一项机器人辅助微创腰椎融合的研究中，术者的辐射暴露从传统开放透视组的70.5 μSv降至机器人组的21.7 μSv。另一项比较导航与透视在多节段微创置钉中应用的研究则显示，导航组术者每枚螺钉的辐射剂量仅为透视组的19.9%。在单髁置换等领域，导航技术同样被证实可显著降低术者剂量。 这种降低的机制在于术者与辐射源的空间关系被改变。在导航或机器人系统中，获取影像数据（如术中3D扫描）时，术者可以离开手术室或退至防护屏后；而在传统透视下，术者需在射线场内手动操作或实时监视。有研究明确指出，术者在3D图像采集期间离开房间，是其辐射暴露大幅降低的关键原因。此外，导航引导下无需反复透视来确认器械位置，也从源头减少了辐射产生的时间。 🧑‍🦽 对患者：取决于影像策略，而非单纯的“降低” 对患者而言，情况更为复杂。机器人或导航系统减少的是“术中实时透视时间”，但它可能以增加“术前或术中一次性影像采集的剂量” 为代价。因此，患者的净辐射暴露取决于这两者之间的权衡。 在单纯透视时间层面，机器人辅助确实带来了显著缩短。 一项纳入8项RCT的meta分析显示，机器人引导脊柱融合术的透视时间较传统透视组减少了39.6%（平均差 -25.65秒）。骨科创伤领域的meta分析同样证实，机器人引导下辐射时间显著缩短。在骨盆等部位，机器人辅助可将透视时间压缩至传统方法的很小一部分。 但在总有效剂量层面，画面则发生分化。 关键在于患者是否接受了额外的CT扫描。 如果机器人/导航系统依赖术前CT进行规划，那么患者的总辐射剂量将是术前CT剂量与术中透视剂量的叠加。一项针对青少年特发性脊柱侧凸的研究明确指出，机器人辅助导航虽然减少了术中透视时间，但增加了患者的总辐射暴露，因为累积剂量中包含了术前CT的贡献（术中透视剂量分别为0.5 mSv vs. 0.4 mSv，但总累积剂量达到12.5 mSv vs. 0.5 mSv）。 如果系统采用术中3D影像（如O臂）进行注册和导航，则患者在一次性的扫描中接受较高剂量，但换来了后续置钉过程中透视次数的大幅减少。一项导航系统的研究显示，其中位有效剂量为0.81 mSv，低于文献报道的常规透视（8.37–15.1 Gy·cm²）和其他导航方式（9.12–9.83 Gy·cm²）的剂量水平。 如果系统能够实现“无辐射”或极低辐射工作流（如基于3D打印导板或术前规划的机器人路径），则患者的总辐射暴露可以获得最大程度的降低。 因此，对于患者辐射，一个诚实的判断是：机器人技术本身并不必然降低总剂量，它改变的是剂量的“时间分布”和“来源构成”。一项系统综述的结论精确地概括了这一现实：术中CT导航对术者的辐射最低，但代价是相对于传统透视增加了患者的辐射暴露；而机器人辅助的患者每枚螺钉辐射剂量（0.04 mSv）低于传统透视（0.26 mSv），但其透视时间（20.07秒/枚）却长于传统透视（11.1秒/枚），提示其剂量优势可能来源于扫描参数或工作流的差异，而非单纯的时间缩短。 🛡️ 对高手术量术者的防护与健康随访建议 鉴于脊柱/骨科手术术者的辐射暴露显著高于其他非脊柱骨科操作（有研究提示可达12倍），且暴露具有累积性，高手术量术者需要一套系统性的防护与监测策略。 防护措施应遵循“距离、屏蔽、时间”的核心原则，并针对导航/机器人工作流的特点进行调整。 最大化距离：这是最有效的防护手段。在导航或机器人系统进行3D影像采集时，术者应离开手术室或退至足够远的屏蔽后方。在传统透视下无法做到这一点的操作，在导航工作流中应被制度化地执行。 屏蔽的规范化与完整性：铅围裙是基础，但不应被视为充分的防护。系统综述呼吁更普遍地使用铅围裙、铅眼镜、甲状腺 shield 以及移动屏蔽。一项量化模型研究通过测量铅围裙内外的剂量（分别为176 mrem和8 mrem），证实了有效屏蔽的必要性和有效性。在高手术量中心，应确保屏蔽装备的铅当量（如0.5 mm Pb）符合标准，并定期进行完整性检查（如透视下检查有无裂纹）。 剂量监测的精细化：不应仅依赖单一的全身剂量计。理想的监测应区分铅围裙内（代表有效防护后的身体核心剂量）和铅围裙外（代表未防护部位的浅表剂量），并考虑对晶状体（使用眼剂量计）和优势手（戒指剂量计） 进行监测，因为这些部位在高手术量术者中可能承受不成比例的累积剂量。 健康随访应聚焦于辐射敏感器官，并以累积剂量而非单次手术作为风险分层依据。 职业辐射的随机性效应（癌症风险）是长期随访的核心关切。一项基于当代防护实践的量化模型研究，在测量了一位脊柱神经外科医生65台连续手术的剂量后，使用BEIR VII风险模型估算，其终生归因癌症风险（LAR）约为0.00042%，大致相当于每24万名接受类似暴露的脊柱外科医生中，出现1例超额癌症。这一绝对风险在群体层面看似微小，但它是在“当代防护实践” 下估算的，意味着防护的依从性和质量是决定个体风险的关键变量。 流行病学证据提示，脊柱术者的辐射相关风险具有器官特异性，研究已将其与甲状腺癌、性腺肿瘤及实体器官癌症的风险升高联系起来。此外，长期累积暴露与辐射诱导的皮肤损伤相关，特别是对于从业超过21年且累积透视时间超过6696分钟的术者，风险更为突出。因此，健康随访不应是泛化的年度体检，而应包含对甲状腺、皮肤（尤其是手部）以及根据性别和年龄相应的性腺/生殖系统的针对性关注。随访的频率和深度，应基于个人累积有效剂量（来自规范化剂量监测的汇总数据）而非单纯的工作年限来个体化制定。 从医师视角的总结： 机器人/导航技术为术者提供了一层真实的、可量化的辐射防护增益，其核心机制在于将术者从实时透视的射线场中“移出”。对于患者，其净获益取决于机构所采用的影像协议是“以CT换透视”还是“以规划消透视”。对于高手术量术者，将辐射安全视为一项需要主动管理的职业健康议题——通过制度化地利用导航工作流中的距离优势、确保屏蔽的完整性、并基于累积剂量数据进行器官针对性的健康监测——是使这项技术的防护优势得以在漫长职业生涯中真正兑现的必要条件。

Conversion to conventional surgery is an established capability, but emergency protocols are not uniformly standardised or sufficiently validated to assume that every robotic orthopaedic team is equally prepared. From a clinical perspective, readiness must be demonstrated for the particular robot, procedure, and operating team. It is important to distinguish three situations: Situation Assessment of preparedness Technical failure without patient injury Conventional fallback is established. Orthopaedic reports describe conversion instruments and continuation with nonrobotic techniques when registration or equipment fails. This demonstrates feasibility, not readiness for catastrophic bleeding. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Major vascular injury Immediate haemorrhage control, resuscitation, and access for definitive repair take priority. Safe robot disengagement is platform-specific; evidence validating emergency conversion during vascular injury in orthopaedic surgery remains limited. Suspected nerve or spinal cord injury The response must address the injury mechanism—not merely switch off robotic guidance. Spine-specific neurological emergency pathways exist, but they are not dedicated robotic-conversion protocols. PMC Orthopaedic conversion also differs from abdominal robotic “undocking.” In robotic joint replacement, the surgeon is generally already at an open operative field; conversion usually means safely withdrawing the robotic instrument and continuing with conventional instrumentation. In percutaneous spinal surgery, gaining sufficient exposure to investigate or treat an injury may require additional steps. Consequently, a single universal disengagement sequence would be inappropriate. For a service to be adequately prepared, I would expect: A rehearsed, device-specific release procedure. Stopping powered motion and safely releasing an instrument are separate actions. An emergency-stop button should not be assumed to free the arm or instrument. Clearly assigned roles. The surgeon directs injury management; anaesthesia manages physiological instability; designated staff handle robot disengagement, equipment, and escalation. Immediate access to conventional instruments and appropriate specialist support. The surgeon must retain competence in the conventional procedure. Simulation that includes actual complications. Drills should test haemorrhage, suspected neurological injury, power failure, and restricted patient access—not only routine technical conversion. Assessment of meaningful response times. Time to haemorrhage control, unobstructed access, or corrective intervention matters more than robot-removal time alone. These are practical readiness criteria, rather than a universally validated orthopaedic checklist. A recent international emergency-undocking consensus supports structured communication and platform-specific procedures, but it does not establish clinical effectiveness across orthopaedic robots. Springer Nature Link For vascular injury, removing equipment must not inadvertently remove temporary bleeding control or worsen tissue damage. A published nonorthopaedic vascular-injury case documented additional injury during incorrect instrument release; it illustrates the importance of device-specific training, but its mechanism should not be generalised to orthopaedic platforms. PMC For neurological deterioration, the team should stop the potentially injurious manoeuvre and activate the relevant neurological emergency pathway, assessing surgical, anaesthetic, and monitoring causes together. AO Spine–PRAXIS guidance recommends neuromonitoring for high-risk spinal cases and supports pre-agreed multidisciplinary protocols; the evidence supporting protocol implementation is graded very low. PMC My assessment is therefore conditional: an experienced, rehearsed team can be well prepared, but robot availability or routine conversion experience alone does not prove emergency readiness. I cannot give a reliable universal conversion time or success rate for vascular or nerve injury specifically during robotic orthopaedic surgery.

From a practicing surgeon's perspective, the answer to whether robotic orthopedic surgery outperforms traditional procedures in long-term complications, implant loosening, and fracture healing is procedure-specific and not uniform. The evidence is strongest—and most favorable to robotics—in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) and in selected high-risk spine and trauma scenarios, but it is notably neutral or conflicting for total knee arthroplasty (TKA) , which is the highest-volume robotic application. I will separate the evidence by procedure and outcome, and flag where the data do not support superiority. 🦵 Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty (UKA): the strongest signal for reduced loosening and complications UKA provides the most consistent long-term evidence favoring robotic assistance. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies encompassing 48,091 knee cases, with follow-up ranging from 36 to 106.4 months, found that robotic-assisted UKA (RAUKA) significantly reduced: Overall complication rate (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.11–0.63). Revision rate (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12–0.67). Postoperative aseptic loosening (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.17–0.50). Fractures (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05–0.79). A separate 2026 meta-analysis of revision causes concluded that compared with conventional UKA, R-UKA may lower the risk of revision related to loosening, disease progression, and limb malalignment. This is clinically coherent: UKA is a more constrained indication in which precise component alignment and avoidance of malalignment-related failure are especially consequential, and the robotic precision advantage translates into measurable differences in aseptic loosening, the outcome the user specifically asks about. 🦵 Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA): conflicting survivorship data, with the largest and most rigorous studies showing no difference TKA is where the evidence is most contested, and where a practicing surgeon must be careful not to overstate the case for robotics. One meta-analysis reports a survivorship advantage. A meta-analysis of 15 studies with an average of 10 years of follow-up found robotic TKA had a higher survivorship rate than conventional techniques (96.2% vs. 92.8%), with a hazard ratio of 0.67 (P = 0.02), attributed to maintenance of the joint line and reduction of polyethylene wear. This is the most favorable long-term TKA data point available. However, multiple high-quality long-term studies directly contradict this. A study with minimum 10-year follow-up found no differences between robotic-assisted and conventional TKA in functional outcome scores, aseptic loosening, overall survivorship, and complications; the authors explicitly noted that despite a small improvement in mechanical axis outliers, there was no between-group difference in aseptic loosening or overall survival, and concluded that considering the additional time and expense, they could not recommend widespread use. A separate 10-year minimum follow-up study reported cumulative 10-year survival of 97.4% in the robotic group vs. 96.6% in the conventional group, with no significant difference (p = 0.447). Another long-term study reported 98.8% vs. 98.5% survival, again with no significant difference (p = 0.563). A pooled analysis similarly concluded that conventional TKA is non-inferior to robotic TKA at short and long-term follow-up with regard to implant survival and complications. The most authoritative synthesis is equally sobering. A 2026 JBJS narrative review synthesizing RCTs, meta-analyses, and national registry data concluded that robotic-assisted arthroplasty consistently improves component positioning precision, but has not demonstrated consistent improvements in patient-reported outcomes, complication rates, or implant survivorship. The review explicitly identifies statistical fragility and platform heterogeneity as barriers to interpreting the literature, and warns of a disconnect between scientific evidence and public enthusiasm. The honest interpretation is that the TKA survivorship question is unresolved: one meta-analysis shows a benefit, but the majority of minimum-10-year primary studies and the most comprehensive narrative review find no difference in aseptic loosening or overall survivorship. The discrepancy likely reflects differences in platform generations, alignment philosophies, and patient selection across studies. A practicing surgeon should not counsel patients that robotic TKA will make their implant last longer based on current evidence. 🦴 Spine: a favorable signal for screw loosening in the specific high-risk context of osteoporosis Spine surgery addresses a different failure mode: pedicle screw loosening, particularly in osteoporotic bone where purchase is compromised. A retrospective study of osteoporotic patients with two-level degenerative lumbar disease undergoing minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) with a bone-mounted robotic system, with long-term imaging follow-up, reported a lower rate of screw loosening and a lesser extent of vertebral compression fracture after spinal fixation and fusion surgery. This is a biologically plausible and clinically important finding: in patients with poor bone quality, robotic-assisted trajectory planning and execution may allow more optimal screw purchase and trajectory within the available osseous corridor, and the study's imaging-based endpoints directly address the user's question about implant loosening. The caveat is that this is a small retrospective series (19 patients) in a specific high-risk subgroup (osteoporosis), not a broad spine population. It supports a targeted indication—osteoporotic patients undergoing instrumented fusion—rather than a general claim that robotic spine surgery reduces loosening across all indications. 🦴 Trauma: fracture healing is generally comparable, with some functional and healing-time advantages in specific fractures Fracture healing is the outcome where the evidence is most heterogeneous, and where "outperformance" is least clearly established. Femoral neck fractures. A retrospective study of 65 patients comparing Holosight robot navigation-assisted percutaneous cannulated screw fixation with conventional freehand technique found no significant difference in the incidence of complications (including screw dislodgement and nonunion), but the fracture healing time and hip Harris score at last follow-up were significantly better in the navigation group (P<0.05). This is a healing-time and functional advantage, not a reduction in the hard endpoint of nonunion. Talar neck fractures. Robot-assisted screw placement achieved clinical outcomes comparable to traditional surgery, with the advantages being shorter operation time and lower intraoperative fluoroscopic dose—not improved healing. Pelvic fractures. A multicenter study of Tile C pelvic fractures with 12-month follow-up assessed fracture union and implant position by CT at 3 and 12 months, alongside complications including screw loosening and nonunion. The study design captures the relevant endpoints, but the primary framing is about reduction quality and functional scores rather than a demonstrated superiority in union rates. The consistent pattern in trauma is that robotic assistance improves the precision of channel creation and reduces radiation and operative time, but fracture healing itself is generally comparable, with healing-time and functional advantages emerging in some specific fractures but not a categorical reduction in nonunion. 💎 The Bottom Line Robotic orthopedic surgery does not uniformly outperform traditional procedures in long-term complications, implant loosening, and fracture healing. The evidence must be read procedure by procedure: UKA: the strongest case for superiority, with significantly lower aseptic loosening, complications, and revision at mid- to long-term follow-up. TKA: conflicting and largely neutral—one meta-analysis reports a survivorship advantage, but multiple minimum-10-year studies and the most comprehensive JBJS review find no difference in aseptic loosening, complications, or survivorship. Spine: a targeted benefit for screw loosening in osteoporotic patients, based on small retrospective imaging data, not a broad population claim. Trauma: fracture healing is generally comparable; advantages are in healing time, functional scores, operative time, and radiation exposure in specific fractures, not in a reduced rate of nonunion. As a practicing surgeon, I would state this plainly to a patient or a colleague: the long-term outcome advantage of robotics is real but narrow. It is most defensible in UKA and in osteoporotic instrumented spine fusion, where the failure mode (loosening) is directly tied to the precision of component or screw placement. For TKA, the highest-volume application, the long-term survivorship benefit has not been consistently demonstrated, and the field's own most rigorous reviews caution against claiming outcome superiority based on improved radiographic precision alone. The value of robotics in TKA currently rests on process accuracy and reproducibility, not on proven long-term durability.

**可以降低部分置钉偏差和操作风险，但尚不能认为机器人能够全面识别、阻止术中误操作，或已被证明普遍减少严重神经血管并发症。**从骨科临床角度，应把它理解为增加安全保障的辅助工具，其效果取决于具体系统、使用条件和术者核验。 首先，“智能辅助”不全是人工智能。三维导航、机械臂导向和虚拟边界约束，与AI自动识别、自动规划属于不同功能，证据不能混为一谈。 1．哪些功能能够帮助降低风险？ 功能 可能带来的安全收益 主要边界 三维规划与轨迹评估 提前选择进点、角度、螺钉长度和直径，识别狭窄骨性通道 影像分割或规划错误仍需医生发现 导航与机械臂导向 帮助维持规划方向，减少空间判断和手工对准偏差 不能完全避免钻头滑移、器械弯曲或骨段移动 虚拟边界、深度或速度限制 在具备这些功能的系统中，限制器械超出规划范围 约束依赖正确配准，且不一定覆盖全部器械和操作 追踪丢失、碰撞或受力异常提示 对系统能够检测到的异常提供警示或暂停 不是所有设备均具备，也不能识别所有损伤 2．减少置钉偏差有临床研究支持。 一项胸腰椎置钉随机对照试验中，特定机器人组螺钉完全位于椎弓根内的比例，即Gertzbein–Robbins A级率，为95.3%，常规透视辅助组为86.1%。这支持该系统在相应研究条件下提高置钉准确度。随机对照试验 但这些是按螺钉统计的影像学指标，不能理解为患者严重并发症风险降低了同样幅度，也不能直接推广至所有设备、节段和复杂病例。 3．AI自动规划有潜力，但仍需逐条审核。 自动规划研究显示，算法可以缩短规划时间、生成可供医生审查的轨迹；然而，规划验证成功不等于实际植入安全，更不等于已经证明减少神经血管损伤。畸形、骨破坏、既往内固定和影像伪影等情况，尤其需要核验算法输出。自动规划验证研究 4．机器人也会引入新的错误来源。 参考架移位、配准错误或骨段移动，可能使屏幕显示与真实解剖不一致；此时机械臂可能稳定地执行一条已经不正确的轨迹。过度信任系统、忽视异常手感和直视所见，也会削弱安全性。 因此，临床上仍需确认手术节段和规划，核验配准，观察真实器械位置，并按需采用透视、探查或其他检查。遇到导航与实际解剖不符，应立即暂停核查，必要时重新配准或转换术式。 目前最稳妥的结论是：机器人对部分定位和执行误差已有降低作用；对于严重损伤、总体并发症及长期安全性的增益，证据仍需按具体设备与术式判断，不能承诺“防止所有误操作”。

From the perspective of a practicing trauma surgeon, the value of robot-assisted percutaneous fixation is not that it can be applied to every fracture, but that it provides a plannable and deterministic execution tool in fractures where conventional freehand or fluoroscopic precision is most fragile and the consequences of error are most severe—narrow osseous corridors, periarticular locations, and fractures where soft-tissue compromise makes open surgery hazardous. The decision rests on two independent questions: can reliable registration and tracking be achieved, and does the precision advantage carry meaningful marginal clinical value over what experienced freehand technique can already deliver. Fracture Patterns Best Suited to Robot-Assisted Percutaneous Fixation Femoral neck fractures have the most concentrated evidence among trauma applications. A 2026 systematic review of 16 comparative studies (1,293 patients) found that robot-assisted fixation was associated with fewer guide-wire manipulations, greater screw-placement accuracy, and 13.9 fewer fluoroscopic acquisitions per procedure (95% CI −20.3 to −7.5), alongside earlier radiographic healing and modestly higher final Harris Hip Scores. Pooled estimates suggested lower risks of union failure, avascular necrosis, and composite complications, although the authors explicitly noted that patient-important clinical superiority and economic value have not been established, and heterogeneity was substantial. The clinical rationale is sound: the femoral neck is a narrow corridor where screw parallelism, dispersion, and cortical purchase directly determine fixation stability and preservation of residual blood supply, and freehand precision is variable. Sacroiliac (SI) disruptions and posterior pelvic ring injuries represent a second strong indication. A 2026 comparative study of Tile C posterior ring injuries reported an excellent-and-good screw placement rate of 97.96% in the robot-assisted group versus 86.36% with conventional fluoroscopy (P=0.042), alongside significantly fewer fluoroscopy exposures (8.2 vs. 18.6), fewer guide-wire adjustments (1.3 vs. 4.2), and less blood loss (45.2 mL vs. 68.5 mL). No severe complications occurred in the robot-assisted group, whereas one L5 nerve-root irritation from screw malposition occurred in the conventional group. The value here is amplified by the extreme narrowness of the SI safe corridor and the proximity of critical neurovascular structures; reducing needle passes and severe breaches has a direct safety logic even if catastrophic events are too rare to quantify in small series. Acetabular column fractures, particularly percutaneous anterior or posterior column screw fixation, are supported by a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of six retrospective cohort studies (168 patients). Robot-assisted percutaneous fixation was associated with shorter operative time, fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy instances, and fewer guide-pin adjustments compared with conventional surgery, with no significant difference in functional scores or estimated blood loss. A separate biomechanical and clinical comparison of both-column acetabular fractures found that robot-assisted percutaneous screw fixation achieved fixed strength and therapeutic effect similar to open reduction and internal fixation with plate fixation, while demonstrating reduced surgical time, blood loss, incision length, and fluoroscopy time. The deep, angularly demanding osseous corridors of the acetabulum make this a technically coherent indication, though the functional outcome equivalence to ORIF should be read in the context of selected, percutaneously feasible fracture patterns. Calcaneal fractures (Sanders type II/III) are an emerging indication with a specific soft-tissue rationale. Robot-assisted percutaneous reduction and fixation is described as particularly suitable for high-risk patients with compromised soft-tissue conditions and Sanders type II/III fractures, and comparative work reports superior perioperative outcomes, earlier functional recovery, and minimal soft-tissue complications compared with conventional approaches. The value proposition is not only screw accuracy but the ability to achieve articular reduction and stable fixation while avoiding the wound-healing risks of extensile open approaches in a soft-tissue envelope that is notoriously unforgiving. Thoracolumbar fractures without neurological deficit are supported by network meta-analytic evidence. Robot-assisted percutaneous pedicle screw fixation demonstrated the lowest complication risk (SUCRA 94.9%) among fixation techniques in thoracolumbar fracture surgery, with significant reductions in fluoroscopy frequency and time, and improved screw accuracy. As with the appendicular indications, the benefit is concentrated in execution precision and radiation reduction, with differences in early functional recovery and implant failure not consistently reaching significance. When Robotic Assistance Is Unnecessary or Contraindicated Simple, stable, minimally displaced fractures constitute the main category where robotic assistance is unnecessary. For nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures that can be treated reliably with conventional percutaneous screws or nonoperative management, the precision increment from robotics does not translate into an observable clinical benefit, while adding cost, workflow burden, and dependence on registration infrastructure. Long-term follow-up of robot-assisted fixation for nondisplaced pelvic fractures has shown effectiveness and minimal invasiveness, but the medical expenses were higher in the robot-assisted group than in the freehand group, and the authors framed the technique as an option rather than a necessity for this pattern. The broader literature notes that the outcome improvement in robot-assisted fracture fixation may be modest—an unweighted pooled reduction of 21 minutes in operative time—which the authors described as low relative to the investment in equipment and training. Absolute contraindications are those that make the procedure unsafe or render the robotic workflow's prerequisites unattainable. Active infection at the operative site is an absolute contraindication to any internal fixation, and robotics does not alter this principle; device labeling for robotic orthopedic systems lists active local infection as a contraindication. Inability to tolerate anesthesia or surgery due to severe systemic disease, uncontrolled coagulopathy, or critical cardiopulmonary compromise is an independent absolute contraindication. Anatomy or image quality that precludes reliable registration and planning constitutes a functional absolute contraindication specific to the robotic workflow: if fracture comminution, displacement, or hardware artifact prevents the system from segmenting bone, acquiring usable registration, or generating a trajectory that falls within the reachable workspace, the robotic procedure cannot proceed safely, and conversion to conventional technique is required. Severe osteoporosis is best characterized as a severity-graded relative or absolute contraindication, not a binary exclusion. The limitation is twofold. First, screw purchase: osteoporotic bone has poor screw purchase, and pedicle or cancellous screws are prone to back-out or loosening even when placed with high image-guided precision. Robotic trajectory accuracy does not improve the bone–metal interface. Second, registration fidelity and breach risk: severe osteoporosis has been identified as a risk factor for unsatisfactory robotic screw placement, and bone density T-scores ≤ −2.5 have been used as an exclusion criterion in robotic fixation studies. The practical threshold is not the diagnosis of osteoporosis itself but bone quality so poor that neither standard nor augmented fixation can achieve stable purchase; in such cases, robotics cannot compensate for biological fixation failure. Where bone stock is marginal but not prohibitive, adjunctive strategies such as cement-augmented screws or cortical screw trajectories may allow the precision advantage of robotics to be retained. Fractures requiring extensive open reduction fall outside the value proposition of percutaneous robotic fixation.
